en: Homage to the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Compendium of the Meaning of Abhidhamma Introduction to the Work
Having paid homage to the incomparable Fully Enlightened One,
together with the supreme Dhamma and the Saṅgha, I shall speak the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
[It consists of] the four categories of ultimate reality.
2. Therein, the categories of Abhidhamma taught are fourfold from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramattha):
consciousness, mental factors, matter, and Nibbāna in every respect.
1. The Analysis of Consciousness (Cittapariccheda)
The Mind Classified by Plane (Bhūmibhedacitta) 3.
Therein, mind is first of all fourfold: sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara), immaterial-sphere (arūpāvacara), and supramundane (lokuttara).
Unwholesome mind (akusalacitta)...
4. Therein, what is the sense-sphere consciousness? One [type] accompanied by joy, associated with views, unprompted;
one prompted; one accompanied by joy, dissociated from views, unprompted; one prompted;
one accompanied by equanimity, associated with views, unprompted; one prompted; one accompanied by equanimity...
One unprompted consciousness dissociated from wrong view and one prompted consciousness [dissociated from wrong view]—these eight are called greed-accompanied consciousnesses. 5.

One unprompted consciousness associated with aversion accompanied by mental pain and one prompted consciousness [associated with aversion accompanied by mental pain]—these two are called aversion-associated consciousnesses. 6.
One consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt and one consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness—these two are called deluded consciousnesses.
7. Thus, in every respect, the twelve unwholesome types of consciousness are concluded.
8. Eight are rooted in greed, two are rooted in hatred, and two are rooted in delusion;
thus there may be twelve unwholesome [types of consciousness].
Rootless consciousness (9):

eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity; likewise ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness accompanied by pain, and receiving-consciousness accompanied by equanimity. Accompanied by equanimity...
And the investigating consciousness—these seven are called unwholesome resultant consciousnesses. 10.

Wholesome-resultant eye-consciousness accompanied by equanimity; likewise ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure, and the receiving consciousness accompanied by equanimity.
The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy and the investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity—these eight are called wholesome-resultant rootless consciousnesses. 11.

The five-door adverting consciousness accompanied by equanimity, likewise the mind-door adverting consciousness, and the smile-producing consciousness accompanied by joy—these three are called rootless functional consciousnesses.
12. Thus, in every respect, the eighteen rootless consciousnesses are completed.
13. Seven are unwholesome resultants, eight are meritorious resultants, and three are functional;
thus, there are eighteen rootless [consciousnesses].
14. Those states that are free from the unwholesome and the rootless are called "beautiful" (sobhana).
There are fifty-nine such consciousnesses, or even ninety-one.
Beautiful consciousness of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara-sobhana-citta): 15.
One accompanied by joy (somanassa-sahagata), associated with knowledge (ñāṇa-sampayutta), unprompted (asaṅkhārika); one prompted (sasaṅkhārika);
one accompanied by joy, dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇa-vippayutta), unprompted; one prompted; and one accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā-sahagata), associated with knowledge.

One unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness, one prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge, and one prompted consciousness [accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge]—these eight are called wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses (kāmāvacara-kusala-citta). 16.

One unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge, one prompted consciousness [accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge], [one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge, and one prompted consciousness... accompanied by joy...
One consciousness dissociated from knowledge and unprompted, one prompted, one accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge and unprompted,
one prompted, one accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge and unprompted,
and one prompted— these eight are called the resultant sense-sphere consciousnesses with roots.

17. One unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge; one prompted consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge;
one prompted consciousness accompanied by joy and dissociated from knowledge; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge;
one prompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge; one unprompted consciousness accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge.
"Volitional" and "single"—these eight are called the wholesome-rooted sense-sphere functional consciousnesses.
Thus, in every way, the twenty-four wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere with roots are completed.
By way of feeling, knowledge, and volition, they are twenty-four.
The wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere are considered to have roots.
In the sense sphere, there are twenty-three resultants, twenty wholesome and unwholesome states, and eleven functionals; thus, in total, there are fifty-four.
Fine-material-sphere consciousness (rūpāvacara-citta):
21. First jhāna wholesome consciousness accompanied by initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), rapture (pīti), pleasure (sukha), and one-pointedness (ekaggatā);

second jhāna wholesome consciousness accompanied by sustained application, rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness; third jhāna wholesome consciousness accompanied by rapture, pleasure, and one-pointedness; [and fourth jhāna wholesome consciousness] accompanied by pleasure and one-pointedness.

The fourth jhāna wholesome consciousness, and the fifth jhāna wholesome consciousness accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness—these five are called fine-material-sphere wholesome consciousnesses. 22.

The first jhāna resultant consciousness accompanied by initial application, sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness; [the second jhāna resultant consciousness] accompanied by sustained application, zest, happiness, and one-pointedness...
The resultant consciousness of the second jhāna, accompanied by rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness; the resultant consciousness of the third jhāna, accompanied by happiness and one-pointedness;

the resultant consciousness of the fourth jhāna, accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness; and the resultant consciousness of the fifth jhāna, accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness—these five are known as the fine-material-sphere resultant consciousnesses.
23. These are: the first jhāna functional consciousness accompanied by applied thought, sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness;

the second jhāna functional consciousness accompanied by sustained thought, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness; the third jhāna functional consciousness accompanied by rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness;
the fourth jhāna functional consciousness accompanied by happiness and one-pointedness; and the fifth jhāna functional consciousness accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness. Thus [are these].
There are also five functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere.
Thus, in every way, the fifteen wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the fine-material sphere are completed.
The fine-material-sphere mind is fivefold according to the distinction of the jhānas.
Through the divisions of meritorious, resultant, and functional, that [formless consciousness] becomes fifteenfold. 26. Form-Sphere Consciousness:

The wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite space, the wholesome consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness, the wholesome consciousness of the base of nothingness, and the wholesome consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these four are called the wholesome consciousnesses of the form-sphere.

27. The resultant consciousness of the base of infinite space, the resultant consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness, the resultant consciousness of the base of nothingness, and the resultant consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these four are called the immaterial-sphere resultant consciousnesses.

28. The functional consciousness of the base of infinite space, the functional consciousness of the base of infinite consciousness, the functional consciousness of the base of nothingness, and the functional consciousness of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these four are called the immaterial-sphere functional consciousnesses.
29. Thus, in every respect, the twelve types of immaterial-sphere wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousness are completed.
30. According to the distinction of their objects, the immaterial mental states are fourfold;
according to the distinction of merit, result, and function, they are further established as twelvefold.
Supramundane Consciousness:

31. The path-consciousness of stream-entry, the path-consciousness of once-returning, the path-consciousness of non-returning, and the path-consciousness of Arahantship—these four are called supramundane wholesome consciousnesses.

32. The fruition-consciousness of stream-entry, the fruition-consciousness of once-returning, the fruition-consciousness of non-returning, and the fruition-consciousness of Arahantship—these four are called supramundane resultant consciousnesses.
33. Thus, in every respect, the eight supramundane wholesome resultant consciousnesses are completed. 34.
By way of the fourfold division of the paths, the wholesome is likewise fourfold;
the resultant is so because it is their fruit. Thus, the supramundane is considered to be eightfold.
The Compendium of the Enumeration of Consciousness: Thus, there are twelve unwholesome consciousnesses,
twenty-one wholesome, thirty-six resultant, and twenty functional consciousnesses.

36. There are fifty-four types of consciousness regarding sense-sphere objects, fifteen regarding fine-material objects, twelve regarding the immaterial, and likewise eight regarding the supramundane. 37.
Thus, the mind is divided into eighty-nine categories.
Or else, the wise analyze them as one hundred and twenty-one. [Section 38:

Detailed Enumeration] How does the ninety-eightfold consciousness become one hundred and twenty-one? [It is when it is] accompanied by initial application, sustained application, zest, bliss, and one-pointedness.
The first jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness; the second jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness accompanied by sustained application, rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness;
the third jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness accompanied by rapture, happiness, and one-pointedness; the fourth jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness accompanied by happiness and one-pointedness;
and the fifth jhāna stream-entry path-consciousness accompanied by equanimity and one-pointedness—these five are known as the stream-entry path-consciousnesses.
39. Likewise, there are twenty path-consciousnesses (maggacitta), namely: the path-consciousness of once-returning, the path-consciousness of non-returning, and the path-consciousness of arahantship.
40. Likewise, including the fruition-consciousnesses (phalacitta), there are forty-four supramundane consciousnesses (lokuttaracitta) in total.
41. By way of the combination with jhāna factors, each one is fivefold.
It is called the "unsurpassed mind" and is said to be of forty kinds.
Just as the fine-material sphere is grasped, so too is the immaterial sphere;
it is included within the first jhāna and so forth, up to the fifth, and also within the fifth [immaterial attainment].
Therefore, the first and subsequent jhānas are said to be elevenfold each;
however, at the end, they become twenty-threefold.
Merit is thirty-sevenfold, and likewise fifty-two-fold.
The wise say that resultant consciousnesses are one hundred and twenty-one.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Compendium of Consciousness," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
2. The Section on Mental Factors:
The Characteristic of Association 1.
Arising and ceasing together, having a single object and a single basis.
Fifty-two mental states associated with consciousness are considered *cetasikas*. 2. How is there "mental concomitance" (*aññasamāna*) among the *cetasikas*?

There are seven *cetasikas* called "universal" (*sabbacittasādhāraṇa*), which accompany every state of consciousness: contact (*phassa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saññā*), volition (*cetanā*), one-pointedness (*ekaggatā*), the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*), and attention (*manasikāra*).

3. Initial application (vitakka), sustained application (vicāra), resolve (adhimokkha), energy (vīriya), rapture (pīti), and desire-to-act (chanda)—these six mental factors are called the miscellaneous (pakiṇṇaka).
4. Thus, these thirteen mental factors should be understood as those that are common to others (aññasamāna). [Now follows] the unwholesome mental factor (akusalacetasika).

5. Delusion, lack of moral shame, lack of moral dread, restlessness, greed, wrong view, conceit, hatred, envy, avarice, worry, sloth, torpor, and doubt—these fourteen mental factors are called unwholesome (akusala).
Beautiful Mental Factors (sobhana-cetasika): 6.
Faith, mindfulness, moral shame, moral dread, non-greed, non-hatred, equanimity, tranquility of body, and tranquility of mind.
Lightness of body, lightness of mind, malleability of body, malleability of mind, wieldiness of body, wieldiness of mind, proficiency of body,
proficiency of mind, rectitude of body, and rectitude of mind— these nineteen mental factors are called the "universals of the beautiful.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are the three called "abstinences."

8. It should be understood that compassion (*karuṇā*) and appreciative joy (*muditā*), known as the two illimitables (*appamaññā*), together with the faculty of wisdom (*paññindriya*), constitute twenty-five beautiful mental factors (*sobhana-cetasika*) in every respect. 9.
And at this point:
"The thirteen associated with perception (*saññā*), and likewise the fourteen unwholesome [factors];"
The twenty-five beautiful [states] are said to be fifty-two.
10. The Method of Association:
Hereafter, according to their respective application, [the association] of those states dissociated from consciousness [will be explained].
In each of the types of consciousness, association is spoken of individually.
Seven [mental factors] are associated everywhere; the miscellaneous ones are associated as appropriate.
Fourteen are found only in the unwholesome; the beautiful ones are found only in the beautiful [consciousness].
The Method of Association with Other Common Mental Factors (Aññasamānacetasika-sampayoga-naya).
12. How so? First, these seven mental factors common to all consciousness are found in all eighty-nine types of consciousness-arisings.

13. Among the miscellaneous factors, initial application (vitakka) arises in fifty-five types of consciousness: namely, in all sense-sphere consciousnesses except for the two sets of fivefold sensory consciousness, and in the eleven types of first-jhāna consciousness.

14. *Vicāra*, however, occurs in those same eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses and thus in sixty-six types of consciousness. 15. *Adhimokkha* (resolution) occurs in all consciousnesses except for the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the consciousness accompanied by doubt. 16.

*Vīriya* (energy) occurs in all consciousnesses except for the five-door adverting consciousness, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the receiving consciousness, and the investigating consciousness.
17. Rapture (pīti) occurs in consciousnesses accompanied by joy, grief, or equanimity, excluding body-consciousness and the fourth jhāna.
18. Desire (chanda) occurs in consciousnesses that are rootless (ahetuka) and exclude delusion (momūha).
19. Those types of consciousness arise in the following order:
Sixty-six, fifty-five, eleven, and sixteen;
seventy, and twenty—these are excluding the miscellaneous [factors].
Fifty-five, sixty-six, seventy-eight, and seventy-three.
Fifty-one and sixty-nine are the miscellaneous [factors].
20. Regarding the method of association with unwholesome mental factors:

among the unwholesome states, these four mental factors—delusion (*moha*), lack of moral shame (*ahirika*), lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and restlessness (*uddhacca*)—are called "common to all unwholesome states," as they are found in all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness.
21. Greed (lobha) is found only in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed. 22.
Wrong view (diṭṭhi) is found in the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view. 23.
Conceit (māna) is found in the four types of consciousness dissociated from wrong view.
24. Hatred, envy, avarice, and worry occur in the two types of consciousness associated with aversion. 25.
Sloth and torpor occur in the five types of prompted consciousness.
26. Doubt occurs only in the consciousness accompanied by doubt.
27. Among all demeritorious states, four are rooted in greed;
three are included among those rooted in greed;
and four are rooted in hatred.
Likewise, there are two [factors] in the volitional states.
With doubt in a doubting consciousness, there are fourteen;
in the twelve agitated types of consciousness, they associate in five ways.

28. The Method of Association with Beautiful Mental Factors (*sobhanacetasika*): Among the beautiful factors, first, nineteen mental factors common to all beautiful states are present in all fifty-nine types of beautiful consciousness. 29.

As for the three abstinences (*virati*), they are invariably found together in all supramundane (*lokuttara*) consciousnesses; however, in mundane (*lokiya*) wholesome sense-sphere consciousnesses, they appear individually and only occasionally.
30. Furthermore, the illimitables (appamaññā) arise occasionally as distinct states within twenty-eight types of consciousness:

namely, in the twelve types of sublime consciousness excluding the fifth jhāna, in the wholesome consciousnesses of the sense sphere, and in the sense-sphere functional consciousnesses accompanied by roots.
However, some maintain that compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) do not exist among those [consciousnesses] associated with equanimity (upekkhā).

31. Wisdom (paññā), however, enters into association with forty-seven types of consciousness: namely, the twelve sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and all thirty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses.
32. Nineteen factors arise in fifty-nine [types of consciousness];
three in sixteen; and two in twenty-eight.
Wisdom has been explained as being of forty-seven kinds;
thus, it is beautiful only when associated with the four beautiful [mental factors] such as envy, avarice, worry, and the abstinences, compassion, and so forth.
33. Envy, avarice, worry, the abstinences, compassion, and so forth.
Sometimes they occur individually, and sometimes conceit along with sloth and torpor.
According to the sequence already stated, the remaining [factors] are invariably associated.
Now I shall explain their grouping as appropriate.
The Method of Compendium:
35. There are thirty-six factors in the supramundane, thirty-five in the sublime, and thirty-eight are found in the beautiful of the sense-sphere.
In the twenty-seven types of meritorious consciousness and the twelve rootless [consciousnesses],
the inclusion therein is fivefold according to their possible combinations.
This is the method for the inclusion of supramundane consciousness.
36. How so? First, regarding the eight supramundane consciousnesses belonging to the first jhāna, thirty-six factors are included:

the thirteen ethically variable mental factors and the twenty-three beautiful mental factors, excluding the illimitables. Likewise, in the consciousnesses of the second jhāna, those same factors are included with the exception of initial application (vitakka);
and in the consciousnesses of the third jhāna, they are included with the exception of both initial and sustained application (vitakka-vicāra).
In the consciousnesses associated with the fourth jhāna, those same factors—excluding applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and zest (*pīti*)—are included;

likewise, in the consciousnesses associated with the fifth jhāna, those same factors accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) are included. Thus, in all eight supramundane consciousnesses, there is a fivefold classification according to the five jhānas.
37. Thirty-six, thirty-five, and thirty-four, respectively.
Thus, thirty-three pairs [of factors] are established in five ways within the supramundane.
38. Regarding the method of classifying sublime consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*):
first, among the three types of first-jhāna sublime consciousness, there are thirteen mental factors common to others.
Twenty-two beautiful mental factors (sobhanacetasika), excluding the three abstinences (virati), comprise thirty-five states that fall under this classification.
Furthermore, compassion (karuṇā) and appreciative joy (muditā) should be applied here separately; likewise, in the consciousnesses of the second jhāna, those excluding initial application (vitakka);

in the consciousnesses of the third jhāna, those excluding both initial and sustained application (vicāra); and in the consciousnesses of the fourth jhāna, those excluding initial application, sustained application, and rapture (pīti).
Furthermore, since the four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) are not found among the fifteen types of fifth-jhāna consciousness,
there is a fivefold classification of all twenty-seven sublime states of consciousness (*mahaggata-citta*) according to the five jhānas.
[The numbers of these are] thirty-five, thirty-four, and thirty-three, respectively.
Thirty-two and thirty [factors]—thus, in the sublime [consciousness], there are fivefold.
40. Regarding the method of classifying the beautiful consciousnesses of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara-sobhana-citta*):
first, among the wholesome [beautiful consciousnesses] of the sense sphere, in the first two types, there are thirteen mental factors common to others.
Together with the twenty-five beautiful mental factors (*sobhanacetasika*), these thirty-eight states are included;
however, here the five immeasurables (*appamaññā*) and the abstinences (*virati*) should each be combined separately. Likewise, in the second pair, those excluding knowledge (*ñāṇa*);

in the third pair, those associated with knowledge but excluding joy (*pīti*); and in the fourth pair, those excluding both knowledge and joy—these alone are included. This is also the case for the functional consciousnesses (*kiriyacitta*).

Excluding the abstinences (*virati*), they are likewise comprised in four ways within each of the four dyads. Similarly, among the resultant [consciousnesses], those same [factors] are comprised, excluding the illimitables (*appamaññā*) and the abstinences.
Thus, in all cases, the grouping of the twenty-four beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-sobhana-citta*) by way of dyads is twelvefold. 41.
Thirty-eight, thirty-seven, two, and thirty-six in the beautiful [consciousnesses].
In the wholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses of the sense sphere accompanied by roots: thirty-five, thirty-four, two, and thirty-three in the functional;
thirty-three in the resultant; and thirty-two, thirty-one, and thirty in the wholesome.
42. Herein, abstinences are purified in the sublime kamma-formations;
the illimitables are purified in the unsurpassed; likewise, the pair [of abstinences] in the ripening of sense-sphere [kamma];
the jhāna-factors and the illimitables are purified in the middle [i.e., the fine-material sphere].
Abstinence and knowledge-joy are the factors that distinguish [wholesome states] from limited [states].
43. The Method for Classifying Unwholesome States:
Regarding the unwholesome states rooted in greed, first, in the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) state, there are thirteen mental factors common to other [unwholesome] states.
The four unwholesome universal factors and the four unwholesome particulars—thus, together with greed and views, nineteen states are included.
44. Likewise, in the second type of unprompted consciousness, [there are eighteen] with greed and conceit. 45.
In the third, likewise, there are eighteen with greed and views, excluding zest.
46. In the fourth [consciousness], it is the same as before, with the addition of greed and conceit.

47. In the fifth, however, in the unprompted consciousness associated with aversion, those same twenty states—excluding joy—are comprised together with four others: hatred, envy, avarice, and worry; namely, envy, avarice, and worry.
In this context, these [factors] should be applied individually.
48. In the pentad of volitionally prompted consciousness (*sasaṅkhārika-pañcaka*) as well, they should be applied in the same way, distinguished by dullness and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*).

49. However, fifteen factors—consisting of eleven common factors excluding desire and rapture (*chanda-pīti*), plus four universal unwholesome factors (*akusala-sādhāraṇa*)—are associated with the consciousness accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca-sahagata*).

50. In the consciousness accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchāsahagata-citta*), fifteen factors—namely those same [fifteen] factors accompanied by doubt but devoid of resolve (*adhimokkha*)—are likewise found.
Thus, although they are applied individually to all twelve types of unwholesome consciousness-arisings, they are comprised in seven ways according to their enumeration.
51. Nineteen, eighteen, twenty, twenty-one, twenty-two, and fifteen—thus the wholesome [states] are established in seven ways. 52.
Four are common, and ten others are shared.
These fourteen are said to belong to all unwholesome consciousnesses.
53. Regarding the inclusion of rootless consciousnesses:
first, in the consciousness of smiling, twelve factors—excluding desire (chanda) and being otherwise common—are included.
54. Likewise, in determining (voṭṭhabbana), [the factors] excluding desire (chanda) and zest (pīti) [are present]. 55.
In pleasant investigating (sukha-santīraṇa), [the factors] excluding desire (chanda) and energy (vīriya) [are present]. 56.

In the threefold mind-element (manodhātu-ttika) and in the pair of rootless rebirth-linking (ahetuka-paṭisandhi-yugala), [the factors] excluding desire (chanda), zest (pīti), and energy (vīriya) [are present].

57. In the two fivefold groups of consciousness, those same [factors] are included, excluding the miscellaneous ones. Thus, in all eighteen types of rootless consciousness, the inclusion is fourfold according to their enumeration.
58. Twelve, eleven, ten, and seven—thus is the fourfold inclusion among the eighteen types of rootless thought-arising.
59. In all cases among the rootless (ahetuka), seven [factors] are present; the remaining ones are included as appropriate.
Thus has been stated in detail the thirty-threefold compendium.
60. In this manner, the association and the compendium of the factors dissociated from consciousness have been explained.
Having understood the distinctions as appropriate, one should indicate them together with consciousness.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Compendium of Mental Factors," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
3. The Section on Miscellaneous Topics 1.
Thirty-five states—consciousness and mental factors—have been explained according to their nature as they correspond. Now, for these, each shall be treated as appropriate.
2. By way of feeling, cause, function, door, object, and basis;
by means of the arising of consciousness alone, the compendium is set forth. This is the Compendium of Feeling (Vedanā-saṅgaha).

3. Regarding the inclusion of feeling (*vedanā-saṅgaha*), there are first three kinds of feeling: pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. However, when divided further, they become fivefold: pleasure, pain, mental joy (*somanassa*), mental grief (*domanassa*), and equanimity (*upekkhā*).
4. Among these, wholesome resultant body-consciousness accompanied by pleasure is only one; likewise, unwholesome resultant [body-consciousness] accompanied by pain is one. 5.
As for consciousnesses accompanied by mental joy, there are four rooted in greed (*lobha-mūla*), twelve beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-sobhana*), and—
Together with the two types of investigating and smiling [consciousnesses] accompanied by pleasure, there are eighteen sense-sphere consciousnesses accompanied by joy;
these, along with the forty-four sublime and supramundane consciousnesses comprised of the first,
second, third, and fourth jhānas, thus constitute sixty-two kinds.
6. Furthermore, the two types of consciousness accompanied by displeasure are exclusively those associated with aversion (*paṭigha*).
7. All the remaining fifty-five types of consciousness are exclusively accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*).
8. Therein, feeling (*vedanā*) is threefold: pleasure, pain, and equanimity.
It is fivefold through the distinction between mental joy (*somanassa*) and mental grief (*domanassa*).
Pleasure (*sukha*) and pain (*dukkha*) each occur in one place; mental grief is established in two places.
Among the sixty-two [types of consciousness], mental joy occurs in fifty-five, while the others occur in the remaining [seven].

**The Compendium of Causes (Hetusaṅgaha)** 10. In the Compendium of Causes, "causes" (hetu) are sixfold: greed (lobha), hatred (dosa), delusion (moha), non-greed (alobha), non-hatred (adosa), and non-delusion (amoha). 11.

Among these, the rootless consciousnesses (ahetukacitta) are so called by way of the five-door adverting consciousness, the two sets of five-fold sense-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, and smiling consciousness.
12. All the remaining seventy-one types of consciousness are exclusively with roots (sahetuka).
13. Among those, two types of utterly deluded consciousness (momūha-citta) have only a single root. 14.

The remaining twenty-two types of consciousness—namely, the ten unwholesome consciousnesses and the twelve sense-sphere beautiful consciousnesses dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta)—are all double-rooted (dvihetuka).

15. There are forty-seven types of consciousness associated with the three roots: namely, the twelve beautiful sense-sphere consciousnesses associated with knowledge, and the thirty-five sublime and supramundane consciousnesses. 16.
Greed, hatred, and delusion—these are the three unwholesome roots.
Non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, as well as the wholesome and the indeterminate;
eighteen are rootless, two have one root, and twenty-two [have two roots]. 17.
They are considered to have two roots or forty-seven roots. 18. Summary of Functions (Kicca-saṅgaha):

In the summary of functions, functions are of fourteen kinds, namely: rebirth-linking, life-continuum, adverting, seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, receiving, investigating, determining, impulsion, registration, and death.
19. Furthermore, their classification of states should be understood as tenfold, by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, adverting, the five types of sense-consciousness, and so forth.

20. Among these, nineteen types of consciousness—namely, the two types of investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity, the eight great resultants, and the nine fine-material and immaterial-sphere resultants—have the functions of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death.
21. The functions of adverting, however, belong to two types of consciousness.
22. Likewise, there are the functions of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and receiving.
23. There are three functions of investigating.
24. Mind-door adverting itself performs the function of determining at the five doors.
25. Fifty-five wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional consciousnesses, excluding the two types of adverting consciousness, perform the function of impulsion (javana).
26. The eleven types of consciousness consisting of the eight great resultants and the three investigating consciousnesses perform the function of registration (tadārammaṇa).
27. Among those, however, the two investigating consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity are said to have five functions: rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, registration, and investigation.
28. The eight great resultant [consciousnesses] are called four-function [consciousnesses] by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, death, and taking an object.
29. The nine sublime resultants are called three-function [consciousnesses] by way of rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death.
30. The investigating consciousness accompanied by joy is two-function [consciousness], by way of investigating and taking an object.
31. Likewise, determining (voṭṭhabbana) [has its function] by way of determining and adverting. 32.

Furthermore, all the remaining types—the seven consciousnesses of the impulsion series, the three mind-elements, and the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions—have each a single function according to their respective occurrence.
33. Thus, there are fourteen functions, beginning with rebirth-linking, distinguished by their functional differences.
The arising of consciousness is explained through tenfold classification of its bases:
sixty-eight, two, nine, eight, and two, respectively. One should now describe the bases for the functions of one, two, three, four, and five.
**The Compendium of Doors (Dvārasaṅgaha)** 35. In the compendium of doors, "doors" are of six kinds: the eye-door, the ear-door, the nose-door, the tongue-door, the body-door, and the mind-door. 36.
Therein, the eye itself is the eye-door.
37. Likewise, the ear and so forth are the ear-door and so forth. 38.
The mind-door, however, is called the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
39. Therein, by way of five-door adverting, eye-consciousness, receiving, investigating, determining, sense-sphere impulsion, and registration—
Forty-six types of consciousness arise in the eye-door as appropriate; likewise, forty-six also occur in the ear-door and so forth by way of five-door adverting, ear-consciousness, and the rest.
Thus, in all cases, fifty-four types of sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousness occur in the five doors.
In the mind-door, however, sixty-seven types of consciousness occur by way of mind-door adverting, fifty-five impulsions (javana), and registration (tadārammaṇa).
41. Nineteen types of consciousness are independent of the sense doors by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
42. Among those, thirty-six—namely, the fivefold sense consciousnesses and the sublime and supramundane javanas—are called single-door consciousnesses, according to their respective cases.
43. The triad of mind-element consciousness, however, is five-door consciousness.
44. The investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure, the determining consciousness, and the sense-sphere javanas are the six-door consciousnesses.
45. The investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity and the great resultants are both six-door consciousnesses and door-freed.
46. The sublime resultants are exclusively door-freed.
47. There are minds with one door, and those with five doors;
those liberated from the six doors, and those liberated in every way.
Thirty-six, three, and thirty-one, respectively.
It should be explained in five ways: as tenfold and ninefold.
48. The Compendium of Objects:
In the compendium of objects, there are six kinds of objects, namely: visible-form object, sound object, odor object, taste object, tangible-object, and mental-phenomena object.
49. Therein, visible form alone is the object of visible form; likewise, sounds and so forth are the objects of sounds and so forth. 50.

The mental-object (dhamma) object, however, is comprised of six kinds by way of the [five] sensitivities, subtle material phenomena, consciousness, mental factors, Nibbāna, and concepts (paññatti). 51.

Therein, for all consciousnesses functioning through the eye-door, visible form alone is the object, and that is exclusively present. Likewise, for consciousnesses and so forth functioning through the ear-door and the others, sounds and so forth are the objects, and those too are exclusively present.
52. For consciousnesses connected with the mind-door, however, the object is sixfold—present, past, future, and timeless—and is appropriate to each case.
53. And for those consciousnesses disconnected from the doors—namely, those termed rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death—the object is sixfold as well;

generally, according to what is possible, it is grasped by any of the six doors in another existence, being present, past, or a conceptualization (paññatti), and is reckoned as kamma, the sign of kamma, or the sign of destiny.
54. Among these, eye-consciousness and the others each have respectively only one object, such as visible form and so forth.
55. The triad of mind-elements (manodhātu), however, has the five objects beginning with visible form.
56. The remaining resultant states of the sense sphere and the smiling consciousness have, in every respect, only sense-sphere objects.
57. Unwholesome states and sense-sphere javanas dissociated from knowledge have all objects except those pertaining to the supramundane. 58.

Sense-sphere wholesome states associated with knowledge and the wholesome supernormal powers (abhiññā) consisting of the fifth jhāna have all objects except those pertaining to the path and fruit of Arahantship. 59.
Sense-sphere functional states associated with knowledge and the functional supernormal powers and the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) have all objects in every respect.
60. Among the formless states, the second and fourth have sublime objects.
61. All remaining sublime consciousnesses have conceptualized objects.
62. Supramundane consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object.
63. Twenty-five [consciousnesses] pertain to the limited (paritta); six consciousnesses pertain to the sublime (mahaggata).
Twenty-one pertain to conventional expression (vohāra); eight have Nibbāna as their object (gocara).
Twenty pertain to the supramundane (anuttara) excluding the highest path and fruit; [one pertains to the highest path and fruit].
"Five everywhere and six"—thus the summary there is sevenfold.
64. Summary of Bases:
In the summary of bases, "bases" refers to the sixfold bases consisting of the eye-base, ear-base, nose-base, tongue-base, body-base, and heart-base.
65. All of these are found in the sense-sphere world (kāmaloka). 66.
However, in the fine-material sphere (rūpaloka), the triad beginning with the nose [olfactory faculty, object, and consciousness] does not exist. 67.
In the immaterial sphere (arūpaloka), however, none of them are present at all.
68. Therein, the five elements of sensory consciousness proceed exclusively by depending upon the five bases of physical sensitivity, respectively. 69.
Furthermore, the mind-element—consisting of the five-door adverting consciousness and the receiving consciousness—proceeds depending solely upon the heart-base. 70.

The remaining factors, namely those comprised within the mind-consciousness-element—consisting of investigating consciousness, the great resultants, the two types of repulsion, the first path consciousness, laughing consciousness, and fine-material-sphere consciousness—proceed depending solely upon the heart-base.
71. As for the remaining wholesome, unwholesome, and functional [consciousness], they exist either depending on or not depending on [the heart-base] by way of the supramundane.
72. By way of the immaterial-sphere resultant, it exists without depending on the heart at all.
73. In the sense-sphere, [consciousness] depends on six bases; in the fine-material sphere, seven; and in the immaterial sphere, fourfold.
The immaterial [states] are considered to be supported by three bases; one element is considered to be supported.
Forty-three [types of consciousness] arise supported by forty-two [bases].
Resultant immaterial states are unsupported, whether they are supported or unsupported.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Compendium of Miscellaneous Matters," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*. 4.
The Chapter on the Cognitive Process (*Vīthi*).
1. Having thus provided this supreme compendium of the arising of consciousness,
determined by its sequence and distinguished according to planes and persons,
[I shall now treat] the compendium of occurrence, which pertains to both rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
I shall explain briefly how [this occurs] according to its possible modes.
(2) However, for those [consciousnesses] outside the cognitive process, the engagement with objects is threefold: by way of kamma, the sign of kamma, and the sign of destiny.
(4) In this regard, the bases, doors, and objects are exactly as described previously.
The Sixfold Consciousness (Viññāṇachakka): 5.
Eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness—these are the six consciousnesses.
The Sixfold Process (Vīthichakka).
6. Furthermore, there are six types of cognitive processes (vīthi):
the eye-door process, the ear-door process, the nose-door process, the tongue-door process, the body-door process, and the mind-door process—classified by way of the doors;

or alternatively, the eye-consciousness process, the ear-consciousness process, the nose-consciousness process, the tongue-consciousness process, the body-consciousness process, and the mind-consciousness process—classified by way of consciousness.
Or, the occurrences of consciousness proceeding through the doors should be correlated accordingly. 7. The Classification of Cognitive Processes:

At the five sense-doors, as well as at the mind-door, the presentation of objects should be understood as sixfold—namely, very great, great, limited, and very limited; and, moreover, as manifest and unmanifest.
8. How so? The three moments consisting of arising, presence, and dissolution are called one mind-moment (*cittakkhaṇa*). 9.
Furthermore, seventeen such mind-moments constitute the lifespan of material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*).
10. Whether they have passed through one moment of consciousness or many moments of consciousness, the five objects reach the range of the five doors only when they have attained stability.

Therefore, if a visible object that has passed through one moment of consciousness reaches the range of the eye, then after the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has vibrated twice, having cut off the stream of the life-continuum, that very [object]—
The five-door adverting consciousness, adverting to the visible-form object, arises and ceases; immediately following that,
the eye-consciousness seeing that same form, the receiving consciousness receiving it, the investigating consciousness investigating it,
and the determining consciousness determining it arise and cease in their respective order.
Thereafter, among the twenty-nine sense-sphere impulsion moments (*javana*), whichever has obtained the necessary conditions generally impels for seven times;
following the impulsions, two registration-resultants (*tadārammaṇa-pāka*) arise as appropriate, after which there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
At this point, fourteen consciousnesses have arisen in the cognitive process, along with two vibrations of the life-continuum, and one preceding moment of consciousness that has already passed.
Having completed seventeen thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*), they fulfill [the process] and cease thereafter; this object is called "too great" (*atimahanta*) as a range. 12.

However, an object that has come into the avenue of the past but is insufficient for the arising of the registration-consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is called "great" (*mahanta*); in that case, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at the conclusion of the impulsion (*javana*), and no arising of registration-consciousness.
13. An object that has come into the avenue of the past but is insufficient even for the arising of the impulsion is called "limited" (*paritta*); therein—
Even without the arising of javana, registration (voṭṭhabbana) occurs two or three times, after which there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). 14.

Furthermore, when the object that has entered the range of the past is too brief for the arising of registration—even if it is near to cessation—it is called "very brief"; in such a case, there is only the vibration of the life-continuum, and no arising of process-consciousness (vīthicitta).
15. Thus, in the eye-door, and likewise in the ear-door and so forth—in all five doors—there are what are termed the "object-advertence," "javana," "registration," and "wave-series" (ogha-vāra).
The occurrence of objects as the fourfold range of the four turns should be understood accordingly. 16.
There are only seven types of process-consciousness and fourteen arisings of consciousness;
in detail, there are fifty-four, as appropriate at the five doors.
This is the method for the occurrence of process-thoughts at the five doors.
17. The Section on Limited Impulsion at the Mind Door:

However, if a clearly manifest object enters the range of the mind door, then following that, after the vibration of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), the adverting of the mind door, and the impulsion, the resultant thoughts taking that same object (tadārammaṇa) occur; thereafter, there is a lapse back into the life-continuum.

18. But when the object has not become manifest, at the conclusion of the impulsion, there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga); there is no arising of registration (tadārammaṇa) at that time.
19. There are only three types of process-consciousness (vīthicitta), but ten types of consciousness-arising (cittuppāda) have been stated.
In detail, however, one should discern forty-one [processes] here.
This concludes the section on the limited impulsion process here. Regarding the absorption impulsion process (appanājavanavāra):
in the absorption impulsion process, there is no distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest, nor does the arising of the registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) occur.
21. For there, after any one of the eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge has arisen and ceased four times or three times respectively—
known as the preliminary (parikamma), access (upacāra), conformity (anuloma), and change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) moments— immediately following that, according to the circumstances,
either the fourth or the fifth [javana] among the twenty-six sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara) javanas arises by way of the specific direction of the mind.
Whatever impulsion enters the path of absorption, after that, at the conclusion of the absorption, there is necessarily a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
In this regard, immediately after an impulsion accompanied by joy, the absorption should be expected to be likewise accompanied by joy;

immediately after an impulsion accompanied by equanimity, it should be accompanied by equanimity; and even therein, immediately after a wholesome impulsion, there is either a wholesome impulsion or [an absorption].
And it includes the three lower fruits: the functional javana immediately following a functional javana, and the fruit of Arahatship.
23. From a pleasant wholesome [consciousness], thirty-two arise; after that, twelve from an equanimous wholesome;
eight from a pleasant functional; and six arise from an equanimous functional.
24. For worldlings and trainees, [the javana arises] from triple-rooted sense-sphere wholesome kamma;
for those free from lust, it arises from triple-rooted sense-sphere functional kamma.
This is the method of the occurrence of process-consciousness in the mind-door herein.
The Rule for Registration: 25.
Furthermore, in all cases here, when the object is undesirable, the fivefold sense-consciousness, reception, investigation, and registration are exclusively unwholesome-resultants. 26.
When the object is desirable, they are wholesome-resultants.

27. However, in the case of over-excitement (*ati-itta*), the investigating consciousnesses (*santīraṇa*) and the registration consciousnesses (*tadārammaṇa*) are accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) alone.

Furthermore, at the conclusion of functional impulsion (*kiriya-javana*) accompanied by joy, the registration consciousnesses are also accompanied by joy; and at the conclusion of functional impulsion accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*), they are accompanied by equanimity.

28. Furthermore, at the conclusion of a javana accompanied by displeasure (*domanassasahagata*), both the registration moments (*tadārammaṇa*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) are exclusively accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*).

Therefore, if there is no occurrence of registration at the conclusion of a javana accompanied by displeasure for one whose rebirth-linking was accompanied by joy (*somanassapaṭisandhika*), then, taking as its object any previously familiar limited object (*parittārammaṇa*), an investigation consciousness accompanied by equanimity arises.
The teachers say that immediately after [the javana] arises, there is simply a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

Likewise, they maintain that at the conclusion of a sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) javana, for sense-sphere beings, there is registration (tadārammaṇa) only upon sense-sphere phenomena serving as the object.
This is so when there is a fixed rule regarding the javana, the being, and the object in the sense sphere.
And when the manifestation is very great, that which has it as its object is said [to arise].
This is the rule for the object (tadārammaṇa) here.
The rule for the impulsion (javana).
31. Among the javanas, in the limited javana process (*parittajavana-vīthi*), sense-sphere javanas run for seven times or only six times.
32. However, in a state of sluggish activity, such as at the time of death and so forth, they run only five times. 33.

But regarding the Blessed One, it is said that during states of swift activity, such as at the time of the Twin Miracle (*yamakapāṭihāriya*), there arise four or five moments of reviewing consciousness (*paccavekkhaṇacitta*).

34. However, for one who is a beginner (*ādikammika*), during the first attainment, the sublime (*mahaggata*) impulsions and the direct-knowledge (*abhiññā*) impulsions impel only once at all times; after that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). 35.

But the four arisings of the paths (*magga*) last for only a single moment of consciousness (*ekacittakkhaṇa*); after that, two or three fruition-consciousnesses (*phalacitta*) arise accordingly, and after that, there is a lapse into the life-continuum.
36. At the time of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the fourth formless-sphere impulsion impels twice; after that, one touches cessation.
37. At the time of emergence, either the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arahantship arises once, as appropriate; when it has ceased, there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). 38.
In all cases within the cognitive process of attainment, since there is no fixed sequence of stages—as there is in the flow of the life-continuum—many [moments] may be obtained.
39. The limited objects are considered to occur seven times; the Path and the direct knowledges (abhiññā) are considered to occur only once.
The remaining [types of consciousness] are obtained; there may even be many impulsions (*javana*).
This is the rule regarding the impulsions in this context. The classification of persons (*puggalabheda*):
40. Furthermore, in this context, functional javanas and absorption javanas are obtained for those with two roots and for those without roots.
41. Likewise, resultant states associated with knowledge are obtained in a happy destination.
42. However, in an unhappy destination, great resultants dissociated from knowledge are not obtained.
43. Among those with three roots, impulsive consciousnesses that are wholesome or unwholesome are not found in those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsavas).
44. Likewise, functional impulsive consciousnesses are not found in trainees (sekkhas) and worldlings (puthujjanas). 45.
Furthermore, impulsive consciousnesses associated with wrong view and doubt are not found in trainees.
46. Furthermore, for non-returner (anāgāmi) individuals, impulsion moments of aversion (paṭigha-javana) are not obtained.
47. And supramundane (lokuttara) impulsions arise only for noble ones (ariya), as appropriate to each.
48. For those beyond training (asekha), there are forty-four; for those in training (sekha), they are specified accordingly.
Of the remaining fifty-five, fifty-four arise from the four [planes].
This, herein, is the classification of persons;
next is the classification of planes.
49. In the sense-sphere plane (kāmāvacara-bhūmi), all these process-consciousnesses (vīthi-citta) are found as appropriate.
50. In the fine-material-sphere plane (rūpāvacara-bhūmi), those [consciousnesses] excluding the impulsion of aversion (paṭigha-javana) and its subsequent registration (tadārammaṇa) are found. 51.

In the immaterial-sphere plane (arūpāvacara-bhūmi), those excluding the first path-consciousness, the fine-material-sphere smiling consciousness (hasana), and the lower immaterial attainments are found.
52. Furthermore, in all instances, those who lack the respective degrees of confidence do not obtain the respective door-adjacent process-thoughts. 53.
For non-percipient beings, however, there is no occurrence of consciousness whatsoever. 54.
There are eighty process-thoughts in the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere, as appropriate.
In such [beings], sixty-four [types of consciousness] are obtained; forty-two are obtained [in others].
This is the analysis of the planes herein. 55.
Thus, in this manner, the occurrence of consciousness through the six doors proceeds uninterruptedly for as long as the life-span lasts, with the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) intervening as appropriate.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Cognitive Processes," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*. 5.
The Chapter on Processes Excluded from the Cognitive Series.
1. Thus has the Compendium of Occurrence been explained by way of the cognitive process (vīthicitta) during the course of existence.
Now, the Compendium of Rebirth-linking (sandhi) will be discussed.

2. In the compendium of process-freed consciousness (vīthimutta), four tetrads are to be understood: the four planes, the fourfold rebirth-linking, the four types of kamma, and the fourfold occurrence of death.

The Fourfold Set of Planes (Bhūmicatukka) 3. Therein, the four planes are known as: the plane of misery (apāyabhūmi), the plane of fortunate existence in the sense-sphere (kāmasugatibhūmi), the fine-material sphere plane (rūpāvacarabhūmi), and the immaterial sphere plane (arūpāvacarabhūmi). 4.
Among these, the plane of misery is fourfold: hell (niraya), the animal realm (tiracchānayoni), the sphere of hungry ghosts (pettivisaya), and the host of asuras (asurakāya).
5. The human realm, the Cātumahārājika, Tāvatiṃsa, Yāma, Tusita, Nimmānarati, and Paranimmitavasavatti—thus the plane of happy destinations pertaining to the sense-sphere consists of seven types.
6. Moreover, these eleven types together are designated as the "sense-sphere plane" (kāmāvacarabhūmi).
7. The Brahmā-pārisajja, Brahmā-purohita, and Mahābrahmā—this is the plane of the first jhāna.
8. The realms of Limited Luster (Parittābhā), Immeasurable Luster (Appamāṇābhā), and Radiant Luster (Ābhassara) constitute the plane of the second jhāna. 9.
The realms of Limited Beauty (Parittasubhā), Immeasurable Beauty (Appamāṇasubhā), and Steady Beauty (Subhakiṇha) constitute the plane of the third jhāna. 10.

The realms of Great Fruit (Vehapphala), Non-percipient Beings (Asaññasatta), and the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa) constitute the plane of the fourth jhāna; thus, the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacarabhūmi) is sixteenfold.
11. The Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsabhūmi*) are fivefold: Avihā, Atappā, Sudassā, Sudassī, and Akaniṭṭhā.

12. The formless plane (*arūpabhūmi*) is fourfold: the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatanabhūmi*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*viññāṇañcāyatanabhūmi*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatanabhūmi*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*nevasaññānāsaññāyatanabhūmi*). 13.
Ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) are not found in the Pure Abodes in any way whatsoever.
In the planes of non-percipient beings and the states of misery, noble persons— both stream-enterers and once-returners—
are not found. In all remaining places, both noble and non-noble persons are found.
This is the fourfold classification of planes here.
The Fourfold Rebirth-linking (Paṭisandhicatukka):

Rebirth-linking is of four kinds, namely: rebirth-linking in the states of misery, rebirth-linking in the happy realms of sense-sphere existence, rebirth-linking in the fine-material sphere, and rebirth-linking in the immaterial sphere.

16. Therein, the unwholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity becomes the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) at the moment of descent into the woeful planes; thereafter it functions as the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and finally, at the end, it becomes the death-consciousness (cavana) and ceases. This is called the single rebirth-linking of the woeful planes. 17.

On the other hand, the wholesome-resultant investigating consciousness accompanied by equanimity occurs in the sense-sphere happy realms as the rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death-consciousness for humans—including those born blind and so forth—as well as for the earth-deities and the fallen Asuras (vinipātika-asura).
18. Furthermore, the eight [types of rebirth] with great fruition (mahāvipāka) occur everywhere within the sense-sphere happy realms by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
19. These nine are called the rebirth-linkings of the sense-sphere happy realms.
20. This tenfold [classification], moreover, is designated simply as "sense-sphere rebirth-linking."
21. Among these, there is no fixed rule for the calculation of the lifespan of beings in the four woeful states, humans, or the fallen asuras. 22.
However, the lifespan of the gods of the Realm of the Four Great Kings is five hundred celestial years, which by human calculation amounts to ninety million years;
that of the Tāvatiṃsa gods is four times that, and that of the Yāma gods is four times that again.

The lifespan of the Yāma devas is four times that; that of the Tusita devas is four times that; that of the Nimmānarati devas is four times that; and that of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas is four times that.
Furthermore, it is twenty-one billion nine hundred million years.
For one hundred and sixty thousand years among the Vasavattī devas.
24. The result of the first jhāna occurs in the plane of the first jhāna by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death.
25. Likewise, the result of the second jhāna and the result of the third jhāna occur in the plane of the second jhāna.
26. The fruition of the fourth jhāna occurs on the plane of the third jhāna.
27. The fruition of the fifth jhāna occurs on the plane of the fourth jhāna. 28.

For non-percipient beings, however, only material form constitutes rebirth-linking. Likewise, thereafter, during the course of existence and at the time of death, only material form continues and ceases. These are called the six types of fine-material-sphere rebirth-linking.
29. Among them, the lifespan of the gods of the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārisajja) is one-third of an eon (kappa).
30. For the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita), it is half an eon.
31. For the Great Brahmās (Mahābrahmā), it is one full eon.
32. For the Parittābha devas, it is two eons.
33. For the Appamāṇābha devas, it is four eons. 34.
For the Ābhassara devas, it is eight eons.
35. For those of Limited Beauty, sixteen eons.
36. For those of Immeasurable Beauty, thirty-two eons.
37. For those of Utmost Purity, sixty-four eons.
38. For the Vehapphala deities and the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta), it is five hundred eons. 39.
For the Aviha deities, it is one thousand eons. 40.
For the Atappa deities, it is two thousand eons.
41. For the Sudassāna devas, it is four thousand eons. 42.
For the Sudassī devas, it is eight thousand eons. 43.
For the Akaniṭṭha devas, it is sixteen thousand eons.

44. The resultant states of the first immaterial sphere and so forth proceed, respectively, by way of rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death in the planes of the first immaterial sphere and so on. These four are called the immaterial rebirth-linkings. 45.
Among them, the lifespan of the deities who have reached the base of infinite space is twenty thousand eons.
46. The lifespan of the deities who have reached the base of infinite consciousness is forty thousand eons.
47. For the gods who have reached the sphere of nothingness, the lifespan is sixty thousand eons.
48. For the gods who have reached the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the lifespan is eighty-four thousand eons. 49.
Rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and likewise the mind at the moment of death.
That which is one, likewise, having the same object,
and of the same kind— this is here the tetrad of rebirth-linking.
The tetrad of kamma.
50. By way of function, there are four types of kamma: supportive, obstructive, oppressive, and destructive. 51.
By way of the sequence of the giving of results, there are four types of kamma: heavy, proximate, habitual, and reserve (kaṭattā-kamma). 52.

By way of the time of ripening, there are four types of kamma: to be experienced in the present life, to be experienced upon rebirth, to be experienced in some subsequent life, and defunct kamma (ahosi-kamma).
53. Likewise, there is unwholesome [kamma], sense-sphere wholesome kamma, fine-material-sphere wholesome kamma, and immaterial-sphere wholesome kamma, according to the mode of ripening. 54.
Therein, unwholesome [kamma] is threefold by way of the doors of action: bodily action, verbal action, and mental action. 55. How so?
Killing, taking what is not given, and sexual misconduct are called "bodily action" because they generally proceed through the bodily door, which is known as bodily intimation (*kāya-viññatti*).

56. False speech, malicious speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter—these, being comprised of vocal intimation at the door of speech, are called verbal action because they generally proceed from that source.
57. Covetousness, ill will, and wrong view—these, even without intimation, are called mental action because they generally proceed within the mind itself. 58.
Among these, killing living beings, harsh speech, and ill will arise from the root of hatred.
59. Sexual misconduct, covetousness, and wrong view arise from the root of greed. 60.
The remaining four also arise from two roots.
61. According to the arising of consciousness, however, this unwholesome [kamma] is altogether twelvefold.

62. Wholesome action pertaining to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) is threefold according to the doors of action: bodily action (*kāyakamma*) occurring at the door of the body, vocal action (*vacīkamma*) occurring at the door of speech, and mental action (*manokamma*) occurring at the door of the mind.
63. Likewise, it is threefold according to giving, virtue, and meditation (*bhāvanā*). 64.
However, according to the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), this is eightfold.

65. It is tenfold by way of giving, virtue, meditation, honoring, service, the gift of the [Three] Refuges, rejoicing in merit, hearing the Dhamma, teaching the Dhamma, and the straightening of views.
66. Furthermore, these twenty types are all reckoned as sense-sphere wholesome kamma.

67. Wholesome kamma of the fine-material sphere, however, is mental kamma alone; it consists of meditation and, having reached absorption, is fivefold according to the distinction of the jhāna factors.

68. Likewise, wholesome kamma of the immaterial sphere is mental action; that too consists of development (bhāvanāmaya) and reaches absorption (appanā). It is fourfold according to the distinction of its objects. 69.
Herein, unwholesome kamma—excluding restlessness—produces rebirth-linking in the woeful planes.

However, during the course of existence, all twelve types of unwholesome kamma ripen as results for sentient beings throughout all places in the sense-sphere world and the fine-material world, as appropriate.

70. Wholesome kamma of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) only within the happy destinies of the sense-sphere; likewise, it produces great resultant states (*mahā-vipāka*) during the course of existence (*pavatti*). However, all eight rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*) ripen as appropriate in both the sense-world and the fine-material world (*rūpa-loka*). 71.

Furthermore, among those, the most excellent wholesome kamma possessing three roots (*tihetuka-mukkaṭṭha*) gives rise to rebirth-linking with three roots and ripens during the course of existence as sixteen resultant states.

72. Wholesome kamma that is three-rooted and inferior, as well as two-rooted and superior, having given a two-rooted rebirth-linking, ripens during the course of existence as twelve resultant states devoid of the three roots.
73. However, wholesome kamma that is two-rooted and inferior gives only a rootless rebirth-linking, and during the course of existence it ripens only as rootless resultants.
74. That which is unprompted does not ripen as prompted resultants.
Some say there are results with effort and results without effort.
For them, there are twelve and eighteen results respectively;
these should be pointed out according to their occurrence, following the sequence already stated.
75. Furthermore, by developing the limited wholesome state of the fine-material sphere as the first jhāna, one is reborn among the Retinue of Brahmā (Brahmapārisajja). 76.
By developing that same [state] to a middling degree, one is reborn among the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita). 77.
By developing it to a superior degree, one is reborn among the Great Brahmās (Mahābrahmā).
78. Likewise, having developed the second and third jhānas to a limited degree, one is reborn among the Parittābha devas; 79.
having developed them to a middling degree, among the Appamāṇābha devas; 80.
having developed them to a sublime degree, among the Ābhassara devas.
81. Having developed the fourth jhāna to a limited degree, [one is reborn] among the Parittasubhas. 82.
Having developed it to a middling degree, [one is reborn] among the Appamāṇasubhas. 83.
Having developed it to a sublime degree, [one is reborn] among the Subhakiṇhas.
84. Having developed the fifth jhāna, [they are reborn] among the Vehapphala [deities].
85. Having developed that same [fifth jhāna] with the fading away of perception, [they are reborn] among the non-percipient beings. 86.
But the non-returners arise in the Pure Abodes.
87. Having developed the wholesome states of the formless realm in due order, beings are reborn in the formless realms.
88. Thus, sublime merit, established according to its respective plane, produces a corresponding result during both the process of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
This is the fourfold classification of kamma here.
89. The process of death and rebirth-linking:
The occurrence of death is fourfold—by the exhaustion of the life-span, by the exhaustion of kamma, by the exhaustion of both, and by an interruptive kamma.

90. Furthermore, for those who are dying, at the time of death, by the power of karma, there appears either the karma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in the next existence according to its fitness;
or the "sign of the deed" (*kamma-nimitta*), which consists of forms and so forth previously perceived at the time of performing that deed and served as its instrumental conditions;
or the "sign of destiny" (*gati-nimitta*), which is to be experienced in the immediately arising existence and serves as the object of enjoyment.
It presents itself at one of the six doors; thereafter, taking that very object thus presented as its basis, the stream of consciousness—
which is either pure or defiled according to the karma about to ripen, or in accordance with the state of existence to be attained—
continues to flow there frequently and predominantly, inclining toward that very [object] which has become the productive cause.
Kamma reaches the "door" by way of being performed anew.

For one whose death is imminent, at the conclusion of the cognitive process (*vīthicitta*), or upon the exhaustion of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*)—which constitutes the end of the present existence—arises and ceases by way of passing away. Immediately after that has ceased, that which was thus grasped [by the dying person]...
Taking an object— whether with or without a physical basis as appropriate—

that consciousness arises precisely at the moment it is being produced by a volitional formation (saṅkhāra) rooted in the underlying tendency of craving and enveloped by the underlying tendency of ignorance; it is grasped by its associated mental factors,
serves as the foundation for co-nascent states, acts as their precursor, and is designated as "rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) by way of connecting to another existence.
It becomes established in another existence.
92. However, in this case, within the process immediately preceding death, it should be expected that there are only five weakly occurring impulsion moments (javana).

Therefore, if death occurs while present objects have merely entered the avenue of the senses and are still persisting, then for the rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) as well—

Since it is held that there is an object in the present, for a sense-sphere rebirth-linking, the kamma-sign and the destination-sign grasped by the six doors are found to have the present as their object, though they are past;
however, the kamma itself is exclusively past, and it is grasped by the mind-door.
Furthermore, all these objects consist solely of limited (paritta) phenomena.
93. However, for the rebirth-linking of the fine-material sphere, the object is exclusively the sign of kamma that has become a concept (paññatti).

94. Likewise, for the rebirth-linking of the immaterial sphere, the object is exclusively the sign of kamma that has become sublime (mahaggata) and has become a concept, according to the circumstances.
95. For non-percipient beings, however, only the vital nonad (jīvita-navaka) establishes itself as the state of rebirth-linking; therefore, they are called those with material rebirth-linking.
96. Those who are formless have a formless rebirth-linking.
97. The rest have both material and immaterial rebirth-linking.
98. Through death in the immaterial realm, they become those who have excluded the lower immaterial realms.
The rebirth-linking of the supreme formless realm, as well as those with two roots in the sense-sphere,
and the death-moment of the fine-material sphere— these may be without roots.
All [rebirth-linkings] from the sense-sphere with two roots occur only within the sense-spheres, while the others occur in both.
This is the process of death and rebirth-linking here.

99. Thus, for those who have taken rebirth-linking in this manner, from the moment immediately following the cessation of that rebirth-linking, that same consciousness—taking that very same object and occurring until the arising of the death-consciousness—is called the "life-continuum series" (bhavaṅgasantati) by way of being a factor of existence, provided there is no arising of process-thoughts (vīthicitta).
The mental continuum proceeds without interruption, like the flow of a river.
At the conclusion, it ceases by way of passing away, having become the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).
Thereafter, the rebirth-linking consciousness and the subsequent states proceed, revolving in due order like the wheel of a chariot.

102. Rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, the cognitive process, and likewise death and transition to another existence—this succession of consciousness revolves again toward rebirth and the life-continuum.
Having attained the deathless state, the wise, having reflected, remove this instability.
Having completely severed the bonds of affection, those of excellent vows will attain peace for a long time.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Analysis of the Compendium of the Path-Independent," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
6. Analysis of Matter 1.
Thus far, mind and mental factors have been analyzed together with their classifications and modes of occurrence. Now, matter (rūpa) shall be explained.
2. Enumeration, classification, origination, by groups, and by the sequence of occurrence—thus the compendium therein is fivefold. This is the enumeration of matter (*rūpasamuddesa*).
3. These two kinds of material form—the four great elements and the derived matter dependent on the four great elements—are subsumed under eleven categories. 4. How so?
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the air element are called "great element matter. 5.
The eye, the ear, the nose, the tongue, and the body are called "sensitive matter."
6. Visible form, sound, odor, flavor, and the tangible object—which is reckoned as the three primary elements excluding the water element—this is called objective form (gocararūpa).
7. Femininity and masculinity are called state-form (bhāvarūpa). 8.
The heart-base is called heart-form (hadayarūpa).
9. The life-faculty is called the materiality of life. 10.
Edible food is called the materiality of nutriment.

11. Thus these eighteen kinds of materiality are included under the categories of: essential materiality, materiality with specific characteristics, produced materiality, materiality that is itself material, and materiality as an object of comprehension.
12. The space element is called delimiting materiality.
13. Bodily intimation and verbal intimation are called intimation-materiality. 14.
The lightness, malleability, and wieldiness of matter, together with the two types of intimation, are called changeable materiality.
15. The characteristic-form (lakkhaṇarūpa) consists of the accumulation (upacaya), continuity (santati), aging (jaratā), and impermanence (aniccatā) of material form.

16. However, since birth-form itself is here designated by the names "accumulation" and "continuity," these eleven kinds of material form become twenty-eightfold according to their specific nature. 17. How so?
The objects of clarity for beings, existence, and also the heart;
likewise, the eighteenfold [materiality] consisting of life-faculty and the nutriments;
and also delimitation, intimation, change, and characteristic.
And ten unproduced [phenomena]; thus there are twenty-eight kinds.
This is the summary of matter herein.
The analysis of matter.

18. Furthermore, all this matter (rūpa)—though it is of a single kind in being causeless [of itself], conditioned, with taints (sāsava), formed (saṅkhata), mundane (lokiya), belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), without an object (anārammaṇa), and not to be abandoned—nevertheless undergoes manifold divisions by way of internal, external, and so forth.
19. How so? That which consists of the five kinds of sensitive matter (pasāda) is called internal matter; the other is external matter. 20.
That which consists of the six kinds of physical basis matter (vatthu-rūpa), including the sensitive matter and heart-matter, is called basis matter; the other is non-basis matter.
21. The sevenfold material phenomenon known as sensitive and intimation is called "door-form" (*dvāra-rūpa*); the other is "non-door-form" (*advāra-rūpa*). 22.
The eightfold material phenomenon known as sensitivity, sex, and life-faculty is called "faculty-form" (*indriya-rūpa*); the other is "non-faculty-form" (*anindriya-rūpa*). 23.

The twelvefold gross material phenomenon known as sensitivity and its objects is "proximate form" (*santika-rūpa*) and "impinging form" (*sappaṭigha-rūpa*); the other is "subtle form" (*sukhuma-rūpa*), "remote form" (*dūra-rūpa*), and "non-impinging form" (*appaṭigha-rūpa*).
24. Matter born of kamma is clung-to matter; the other is unclung-to matter. 25.
The visible base is visible matter; the other is invisible matter. 26.

The dyad beginning with the eye, by way of non-arrival, and the triad beginning with the nose, by way of arrival—these five types are matter that grasps its objective field; the other is matter that does not grasp its objective field.
27. Color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, and the primary quartet—these eight types are inseparable matter; the rest is separable matter.
28. Thus, the wise analyze these twenty-eight kinds [of material phenomena] appropriately according to their internal and other divisions.
This is the analysis of matter herein.
29. The Method of the Origination of Matter:
There are four origins of matter, namely: kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment.

30. Therein, the twenty-fivefold wholesome and unwholesome kamma pertaining to the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere, once performed, produces, from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) onward, kamma-originated materiality within the internal continuum at every moment.

31. The seventy-five types of consciousness—excluding the two types of immaterial-sphere resultant consciousness and the five types of sense-sphere consciousness—produce mind-originated materiality as soon as they arise, beginning from the first bhavaṅga moment.
32. Among these, the javana of absorption (appanājavana) also molds the postures (iriyāpatha).
33. Furthermore, the registration, sense-sphere javanas, and direct knowledges also originate intimation.
34. Herein, the thirteen javanas accompanied by joy also produce laughter. 35.
The fire element, known as cold, heat, and temperature, when it reaches its state of stability, originates temperature-born matter both internally and externally, as appropriate.
36. The nutriment known as *ojā* (nutritive essence) produces matter originated by nutriment (*āhārasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa*) at the very moment it reaches its location during the act of ingestion. 37.
