Among those, the heart and the sense-faculties are produced solely by kamma (*kammaja*). 38.
The two types of intimation (*viññatti*) are produced solely by consciousness (*cittaja*).
39. Sound is born of consciousness and temperature.
40. The triad of lightness and so forth arises from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.
41. The inseparable material phenomena and the space element arise from four [causes].
42. The characteristic material phenomena do not arise from anywhere.
43. Eighteen, fifteen, thirteen, and twelve respectively;
they are born of kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment, in that order.

44. It has been declared that because the states of being "arising" and so forth are merely intrinsic natures (sabhāva), these characteristics do not themselves arise; they are not produced by anything else.
This is the method regarding the origination of matter (rūpasamuṭṭhānanaya) in this context.
Kalāpayojanā 45.
There are twenty-one material groups (rūpakalāpa) which arise together, cease together, have a common basis, and coexist. 46.
Among these, life-faculty and the inseparable material phenomena, together with the eye, are called the "eye-decad. Likewise...
Together with the ear and the others, the ear-decad, nose-decad, tongue-decad, body-decad, female-faculty decad, male-faculty decad, and the base-decad should be applied in their respective order.
The inseparable material phenomena together with vitality are called the "vitality-nonad. These are the nine groups originated by kamma.

47. As for inseparable material phenomena (*avinibbhogarūpa*), there are six groups originating from consciousness (*cittasamuṭṭhāna*): the pure octad; that same [octad] together with bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) as the ninefold group of bodily intimation;

together with vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*) and sound (*sadda*) as the tenfold group of vocal intimation; together with lightness and so forth (*lahutādi*) as the elevenfold group of lightness and so forth; together with bodily intimation and lightness and so forth as the twelvefold group of bodily intimation, lightness and so forth;
and together with vocal intimation, sound, and lightness and so forth as the thirteenfold group of vocal intimation, sound, and lightness and so forth.
48. There are four groups produced by temperature (*utu-samuṭṭhāna-kalāpa*): the pure octad, the sound nonad, the lightness-undecad, and the sound-lightness-dodecad.
49. There are two groups produced by nutriment (*āhāra-samuṭṭhāna-kalāpa*): the pure octad and the lightness-undecad. 50.
Among these, the two groups produced by temperature—the pure octad and the sound nonad—are found externally as well; however, all the remaining ones are exclusively internal.
51. Arising from kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment, respectively, there are nine, six, four, and two groups—thus twenty-one groups in total.
Because they define the characteristics of these groups, the wise [should understand them].
They say that space and the characteristics are not factors of the aggregate;
this is the application of the aggregate in this context.
The sequence of the occurrence of matter.
52. Furthermore, all these material phenomena are found, without exception, in their appropriate manner during the course of existence (*pavatti*) in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*).

53. At rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), however, for moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) and spontaneously born (*opapātika*) beings, seven decads appear at most—namely, the decads of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and sex-base;
but at the minimum, the decads of the eye, ear, nose, and sex-base appear.
Sometimes these are not obtained; therefore, the loss of the group [of kamma-results] should be understood by way of those instances.
54. However, for beings born from the womb, three decads arise—namely, the decad of the physical body, the decad of sex, and the decad of the heart-base.
Even there, the decad of sex is sometimes not obtained. Beyond that, during the course of existence, the eye-decad and so forth gradually manifest.
55. Thus, from the moment of rebirth-linking, there occurs a continuity of material groups produced by fourfold origination:

produced by kamma, produced by consciousness from the second moment of consciousness onward, produced by temperature during the period of maintenance, and produced by nutriment through the diffusion of nutritive essence.
In the sense-sphere world, this proceeds uninterruptedly for the duration of the life-span, like the flame of a lamp or the current of a river.

56. At the time of death, however, starting from the moment of the stability of the seventeenth consciousness following the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), kamma-born material phenomena (*kammajarūpa*) no longer arise.

Those kamma-born material phenomena that had arisen previously continue to function until the very moment of the death-consciousness and then cease. After that, the material phenomena born of consciousness (*cittaja*) and those born of nutriment (*āhāraja*) are cut off; thereafter, there remains only the succession of material phenomena produced by temperature (*utusamutthāna*).
Thus, for deceased beings, in another existence, material form proceeds in the same way, beginning from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), until what is reckoned as a corpse comes to pass.
58. Furthermore, in the fine-material world (rūpaloka), the decads of nose, tongue, body, and sex, as well as the nutriment-born groups, are not found.
Therefore, at the moment of rebirth-linking, there are four kamma-originated groups: three decads based on the eye, ear, and heart-bases, and the life-nonad;
during the course of existence, those originated by consciousness and temperature are also found.

59. Furthermore, among non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*), even the eye, ear, and their bases, as well as sounds, are not found; likewise, all material qualities born of consciousness (*cittaja-rūpa*) are absent.

Therefore, at the moment of their rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), only the life-nonad (*jīvitanavaka*) exists, and during the course of existence (*pavatti*), it exceeds that by including temperature-born materiality (*utusamutthāna-rūpa*), with the exception of sound. 60.

Thus, in these three locations known as the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the non-percipient realm, the occurrence of materiality should be understood as twofold, by way of rebirth-linking and the course of existence.
61. There are twenty-eight [factors] among the sense-sphere beings (kāma), twenty-three among those in the fine-material realm (rūpa).
Among those with perception (saññī) in the immaterial realm (arūpa), there are only seventeen; in the formless state, nothing at all exists.
Sound, change, aging, and death are absent from the moment of rebirth.
In the course of existence, nothing whatsoever is not obtained;
this is the sequence of the occurrence of form therein. The classification of Nibbāna.

62. Nibbāna, however, which is reckoned as supramundane, is to be realized by means of the knowledge of the four paths; it is the object of the paths and fruits, and because it has emerged from craving—which is termed *vāna*—it is called "Nibbāna. 63.

Although this is of a single kind by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), it is twofold by way of a functional description (*kāraṇapariyāya*): namely, the element of Nibbāna with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*) and the element of Nibbāna without residue remaining (*anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).
64. Likewise, it is threefold by way of the distinction of its aspects (*ākārabheda*): namely, emptiness (*suññatā*), the signless (*animitta*), and the desireless (*appaṇihita*).
65. "The deathless state, the ultimate end, unconditioned and unsurpassed—this they call Nibbāna," so say the great seers who have cast off craving.
Thus: mind, mental factors, form, and also Nibbāna.
The Tathāgatas reveal the ultimate meaning in four ways.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Matter," in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
7. The Chapter on Compendium (Samuccayapariccheda) 1.
Seventy-two kinds of entities with their specific characteristics have been stated.
Now, I shall explain their compendium according to their respective application.

2. The compendium of synthesis should be understood as fourfold: the compendium of the unwholesome, the compendium of the mixed, the compendium of the factors conducive to enlightenment, and the compendium of all things. Regarding the compendium of the unwholesome (3): How so?
First, in the compendium of the unwholesome, there are four taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, the taint of views, and the taint of ignorance.
4. Four floods: the flood of sensual desire, the flood of existence, the flood of views, and the flood of ignorance.
5. Four yokes: the yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance.
6. Four ties: the bodily tie of covetousness, the bodily tie of ill will, the bodily tie of adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily tie of dogmatic insistence on "this alone is the truth."
7. Four kinds of clinging: clinging to sensual pleasures, clinging to views, clinging to rules and observances, and clinging to a doctrine of self.

8. Six hindrances: the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt, and the hindrance of ignorance.

9. Seven underlying tendencies: the underlying tendency to sensual lust, the underlying tendency to lust for existence, the underlying tendency to aversion, the underlying tendency to conceit, the underlying tendency to views, the underlying tendency to doubt, and the underlying tendency to ignorance.

10. Ten fetters: the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of lust for form, the fetter of lust for the formless, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of restlessness, and the fetter of ignorance—thus in the Discourses.

11. Furthermore, there are ten fetters according to the Abhidhamma: the fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of lust for existence, the fetter of aversion, the fetter of conceit, the fetter of views, the fetter of adherence to rules and observances, the fetter of doubt, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, and the fetter of ignorance.
12. Ten defilements (kilesa): greed, hatred, delusion, conceit, wrong view, doubt, sloth, restlessness, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread.

13. Regarding the taints (āsava) and so forth here: by the terms "sensuality" (kāma) and "existence" (bhava), craving (taṇhā) which has them as its basis is intended. The adherence to rules and observances, the dogmatic insistence that "this alone is the truth," and the clinging to a self-theory are likewise said to be merely types of wrong view (diṭṭhigata) as they occur.
14. The taints (āsava), the floods (ogha), and the yokes (yoga)...
There are three fetters by way of their basis;
two kinds of clinging are taught;
and there may be eight hindrances.
There are six underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are recognized, and ten defilements (*kilesa*) are spoken of;
this is the ninefold compendium of evil. This is the Compendium of Mixtures (*missaka-saṅgaha*).
15. In the compendium of mixed factors, there are six roots: greed, hatred, delusion, non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
16. There are seven jhāna factors: initial application, sustained application, rapture, one-pointedness, mental pleasure, mental pain, and equanimity.

17. There are twelve path factors: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, wrong view, wrong intention, wrong effort, and wrong concentration.

18. The twenty-two faculties (indriyāni): the eye faculty, the ear faculty, the nose faculty, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, the mind faculty, the pleasure faculty, the pain faculty, the joy faculty, the grief faculty, the equanimity faculty, the faith faculty, the energy faculty, the mindfulness faculty, and the concentration faculty.
The faculty of wisdom, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of final knowledge, and the faculty of one who has known.

19. Nine powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, the power of wisdom, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of lack of moral shame, and the power of lack of moral dread.
20. Four predominants: the predominant of desire, the predominant of energy, the predominant of consciousness, and the predominant of investigation.
21. There are four nutriments: physical food as nutriment, contact as the second, mental volition as the third, and consciousness as the fourth.
22. Among the faculties, here the knowledge of the path of stream-entry is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
23. The knowledge of the fruit of arahantship is the faculty of one who has known.
24. The six knowledges in the middle are called the faculty of final knowledge (*aññindriya*). 25.
The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is twofold, according to whether it is material or immaterial.

26. Among the fivefold consciousnesses, the factors of jhāna are not found; among those lacking vigor, the powers (*bala*) are not found; and among those without roots (*ahetuka*), the path-factors (*maggaṅga*) are not found.
27. Likewise, one-pointedness in a mind accompanied by doubt does not attain the status of a path-factor (*magga*), a faculty (*indriya*), or a power (*bala*).
28. Only one predominance (*adhipati*) is obtained, as the case may be, within impulsions (*javana*) that possess two or three roots. 29.
There are six roots, five jhāna-factors, and nine path-factors in terms of their actual entities (*vatthu*).
The sixteen states that are faculties, the nine states that are powers, the four stated as predominants,
and likewise the four nutriments— thus in seven ways, the mixed compendium is stated,
interspersed with the wholesome and so forth.
The Compendium of Factors Conducive to Enlightenment: 30.

In the compendium of factors conducive to enlightenment, there are four foundations of mindfulness: the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the body, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness consisting in contemplation of mental phenomena.
31. There are four right efforts: the effort to abandon unwholesome states that have arisen, and [the effort to prevent] unwholesome states that have not yet arisen...
The effort for the non-arising [of unwholesome states], the effort for the arising of unarisen wholesome states, and the effort for the increase of arisen wholesome states.

32. The four bases of psychic power: the basis of psychic power consisting of desire, the basis of psychic power consisting of energy, the basis of psychic power consisting of consciousness, and the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation.
33. The five faculties: the faculty of faith, the faculty of energy, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom.
34. The five powers: the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.

35. The seven factors of enlightenment: the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the enlightenment factor of energy, the enlightenment factor of rapture, the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity.
36. The eight path-factors: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
37. Herein, however, the four foundations of mindfulness are said to be simply right mindfulness.
38. Likewise, the four right endeavors are right effort.
39. Zeal, consciousness, equanimity, faith, tranquility, and joy.
Right view, intention, effort, the three abstinences,
right mindfulness, and concentration— these fourteen factors by their intrinsic nature are subsumed there into seven groups according to their thirty-sevenfold classification.
40. Tranquility of intention, zest, and equanimity;
zeal, consciousness, and the three abstinences;
energy as one place and nine as eight.
Mindfulness, concentration, the four [bases of power],
and wisdom; faith, energy, and the supreme thirty-seven factors—
this is the preeminent classification of these phenomena.
41. All [factors] are present in the supramundane, or else there are no [mental] intentions and raptures.
In the mundane as well, they occur according to the circumstances during the process of the sixfold purification.
This is the summary of all.

42. In the Compendium of All, there are five aggregates (khandhas): the aggregate of form (rūpa), the aggregate of feeling (vedanā), the aggregate of perception (saññā), the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhāra), and the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇa).

43. There are five aggregates of clinging (upādānakkhandhas): the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to mental formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.

44. There are twelve bases (āyatanas): the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, [the mind base, the visible-object base, the sound base, the odor base, the flavor base, the tangible-object base, and the mental-phenomena base].
The mind-base, the visible-form base, the sound base, the odor base, the taste base, the tangible-object base, and the mental-phenomena base.

45. The eighteen elements: the eye element, the ear element, the nose element, the tongue element, the body element, the visible-form element, the sound element, the odor element, the taste element, the tangible-object element, the eye-consciousness element, the ear-consciousness element... [and so forth].
The nose-consciousness element, the tongue-consciousness element, the body-consciousness element, the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element. 46.

The Four Noble Truths: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
47. Herein, sixty-nine phenomena—consisting of the mental factors, subtle matter, and Nibbāna—are designated as the "mental-object base" (dhammāyatana) and the "mental-object element" (dhammadhātu).
48. The mind-base itself is divided according to the seven elements of consciousness.
49. Matter, feeling, perception, the remaining mental factors, and likewise consciousness—these five are declared to be the five aggregates.
50. "The five aggregates of clinging" (pañcupādānakkhandhā) are likewise considered to belong to the three planes of existence.
Nibbāna, being devoid of differentiation, is excluded from the inclusion within the aggregates.
51. And the bases (āyatana) exist through the differentiation of doors and objects.
The elements are [defined] by way of the door, the object, and that which arises therefrom. 52.
Suffering is the round of existence belonging to the three planes; craving is its origin.
Cessation is called Nibbāna; the path is considered supramundane.
53. Those associated with the path and those that are fruits, which are excluded from the four truths—thus has the Compendium of All Categories been set forth in five divisions.
Thus ends the section on the Compendium of Categories in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
The Seventh Chapter:
8. The Section on Conditions (Paccayapariccheda) 1.
Of which conditioned phenomena, which phenomena are conditions, and in what manner.
I shall now explain that classification here as it is appropriate.
2. The compendium of conditions should be understood as twofold: the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-naya*) and the method of the foundations (*paṭṭhāna-naya*). 3.

Therein, the method of dependent origination is characterized merely by the mode of the occurrence of a state when another state exists; however, the method of the foundations is expounded with reference to the actual establishment of specific conditions. Yet, the teachers elaborate by blending both methods together.
The Method of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādanaya) 4.
Therein: with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise; with volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises;

with consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise; with the six sense bases as condition, contact arises; with contact as condition, feeling arises; with feeling as condition...
Craving; with craving as condition, clinging; with clinging as condition, existence; with existence as condition, birth;
with birth as condition, aging and death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come into being. Thus there is the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
This is the method of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in this context.
5. In this context, it should be understood that there are three periods, twelve factors, twenty modes, three connections, four groups, three rounds, and two roots.

6. How so? Ignorance and volitional formations are the past period; birth and aging-and-death are the future period; and the eight [factors] in between are the present period—thus there are three periods. 7.
Ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, existence, birth, and aging-and-death—these are the twelve factors.
8. Furthermore, the mention of "sorrow" and so forth here is an indication of the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*). 9.

Moreover, by the inclusion of ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*) are also included; likewise, by the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming, ignorance and volitional formations are included;
and by the inclusion of birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the pentad of results beginning with consciousness (*viññāṇa*) is included. Having taken this into account—
10. Five causes in the past, five fruits now;
five causes now, five fruits in the future—thus there are twenty aspects, three connections, and four summaries.

11. Ignorance, craving, and clinging constitute the cycle of defilements (*kilesa-vatta*); the portion of existence termed "kamma-existence" and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) constitute the cycle of kamma (*kamma-vatta*); and the portion of existence termed "rebirth-existence" along with the remaining factors constitute the cycle of result (*vipāka-vatta*). Thus, there are three cycles. 12.
Furthermore, two roots should be understood by way of ignorance and craving.
13. And through the cessation of those very roots, [the cycle] ceases.
For those who are constantly oppressed by the intoxication of aging and death,
ignorance arises from the emergence of the taints (āsava).
Thus is the beginningless cycle of existence in the three realms bound together.
"The Great Sage established what is called dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). The method of establishment (paṭṭhānanaya):

the root-condition (hetupaccaya), the object-condition (ārammaṇapaccaya), the predominance-condition (adhipatipaccaya), the proximity-condition (anantarapaccaya), and the contiguity-condition (samanantarapaccaya)."
Conascence condition, mutuality condition, dependence condition, strong-dependence condition,
prenascence condition, postnascence condition, repetition condition, kamma condition, resultant condition,
nutriment condition, faculty condition, jhāna condition, path condition, association condition, dissociation condition, presence condition, absence condition.
"Condition that has disappeared" and "condition that has not disappeared"—this is the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* (Conditional Relations) here.
Namely, name is related to name in six ways; name-and-form to name-and-form in five ways;
again, form to form in one way; and form to name in one way.
Designations, mind, and matter; for mind, there are two kinds of conditions for the pair [of mind and matter];
and for the pair, there are nine kinds—thus, how are there six kinds of conditions? 16.
Mental states and mental factors that have ceased immediately prior [are conditions] for present mental states and mental factors.
Name is a condition for name in six ways: by way of immediate, contiguous, absence, and disappearance; by way of repetition, as the preceding impulsions are to the subsequent impulsions;
and by way of association, as co-nascent mind and mental factors are to one another.
(17) The roots, jhāna-factors, and path-factors are conditions for co-nascent mind and matter by way of being roots and so forth; likewise, co-nascent volition [is a condition].
Volition occurring at different moments is a condition for name-and-form produced by karma through the power of karma;
and the resultant aggregates are a condition for their co-nascent material phenomena through the power of result. Thus, name is a condition for name-and-form in five ways.
(18) Mind and mental factors arising later are a condition for this body arising earlier solely in one way: through the power of postnascent [condition].

19. In the course of existence, the six bases and the five objects serve as conditions for the seven consciousness-elements by way of the fivefold sense-consciousness process through the relation of pre-existence;
thus, in one way, matter is a condition for mind. 20. By way of object and by way of decisive support, the two types of designations—mind and matter—are conditions for mind alone. 21.
Therein, the object is sixfold, consisting of visible forms and so forth.

22. Furthermore, decisive support (upanissaya) is threefold: object-decisive-support (ārammaṇūpanissaya), proximity-decisive-support (anantarūpanissaya), and natural-decisive-support (pakatūpanissaya).
23. Among these, an object that is treated with esteem is the object-decisive-support. 24.
Mental states and mental factors that have ceased immediately prior are the proximity-decisive-support.
Furthermore, states such as lust and so forth, as well as faith and so forth; happiness and suffering; the person; food;

and lodgings—whether internal or external, as appropriate—are the natural decisive support (pakatūpanissaya) for wholesome and other states, and likewise karma is [the support] for its results; thus it is manifold.

26. By way of predominance (*adhipati*), conascence (*sahajāta*), mutuality (*aññamañña*), dependence (*nissaya*), nutriment (*āhāra*), faculty (*indriya*), dissociation (*vippayutta*), presence (*atthi*), and non-disappearance (*avigata*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) become conditions for name-and-form in nine ways, as appropriate.

27. Therein, the object-condition (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) is twofold: the emphasized object acts as a condition for mental states by way of objective predominance (*ārammaṇādhipati*), and the fourfold conascent predominance acts as a condition for conascent name-and-form by way of conascence (*sahajāta*). Thus, the predominance-condition is of two kinds.

28. The co-nascence condition (*sahajāta-paccaya*) is threefold: (1) mental states and mental factors (*citta-cetasika-dhamma*) are related to one another and to the co-nascent material phenomena; (2) the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are related to one another and to the derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*); and (3) at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-kkhane*), the physical basis (*vatthu*) and the resultant consciousness (*vipāka*) are related to one another.

29. The mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccaya*) is threefold: (1) mental states and mental factors are related to one another; (2) the primary elements are related to one another; and (3) at the moment of rebirth-linking, the physical basis and the resultant consciousness are related to one another.

30. The condition of support (nissaya-paccaya) is threefold: mental states and mental factors are the support for one another and for co-nascent material phenomena; the great primary elements (mahābhūta) are the support for one another and for derived material phenomena (upādārūpa); and the six bases are the support for the seven consciousness-elements. 31. The condition of nutriment (āhāra-paccaya) is twofold:
edible food is the support for this body, and the immaterial nutriments are the support for co-nascent mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa).

32. The five sensitive organs (*pasāda*) are a condition for the five types of consciousness; the material life-faculty (*rūpa-jīvitindriya*) is a condition for derived matter (*upādinnarūpa*); and the immaterial faculties are a condition for the co-nascent mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*). Thus, the faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) is threefold. 33.

At the moment of conception (*okkantikkhaṇa*), the physical base (*vatthu*) is a condition for resultant states by way of co-nascence; the mental states and mental factors (*cittacetasika-dhammā*) are a condition for co-nascent matter by way of co-nascence;
and the subsequently arisen mental states and mental factors are a condition for this pre-arisen body by way of post-nascence. These constitute the six bases (*cha vatthūni*).
In the course of existence, the dissociation condition (vippayutta-paccaya) is threefold, by way of the pre-arisen state for the seven consciousness-elements.
[It is stated: "The conascent, the pre-arisen, and the post-arisen in every way;
as well as edible food and material life."
The presence condition (atthipaccaya) and the non-disappearance condition (avigatapaccaya) are each fivefold.
35. Furthermore, all conditions are subsumed within the object condition (ārammaṇa), decisive support condition (upanissaya), kamma condition (kamma), and presence condition (atthi).

36. Herein, "conascent materiality" (sahajātarūpa) should be understood as being twofold throughout: in the course of existence (pavatta), it consists of mind-produced materiality; and at rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), it consists of kamma-born materiality.
37. Thus, phenomena are threefold: those pertaining to the three times and those that are timeless;
internal and external; likewise, conditioned and unconditioned;
established by way of designation, name, and form.
In the *Paṭṭhāna*, conditions (*paccaya*) are of twenty-four kinds in every way.

(38) Therein, material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) are simply the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*). The four immaterial aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*)—comprising consciousness and mental factors—and Nibbāna are called both "immaterial" (*arūpa*) and "name" (*nāma*).
This is the classification of concepts (*paññatti*).

39. Furthermore, the remaining "description" (*paññatti*) is twofold: it is a "description" in the sense of being made known (*paññāpiyattā*), and it is a "description" in the sense of describing (*paññāpanato*).
40. How so? There are things such as the earth and mountains, which are described in various ways by taking their respective modes of transformation of primary elements as the basis;

there are things such as houses, chariots, and carts, which are described by taking the mode of arrangement of constituent parts as the basis; and there are things such as persons and individuals, which are described by taking the five aggregates as the basis.
Furthermore, these various classifications— such as those based on direction and time starting with the fierce whirlwind (candāvaṭṭanādi),

those based on unobstructed form starting with wells and caves, and those based on the signs of the respective elements and specific meditative developments starting with the kasiṇa signs— are, although non-existent in the ultimate sense (paramattha),
objects for the arising of consciousness in the manner of a shadow of an object (atthacchāyākāra), depending upon and in relation to each of those [bases].
When it is conceptualized in such and such ways by taking [something] as its cause, it is reckoned, designated, expressed, and made known;
thus it is called a "conceptualization" (*paññatti*). This conceptualization is called a "conceptualization" because it is that which is made known.
Furthermore, conceptualization by way of making known is illustrated by such terms as "name" (*nāma*) and "name-action" (*nāmakamma*); this is the "existent conceptualization" (*vijjamāna-paññatti*).

There are six kinds [of designation]: designation of the non-existent, designation of the non-existent by means of the existent, designation of the existent by means of the non-existent, designation of the existent by means of the existent, and designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.
In that context, when they designate by means of this [designation] that which exists in the ultimate sense, such as form, feeling, and so forth, then this—

It is a designation of what exists (*vijjamānapaññatti*). However, when they designate things such as the earth or mountains—which do not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*)—by means of this [designation], it is then called a designation of what does not exist (*avijjamānapaññatti*).

But by way of mixing both, the remaining four should be understood respectively as: "one possessing the six direct knowledges" (*chaḷabhiñño*), the word "woman" (*itthisaddo*), "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇaṃ*), and "king's son" (*rājaputto*).
43. By means of the sound of speech, through the process of ear-consciousness, objects that arise immediately thereafter become the domain of the mind-door;
it is by following those [objects] that what is to be known is subsequently understood.
This designation is to be understood as conventional, fashioned by worldly convention.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Conditions," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
9. The Section on Meditation Subjects (Kammaṭṭhānapariccheda) 1.
Hereafter, I shall explain in due order the two kinds of meditation subjects for the development of serenity and insight.
The Meditation Subject for Serenity (Samatha-kammaṭṭhāna) 2.

Therein, in the summary of serenity, the summary of the meditation subjects for serenity is sevenfold: namely, the ten kasinas, the ten foulness subjects, the ten recollections, the four illimitables, one perception, one analysis, and the four formless attainments.

The Classification of Temperaments (Caritabheda): The compendium of temperaments is sixfold, consisting of those of lustful temperament, of hateful temperament, of deluded temperament, of faithful temperament, of intellectual temperament, and of discursive temperament. The Classification of Meditative Development (Bhāvanābheda).
4. There are three kinds of development: preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā), access development (upacāra-bhāvanā), and absorption development (appanā-bhāvanā). 5.
Furthermore, three kinds of signs should be understood: the preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta), the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta), and the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta).
6. How so? The earth-kasina, water-kasina, fire-kasina, air-kasina, blue-kasina, yellow-kasina, red-kasina, white-kasina, space-kasina, and light-kasina—these are called the ten kasinas. 7.

The bloated, the livid, the festering, the cut up, the gnawed, the scattered, the hacked and scattered, the blood-stained, the worm-infested, and the skeleton—these are called the ten foulnesses (asubha).

8. These ten are called the recollections (*anussati*): recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dhamma, recollection of the Saṅgha, recollection of virtue, recollection of generosity, recollection of the deities, recollection of peace, recollection of death, mindfulness directed to the body, and mindfulness of breathing.
9. Loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—these four are called the immeasurables (*appamaññā*), and they are also termed the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
10. The perception of the repulsiveness of food is one single perception.
11. The analysis of the four elements is one type of analysis.

12. The four formless states, beginning with the base of infinite space, are called the four formless [attainments]. Thus, in total, there are forty meditation subjects described in the exposition of serenity. This is the classification according to suitability.

13. Furthermore, the ten foulness subjects and the meditation on the parts of the body, known as mindfulness directed to the body (*kāyagatāsati*), are suitable for one of lustful temperament (*rāgacarita*). 14.
The four immeasurables (*appamaññā*) and the four kasiṇas beginning with the blue are suitable for one of hateful temperament (*dosacarita*). 15.
Mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*) is suitable for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*) and for one of discursive temperament (*vitakkacarita*).
16. The six beginning with the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati) are suitable for one of faithful temperament (saddhācarita).
17. Death, peace, and the perception of repulsiveness are suitable for one of intellectual temperament (buddhicarita).

18. All the remaining meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna), however, are suitable for all temperaments; yet even among those, the large kasiṇas are for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita), while the small ones are for one of discursive temperament (vitakkacarita).
This is the classification according to suitability here. 19. Classification according to development:

In all instances of development, preliminary development (*parikamma-bhāvanā*) is indeed found. However, in these ten meditation subjects—the eight recollections beginning with the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*), etc., and the four foundations of perception (*saññāvavatthāna*)—only access development (*upacāra-bhāvanā*) is achieved; there is no absorption (*appanā*).
20. Furthermore, among the remaining thirty meditation subjects, absorption development (appanā-bhāvanā) is also achieved.
21. Among those, the ten kasinas and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) consist of five jhānas each. 22.
The ten foulness subjects (asubha) and mindfulness directed to the body (kāyagatāsati) consist of the first jhāna.
23. The three beginning with loving-kindness (mettā) have four jhānas each.
24. Equanimity (upekkhā) has five jhānas; thus, there are twenty-six meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) belonging to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara). 25.
Furthermore, the four immaterial states (āruppa) belong to the immaterial-sphere jhānas.
This is the classification of development here. As for the classification of the object (gocara-bheda):
among the signs, both the preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta) and the learning sign (uggaha-nimitta) are indeed obtainable everywhere as appropriate by way of synonyms.

27. However, the counterpart sign (paṭibhāganimitta) is obtained only in the case of the kasiṇas, the foulness subjects (asubha), and mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna); for it is with reference to the counterpart sign in these instances that access concentration and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi) proceed.

28. How so? For when a beginner is grasping the sign in the earth-circle and so forth, that object is called the preliminary sign (parikamma-nimitta), and that meditation is known as preliminary development (parikamma-bhāvanā).

29. But when that sign has been fully grasped by the mind and has come into the range of the mind-door even while one is looking with the eye, then that very object is called the "learning sign" (uggahanimitta), and that meditation becomes concentrated.

30. For one who is thus concentrated and thereafter devotes himself to the development of that learning sign through preliminary concentration (parikamma-samādhi), when there appears its counterpart (tappaṭibhāga)—which is freed from the physical basis and consists of a mental concept—
When the object consisting of mental development has become firmly settled and well-established in the mind,
it is then said that the counterpart sign has arisen.
From that point on, access development— known as sense-sphere concentration— is said to be accomplished, being now free from obstacles.

32. Thereafter, for one who repeatedly cultivates that very same sign of the analyzed parts by means of access concentration (*upacāra-samādhi*), the first absorption (*pathamajjhāna*) of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*) arises.

33. Thereafter, having brought that very first absorption to mastery through these five masteries—namely, adverting (*āvajjana*), entering (*samāpajjana*), resolving (*adhiṭṭhāna*), emerging (*vuṭṭhāna*), and reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*)—one [abandons] the gross factors such as applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth.

For one who strives for the attainment of the subtle factors such as sustained application (*vicāra*) and so forth in order to abandon [the grosser ones], the second jhāna and the subsequent states arise in due order, each according to its suitability.
Thus, in this way, the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*) is found in twenty-two meditation subjects, beginning with the earth-kasiṇa.
However, among the remaining subjects, the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) occur in relation to the designation of beings (*sattapaññatti*).

36. Among the kasiṇas excluding the space-kasiṇa, however, for one who performs the preliminary work by regarding as infinite the space obtained after removing any kasiṇa whatsoever, the first immaterial attainment (āruppa) arises. 37.
For one who performs the preliminary work by regarding that very consciousness of the first immaterial attainment as infinite, the second immaterial attainment arises. 38.

But for one who performs the preliminary work regarding the absence of that very consciousness of the first immaterial attainment as "there is nothing whatsoever," the third immaterial attainment arises.
39. For one who performs the preliminary work (*parikamma*) thinking, "This is peaceful, this is sublime," regarding the third immaterial state, the fourth immaterial state arises. 40.

And in the case of the remaining ten meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*), having performed the preliminary work by taking the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as the object, once that sign (*nimitta*) has been well grasped, the preliminary work becomes concentrated right there, and access concentration (*upacāra*) is achieved.
41. However, the fifth fine-material-sphere jhāna occurring by way of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) [arises] from the fifth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge.

Having emerged from that attainment, after reflecting upon the resolution and so forth, it occurs appropriately for one who performs the preliminary work with respect to objects such as visible forms. 42.
And what is called direct knowledge (abhiññā) consists of:
the various supernormal powers (iddhividha), the divine ear (dibbasota), and the knowledge of others' minds (paracittavijānanā).
Recollection of past lives and the divine eye—thus it is fivefold.
This is the classification of its objective domain herein.
The method for the meditation subject of serenity is concluded.
The Stages of Purification in the Meditation Subject of Insight (Vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna) 43. In the meditation subject of insight, however, there are:
purification of virtue, purification of mind, purification of view, and purification by overcoming doubt.

The compendium of purification is sevenfold: purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision. 44.
The three characteristics are: the characteristic of impermanence, the characteristic of suffering, and the characteristic of non-self.
45. There are three contemplations: the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), the contemplation of suffering (*dukkhānupassanā*), and the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*).

46. There are ten knowledges of insight (*vipassanāñāṇa*): knowledge of comprehension (*sammasanañāṇa*), knowledge of arising and passing away (*udayabbayañāṇa*), knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅgañāṇa*), knowledge of fearfulness (*bhayañāṇa*), knowledge of danger (*ādīnavañāṇa*), knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidāñāṇa*), knowledge of the desire for deliverance (*muñcitukamyatāñāṇa*), knowledge of reflective contemplation (*paṭisaṅkhāñāṇa*), knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhāñāṇa*), and knowledge of conformity (*anulomañāṇa*).
47. There are three liberations (*vimokkha*): the void liberation (*suññato vimokkho*), the signless liberation (*animitto vimokkho*), and the desireless liberation (*appaṇihito vimokkho*).

48. Furthermore, the three gateways to liberation—contemplation of emptiness (*suññatānupassanā*), contemplation of the signless (*animittānupassanā*), and contemplation of the desireless (*appaṇihitānupassanā*)—should be understood.

49. How so? The fourfold purification of virtue—namely, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha, the virtue of restraint of the sense faculties, the virtue of purity of livelihood, and the virtue concerning the requisites—is called purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*).
50. Both types of concentration—access concentration (*upacārasamādhi*) and absorption concentration (*appanāsamādhi*)—are called purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*).
51. The discernment of mind-and-matter by way of its characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes is called Purification of View.
52. And the discernment of the conditions for that same mind-and-matter is called Purification by Overcoming Doubt.
53. Following that, however, with regard to those conditioned formations of the three planes that have been thus discerned and which are divided into the categories of the past and so forth:

Having begun with the method of the aggregates (khandha) and so forth, and having condensed them by way of groups (kalāpa), one who comprehends the three characteristics— “impermanent in the sense of destruction, suffering in the sense of terror, and non-self in the sense of corelessness”—

by means of comprehension-knowledge (sammasana-ñāṇa) according to duration, continuity, or moment, [then perceives] within those very same phenomena, by way of conditions and by way of moments, through knowledge of rise and fall (udayabbaya-ñāṇa).
And for one who contemplates rise and fall:
“Radiance, rapture, tranquility, resolution,
exertion, pleasure, knowledge, establishment, equanimity, and attachment.”

The purification by knowledge and vision of what is the path and what is not the path consists in the defining of the characteristics of the path and the non-path by means of discerning the hindrances consisting of the imperfections of insight,
such as illumination and the rest. Furthermore, for one who is thus freed from those hindrances,
the purification by knowledge and vision of the way consists in the nine successive insights that proceed in conformity with the three characteristics, beginning from the knowledge of rise and fall.
55. As he practices in this way, through the ripening of insight (*vipassanā*), with the thought "Now absorption (*appanā*) will arise," the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is interrupted.

Immediately following the mind-door adverting consciousness (*manodvārāvajjana*) that has arisen, two or three insight-consciousnesses proceed under the names of preliminary work (*parikamma*), access (*upacāra*), and conformity (*anuloma*), taking any one of the characteristics such as impermanence as their object.
56. That which has reached the peak is called equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*) accompanied by conformity, and it is also termed insight leading to emergence.

57. Following that, the change-of-lineage consciousness (*gotrabhucitta*) occurs, taking Nibbāna as its object, overcoming the lineage of the worldling (*puthujjana*), and attaining the lineage of the noble ones (*ariya*). 58.

Immediately after that, the Path, fully understanding the truth of suffering, abandoning the truth of its origin, realizing the truth of its cessation, and developing the truth of the path, enters the avenue of absorption (*appanāvīthi*).

59. After that, two or three fruition-consciousnesses (phala-citta) arise, and then there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Again, having interrupted the life-continuum, the reviewing knowledges (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) arise. 60.
The wise one reviews the Path, the Fruition, and Nibbāna;
he may also review the defilements that have been abandoned and those that remain.
Thus, by means of the sixfold purification, the fourfold path called "purification by knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassanavisuddhi) is to be developed. This,
herein, is the classification of purifications.

61. Regarding the classification of the liberations (*vimokkha*): therein, the contemplation of non-self (*anattānupassanā*), which relinquishes the adherence to a self, is the gateway to liberation called the "contemplation of emptiness" (*suññatānupassanā*).
62. The contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*), which relinquishes the sign of perversion (*vipallāsanimitta*), is the "contemplation of the signless" (*animittānupassanā*).
63. Contemplation of suffering, which releases the longing of craving, is called the contemplation of the wishless (*appaṇihitānupassanā*). 64.
Therefore, if insight leading to emergence contemplates [the aggregates] as non-self, it becomes the path known as the emptiness liberation (*suññato vimokkho*). 65.
If it contemplates them as impermanent, it is known as the signless liberation (*animitto vimokkho*).

66. If one contemplates [the aggregates] as suffering, it is called the "desireless liberation. Thus, both the path and the fruit receive three names according to their approach: the path receives them by way of its approach to insight (*vipassanā*), and likewise the fruit receives them by way of its approach to the path within the sequence of the path.

67. However, in the sequence of the attainment of the fruit (*phalasamāpatti*), although each respective fruit arises for those who are contemplating in the manner already described, it is nevertheless called the "emptiness liberation" and so forth by way of its approach to insight;
yet, by way of its object and its own inherent nature, it is designated accordingly.
And the three names apply equally to all in every respect.
This, then, is the classification of liberations (vimokkha) here; [next is] the classification of persons (puggala).

68. Herein, having developed the path of stream-entry, by the abandoning of wrong view and doubt, one who has abandoned rebirth in the states of deprivation is called a "stream-enterer" (sotāpanna), limited to seven more births at most. 69.
Having developed the path of once-returning, because of the attenuation of lust, hatred, and delusion, one is called a "once-returner" (sakadāgāmī), returning to this world only once more.
70. Having developed the path of non-returning, by the complete abandoning of sensual lust and ill-will, one is called a "non-returner" (anāgāmī), not returning to this state of existence.

71. Having developed the path of arahantship, through the abandonment of all defilements without remainder, one becomes known as an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed, the supreme recipient of offerings in the world.
This, in this context, is the classification of persons.
Now, the classification of attainments:
72. However, in this context, within the process of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*), these [factors] are common to all according to their respective fruits.
73. But the attainment of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is obtainable only for non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arahants;
therein, having successively entered and emerged from the sublime attainments beginning with the first jhāna, and having proceeded to that [state],...
Insighting into the conditioned phenomena right there where they arise, he proceeds as far as the base of nothingness;
then, having performed the preliminary duties such as the resolution and so forth, he enters the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Following two moments of absorption-javana, the continuity of consciousness is cut off for him; from that point, he is said to have attained cessation.

74. At the time of emergence, however, for a non-returner, the fruit-consciousness of non-returning, and for an arahant, the fruit-consciousness of arahantship, occur only once, after which there is a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). Following that, the knowledge of reviewing occurs.
This is the classification of attainments herein.
The method of the meditation subject of insight is concluded.
75. Thus, "it should be developed" refers to these two supreme forms of development.
For one who desires the flavor of practice within the Dispensation, [this] is the exhortation.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Compendium of Meditation Subjects," in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
The Conclusion.
By one named Nampa, born into a noble family adorned by virtuous conduct,
whose pure qualities have increased through faith,
having conceived compassion for others—
This treatise, which was intended, has been completed.
By this vast merit, may Mūlasoma— whose dwelling is blessed with grain,
who is joyful and exalted, and whose life is desirable— prosper.
May the modest bhikkhus, adorned with the virtue of wisdom purified by insight,
consider this for the auspicious arising of the power of merit.
Thus was it composed by the teacher Anuruddha.
The Treatise known as the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary: *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
Having paid homage to the Buddha, whose wisdom and compassion are purified and who is worshipped by the Fully Enlightened Ones;
to the Dhamma, which has arisen from the True Dhamma; and to the Saṅgha, free from all defilements.
(Kha) Having bowed my head to the great elder Sāriputta—
the wise one, skilled in the mastery of the scriptures, venerable,
and a worthy recipient of reverence— (Ga) I shall briefly explain the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha*.
(Gha) This is for the sake of increasing the joy of the bhikkhus learned in the Abhidhamma.
As for the many commentaries composed by the ancients,
it is not possible here to understand their meaning in every detail.
(Ṅa) Therefore, elucidating here in brief the words that are obscure and the great path together with its purpose,
I shall compose this commentary. Commentary on the Introduction to the Text.
1. As this master commences this treatise— which is endowed with most wonderful methods, capable of penetrating the depths of both his own system and other systems,
and which generates the clarity of perfectly pure and vast wisdom— he first states "The Perfectly Enlightened One," etc., in order to demonstrate the homage to the Triple Gem,
the title of the work, the means of composition, and the purpose of the treatise.

For here, by the words “I pay homage to the Fully Enlightened One... [etc. ...I salute,” the salutation to the Triple Gem is stated. By the phrase “Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha,” the subject matter, the composition, the manner of treatment, and the title of the treatise are expressed;

this is because, by showing that the categories of the Abhidhamma are to be compiled herein, it demonstrates through this combined expression that they are to be presented in this specific order, and because it demonstrates the manner in which they are to be spoken after being compiled into a single place.
And it is because it elucidates the conventional designations (saññā) that follow from their meanings. As for the purpose, it is shown by implication through the word "compendium" (saṅgaha):

when there is a compendium of the Abhidhamma topics in one place, there arises an effortless mastery through the means of learning them and inquiring into them, which leads to the realization of their true nature and, rooted therein, to the accomplishment of welfare pertaining to both the present life and the future life.
Regarding this, the teachers elaborate in many ways upon the purpose of the homage to the Triple Gem;
specifically, however, they expect the warding off of obstacles. For it has been said by the compilers: "By its power, may obstacles be destroyed.

In its essential meaning, the homage to the Triple Gem is a wholesome volition (kusala-cetanā) that brings about the act of paying homage; and that [volition] pertains to both those who are worthy of worship and those who perform the worship.
Through the perfection of field and intention, by way of providing reinforcement for karma that has its result experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*)—

which is caused by the attainment of whatever prosperity has been obtained— one wards off obstructive and interrupting karmas (*upapīḷaka-upacchedaka-kamma*) that would otherwise cause obstacles to the continuity of the resultant (*vipāka-santati*) produced therefrom;
and thus one ensures the non-occurrence of obstacles such as disease, which are the causes of those [karmas] and which would hinder the accomplishment of one's intended goals.

He accomplishes [this]. Therefore, at the commencement of the treatise, the act of paying homage to the Triple Gem is for the purpose of completing the treatise as it has been begun without obstacle, and for the purpose of ensuring that the listeners’ mastery, retention, and so forth, of the practice preceded by such veneration are accomplished without obstacle.
Furthermore, the statement of the subject matter is because a wise person should engage with a work—once its subject matter is known—by means of learning it and so forth.
The demonstration of the instrument, the method, and the purpose is for the sake of generating enthusiasm in those who hear;
the statement of the title, however, is for the sake of ease of communication—this is the collective meaning here. As for the individual meanings:

"Having paid homage to the peerless, perfectly enlightened Buddha, who is supreme among the assemblies of his own true Dhamma, he will speak the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*"—this is the connection [of the words].
In this context, he is the "Perfectly Enlightened One" (*sammāsambuddho*), the Blessed One, because he has perfectly and by himself awakened to all phenomena.

For he himself, through his own self-arisen knowledge (*sayambhūñāṇa*)—produced by the various and accumulated perfections (*pāramitā*)—has perfectly awakened to and known the entire range of phenomena, including both the conditioned and the unconditioned, by way of penetrating their true nature and specific characteristics. As it is said:

“Having realized it by himself, whom would he point to? Alternatively, because the element of the Buddha (*budhadhātu*) functions in the senses of awakening and blossoming, he has awakened perfectly and personally, being one whose awakening is not dependent on another;

he has himself utterly transcended the sleep of delusion along with its latent tendencies (*savāsana*), like a flower that has blossomed through contact with the rays of the sun, attaining the highest excellence of radiant splendor.

The lotus (*paduma*) has blossomed perfectly by itself through the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), which is adorned with an immeasurable multitude of qualities due to its union with the knowledge of the supreme path; the meaning is that it has reached full blooming.

Even though the word-meaning of the term *sammāsambuddha* applies here according to its conventional usage for the Blessed One, he is distinguished by the word "incomparable" (*atula*). That which is measured by a scale is "comparable" (*tulya*); [the Buddha is not so].
It is simply by the elision of the letter *ya* from *tulaya*. Alternatively, it is derived by adding the suffix *aka* in the sense of "measured":
that which is measured by a scale is *tula*; what is not so measured is *atula*. He is incomparable in qualities such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth;

or, there is no one equal to him, thus he is *atula*, because of his status as the supreme person in the world including the devas. As it is said: "Bhikkhus, as far as beings exist, whether footless..."
“Whether they be two-footed or four-footed... [and so on] ...the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them,” and so forth.
Up to this point, the praise of the Blessed One has been performed by way of three aspects: the perfection of cause, the perfection of fruit, and the perfection of assistance to sentient beings.

Therein, the “perfection of cause” refers to the conjunction with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*). The “perfection of fruit”...
Furthermore, it is fourfold by way of the perfection of knowledge, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of power, and the perfection of the form-body.

Among these, the perfection of knowledge consists of the knowledge of the path, which has omniscience as its proximate cause, and the ten powers and other knowledges rooted therein. The perfection of abandonment is the bringing about of the state of absolute non-arising for all defilements along with their latent tendencies.
The perfection of power is the sovereignty in the accomplishment of whatever is desired. [The perfection of the form-body] is that which serves as the consecration for the eyes of the entire world.
Furthermore, the excellence of the personal form adorned with the primary and secondary marks is called the perfection of the material body (*rūpakāya-sampadā*).

As for the assistance to beings, it is twofold according to intention (*āsaya*) and application (*payoga*). Among these, "intention" refers to the constant disposition toward the welfare of even hostile beings such as Devadatta and others, as well as the arrival at the time for the ripening of the faculties of those whose faculties have not yet reached maturity. As for other beings...
The teaching of the Dhamma that leads out from all suffering by way of the Three Vehicles for one whose mind is indifferent to gain, honor, and so forth, is called the "application" (*payoga*).
Among those, the first two perfections of fruit are shown by the term "Sammāsambuddha";
the other two, as well as the perfection of benefit to beings, are shown by the term "Atula"; and the perfection of cause, which serves as the means for those, is shown by both.
It is shown by way of capacity, because the perfection of both [the Buddha and the Dhamma] is impossible without such causes;
and if they were causeless, it would follow that they could exist everywhere.
Thus, having paid homage to the Jewel of the Buddha preceded by praise encompassing the three states, [the author now proceeds] with the remaining Jewels as well.
Beginning the salutation, he says: "To the Buddha, the True Dhamma, and the Supreme Assembly.

For even though the Dhamma and the Saṅgha are subordinate [to the Buddha], their status as objects of veneration is understood through their association with him, just as when one says, "He has arrived with his sons and wife," it is understood that the sons and wife have also arrived.

In this context, [the Buddha] is so called because he sustains himself by holding others up, preventing them from falling into the four states of misery and the sufferings of the round of existence (vaṭṭa).
The Dhamma is ninefold by way of the four paths, the four fruits, and Nibbāna; or it is tenfold when including the scriptures (pariyatti).
Furthermore, its "retention" consists in the destruction of the defilements that produce rebirth in the woeful states and so forth;

this is obtained in the primary sense because the Noble Path possesses the nature of completely cutting off the defilements, and because Nibbāna—by being its object—is the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose.
However, it should be understood that both [the fruit and the teaching] are so called by way of a figurative designation (*pariyāya*):

because the fruit proceeds in conformity with the path through the subsiding of the defilements, and because the teaching is the cause for its attainment. "Of the good" means of the true persons, the noble individuals (*ariyapuggala*);
or, "good" means existing, not non-existent in the ultimate sense like the self imagined by the non-Buddhist sectarians.
It is the True Dhamma (*saddhamma*) because it is praised due to its possession of qualities such as being well-expounded, and not like the Dhamma of outsiders which is entirely censured.

It is the Supreme Assembly (*gaṇuttama*) because it is a multitude of the eight types of noble persons (*ariyapuggala*), and because it is supreme among assemblies due to its possession of distinguished qualities such as right practice;
or, it is the Supreme Assembly among assemblies—that is, among the multitudes of gods, humans, and others—by virtue of the aforementioned qualities.
"Accompanied by the true Dhamma and the supreme assembly" means together with the true Dhamma and the supreme assembly; thus, "together with the true Dhamma and the supreme assembly.

"Having paid homage" means having especially venerated; the sense is that one has venerated with body, speech, and mind through carefulness and reverence, being free from fear, desire for gain, or mere social custom.
"I shall speak" means I will explain. [They are] distinguished (*abhi-visiṭṭhā*) by virtue of having produced the ultimate meaning (*paramattha*).

"Abhidhamma" refers to that which is "dhammas here," and so forth; it consists of the seven treatises beginning with the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*. The "Abhidhamma-piṭaka" is the collection of those [treatises].
The "meanings of the Abhidhamma" (*abhidhammattha*) are the subjects explained therein. That in which, or by means of which, these meanings are compiled is the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*.
This is a commentary on the ultimate nature of phenomena (*paramatthadhammavaṇṇanā*).

2. Thus, having first performed the homage to the Triple Gem and other such acts intended as a preliminary for the purpose at hand, he now says "Therein stated," etc., while briefly indicating those for whose sake this treatise is composed by way of summarizing the subjects of the Abhidhamma.
Therein, in that Abhidhamma, in every respect, by way of the wholesome and so forth...

The categories of the Abhidhamma taught by way of the aggregates and so forth are, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramattha*), fourfold—excluding conventional designations (*sammuti*)—according to the ultimate reality that has been produced:

consciousness as the aggregate of consciousness; mental factors as the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling; matter, divided into the primary elements and their derivatives, as the aggregate of matter;
and Nibbāna, which is the unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṅkhata-dhamma*) serving as the object of the paths and fruits. Thus it is fourfold.

The construction is: "It exists in four ways. In this context, *paramattha* means the supreme, highest, or non-erroneous meaning; or, it is the object (*attha*) or sphere (*gocara*) of the supreme or highest knowledge (*ñāṇa*), hence it is the ultimate meaning.
It is called *citta* because it thinks; the meaning is that it cognizes the object. As it has been said: "Citta has the characteristic of cognizing its object."

For since consciousness arises even without the conditions of support (*nissaya*), immediate antecedent (*samanantara*), and so forth, but with an object (*ārammaṇa*), its definition as such has been stated;

by this, the doctrine of those who maintain that there is no object is refuted. Or, it is "consciousness" (*citta*) because associated states think (*cintenti*) by means of it acting as an instrument.
Alternatively, consciousness is merely the act of thinking (*cintanamatta*). For, according to conditions, it is merely a state of occurrence.
That is to say, it is what is called "the phenomenon of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvadhamma*).

And having established it thus, it should be understood that, in the ultimate sense, the derivation of all phenomena as "existence" (*bhāva*) alone is obtained; however, the etymological analysis by way of agent and instrument is merely a figurative explanation (*pariyāya-kathā*).

For the status of being an agent (*kattubhāva*) in phenomena belongs to them when their own predominance is attributed to them in their respective functions, and [the status of instrument] by virtue of their being conducive thereto.
By superimposing the status of an agent upon a collection of co-arisen phenomena, the state of being the instrument for the phenomenon to be accomplished is obtained only figuratively;
however, it should be understood that such a demonstration is intended to illustrate the non-existence of an agent and so forth apart from the intrinsic nature (sabhāva) of phenomena.
They also elaborate on the meaning of the word *citta* as "that which makes variegated" (*vicittakaraṇa*) and so forth. Herein, this is the summary:
“Because it makes various, or because it is the state of being conscious for itself;
because it is accumulated by kamma and defilements, or because it protects that which has been so accumulated;
because it accumulates its own continuity, and because it has a manifold object—thus it is called ‘citta’.”
It is called *cetasika* because it exists in the mind (*cetasi*), owing to its dependence on that [mind] for its occurrence. For it is not capable of grasping an object without the mind;

since it does not arise at all when the mind is absent, whereas the mind can proceed toward an object even without any particular mental factor (*cetasika*), it is the mental factor alone that is said to have its existence dependent on the mind. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Mind precedes..."
By the term "mental phenomena" (*dhammā*), misconceptions such as the lack of sentience and impermanence regarding pleasure and so forth are also rejected.
Alternatively, it is "mental" (*cetasika*) because it is connected with the mind (*cetasi*).
It is "form" (*rūpa*) because it is affected (*ruppati*); that is, it undergoes change through opposing conditions such as cold and heat, or its meaning is "that which is appropriated."

Therefore the Blessed One said: "It is affected by cold, it is affected by heat," and so forth. Here, "being affected" (*ruppana*) refers precisely to the arising of something different when there is a concurrence of opposing conditions such as cold and so on.
If this is so, does it not follow that non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) would also receive the designation "matter" (*rūpa*)?

It does not follow, because the mention of cold and so on implies that only a more manifest form of being affected is intended. For otherwise, by the general term "it is affected" alone—[the meaning would be too broad].

Regarding the phrase "to be experienced": what is the purpose of mentioning cold and so forth? Since the deformation (*ruppana*) of one who is touched by cold and so forth is more manifest, the mention of cold and so forth is made for the purpose of making it known that this [deformation] alone is intended here.
If this is so, how is there the designation "form" (*rūpa*) in the Brahma-world, for there are no cold things or the like there to cause affliction?
Although there are no such afflictive things, [the designation still applies].

However, there are supporting factors; therefore, in this context, "being affected by change" (ruppana) occurs by way of those [factors]. Alternatively, because it does not transcend its own intrinsic nature, the designation "form" (rūpa) is applied to it. Enough with this excessive elaboration.

It is called *nibbāna* because it has emerged from craving—which is designated as "weaving" (*vāna*)—by means of discerning existence and non-existence, or because of binding together; or else, it is *nibbāna* because by means of it the fire of passion and so forth is extinguished (*nibbāti*).
1. Explanation of the Analysis of Consciousness; 2. Explanation of Consciousness according to the Distinction of Planes. 3.
Now, since the manifestation of the intrinsic nature of phenomena that possess distinctions cannot occur without analysis, [the following is presented].

Therefore, in order to show the analysis of the Abhidhamma categories as they were enumerated according to the order of their listing, he begins by explaining consciousness (*citta*) after first classifying it by way of plane, genus, association, and so forth, saying: "Therein, first, consciousness...
The word *tāva* (first) has the sense of "first. Among the four Abhidhamma categories as they were enumerated, this refers to the first.
"Mind is explained"—this is the meaning here. "Fourfold" means having four modes or ways.

However, because these phenomena belonging to the four planes are progressively more refined, their explanation is made according to the sequence of inferior, superior, more superior, and most superior.
In that context, it "desires," thus it is *kāma*; it is craving for sensual pleasure (*kāmataṇhā*), and that [craving] ranges over this [plane] by way of making it its object.

It belongs to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*). Alternatively, it is called "sense-desire" (*kāma*) because it is desired; the elevenfold existence of sense-desire (*kāmabhava*) is that [realm], and since it mostly moves within that, it is "belonging to the sense-sphere.

For since movement therein is intended as the primary factor, its status as belonging to the sense-sphere is established even when it occurs in the fine-material and immaterial existences (*rūpārūpabhava*).
Or else, it is "belonging to the sense-sphere" because sense-desire itself—that is, the existence of sense-desire—moves within it.

In this context, even though consciousness occurs [in the sense-sphere], it is designated as "sense-sphere" (kāmāvacara) by way of its dependence on what it depends upon, just as in such expressions as "the beds are making a noise.
Enough with this overly prolix discussion. And here there is a verse: "Regarding the term *kāmovacaratī*:
either 'it moves within the sense-spheres' (*kāmesu avacaratī*), or..."
"Or else, by way of proximity to its basis, that [consciousness] would belong to the sense-sphere.
This same method should be understood as applicable, as appropriate, to the fine-material and immaterial spheres as well.

It is called "supramundane" (*lokuttara*) because it transcends the world—defined here as the aggregates of clinging—by virtue of being free from taints (*anāsava*); this refers to the path-consciousness (*magga-citta*). As for the fruition-consciousness (*phala-citta*), however, it has already crossed over from that.
Supramundane (*lokuttara*). Or, both [the paths and fruits] together with Nibbāna are "supramundane" because they transcend and exceed the world by virtue of the aforementioned qualities.
The commentary on the classification of the planes of consciousness is finished.
Commentary on the unwholesome consciousnesses.

4. Furthermore, although these four types of consciousness are fourfold—being divided into the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, and functional within the sense-sphere consciousness (kāmāvacara)—for the purpose of designating fifty-nine or ninety-one types of consciousness as "beautiful" (sobhana), excluding the unwholesome and the rootless (ahetuka), it is said: "Those [consciousnesses] excluding the unwholesome and the rootless are called 'beautiful'.
This is in accordance with the method that will be explained hereafter; thus, [the term "beautiful"] applies only to those excluding the unwholesome and the rootless.

Showing the first [category] among those [three types of existence], and because for a being who has taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) in those existences, only the arising of consciousness accompanied by greed is possible at the very beginning by way of process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*), he shows those first;
immediately after that, he shows those accompanied by displeasure (*domanassasahagata*) due to their commonality as being twofold-rooted (*dvihetuka*);
and immediately after that, in order to show those with a single root (*ekahetuka*), he says "accompanied by joy" (*somanassasahagata*), and so forth.
First, that which is rooted in greed (*lobha*) is shown by dividing it into eight types through the distinctions of feeling (*vedanā*), view (*diṭṭhi*), and volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).
In this context, "sumana" means a beautiful mind; or, one who possesses that [mind] is "sumano," referring to the consciousness or the person endowed with it.

Its state, or its being the cause for the application of the designation and the cognition [of "sumana"] toward that [person], is "somanassa" (mental joy); this refers to a pleasant mental feeling (*mānasika-sukha-vedanā*).
It is a designation; "accompanied by joy" means associated with it by way of arising together and so forth, or having attained the state of arising together and so forth with it.
"Views wrongly" refers to *diṭṭhi* (view). For even a general term acquires a specific scope through context and other factors;
thus, here it is specifically wrong view that is called "view. View itself is "gone-to-view" (*diṭṭhigata*).
Because the word *gata* functions in the sense of "becoming that state," as in such expressions as "gone to the state of formations" (*saṅkhāragata*) or "gone to firmness" (*thāmagata*).

Alternatively, it is "gone among" (*gata*) or "included within" (*antogata*) the sixty-two views; or, it is the mere movement (*gamana-matta*) of view. It is called "view-activity" (*diṭṭhigata*) because there is no entity such as a self (*attā*) or anything belonging to a self (*attaniya*) to be found here.
It is the adherence (*abhinivesa*) to a self and what belongs to a self, proceeding in the form: "Only this is true, all else is false."
"Associated with views" means being conjoined with them through such modes as arising together (*ekuppāda*).

It is called "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*) because it prepares the mind by adorning it with the distinction of sharpness, or because it is prepared—that is, it is adorned—by means of that [sharpness] according to the method already described;
[it functions] by providing supporting power to the mind when it is sinking in its various tasks.
It is a previously applied effort, whether by oneself or by others;

moreover, it occurs both in one’s own mental continuum that has arisen in a prior stage and in the continua of others. This specific quality of sharpness produced thereby is called "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*).
That which lacks this is "without volitional formation" (*asaṅkhāra*), and that itself is "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*). That which is accompanied by volitional formation is [prompted].
It is "prompted" (sasaṅkhārika). And so they say:
