it is the seeking after an object, characterized by the wish to act. For it is said that "in the grasping of an object, it is like the stretching out of the mind's hand.
Even at the time when it functions through the relinquishing of the basis for giving, it [is characterized] by that which is to be relinquished...
Therefore, one who desires [the beautiful] must indeed grasp the arrows that have been shot, just like an archer.
They are called *pakiṇṇaka* (miscellaneous) because they are scattered and strewn about in various ways among both the beautiful and the others. 4.

In relation to the beautiful, the others are "others"; and in relation to the others, the beautiful are also "others. These are called "similar to others" (*aññasamāna*) because, unlike restlessness, faith, and so forth, they do not possess an exclusively unwholesome nature or the like.
The commentary on the mental factors common to other [types of consciousness] is concluded.
Commentary on the Unwholesome Mental Factors: 5.
Thus, first, by way of those common to all consciousness, and by way of the miscellaneous, there are thirteen [factors] of a beautiful or otherwise nature.

Having pointed out the states (dhammas), [the author] now speaks the words beginning with "delusion" (moha) in order to show first those included among the unwholesome states, and then those included among the beautiful states, according to the sequence indicated below in the analysis of consciousness (cittavibhāga).
However, because there are no rootless (ahetuka) states that are unique (āveṇika), they are not mentioned separately.
It is called delusion (moha) because it is bewildered (muyhati) regarding the object; it is ignorance (aññāṇa), and its characteristic is the obscuring of the true nature of the object.
For even when this [mind] proceeds by way of grasping an object, it proceeds precisely by way of concealing its true nature.

One who does not feel shame and does not feel abashment is "shameless" (*ahirika*), whether referring to a person or a collection of phenomena. The state of being shameless is "shamelessness" (*ahirikka*);

that itself is *ahirika*. That which does not cause one to tremble is "fearlessness of wrongdoing" (*anottappa*). In this context, just as a village pig [is indifferent] to excrement, [the shameless person is indifferent] to bodily misconduct and so forth.

Lack of moral shame (*ahirika*) has the characteristic of not being disgusted [by evil]. Lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) has the characteristic of not being afraid of that [evil], like a moth before a fire. Thus the ancients said:
“The one who lacks moral shame is not disgusted by evil, just as a pig is not by dung;
The one who lacks moral dread does not fear it, like a moth before a flame.”
Agitation (*uddhacca*) is the state of being agitated; its characteristic is the lack of composure in the mind, like ashes blown up by the impact of a stone.
Greed (*lobha*) is that which covets; its characteristic is clinging to an object, like the saliva of a monkey.
Desire (*chanda*) is merely the mind’s wish to seize an object, whereas greed is the intense craving for it—this is the distinction between them. “This very...”

The view has the characteristic of wrong adherence, such as [thinking] "this is true, the other is false. For while knowledge knows its object according to its actual nature, view grasps it falsely by abandoning its actual nature;
this is the distinction between them. Pride is that which conceives [itself] by means of [thoughts] such as "I am superior";
it has the characteristic of inflation, for it is described as having "the desire for self-display" as its manifestation.
*Dūsati* means "to corrupt"; it has the characteristic of ferocity, like a struck venomous snake. *Issati* means "to envy"; it has the characteristic of being envious of the success of others.
The state of being stingy (*macchara*) is stinginess (*macchariya*); or, stinginess is that which occurs with the thought, "May this wonder not belong to others, but to me alone.
It has the characteristic of concealing one's own success. That which is done in a contemptible way is a "bad deed" (*kukata*).
"Bad conduct and good conduct done and not done. For they say of even what has not been done, "That which was not done by me is a bad deed (*kukata*).
Here, however, the arising of a state of mental remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) with respect to what has been done and not done is "bad deed" (*kukata*);
its state is "remorse" (*kukkucca*). It is characterized by grieving over bad conduct and good conduct done and not done. *Thinanaṃ* is "stiffness" (*thina*).
The state of being congealed is by way of the influence of incitement and the influence of despondency. *Middha* is sleep; it is the loss of capacity, or the impairment of power.
In this context, *thina* has the characteristic of unworkability of the mind, while *middha* [has that characteristic] of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).
This is the distinction between them. For thus it is said in the Pāḷi: "In this regard, what is *thina*? That which is the unwieldiness of the mind..."
“Unwieldiness. In that context, what is torpor? It is defined by such passages as: “That which is the body’s lack of health, its unwieldiness,” and so forth.
Now, one might object: since it says “of the body,” does this not imply that unwieldiness belongs even to the material body, and thus torpor would also possess a material nature?
This does not follow; for its [nature] is established solely through the reasons brought forward by the teachers in various places.

Because it has been rejected. For indeed, in order to refute the opinion of those who maintain that torpor (*middha*) is material form (*rūpa*), the teachers extensively explain this in various ways in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other works, preceded by the rejection of their doctrine.
Herein is the summary: "Some say that even torpor is material form; this is not tenable."
Because it is stated among those things to be abandoned, like sensual desire and so forth:
"This has indeed been declared among the hindrances as things to be abandoned;
but form has not been declared as something to be abandoned by means of vision and the rest."
“‘Monks, you should abandon form’—this is the reading from the text;
yet even a trace of the state of being abandoned is seen in the case of form.
Therein, the abandonment of desire and lust for its object is made manifest.”
For it is said there: "That which is the casting off of desire and lust," and so forth. [Objection:
"Among the states of torpor in the realms of form and formlessness, the formless is taught therein;
if you say this is not the case because the text does not specify [a particular realm], [we reply: it is not so."
“It may indeed be inferred that what is considered ‘matter’ (rūpa) is actually torpor (middha);
for that too is an hindrance (nīvaraṇa) by virtue of its being torpor, just like the others.
And because it is designated as a mental concomitant (sampayoga), it is certain that it is not matter.”
"For it is said that there is association (sampayoga) of the formless aggregates (arūpīnaṃ khandhānaṃ).
In such a case, their simultaneous arising (samuppatti) is established; there is no state of being material (rūpatā) according to the text.
However, for those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), sleep may occur due to bodily fatigue."
The commentary on the unwholesome mental factors is concluded.
Commentary on the Beautiful Mental Factors: 6.
It is called *saddhā* because one has faith; it is confidence in the Buddha and so forth. Its characteristic is the clarification of associated states.
Like a water-clearing gem, mindfulness (*sati*) is non-forgetfulness; it has the characteristic of recollecting associated mental states.
*Hirī* is so called because one feels shame (*hiriyati*)—that is, disgust—with bodily misconduct and the like; it has the characteristic of disgust toward evil.
*Ottappa* is so called because one is afraid (*ottappati*) of evil; it has the characteristic of dread of evil. Because she feels disgust toward evil by way of self-respect, she is like a noble lady.

Moral shame (*hiri*) is like a father, because it causes one to shrink from evil out of respect for oneself; moral dread (*ottappa*) is like a courtesan, because it causes one to shrink from evil out of regard for others.
Non-greed (*alobha*), the opposite of greed, has the characteristic of non-attachment of the mind to an object, like a monk who has renounced his possessions.

Non-hatred (*adosa*), the opposite of hatred, has the characteristic of absence of ferocity, like a friendly companion. Equanimity toward these states is "equanimity regarding the middle" (*tatramajjhattatā*).
It has the characteristic of looking on with equanimity at the mind and mental factors; it is like a charioteer who looks on with equanimity at the horses as they proceed evenly.
Tranquillization of the body is bodily tranquillity (*kāyappassaddhi*); tranquillization of the mind is mental tranquillity (*cittappassaddhi*).
Both of these have the characteristic of the subsiding of bodily and mental distress. Lightness of the body is bodily lightness (*kāyalahutā*); likewise for mental lightness (*cittalahutā*).

These have the characteristic of the subsiding of stiffness in body and mind. Bodily pliancy is the state of suppleness of the body; likewise for mental pliancy. These have the characteristic of the subsiding of rigidity in body and mind.
Serviceability means being good at work; its state is serviceability (*kammaññatā*).
Bodily serviceability is the serviceability of the body; likewise for mental serviceability. These have the characteristic of the subsiding of unserviceability in body and mind.
The state of being fit (*paguṇa*) is fitness (*pāguñña*); that itself is fitness (*pāguññatā*). Fitness of the body is bodily fitness (*kāyapāguññatā*).

Likewise for mental fitness (*cittapāguññatā*). These two have the characteristic of the subsiding of sickness in the body and mind. Rectitude of the body is bodily rectitude (*kāyujukatā*); likewise for mental rectitude (*cittujukatā*).
These two have the characteristic of straightness in the body and mind, respectively. Furthermore, these [qualities] belong to the body and mind...

It arises from conditions that are the opposites of the disturbances of the elements caused by exertion and so forth; and here, by "body," there is the inclusion of the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling.

Furthermore, because these two pairs of phenomena together strike down their respective opposing factors, their twofold nature is stated only in this context and not in the case of concentration and the others.
Moreover, [this is not the case] for the mind itself, due to mental tranquility and so forth.

There is the state of serenity and so forth; however, because the physical body is also pervaded by the sublime matter originated from bodily serenity and the rest, the twofold nature is stated here for the purpose of demonstrating that meaning.
They are called "common to the beautiful" because they are common to all beautiful [states] and arise among them as a rule.
7. It is called right speech (*sammāvācā*) because one speaks rightly by means of it; it is the abstention from verbal misconduct. It is fourfold:
abstention from false speech, abstention from malicious speech, abstention from harsh speech, and abstention from idle chatter.

Just as "kamma" itself is "kammanta" (the course of action), as in the cases of *suttanta* and *vananta*, so too "rightly proceeding action" is "right action" (*sammākammanta*), which is the abstention from bodily misconduct.
That [abstinence] is threefold: abstinence from taking life, abstinence from taking what is not given, and abstinence from sexual misconduct.
Right livelihood (*sammā-ājīva*) is that by which one lives rightly; it is the refraining from wrong livelihood.

Furthermore, it is sevenfold by way of abstaining from bodily and verbal misconduct caused by livelihood, or it is manifold by way of abstaining from wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy, flattery, and so forth. All three types...

These three types of abstinence—each consisting of the undertaking, the severance, and the avoidance of what has been attained—are so called because they involve refraining from the aforementioned misconducts.
8. It is *karuṇā* (compassion) because, when there is suffering in others, it produces heartache for the virtuous; or because it scatters (*kirati*) or disperses the suffering of others;
or because it buys (*kiṇāti*) or harms that [suffering]; or because it is extended toward those who are suffering (*kiriyati*). Its characteristic is the desire to remove the suffering of others.
For even if the suffering of others is not actually removed by that [compassion], it still proceeds in that very manner. It is called *muditā* (altruistic joy) because beings rejoice by means of it;
its characteristic is rejoicing in the success of others. It is "immeasurable" (*appamāṇā*) because it has immeasurable sentient beings as its object;
these are thus the "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*). But will he not say later, "There are four immeasurables"? Why, then, are only two mentioned here?

Because loving-kindness (*mettā*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*) are included within non-hatred (*adosa*) and neutrality (*tatramajjhattatā*). For it is non-hatred itself, when proceeding with a disposition toward the welfare of beings, that is called loving-kindness.
And it is neutrality itself, when proceeding as the subsiding of aversion and attachment toward them, that is called equanimity. Thus the ancients said:
“Loving-kindness is indeed through non-ill-will, and through neutrality...”
“Since equanimity (*upekkhā*) has been taken [as a faculty], therefore both have not been taken.
It is wisdom (*paññā*) because it knows by way of its specific mode, awakening [to things] through their impermanence and so forth;

that very same wisdom is called the “faculty of wisdom” (*paññindriya*) due to its predominance in the awakening to the true nature of things (*yathāsabhāvāvabodhana*). Now, what is the distinction between perception (*saññā*), consciousness (*viññāṇa*), and wisdom (*paññā*)?
Perception (saññā) performs the mere act of perceiving by way of blue and so forth, but it is not able to effect the penetration of characteristics (lakkhaṇappaṭivedha).
Consciousness (viññāṇa) accomplishes even the penetration of characteristics, yet it is not able to bring one to the Path after having exerted itself.
Wisdom (paññā), however, performs all three functions; the illustration here is the understanding of a coin by a child, a villager, and a money-changer.
Furthermore, at the time when consciousness arises by way of grasping the aspect of a perception dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇavippayutta-saññā*), it is not conventionally designated as such;
at other times, however, it is powerful. But when associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta*), both [perception and consciousness] follow that [knowledge]. The connection is:
"in all ways, twenty-five. 9. The summary of those stated in three groups, beginning with "thirteen are similar to perception," etc.
The commentary on the beautiful mental factors (*sobhanacetasika*) is finished.
Commentary on the method of association:
"Inseparable from consciousness" means not dissociated from consciousness; what is meant is "mental factors. "Arises" means *uppāda*.
“Cittuppāda” (arising of mind) means the arising itself is the mind. In other contexts, however, the mind together with its associated factors is called “cittuppāda,” based on the analysis:
“It is an arising because the mind arises by means of it; it is a collection of phenomena (dhamma-samūha); and it is both that mind and an arising—thus, ‘cittuppāda’.
For grammarians maintain that even in a collective dvanda compound, the masculine gender may sometimes be used. Of those [factors] inseparable from the mind...
The connection is as follows: "In the arising of consciousnesses, the specific association will be explained hereafter as appropriate.
13. Commentary on the Method of Association with Other Common Mental Factors:

Because they are by nature without applied thought (*vitakka*), the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness are excluded from these [mental factors], or rather, these [consciousnesses] are excluded from them.

Excluding the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousnesses, there are forty-four sense-sphere consciousnesses (*kāmāvacara-citta*). Among these, as well as among the eleven first-jhāna consciousnesses, applied thought (*vitakka*) arises;
the intention is that for the remaining [consciousnesses], it is absent due to the power of meditation (*bhāvanā-bala*).

14. Among those fifty-five consciousnesses accompanied by applied thought (*savitakka*), as well as among the eleven second-jhāna consciousnesses—that is, among sixty-six consciousnesses—sustained thought (*vicāra*) arises.
15. Resolution arises in seventy-eight consciousnesses, excluding eleven: namely, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and that accompanied by doubt.

16. Energy arises in seventy-three consciousnesses, excluding sixteen: namely, the five-door adverting consciousness, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the two types of receiving consciousness, and the three types of investigating consciousness.

17. Joy arises in fifty-one types of consciousness, excluding seventy-seven: namely, the two types accompanied by displeasure, the fifty-five types accompanied by equanimity, the two types of body-consciousness, and the eleven types of the fourth jhāna.
18. Interest arises in sixty-nine types of consciousness, excluding twenty: namely, the eighteen rootless types and the two types of sheer delusion. 19.

"But those" refers to those associated with [the factors] excluding the miscellaneous ones. "In due order" means according to the sequence corresponding to their respective association, excluding the six miscellaneous factors beginning with applied thought (vitakka).
“Sixty-one, fifty-five,” and so forth, should be applied accordingly according to the reckoning of one hundred and twenty-one and the reckoning of eighty-nine.
The commentary on the method of association with other common mental factors is concluded.
Commentary on the Mode of Association with Unwholesome Mental Factors (Akusalacetasika-sampayoga-naya-vaṇṇanā) 20.
Having stated that they are "common to all unwholesome states," the phrase beginning with "in all [unwholesome states]" was spoken in order to substantiate that very point.
For whoever engages in such acts as the destruction of life, all of them do so through delusion (*moha*), failing to see the danger therein, and through shamelessness (*ahirika*).

Therefore, being unashamed due to lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), and being unpacified due to restlessness (*uddhacca*), these [factors] are found in all unwholesome states. 21. Regarding the phrase "only in consciousnesses accompanied by greed":
the particle *eva* (only) also serves the purpose of restriction; thus, it applies to the subsequent phrases such as "in consciousnesses accompanied by views," and so forth.

The restriction is to be understood as follows: because for one who is intent upon personality (*sakkāya*) and so forth, the arising of self-cherishing (*mamāyana*) occurs therein, view is found only in consciousnesses accompanied by greed (*lobha*).
Pride (*māna*), too, since it proceeds by way of the conceit "I am," functions in a manner similar to view;
thus, it arises together with view within a single moment of consciousness, like a maned lion [arising] with another of its kind.
It does not arise even in a single cave, nor in the roots of faults and so forth, because it is based on self-attachment and has absolute greed as its proximate cause;
thus, it is found only among those dissociated from wrong view.
24. Likewise, it arises in one who envies the success of others and who is unwilling for their own success to be shared with others.

Envy, avarice, and worry occur only in states of mind associated with aversion (paṭigha-citta), because they function by way of resistance toward various objects while one grieves over past misconduct or the lack thereof. 25.

Since lethargy and drowsiness cannot occur in spontaneous (asaṅkhārika) states—which are of such a nature that they are characterized by unwieldiness—they are found only in prompted (sasaṅkhārika) states.

27. The application [of the factors] is as follows: the four mental concomitants (cetasika) are included in all unwholesome states (apuñña); the three are included in those rooted in greed (lobha-mūla) according to their occurrence;
the four are included in the two rooted in hatred (dosa-mūla); likewise, the two are included only in those accompanied by volitional effort (sasaṅkhāra).
In the phrase "doubt (vicikicchā) [is included] in the mind of doubt," the word *ca* (and) is used for emphasis. The connection is: "Doubt is included only in the mind of doubt."
The explanation of the method for association with unwholesome mental factors is finished.
29. Explanation of the method for association with beautiful mental factors:
In supramundane consciousnesses, there may occasionally be an absence of right intention due to the influence of the foundational jhānas and so forth; however, [it is never absent].

The absence of non-abstention (*virati*) in the case of the Path is due to the total eradication of bodily misconduct and so forth, while in the case of the Fruit, it is because [the Path] proceeds in a manner conducive to that eradication;
thus it is said, “But as for the abstentions,” and so on. “In every way” means by all those modes of proceeding which function to dispel each respective misconduct and wrong livelihood.
For these [abstentions], unlike those in the mundane sphere, do not [apply to] lying and so forth even in the supramundane realm.

The occurrence takes place through the abandoning of each [type] individually—that is, of all misconducts and wrong livelihoods—either entirely for some by means of this or that path, or for others by way of abandoning them at a single moment in the state of those leading to the states of misery and so forth.
But is this meaning not already established by the phrase "on one side" (*ekatovā*) alone? That is not so, because of the three...
Because it is not indicated that the fourfold verbal misconduct and so forth proceed as their opposites by the mere indication of their occurrence on one side.
However, some, failing to perceive this point, say: "The phrase 'in every way' (sabbathāpi) is redundant.
In that case, their ignorance alone is the reason. By the word "fixed" (niyatā), [it is shown that] unlike in worldly matters, it does not occur only occasionally.

It precludes their occurrence. Likewise, while those [factors] were taught in the *Lokiyas* by way of being merely included (*yevāpanaka*), here they are taught in their own specific form (*sarūpena*).

By the restriction "only among the wholesome states of the sense-sphere" (*kāmāvacara-kusalesveva*), it precludes their occurrence in the resultant and functional states of the sense-sphere, as well as in the sublime (*mahaggata*) states;
he will state this very point further below. "Sometimes" (*kadāci*) refers to the time of abstaining from each individual misconduct, such as false speech and so forth.
Even when they do arise, they do not arise simultaneously, because they depend upon the occurrence of their respective objects, which consist of the bases to be transgressed;

thus it is said, "separately. 30. For the illimitables that have reached absorption (*appanā*), there is never an occurrence devoid of mental joy (*somanassa*); thus it is said, "the fifth... and so forth.
And it is said, "in the minds. They have reached greatness because they are free from hindrances (*vinīvaraṇa*), or because they have been reached and attained by great meditators;

thus, they are "lofty" (*mahaggata*). "Having become diverse" means having become separate due to their different objects, owing to the requirement of coming into the range of suffering and happy beings who constitute their respective objects.
"In these" refers to these wholesome sense-sphere minds (*kāmāvacara-kusala-citta*).
At the time of developing compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*), prior to the path of absorption (*appanāvīthi*),

there is preliminary work (*parikamma*) by means of consciousnesses accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) due to the power of prior familiarity; just as one who is reciting a well-mastered text may sometimes continue the recitation even when distracted,

or as one who is comprehending formations (*saṅkhāra*) through well-practiced insight (*vipassanā*) may, by the force of habituation, do so even with consciousness dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa*).

Regarding "comprehension" (*sammasana*): the claim that compassion (*karuṇā*) and gladness (*muditā*) cannot occur in sense-sphere states accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) is merely the opinion of some.

However, it should be understood that in the cognitive process of absorption (*appanāvīthi*), these two arise exclusively in those states accompanied by joy (*somanassa*), because there is no condition of repetition (*āsevanapaccaya*) for factors of a different class or a different feeling-tone.

32. "Three [factors] in sixteen types of consciousness": the three factors beginning with right speech arise in sixteen types of consciousness by way of the eight supramundane and the eight sense-sphere wholesome [consciousnesses].

33. Having thus shown together the indeterminate factors mentioned in terms of their association with both determinate and indeterminate [states], the following was stated—"envy, avarice," etc.—to illustrate the determinate nature of the remaining factors: envy, avarice, remorse, abstinence, compassion, and so forth.
The construction is as follows: various [hindrances] arise at different times, while conceit (*māna*) arises at times through the occurrence of such states as "I am superior.
Likewise, sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*) arise at times through the occurrence of unwieldiness, arising together with one another in a state of non-separation.
Alternatively, having also connected the word *ca* ("and") in the phrase "conceit and" (*māno ca*) with the word "together" (*saha*), [the meaning is that] sloth and torpor likewise [arise together].

The construction should be understood as follows: sometimes [the unwholesome roots] arise together with impulsive resistance (*sasaṅkhārika-paṭigha*), and with envy (*issā*), avarice (*macchariya*), and worry (*kukkucca*) when associated with impulsions dissociated from views (*diṭṭhigata-vippayutta-sasaṅkhārika*);
and sometimes they arise separately at the time of association with other impulsive consciousnesses, or even at the time of association with those [specific ones].
However, other teachers [hold that] "conceit (*māna*) and sloth-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*)..."
They joined [the text] with only this much: “Thus, sometimes they arise separately, and sometimes together.
34. “The rest” means the forty-one others besides the eleven indeterminate factors already mentioned.
However, some explain that “the rest are the determinate factors included by way of inclusion,” but that is merely their own opinion; here [the meaning is as stated].
Because some [mental factors] have not been specifically mentioned by the name "occasional" (yevāpanaka).

Here, the Master has merely demonstrated the mental concomitants as they are obtained among the arising of consciousnesses according to their respective suitability, classifying them as either fixed or unfixed; he has not, however, specifically mentioned any by the name "occasional.
Thus, first of all, this is by way of delimiting the consciousnesses, showing that "this state is found in so many types of consciousness," starting with contact (phassa) and so forth.

Having shown the association [of mental factors], the passage beginning with “And the compendium” is now stated in order to show the compendium by way of delimiting the groups of mental factors, namely: “In this arising of consciousness, there are so many mental factors.
The commentary on the method of association with beautiful mental factors is concluded.
The commentary on the method of conjunction is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the method of inclusion (saṅgahanaya): “Thirty-six,” and so forth, refers to a numerical inclusion based on the phenomena as they are found appropriate in each respective context.
36. Those consciousnesses associated with the first jhāna, or those that possess it, are called "first-jhāna consciousnesses.

Because the illimitables have sentient beings as their object, and because supramundane consciousnesses have Nibbāna as their object, it is said: "excluding the illimitables. By the word "likewise," it is indicated that they are similar to others;
thus, the beautiful mental factors (sobhana-cetasika), excluding the illimitables, are included [in this category].

It draws [the mind] toward itself. "Accompanied by equanimity" means accompanied by that equanimity which has entered the place of bliss, being devoid of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), and pleasure (*sukha*).

"By way of the fivefold jhāna" refers to the fivefold jhāna taught for one of moderately sharp wisdom who develops it by transcending applied and sustained thought individually; however, for one who transcends them both together—

The intention is that for one developing [insight] by way of sharp knowledge, there is a fourfold inclusion alone, because among those possessing the second jhāna, [the factors] excluding applied thought (*vitakka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) are possible by way of the four jhānas taught [in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*]. 37.
The "pair of thirty-three" refers to the fourth and fifth jhāna consciousnesses.
Commentary on the Compendium of Lofty Consciousness (Mahaggatacittasaṅgahanayavaṇṇanā) 38.
Regarding the phrase "in the three": this refers to the threefold [consciousness] by way of the wholesome, the resultant, and the functional.

For one whose bodily and vocal applications have been thoroughly purified by means of purification of virtue, the lofty jhānas proceed merely through the stabilization of the mind, but not through bodily and vocal actions.

It is said to be "excluding abstinence" because it does not function by way of purification, nor by way of cutting off or pacifying misconduct and wrong livelihood. "Each separately" means individually.

"In fifteen" refers to the three [planes] by way of the fine-material sphere and the twelve by way of the immaterial sphere, thus making fifteen. The reason why the illimitables are not found there has already been stated.
The commentary on the method for classifying the sublime consciousnesses is finished.
Commentary on the Method for Classifying the Beautiful Consciousnesses of the Sense-Sphere (Kāmāvacara-sobhana-citta): 40.

"Each individually" means one by one. This is because the illimitables (appamaññā) have sentient beings as their object, and the abstinences (virati) have the objects that are to be abstained from as their domain.
Because worldly abstinences (*lokiya-virati*) are exclusively of a wholesome nature, they cannot arise even in a single moment of consciousness;

thus, it is said that they do not occur among the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states, for which reason it is stated: “excluding abstinence. Therefore he says: “The five training precepts (*sikkhāpada*) are exclusively wholesome.
Otherwise, he would have said that they “may be wholesome or may be indeterminate,” just as in the case of faith, mindfulness, and so forth. However, regarding the fruit...
Because they are counter-images of the Path and because they suppress misconduct and wrong livelihood, it is not logical that the supramundane abstinences (virati) are exclusively wholesome;

therefore, they are not included therein. Furthermore, because even the sense-sphere resultant states have exclusively limited objects, and because the immeasurables (appamaññā) have sentient beings as their object, and because the abstinences are exclusively wholesome, it is said: "excluding the immeasurables and the abstinences."

But surely, since even wholesome consciousness of the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*) has concepts and so forth as its objects, its result (*vipāka*) should also have an object similar to that which is wholesome—just as it is with the results of sublime (*mahaggata*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*) consciousness? This is not so, because [the sense-sphere result] is a fruit dependent upon craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmatanha*).
For just as the son of a slave-girl, being unable to do what his mother desires, must do whatever his master desires; so too is this the case here.

It acts thus: because of its dependence on sensual craving, the consciousness—which is the result of sense-sphere karma that resembles a slave—does not grasp the object previously taken up by that [karma], but grasps only the object of sensual craving.

"In twelve ways" means that within the divisions of wholesome-resultant and functional [consciousness], there are four types each for the three [realms] when categorized as pairs, thus making twelve ways.
42. Now, in order to show the distinguishing factors that differentiate the second jhāna and so forth from the first jhāna and so forth among these [states], it is said:

“In the unsurpassed mind, the jhāna-factors,” and so on. In the unsurpassed mind, the jhāna-factors—consisting of applied thought (*vitakka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), rapture (*pīti*), and bliss (*sukha*)—are the specific qualities that serve as differentiators.

In the middling and exalted [minds], both the immeasurables (*appamaññā*) and the jhāna-factors are present. In the limited [minds] of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), [only the immeasurables are present].
The abstinences, knowledge-joy, and the immeasurables are the distinguishing factors. In this context, the abstinences distinguish the wholesome resultant and functional states from one another;

the immeasurables distinguish the resultants from the wholesome and functional states; and as for knowledge-joy, it should be understood that among the three dyads, each subsequent dyad distinguishes itself from the preceding one.
The commentary on the method for classifying the beautiful consciousnesses of the sense sphere is concluded.
Commentary on the Method for Classifying Unwholesome Consciousness: 44.

Regarding the second [consciousness], "unprompted" (*asaṅkhārika*), the connection is as follows: in that which is dissociated from views and unprompted, there are nineteen factors—namely, the same as those associated with greed and conceit, plus the universal unwholesome factors (*akusala-sādhāraṇa*).
45. In the third [jhāna], it is the unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness associated with view and accompanied by equanimity.
46. In the fourth, it is the unprompted consciousness dissociated from view. 47.
However, envy, avarice, and worry should be applied here separately, because their objects are distinct; this is the intended meaning.

50. Because resolution (adhimokkha) functions in the mode of certainty, it cannot arise in the state of doubt (vicikicchā), which is characterized by indecision; therefore, it is said that [the latter] is "devoid of resolution. 51.

There are nineteen factors in the first and second types of unprompted (asaṅkhārika) consciousness; eighteen in the third and fourth types of unprompted consciousness; twenty in the fifth type of unprompted consciousness;
twenty-one in the first and second types of prompted (sasaṅkhārika) consciousness; and twenty in the third and fourth types of prompted consciousness.

The construction is as follows: "In the fifth [consciousness], the one with volitional effort (*sasaṅkhārika*), there are twenty-two; in the two types of deluded (*momūha*) consciousness, fifteen. Thus, the unwholesome states are established in seven ways. 52. The construction is as follows:

"Common" means those four factors that are common to all unwholesome states, and another ten that are "partially common," excluding desire (*chanda*), joy (*pīti*), and resolve (*adhimokkha*). These fourteen factors are called "associated with all unwholesome states."
The commentary on the method for classifying unwholesome consciousness is finished.
Commentary on the method for classifying rootless consciousness: 54.
By the word “likewise” (tathā), he refers back to what is similar to the others.

56. Because it is associated with the specific function of cognizing (*manana*)—unlike the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*)—it is the "mind-element" (*manodhātu*), being merely the act of cognizing. In the pair of rootless rebirth-linking moments, that is, in the two types of equanimity-resultant investigating consciousness (*upekkhā-santīraṇa*).

58. There is a fourfold inclusion among the eighteen rootless (ahetuka) thought-arising states: twelve in the smiling consciousness; eleven in the determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) and the pleasant-resultant investigating consciousnesses;
ten in the five instances of the triad of mind-elements and the rootless rebirth-linking pair; and seven in the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness. This is how the inclusion is fourfold.
59. The thirty-threefold grouping: there are five in the supramundane, likewise five in the sublime, twelve in the beautiful of the sense-sphere, seven in the unwholesome, and four in the rootless;

thus is the thirty-threefold grouping. 60. Thus, having understood the association of mental factors dissociated from consciousness as described by way of the classification of consciousness, and the grouping as described by way of the classification of the heap of mental factors, one should [apply them] to the mind according to their respective fitness.

One should point out the classification by way of equality thus: "First, the seven universal mental factors (sabbacittasādhāraṇā) are each of eighty-nine types because they arise in all eighty-nine types of consciousness;
among the occasionals (pakiṇṇaka), initial application (vitakka) is of fifty-five types because it arises in fifty-five types of consciousness," and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the method for classifying rootless consciousness (ahetukacitta).
Thus ends the commentary on the Section on Mental Factors within the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammattha-vibhāvinī*. 3.
Commentary on the Section on Miscellaneous Topics (*Pakiṇṇaka-pariccheda*).

1. Now, in order to show the compendium of miscellaneous factors (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅgaha*) by way of the classification of the aforementioned consciousnesses and mental concomitants according to their feeling and so forth, and by way of the classification of the arising of consciousnesses as distinguished by the various types of those respective feelings and so forth, the passage beginning with "Associated, as appropriate" is commenced.

Consciousness and mental concomitant phenomena associated as appropriate, by their own intrinsic nature—that is, by virtue of their respective individual natures—[encompass] the ninety-ninefold consciousness.

They are of one kind by way of the commonality of their intrinsic nature as the cognition of an object; they become thirty-five [factors] through such [classifications] as "contact, which is common to all consciousness, is of one kind by way of its intrinsic nature as touching," and so forth. 2.
Now, the compendium of these states according to their respective [categories], beginning with the compendium by feeling and so on, is called the "Compendium by Way of Basis" (*vatthusaṅgaha*).

The Compendium of Miscellaneous Items (*pakiṇṇaka-saṅgaha*) is presented and brought forth solely by way of the arising of consciousness (*cittuppāda*), distinguished by its various types such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so on;
it is not led anywhere apart from that [classification]. This is the meaning of "it is brought forth.
Commentary on the Compendium of Feeling (*Vedanā-saṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*).

3. *Tattha* means "among those six types of inclusion. The inclusion by way of feeling (*vedanā-saṅgaha*) is the inclusion based on the classification of pleasant and other feelings, as well as the mental states associated with them.
[The term] "neither-painful-nor-pleasant" (*adukkhamasukhā*) refers to that which is other than painful and pleasant, due to the occurrence of the letter *m*.
But is it not the case that there are only two feelings, because of the statement: "Bhikkhus, there are these two feelings: pleasant and painful"? True.
That [feeling], however, is stated by including the blameless side under neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling within pleasant feeling, and the blameworthy side under painful feeling.

As for the statement found in some suttas, "Whatever is felt, that is here included in suffering," that is said because all feelings have the nature of suffering due to the suffering inherent in conditioned formations (saṅkhāradukkhatā). As it has been said:
“Ānanda, it was with reference to the impermanence of formations and the changeability of formations that I said:
‘Whatever is felt, that is here [included] in suffering. Therefore, it should be understood that there are only three feelings. Thus the Blessed One said:
‘Bhikkhus, these three feelings are pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant. In this way, although they are of three kinds, in the teaching on the faculties...”

The fivefold teaching—“the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of pain, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of mental grief, and the faculty of equanimity”—is given here in order to demonstrate the classification according to those very [faculties].
Thus, it is said: “Pleasure, pain,” and so forth. For pleasure and pain are each divided into two types based on the distinction between bodily and mental;
having thus divided them, [the text continues]: “the faculty of pleasure, the faculty of mental joy, the faculty of pain...”

The faculty of mental displeasure (*domanassindriya*) is thus taught; however, because equanimity (*upekkhā*) lacks such differentiation, it is taught as a single entity, namely the faculty of equanimity (*upekkhindriya*).
For while pleasure and pain benefit or afflict the body in one way and the mind in another, equanimity does not do so;
therefore, it is taught as a single entity. Thus the Ancients said:
“Bodily and mental suffering, pleasure, and the feeling of equanimity—these are one [mental] only, according to the division of the five faculties.
Therein, pleasure has the characteristic of experiencing a desirable tangible object. Suffering has the characteristic of experiencing an undesirable tangible object.
Suffering (*dukkha*). Joy (*somanassa*) has the characteristic of experiencing what is desirable, whether by way of its intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) or through conceptualization (*parikappa*).
Likewise, grief (*domanassa*) has the characteristic of experiencing what is undesirable. Equanimity (*upekkhā*) has the characteristic of experiencing what is neutral.
5. There are forty-four [factors], each being elevenfold through the division into mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*).

7. "The rest" refers to all fifty-five remaining [consciousnesses]: six unwholesome ones accompanied by pleasure, pain, joy, and grief; fourteen rootless ones; twelve beautiful sense-sphere ones; and twenty-three fifth-jhāna ones.
The commentary on the Compendium of Feeling is finished.
The commentary on the Compendium of Roots begins.
10. The "Inclusion of Causes" (*hetusaṅgaha*) is the inclusion [of factors] by way of the classification of causes such as greed (*lobha*), and by way of their association with those [causes].

The connection [of the sentence] is: "Causes (*hetu*) are of six kinds. Their state of being a cause (*hetubhāva*), however, is the state of being a root (*mūlabhāva*), which consists in establishing the well-established nature of the associated states.
For phenomena that have obtained the causal condition (*hetupaccaya*) become firm like trees with well-developed roots; those without a cause do not.
They are like moss upon the surface of water. Having established this, these are called "roots" (*mūla*) because of their similarity to roots.
Others, however, say that they are "the state of being a cause that establishes the wholesome nature, etc., of the wholesome factors, etc.

If that were so, another cause would have to be sought to establish the wholesome nature, etc., of those causes themselves. [If one objects: "In that case, it is dependent on the other associated causes..."

In that case, the status of [the cause] as wholesome and so forth would be independent; thus, even for a cause associated with a state of delusion (*momūha-citta*), its unwholesome nature would be independent.

If, on the other hand, it were to have an unwholesome nature by virtue of its own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), then since the same would apply to the remaining causes—their being wholesome and so forth being due solely to their own intrinsic nature—that [unwholesomeness] would not be dependent upon the associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*) in the same way as those [other causes]. If...

Furthermore, if the state of being wholesome and so forth were dependent on a cause, then the state of being indeterminate for those things that lack a cause would not be possible; enough, then, with this excessive pressing.
Rather, the state of being wholesome and so forth in wholesome and unwholesome states is dependent upon wise and unwise attention (*yoniso-ayoniso-manasikāra*). As it has been said:
"Bhikkhus, for one who attends wisely, both unarisen wholesome states arise and arisen [wholesome states]..."

"...and wholesome states increase," and so forth. However, it should be understood that the indeterminate nature of indeterminate states is dependent upon a continuum free from underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), dependent upon karma, and dependent upon the state of being non-resultant. 16.
Now, in order to show the classification of the roots (*hetu*) by way of their types, it is said: "Greed, hatred... and so forth.
The commentary on the Compendium of Causes is finished.
Commentary on the Compendium of Functions: 18.
This compendium is presented by way of the classification of functions such as rebirth-linking and so forth, and by way of the delimitation of those factors possessing such functions.
The Summary of Functions: The function of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-kicca*) is the linking of one existence to another existence.
The function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga-kicca*) is being a factor of existence by way of being the cause for its uninterrupted occurrence.

The functions of adverting (*āvajjana-kicca*) and so forth should be applied as appropriate according to the meanings of the words explained above. [These functions] occur many times or once, by way of accomplishing their respective functions with respect to an object.

The function of impulsion (*javana-kicca*) is like the movement of one who is running fast. The function of registration (*tadārammaṇa-kicca*) is the taking of an object by means of making that very object which was grasped by the respective impulsion its own object. The function of death (*cuti-kicca*) is the slipping away from the existence that has been produced. 19.
Since these functions are evident according to their locations, he now shows them in detail with the words beginning "rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi*).
It has been stated; therein, the "place of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhi-ṭhāna*) is the locus of rebirth-linking. Granted, there is no such thing as a "place" separate from rebirth-linking itself;

however, for the sake of easy comprehension, it should be understood that even where there is no actual difference, a distinction is conceptually constructed—as in the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*silāputtakassa sarīra*).
The same applies to the remaining cases. It is the locus of the five consciousnesses, beginning with seeing.
The basis for the fivefold sense-consciousness. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the basis for reception and so forth is intended.

Among these, the basis for rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is that which occurs between the death-moment and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). [The sequence includes] the rebirth-linking and adverting moments;

the impulsion and adverting moments; the registration and adverting moments; the determining and adverting moments; and occasionally the impulsion and death moments, as well as the registration and death moments.

The position of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is between [the registration consciousness and the next bhavaṅga]. The position of adverting (āvajjana) is between the life-continuum and the fivefold sense-consciousnesses, as well as between the life-continuum and the javanas.

The position of the fivefold sense-consciousnesses is between the five-door adverting consciousness and the receiving consciousnesses. The position of receiving (sampaṭicchana) is between the fivefold sense-consciousnesses and the investigating consciousnesses (santīraṇa).
The position of investigating is between the receiving and the determining (voṭṭhabbana) consciousnesses. [The position of javana is] between the investigating and the javanas...

Between the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) and the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), there is the position of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*). Between the determining consciousness and its object, between the determining consciousness and the life-continuum, between the determining consciousness and death, between the mind-door adverting consciousness and its object, between the mind-door adverting consciousness and the life-continuum, and between the mind-door adverting consciousness and death, there is the position of the impulsion (*javana*).
[There is also the position] between the impulsion and the life-continuum, and between the impulsion and death.

The interval between that [registering consciousness] and the registration-moment is called the death-moment (*cuti-ṭhāna*). It occurs either between a javana and rebirth-linking, between a registration and rebirth-linking, or between the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and rebirth-linking.

The intention is that there are two types of equanimity-accompanied investigating consciousness (*upekkhā-sahagata-santīraṇa*), because for the investigating consciousness accompanied by pleasure, there is no occurrence of rebirth-linking or the life-continuum.

And having done so, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, regarding the passage that comes down thus: "Dependent on a state accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhāsahagata*), a state accompanied by equanimity arises, not by way of the root-condition (*na hetupaccayā*)," the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the term "accompanied by equanimity" states:
"Dependent on one rootless aggregate accompanied by equanimity, two aggregates [arise]; dependent on two aggregates, one aggregate [arises]; at the moment of rootless rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)."
“Dependent on one aggregate accompanied by equanimity, two aggregates [arise];

dependent on two aggregates, one aggregate [arises]”—thus the method of dependence (*paṭiccanaya*) has been set forth by way of the process of existence (*pavatti*) and rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). However, in the analysis of the terms for that which is accompanied by rapture (*pītisahagata*) and that which is accompanied by pleasure (*sukhasahagata*), it says:
“Dependent on one rootless (*ahetuka*) aggregate accompanied by rapture, three aggregates [arise]... [and so on]... two aggregates. Rootless...”
The statement, "Dependent on one aggregate accompanied by pleasure, two aggregates [arise]... [and so on]...

one aggregate," is cited solely by way of the process of occurrence (*pavatti*), and not by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) as in the passage beginning, "At the moment of rootless rebirth-linking. Therefore, since even the non-mention [of such a state] in the teaching according to the nature of phenomena indicates its non-existence, there is no occurrence of that [state] by way of rebirth-linking. However, where...
There is also the non-occurrence of certain [consciousnesses] even when they are capable of arising; the reason for this will be made clear further on.

25. Even though mind-door adverting consciousness occurs two or three times with respect to a limited object, it lacks the function of impulsion because it lacks the experience of the object's flavor;
thus it is said, "excluding the two types of adverting. And having done so...
It is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Having stood in the position of javana. Otherwise, it would have had to be said, “having become javana.

The wholesome, unwholesome, fruition, and functional consciousnesses consist of twenty-one mundane and supramundane wholesome consciousnesses, twelve unwholesome consciousnesses, four supramundane fruition consciousnesses, and eighteen functional consciousnesses of the three planes. Even for that which lasts for a single moment of consciousness...
For that which begins with the supramundane path possesses the function of impulsion by virtue of its own intrinsic nature;
just as omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), even though it has only a single object within its range, never loses that name because of its capacity to comprehend the entire range of objects. 27.

Thus, having explained [the functions] according to their different types, the passage beginning with "Among these, however" was stated in order to show them grouped together according to the number of functions each actually possesses.
33. The arising of consciousnesses beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) are fourteenfold according to the distinction of the names and functions of rebirth-linking and so forth;

or alternatively, the "names" such as rebirth-linking refer to those consciousness-arising states so named, which are shown to be fourteen by way of the distinction of the functions of rebirth-linking and so forth, and tenfold by way of the distinction of the stations (ṭhāna) of rebirth-linking and so forth themselves.

The construction [of the verse] is as follows: the states of consciousness with one function, two functions, three functions, four functions, and five functions—namely sixty-eight, two, nine, eight, and two respectively—are to be pointed out. This is the connection.
The commentary on the Compendium of Functions is finished.
**Commentary on the Compendium of Doors (Dvārasaṅgahavaṇṇanā)** 35.

The compendium of doors (*dvārasaṅgaha*) is the grouping together of the doors and of the consciousnesses that proceed through those doors by way of their delimitation. They are called "doors" because, as the means for the occurrence of immaterial phenomena such as adverting and so forth, they are like doors.
36. "The eye alone" refers specifically to the sensitive eye-organ (*pasādacakkhu*).

37. The mind-door (manodvāra) is either the mental states beginning with adverting (āvajjana), or the mind itself as the door. Regarding "the life-continuum" (bhavaṅga): immediately after adverting, there is the life-continuum. Thus the ancients said:
"The life-continuum together with adverting is called the mind-door. 39. "Therein" means:
among those doors such as the eye and so forth, forty-six types of consciousness arise in the eye-door according to their respective fitness.
The connection: There is one five-door adverting consciousness; seven [consciousnesses] consisting of eye-consciousness and the rest by way of both types of resultant; one determining consciousness;

twenty-nine sense-sphere javanas by way of wholesome, unwholesome, non-adverting functional, and [functional]; and eight registration consciousnesses by way of taking what was not previously grasped—thus there are forty-six.

"According to suitability" refers to the mental continuum’s state of wise attention, unwise attention, absence of underlying tendencies, and so forth, with respect to desirable and other types of objects.

"By way of correspondence. "In every respect" (*sabbathāpi*) means that all [these states] belong exclusively to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), whether considered from the perspective of the entire process beginning with adverting (*āvajjana*) and ending with the registration of that object;
or it may be construed as "in every respect, there are fifty-four types of consciousness.

"In every respect" refers to those states existing by way of their respective doors, including—by the method of taking what has not yet been taken—the forty-six types of consciousness belonging to the eye-door.
The meaning is that there are fifty-four [types of consciousness] by excluding the four pairs beginning with ear-consciousness. 41.

Because they do not occur at the eye and other doors, and because they do not occur by way of grasping another object from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) known as the mind-door, the nineteen types occurring by way of rebirth-linking and so forth are "door-freed" (dvāravimutta).

42. Since the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness arise at their respective doors, and the twenty-six sublime and supramundane javanas arise only in the mind-door, these thirty-six types of consciousness are, as appropriate, "single-door" consciousnesses corresponding to their respective doors.

45. Because they proceed by way of investigation (*santīraṇa*) and registration (*tadārammaṇa*) in the five doors, and by way of registration in the mind door, they are both "six-door" (*chadvārika*) and "door-freed" (*dvāravimutta*) in their occurrence from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) onwards throughout the course of existence. 47. Those that are five-door and those that are six-door are the "five-and-six-door" (*pañcachadvārika*).
Those that are six-door and sometimes door-freed are the "six-door-and-freed" (*chadvārikavimutta*). Alternatively, they are the "six-door-and-six-door-freed."
And the phrase "the sixfold doors of liberation" (*chadvārikavimuttāni*) should be understood as a *ekadesasarūpekaśeṣa* (a collective singular formed from a portion of similar items).
The commentary on the Compendium of Doors is finished.
Commentary on the Compendium of Objects.
48. The summary of objects (ārammaṇa-saṅgaha) is the grouping together [of objects] by way of their intrinsic nature, their classification, and the consciousness that has them as its domain.
It is called "form" (rūpa) because it undergoes transformation (rūpayati) through changes in color and manifests the state of being present in the heart.

That very thing is "objected to" (ālambīyati) by consciousness and mental factors, just as a staff and so forth are used by a weak man; or else, it is called an "object" (ārammaṇa) because consciousness and mental factors come to it and take delight (ramanti) therein.
The visible form is the object. It is called "sound" (*sadda*) because it is sounded; that very thing as an object is the "sound-object" (*saddārammaṇa*).
It is called "odor" (*gandha*) because it makes its own basis known, as if whispering, "This is here," like one who slanders;
that very thing as an object is the "odor-object" (*gandhārammaṇa*). It is called "flavor" (*rasa*) because beings relish it; that very thing as an object is the "flavor-object" (*rasārammaṇa*).

It is touched (*phuṭṭha*), thus it is the tangible (*phoṭṭhabba*); that very object is the "tangible-object" (*phoṭṭhabbārammaṇa*). A mental state (*dhamma*) itself as an object is the "mental-object" (*dhammārammaṇa*).

49. "Therein" means among those objects such as visible form and so forth. "Visible form itself" means visible form known as the sphere of visible forms (*vaṇṇāyatana*). "Sounds and so forth" refers to sounds and so forth known as the spheres of sound and so forth, as well as the sphere of the tangible, which consists of the three primary elements excluding the water element.
50. Excluding the five sensitive faculties (*pasāda*) as objects, the remaining sixteen are subtle material phenomena (*sukhumarūpa*).
51. "Present" means occurring at the present moment.

52. "All sixfold" means all sixfold by way of visible form and so forth. Because it lacks the state of destruction and cannot be designated in terms of past time and so on, Nibbāna and concepts (paññatti) are called "time-free.
"As appropriate" refers to the sense-sphere impulsion, the super-knowledge (abhiññā), and all other sublime (mahaggata) impulsions and the rest.

According to their suitability: for the sense-sphere javanas—excluding those that arise as laughter—the object is of six kinds, pertaining to the three periods of time and being timeless (kālavimutta).
For the javana arising as laughter, it is only of the three periods of time; for he will later state that its object is exclusively limited (paritta).
However, for the super-knowledge javanas occurring through the divine eye and so forth, the object is likewise of six kinds, as appropriate.
The object is both of the three periods of time and timeless (*kālavimutta*). The analysis of this will be made clear in the ninth chapter.
As for the remaining [consciousnesses], their object is either timeless or past, as appropriate.
53. Regarding the phrase "of those reckoned by way of doors... the object is sixfold," the connection is that it is the object of these in all six ways. Furthermore, of them...
The object does not become a range of experience in such a way that it is ungrasped by anything, as is the case with adverting;
nor is it exclusively present, as with five-door impulsion; nor is it restricted to the three times, as with mind-door impulsion; nor is it entirely independent of time;
nor is it devoid of the conventional designations established by scriptural authority regarding kamma and its signs, as is the case with the preceding impulsions prior to the moment of death.

He said: “…according to possibility… agreed upon. In this context, “according to possibility” means in accordance with the occurrence of the rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and death-moments of each respective plane, by way of their being apprehended through the various doors and so forth.
For instance, the objects of the rebirth-linking and life-continuum of those belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consist of the five objects such as visible forms;
they are apprehended through the six doors and, as appropriate, have as their objects either present or past kamma, kamma-signs, or conventional signs.

Likewise, for the death-consciousness, [the object] has already passed. However, for those three [types of rebirth-linking], the mental-object (dhamma) is apprehended solely by the mind-door and is past, being considered either kamma or a kamma-sign;
likewise, the visible-form (rūpa) object is apprehended by the mind-door alone and is exclusively present, being considered a sign of destiny (gatinimitta).
Thus, for the sense-sphere rebirth-linking and so forth, [the object] is apprehended by whichever of the six doors is applicable.
The object consists of the present and the past, recognized as kamma, the sign of kamma (*kamma-nimitta*), and the sign of destiny (*gati-nimitta*).

However, in the case of rebirth-linking in the sublime realms and so forth, for those in the fine-material sphere and the first and third immaterial planes, the object is exclusively a mental state (*dhamma-ārammaṇa*) apprehended by the mind-door, which is a conceptual construct (*paññatti*) recognized as the sign of kamma; the same applies to the second and fourth immaterial planes.
"Only past" means that the object consists of what is grasped by the mind-door—namely, the conception, the life-continuum, and the death-moment of a sublime state—which is a conceptual construct;
or else, it is simply the sign of the kamma considered as past.

For the most part, it is grasped by the six doors in another existence; that is, by the javanas occurring at the time of death in the immediately preceding past birth, which function through the six doors.

It is grasped. For there is no grasping by any door whatsoever of the object of rebirth-linking for those who have passed away from the non-percipient realm (*asaññībhava*) in the immediately preceding past existence;
thus, this [definition] is rendered inconclusive here by the inclusion of the majority.

Indeed, for them, the object of rebirth-linking—such as the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) and so forth—manifests solely through the power of karma. Thus, it is said in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*: "From the non-percipient realm..."
Having asked about the sign of rebirth for one who has passed away:
"The karma performed in another existence, whichever opportunity it finds,
by that very [karma] is the rebirth-linking established within the presented field of experience."
It has been stated that the presentation of the object of rebirth-linking occurs solely through the power of kamma.

Otherwise, since even an object grasped by the impulsion (javana) would be presented only through the power of kamma, the restrictive statement "by that alone" would be rendered devoid of its intended meaning.
But is it not the case that for those [types of consciousness] as well, the object of rebirth-linking is grasped by some door during the existence of kamma?
Is it possible? It is true that what is designated as "kamma" and "the sign of kamma" (kamma-nimitta) is possible;

however, since that which is designated as "the sign of destiny" (gati-nimitta) appears for everyone only at the very moment of death, how could there be any possibility of its being grasped within the existence of kamma?
Furthermore, in this context, the phrase "grasped by the six doors" is stated with reference specifically to what has been grasped by the javanas occurring immediately prior to death; and thus...
Having done so, the Master has stated in this very context of the *Paramatthavinicchaya*:
"For a being at the point of death, according to the object that appears,
rebirth-linking occurs in another existence, directed toward that [object] through the six doors."
By the words beginning with “the present,” he excludes the possibility of the future being the object of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

For that [future] has not been experienced like past kamma and the signs of kamma (*kamma-nimitta*), nor has it entered the range of the senses like present kamma, the signs of kamma, or the signs of the destination (*gati-nimitta*);
and he himself will later describe the specific nature of kamma, the signs of kamma, and so forth.

54. "In these" means in those consciousnesses that have as their objects present forms and so forth, or kamma and so forth. "Having each of the forms and so forth as their object" means those for which each individual object among the forms and so forth is an object.
55. "That which has the fivefold object consisting of form and so forth" means that whose object is the five kinds beginning with form. 56.
"The remaining ones" refers to the eleven sense-sphere resultant consciousnesses other than the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the receiving consciousnesses.

"Even all those having sense-sphere objects" means that although they are produced in every way—whether by way of the six doors, or by way of the door-freed, or by way of proceeding toward the six objects—they nevertheless have exclusively the nature of the sense sphere and have the six objects as their domain.
For herein, the resultant [consciousnesses] proceed toward the five objects such as visible form, etc., by way of investigation (*santīraṇa*), and so forth;
and toward the sense-sphere objects designated as the "six objects" by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and so forth.
When he sees a place suitable for striving and is satisfied even with a mind that has become joyful, there is [attachment] to the object of visible form;
when he hears a great noise at the place where goods and vessels are kept and is satisfied thinking, "Such greedy craving has been abandoned by me," there is [attachment] to the object of sound;

when he is satisfied at the time of worshipping a cetiya with perfumes and so forth, there is [attachment] to the object of fragrance; and when [he receives] almsfood endowed with excellent flavor from his fellow celibates...
It occurs with respect to the six objects included within limited phenomena (paritta-dhamma) as follows: when one is satisfied while enjoying food after it has been divided;
when one is satisfied with the tangible object at the time of fulfilling the duties of proper conduct (ābhisamācārika-vatta);

and when one is satisfied with respect to sense-sphere phenomena grasped through the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) and so forth, taking them as a mental object (dhammārammaṇa). Thus, it operates only upon these six objects comprised within limited phenomena.

57. Because the twenty consciousnesses—consisting of the twelve unwholesome types and the eight types of javana dissociated from knowledge—are dull by nature, they are unable to occur with respect to supramundane states.

Therefore, it is said that "the unwholesome [consciousnesses]... and so forth, meaning that they occur by taking as their object the three planes of existence and conceptual designations (paññatti), excluding the ninefold supramundane states. For among these...

Regarding the unwholesome, the four types of consciousness associated with wrong view (*diṭṭhigata*) have a sense-sphere object (*kāmāvacarārammaṇa*) at the time of misapprehending, relishing, and delighting in limited phenomena (*parittadhamma*).
In that same manner, when occurring in relation to sublime phenomena (*mahaggatadhamma*), twenty-seven such states have a sublime object (*mahaggatārammaṇa*);

and when occurring in relation to conventional phenomena (*sammutidhamma*), they have a concept as their object (*paññattārammaṇa*). The types of consciousness dissociated from views are also exactly those same [twenty-seven].
With respect to mental phenomena (*dhamma*), when it occurs solely through the mode of gratification and delight,
or through association with aversion by way of malice and remorse, or through association with doubt by way of non-arrival at the goal,
or through association with restlessness by way of distraction and lack of tranquility, its object is a limited or sublime concept (*paññatti*).

There are eight types of consciousness dissociated from knowledge—four wholesome and four functional—which, when occurring for trainees (*sekkha*), worldlings (*puthujjana*), or those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) during the reviewing of careless giving, hearing the Dhamma, and so forth, have sense-sphere objects;

when occurring during the reviewing of highly proficient jhānas, they have sublime objects; and when occurring during the preliminary work (*parikamma*) and so forth regarding the kasiṇa-signs and the like, [they have those as their objects].
It should be understood that they have concepts as their objects.
This is because, with the exception of the path and fruit of Arahantship, all other objects occur only within the mental continuums of those in training (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana).
For even those in training, setting aside mundane consciousness, possess individual consciousness consisting of the path and fruit of an Arahant.
They are unable to know [them] because they have not attained them; likewise, ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others cannot know the stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and so forth.

However, for those in training (*sekha*), at the time of the preliminary work (*parikamma*) for the higher knowledge (*abhiññā*) whose object is the path and fruit existing in another's continuum during their own respective reviewings of the path and fruit, and at the time of delimiting the paths and fruits by means of the higher-knowledge consciousness itself, [they know] their own respective...
Since there is the occurrence of wholesome javanas directed toward the states of the paths and fruits of both the common [worldlings] and those below,
the negation applies specifically to the path and fruit of Arahantship alone. However, in the case of sense-sphere objects, sublime objects, concepts, and Nibbāna,

there is the occurrence of javanas for trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana) during such activities as careful reflection on giving, listening to the Dhamma, comprehension of formations, and the preliminary work for the kasiṇas.

At the time of the preliminary work for those higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) having that as their object, at the time of the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*) and purification (*vodāna*), and at the time of cognizing visible forms by means of the divine eye and so forth, they become the objective range (*gocara*) of wholesome impulsion (*javana*) consciousnesses.
(59) "In every way, all objects" means: in every way, by way of the sense-sphere, the sublime, and the supramundane, as well as by way of the conceptualized (*paññatti*).
The meaning is that they have all things as their object, but unlike unwholesome states and so forth, they do not have "all things" as their object in a limited sense.
For when the functional javanas proceed by way of the range of omniscient knowledge and so on, and when the determining consciousness proceeds by way of its respective preliminary ranges,
there is nothing whatsoever that is not within their domain.
60. Because they have the first and third immaterial states as their objects, the second and fourth immaterial states among the immaterial consciousnesses have sublime objects.

61. The remaining... [as follows] ...have concepts as their objects: the fifteen sense-sphere consciousnesses and the first and third immaterial consciousnesses—these twenty-one—have concepts as their objects because they occur with respect to the conceptual designations (paññatti) such as the kasiṇas.

63. Twenty-five consciousnesses—namely, the twenty-three sense-sphere resultants together with the five-door adverting consciousness and the smile-producing consciousness—occur with respect to the limited.

They have only sense-sphere objects as their objective support. For the sense-sphere [consciousness] is called "limited" (paritta) because, compared to the sublime and other types of consciousness, it is of weak power and thus its self-nature is, as it were, broken all around.
In every instance, such as "six consciousnesses occur only in the sublime," the application of the restrictive particle "only" (eva) should be understood.
The commentary on the Compendium of Objects is finished. 64.

The Compendium of Bases (vatthusaṅgaha) is a compendium by way of the classification of bases and by way of delimiting the consciousnesses that have those as their physical basis. They are called "bases" (vatthūni) because consciousness and mental factors dwell (vasanti) in them, taking them as their support.

65. All of those are found in the sense-sphere world (*kāmaloka*), because they are obtained there by one whose faculties are complete. However, by the word "also" (*pi*), he indicates that for some—such as the blind or the deaf—they are not possible.

66. The triad beginning with the nose does not exist among the Brahmās. This is because, through the cultivation of detachment from sensual pleasures, they have become dispassionate toward odors, tastes, and tangibles;

consequently, their faculties directed toward those objects are also of a nature characterized by dispassion. [They do possess them] for the purpose of seeing the Buddha, hearing the Dhamma, and so forth.
However, because of the state of non-detachment from the eye-faculties, the dyad of the eye and so forth is found there. 67.

In the immaterial world (arūpaloka), none of the six bases (vatthu) exist, because for those who are immaterial, due to the power of the cultivation of dispassion toward form, there is a total absence of the occurrence of form in every respect.
68. The five consciousnesses themselves are called the "five consciousness-elements" (pañcaviññāṇadhātu) in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being and devoid of a soul.
69. The element that consists merely in the act of cognizing is the mind-element (*manodhātu*). 70.

That which is simply the mind, by virtue of its association with the specific function of discerning, is consciousness (*viññāṇa*); and in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul, it is an element (*dhātu*);

thus it is the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). Alternatively, it is the consciousness-element of the mind, hence the mind-consciousness-element. For it arises precisely from the mind as its immediately preceding condition (*anantarapaccaya*).
Because it arises immediately after the mind itself as its proximate condition, it is "connected with the mind.

It is designated as the "mind-consciousness element" (manoviññāṇadhātu), which consists of all consciousness remaining after excluding the aforementioned mind-element (manodhātu) and the five sense-consciousness elements; it functions by way of the three types of investigating consciousness (santīraṇa), the eight great resultants (mahāvipāka), the two types of repulsive consciousness (paṭigha), the first path consciousness, the smile-producing consciousness, and the fifteen fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) consciousnesses.
The connection is that these thirty factors do not arise solely in the mind-element (*manodhātu*), nor do they function depending on the heart-base alone.

Indeed, the eleven [types of consciousness], namely the investigating consciousnesses (*santīraṇa*) and the great resultants (*mahāvipāka*), do not arise in the formless realm due to the absence of sense doors and the absence of their respective functions.

Furthermore, because of the absence of resentment (*paṭigha*)—which exists as a state free from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*)—the two types of consciousness associated with it do not exist even in the fine-material realm (*rūpaloka*).
The same applies to the formless realms (*ārūpa*). First, the first path does not arise for disciples (*sāvaka*) in the absence of the condition of another's voice;

furthermore, Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas do not take birth elsewhere than in the human world. Also, the smiling consciousness cannot arise there due to the absence of a body. And as for the fine-material-sphere states, because those in the formless realms have developed detachment from form, they are dispassionate even toward the jhānas that take those [fine-material] forms as their object; thus, these states do not arise in the formless existence.
All these thirty-three types of consciousness proceed solely in dependence upon the heart-base (hadaya).
71. The twelve mundane wholesome states remaining from the five fine-material-sphere wholesome states;

the ten unwholesome states remaining from the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (paṭigha); and the thirteen functional consciousnesses remaining from the five-door adverting, laughing, and fine-material-sphere functional states.

By way of these—the first path-consciousness and the remaining seven supramundane consciousnesses—there are forty-two kinds of phenomena classified as the mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*).
