These proceed either depending on the heart-base, by way of the five-aggregate existence (*pañcavokārabhava*), or without depending on it, by way of the four-aggregate existence (*catuvokārabhava*).
In the sensual-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), the seven consciousness elements depend on six physical bases; in the fine-material-sphere existence (*rūpabhava*), they depend on three bases.

The construction is as follows: the fourfold consciousness-elements, excluding the triad beginning with nose-consciousness, and the single mind-consciousness-element which is independent in the formless existence (āruppa-bhava), are reckoned as such.

74. Twenty-seven [consciousnesses] belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara) by way of the five-door adverting consciousness of the sense-sphere resultants, the two types of resistance consciousness, and the smile-producing consciousness;
fifteen belong to the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara); and the first Path [consciousness]—thus, forty-three arise depending on those very [bases], and from those alone the remainder [arise].

The connection is as follows: forty-two types of consciousness, excluding the immaterial-sphere resultants, arise both with and without a physical basis; the four immaterial-sphere resultants arise only without a basis.
The commentary on the compendium of bases is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Chapter on Miscellaneous Matters in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*. 4.
Commentary on the Chapter on the Cognitive Process (*Vīthipariccheda*).

1. Thus, having made this supreme compendium of the classifications of the four aggregates of consciousness arising according to the method already stated—by way of their inclusion within feeling and so forth—one should again characterize the three planes, such as the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and the types of persons with double-rooted faculties and so on, [thinking]:
"This [consciousness] is followed by so many; immediately after this, there are so many consciousnesses. In this manner...

The construction is as follows: "I shall briefly explain, according to their occurrence, the compendium of mental states (cittuppāda) during rebirth-linking and the course of existence, which is determined by preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness, and which bears that name.
Although the compendiums of bases, doors, and objects were already discussed above, they are set forth again here in order to present the compendium of the course of existence in its full detail.
3. The occurrence of objects at the doors and the occurrence of consciousnesses with respect to those objects is "the occurrence of objects" (*visayappavatti*).
4. "Therein" (*tattha*) means in those six sets of six.
[End of] the commentary on the wheel of the cognitive process (*vīthicakka*).

6. To show that the application of the name "path" (*vīthi*) to these mental processes may be made either by way of the door—such as "the succession of consciousnesses occurring at the eye-door is the eye-door path"—or by way of the consciousness—such as "the path associated with eye-consciousness is the eye-consciousness path, because of its state of co-occurrence through sharing the same object and the same door"—it is said: [the following].
“‘The avenue of the eye-door,’ and so forth, has been stated.
The commentary on the six avenues is finished.
Commentary on the classification of the avenues.

7. Regarding the terms "extremely large" (*atimahanta*) and so forth: having passed one mind-moment (*cittakkhaṇa*) and having entered the range of the senses, that which lasts for sixteen mind-moments is called "extremely large. Having passed two or three mind-moments and lasting for fifteen or fourteen mind-moments, it is called "large.
From four mind-moments onwards, up to and including nine mind-moments having passed, [it lasts] from thirteen mind-moments...
From the first moment up until it has lasted for eight mind-moments, it is called "limited" (*paritta*).
From ten mind-moments onwards, up until fifteen mind-moments have passed, it is called "very limited" (*atiparitta*)—lasting from seven mind-moments up to two mind-moments.
Having established this, he will say: "passed by one mind-moment," and so forth. "Vibhūta" means manifest; "avibhūta" means unmanifest.
The commentary on the classification of the cognitive process (*vīthibheda*) is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the five-door process (*pañcadvāravīthivaṇṇanā*):
Having asked "How? In what manner is the determination of the object by way of its being 'excessively large' and so forth? [the answer is given] by way of mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*).
To explain this, the passage beginning with “arising and presence” (*uppādaṭhiti*) has been commenced. Arising (*uppāda*) is the act of coming into being; it is the acquisition of self-existence.
Dissolution (*bhaṅga*) is the act of breaking up; it is the destruction of its own form. That which occurs in the interval between these two, tending toward dissolution, is called presence (*ṭhiti*).
However, some deny that there is a moment of presence for consciousness. For their intention is as follows: in the *Cittayamaka*, [it is stated] “the arisen...”.
In the *Vibhaṅga* on such terms as "arising" (*uppajjamāna*), only dissolution and arising are mentioned—stating, for example: "At the moment of dissolution it has arisen, but is not arising;
at the moment of origination it has both arisen and is arising"—but the moment of presence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) is not mentioned.
If there were also a moment of presence for consciousness, one would have to say: "at the moment of presence and at the moment of dissolution."

Now, if it is thought that "the moment of duration exists because of the Sutta passage: 'Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned,'" even there, because alteration does not occur within a single dharma and because it is spoken of as a state of discernment (*paññāṇa*), only continuous duration (*pabandhaṭṭhiti*) is intended, not momentary duration (*khaṇaṭṭhiti*); nor is it something obtainable in the Abhidhamma.
There is a reason for not stating it; therefore, in the teaching of the Dhamma, even non-statement indicates non-existence.

To this, it is said: For just as, although they share a single substratum in one phenomenon, the moment of arising (*uppādakkhaṇa*) is distinct from the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), and thus the state of dissolution is held to be different from the state of arising. Otherwise, [the statement] "it is indeed another... [would be untenable].

One might fall into the position that "one phenomenon arises while another ceases"; likewise, a state distinct from the states of arising and dissolution, which is the state facing dissolution, must also be admitted—this is what is called "stability" (*ṭhiti*).
However, it was not mentioned in the Discourse (*pāḷi*) because it was presented as a method of instruction in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
For even the teaching of the Abhidhamma is sometimes given in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained.
It proceeds; just as the arising of matter (*rūpa*) was taught by dividing it into two ways—namely, accumulation (*upacaya*) and continuity (*santati*)—and as in the Sutta:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three conditioned characteristics of the conditioned. Which three?
Arising is discerned, passing away is discerned, and the alteration of that which stands is discerned"—thus it is for the purpose of showing the characteristics of conditioned phenomena alone.

Because arising and so forth have been mentioned, it cannot be understood that the stationing (*ṭhiti*) of the continuity—which is a conceptual designation (*paññatti-sabhāva*) and unconditioned (*asaṅkhata*)—has been mentioned therein.
Furthermore, since a prefix functions only within the meaning of the verbal root, the meaning of "is made known" (*paññāyati*) is "is cognized" (*viññāyati*).
Therefore, it is well said that the moment of stationing of consciousness cannot be excluded by this much alone.

“By way of arising, presence, and dissolution. And having established it thus, it is said in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well: “For each [dhamma], there are three moments by way of arising, presence, and dissolution. 9.

The immaterial (arūpa) is of light transformation, while the material (rūpa) is of heavy transformation, because they arise according to their respective moments in the state of being the grasper and the grasped.
Therefore he says “those,” and so forth. “Those” means such [moments]. Just like the moments of the seventeen types of consciousness...
The moments (*khaṇa*) consist of seventeen mind-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*); the connection is that those mind-moments are seventeen.

However, individually, they amount to fifty-one mind-moments. "Of material phenomena" (*rūpadhammānaṃ*) means of material phenomena excluding the two types of intimation (*viññatti*), which have the characteristic of making known.
For those two intimations have a lifespan of only a single mind-moment; thus, among the phenomena that follow the mind, they are excluded.

It has been stated. Among the material phenomena possessing characteristics (*lakkhaṇarūpa*), both birth (*jāti*) and impermanence (*aniccatā*) have a duration equal to the moments of arising and dissolution of consciousness, whereas aging (*jaratā*) lasts for forty-nine moments of consciousness. And having established this, they say:
"That [aging] lasts seventeen moments of consciousness, excluding the characteristics of intimation (*viññatti*)."
Some, however, say: "In the *Paṭiccasamuppāda-aṭṭhakathā*, because of the statement, 'At this point eleven consciousness-moments have passed;
then [the material phenomena] have a lifespan of the remaining five consciousness-moments,' the lifespan of material phenomena is sixteen consciousness-moments.
For it is the material phenomenon as it is actually arising that becomes the condition for the vibration of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*). This, however, is without substance.
"Materiality born of kamma that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness ceases along with the seventeenth [consciousness] from that point onward;

that which arose at the moment of the rebirth-linking consciousness's presence ceases at the moment of arising of the eighteenth," and so forth—since it is precisely in the Aṭṭhakathā that the seventeen thought-moments are mentioned.
However, where only sixteen thought-moments are [mentioned],...
They appear; therein, the method is established by way of the moment suitable for being a condition for the occurrence of consciousness.

For even when material phenomena have exceeded a single moment of consciousness by their lower limit, they possess the capacity to come into the range [of cognition]. Enough of this over-elaboration. 10.
A "moment of a single consciousness" (*ekacittakkhaṇa*) is a moment like that of a single consciousness; those [phenomena] have passed that [moment], or these [moments] belong to it.

"Past" means those that have passed away from a single moment of consciousness. "Come into range" means that visible forms, sounds, and other sense objects, while remaining in their respective locations, come into the range of perception according to the corresponding mental application (*ābhoga*), having reached a state of being a field of experience through many groups of moments (*kalāpa*).

However, the others—namely, odors and so forth—become causes for the arising of consciousness only when they have attached themselves to the bases such as the nose; thus, they come into range even when occurring within a single group of moments.
For even when they have entered into a single momentary unit (*ekakkhaṇika-kalāpa*), the translucent elements (*pasāda*) serve as the support for consciousness;

however, they arise together with the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) which acts as the immediately preceding condition (*anantara-paccaya*) for the movement of the life-continuum. Others say: "They arise together with the adverting consciousness (*āvajjana*).
[The phrase] "the life-continuum has moved twice" refers to the movement of the life-continuum, which is defined as the cause for the arising of a dissimilar consciousness.
When the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) has proceeded twice over the very same object previously grasped:

for when an object strikes the five sensitive organs by way of being in a suitable place and condition, the continuity of the life-continuum—though about to be interrupted by the force of that impact on the sensitive organ—does not suddenly cease.
Rather, it is like a man running with speed who, even though he wishes to stop, continues for one or two steps before standing still; even so, [the life-continuum proceeds].

Having arisen twice, it ceases. In that context, the first consciousness arises as if shaking the continuity of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and is thus called "the shaking of the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgacalana);
the second arises in the manner of its cessation, and is therefore conventionally termed "the cutting off of the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgupaccheda).
However, here it is stated without distinction: "when the life-continuum has shaken twice."
But surely, when the sensitive organ (*pasāda*) is struck by a visible form or other object, it is logical that only what is supported by it should vibrate;
how then can this apply to the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), which is supported by the heart-base? Because they are bound together as a single continuity.

For example, when a fly is sitting on a pebble placed on one surface of a drum and that other surface is struck with a stick or the like, [the vibration] gradually reaches the drum-skin, the leather straps, and so forth.

Just as when a pebble is moved, flies take flight and depart, even so, when the sensitive matter (pasāda) is struck by visible form and so forth, the primary elements (mahābhūta) that support it are set in motion;

through their successive movement, the remaining material phenomena connected to them are also moved, and when the heart-base (hadayavatthu) is moved, the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) supported by it proceeds in the manner of a vibration. And it is said:
“When one place is struck, there is a shaking dependent on another;
this occurs because they are bound together—so speak by way of the simile of the pebble.
The “stream of the life-continuum” (bhavaṅgasota) refers to the flow of the life-continuum. “Adverting” means an application of attention as if saying, “What is this?”

"Performing": seeing directly before one's eyes. Now, is it not the case that, according to the statement "having seen a form with the eye," it is the eye-faculty alone that accomplishes the function of seeing, and not consciousness? This is not so;
for the eye is blind by nature and thus incapable of seeing forms. And if that [eye] were to see the form, then even one possessing a different consciousness [at that time] would likewise [see].

There would be the consequence of seeing forms [even when obstructed]. If consciousness performs that function in this way, then because consciousness is unimpeded, there would be seeing even of a form that is screened off.

Let there be seeing even of what is screened off—namely, that which is hidden by crystal and the like where there is no obstruction to light—but as for that which is screened off by a wall and the like, there is an obstruction to light. In that case:
Because of the absence of conditions, consciousness does not arise; thus, there is no apprehension of it by visual consciousness.

However, the intention here in the phrase "by the eye" is that it is by means of that door acting as the instrument (*karaṇa*). Alternatively, the action of depending is said to be bound to its support (*nissaya*), just as in the expression, "the beds are making a noise."
"Accepting" means as if receiving that very same form. "Examining" means as if investigating that very same form. "Determining" means as if clearly discerning that very same form.

"Having obtained conditions" means that by which conditions have been obtained through such means as appropriate attention (*yonisomanasikāra*). "Any impulsion whatsoever" is the connection [to the preceding]. During times close to fainting or death...
And because even six or five impulsions (javana) may occur, he said “for the most part.

“Following upon the impulsion” means that for a short time they follow after the impulsion, just as the current of a river follows a boat going against the stream. They have that impulsion’s object as their own object;
thus they are “tadārammaṇa,” by the elision of the middle term as in the case of “Brahmāsara” and so on. And these are the tadārammaṇas.

"And the results" refers to the results that have those [preceding consciousnesses] as their object. "As appropriate" means in accordance with the object, the impulsion (javana), and the sentient being.

However, he will explain the occurrence [of the result] himself later. "Falling back into the life-continuum" (bhavaṅgapāta) means, as it were, the falling back of the consciousness into the life-continuum because it does not proceed further by way of process-consciousness (vīthicitta);
what is meant is that it arises by way of the life-continuum itself. And here, regarding the occurrence of process-consciousness...
For the sake of easy comprehension, they cite the mango simile and others; here is the essence of that mango simile:
it is said that a certain man, having covered his head while sleeping at the foot of a flowering mango tree, woke up at the sound of a single mango fruit falling nearby.
He removed the cloth from his head, opened his eyes, and having seen it, he took hold of the fruit.
Having crushed it, smelled it, recognized its ripeness, eaten it, swallowed what was in his mouth along with the phlegm, he falls asleep once again right there.
In this context, the time of the man’s sleeping is like the moment of the *bhavaṅga* (life-continuum);
the time when the fruit strikes the sense-faculty is like the moment the object strikes the sensitivity; and the time when he is awakened by its sound is like the moment of adverting (*āvajjana*).
The moment of the arising of eye-consciousness is like the time of looking after having opened the eyes;
the moment of reception is like the time of grasping; the moment of investigation is like the time of chewing; the moment of determining is like the time of sniffing;
the moment of impulsion is like the time of enjoyment; the moment of registration is like the time of swallowing what has reached the mouth along with saliva; and again...
The period of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is like the time of falling asleep.
And what is illustrated by this simile? The function of the object is merely to strike the sensitive matter;
that of adverting (āvajjana) is merely to turn toward the object; that of eye-consciousness is merely seeing; and those of receiving (sampaṭicchana) and the rest are merely receiving and so forth.
Furthermore, the experience of the object’s flavor belongs specifically to the javana, while the registration consciousness experiences precisely that which was already experienced by it;
thus, the non-confusion of the functions of these phenomena with one another is illustrated. As the mind proceeds in this way, [it is said]:
"Having become what is called adverting, it occurs immediately after the life-continuum; you [the adverting] are one among seeing and the others..."

It should be understood that even when there is no directing agent (kāraka) who enjoins [the process] by means of the phrase "having sacrificed, immediately after adverting," etc., it proceeds solely through the determination of consciousness (*cittaniyāma*), just like the determination of season (*utu*),
seed (*bīja*), and so forth. At this point, the connection is that seventeen thought-moments (*cittakkhaṇa*) are fulfilled.
12. *Appahontātītaṃ* means that which has passed away while still being insufficient [to produce registration].

"There is no arising of registration" (*tadārammaṇuppādo*) means that, first of all, because the object has already ceased within the fourteen mind-moments [of the cognitive process], registration does not arise.

Indeed, within a single cognitive series (*ekavīthi*), some objects are present while others are past. Even in the case of those [processes] lasting fifteen mind-moments, [registration does not arise] from the moment the impulsion (*javana*) occurs.

However, because only a single moment of consciousness remains, and since that is insufficient for the arising of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) a second time, there is no arising of a second registration consciousness; thus, even the first does not arise.

For the arising of the registration consciousness is restricted to exactly two occasions throughout all instances in the enumeration of the occurrence of consciousness in the Canon, as it is stated: "The registrations are two."

Because it has come down in the *Cittavārāṇa*. As for what was stated in the *Paramatthavinicchaya*—“Once or twice that object, once the adverting and so forth”—that should be understood as having been stated according to the tradition of the Majjhima reciters (*majjhimabhāṇaka*).
For the doctrine of the Majjhima reciters does not accord with the canonical text (*pāḷi*) cited above; thus, [this view] is [rejected] in the *Sammohavinodanī*.

It is indeed excluded; therefore, because it is not intended by the Master himself, the arising of the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) has not been mentioned here either in this section or in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda*.
13. Even though the object remains for a lifespan of six mind-moments after the arising of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*), it is considered short-lived.

Due to extreme weakness, it does not serve as a condition for the arising of javana. For the intention is that when javana arises, it necessarily arises with a lifespan of only seven consciousness-moments;
thus he said, "even without the arising of javana. Furthermore, this suffix *-tvā* is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), meaning "due to the non-arising of javana as well.
Otherwise, the identity of the agent (*samānakattukatā*) for a subsequent action would not be obtained.
“Twice or thrice” means either twice or thrice. Some, however, say that the word “thrice” is used merely for the sake of euphony; but that is merely their own insistence.
For there is no lack of euphony in the statement, “The determining [consciousness] itself turns back twice,” nor is there anything to contradict its occurrence three times.

This statement is found in the *Aṭṭhakathā* and other commentaries. Having established this, the authors of the Sinhalese commentaries (*saṃvaṇṇanā*) in various places also describe it simply as "twice or thrice.
"The determining consciousness (*voṭṭhabbana*) alone turns back" means that the determining consciousness itself arises again and again.
However, until that [determining consciousness] is reached, there is no turning back of the mental process by halting midway within the eye-consciousness and the others.
However, Master Ānanda, because it is stated here that "adverting is a condition for wholesome and unwholesome aggregates by way of proximity-condition" (*anantara-paccaya*),
and because there is no difference in meaning between determining (*voṭṭhabbana*) and adverting,
when [a consciousness] arises, determining is a condition for the sense-sphere wholesome, unwholesome, and functional impulsion-moments (*javana*).
It indicates that [the javana] would proceed only by way of being an immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*) and not otherwise;

thus, during times such as fainting, because its momentum has become weak, the limited object must be determined for the completion of the javana, rather than through the occurrence of the determining consciousness (*voṭṭhapana*) two or three times.
Even though it is explained in this way, nevertheless, the three-rooted resultant states (*tihetuka-vipāka*) are indeed stated to function as immediate conditions.
Since the states occurring by way of the death-moment of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) do not become the proximity condition for anyone,
it cannot be said that the determining consciousness (voṭṭhapana) is likewise not a proximity condition for the wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, due to a deficiency of conditions;
therefore, it is precisely according to the method handed down in the Commentaries that the limited object (parittārammaṇa) is here determined.

14. "There is no arising of process-thoughts" (natthi vīthicittuppādo): because even for one whose life-span lasts for seven thought-moments at the maximum, there is no occurrence of process-thoughts due to their being insufficient for the registration-thought (voṭṭhabbana) to arise two or three times;

the intention is that there is only a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga). The phrase "there is no arising of process-thoughts" is used to show the result of the restriction "only the movement of the life-continuum."
Thus it was said. Others, however, point out that the purpose of the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is to show that "there is no cutting off of the life-continuum" (*bhavaṅgupaccheda*).

But that is already established by the very statement regarding the absence of the arising of process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*); for it is only when there is the arising of a process-thought that the life-continuum is cut off.
Furthermore, because the cutting off of the life-continuum was not mentioned separately below, it is stated here without distinction.
15. Because there is an absolute absence of the arising of process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*), the final section is described as the "vain section" (*moghavāra*).
Elsewhere, however, even the second and third sections are called "vain sections" because they are devoid of registration and impulsion (*tadārammaṇa-javana*).

"Becoming objects" (*ārammaṇabhūtā*) means becoming sense-fields (*visaya*) and becoming conditions (*paccaya*); for even a condition is called an "object," as in: "Māra shall not find [an opportunity]."

...as in the passages beginning with "Māra will not find an opportunity" and "an objective support. For this very reason, it is established here that the occurrence of objects constitutes the objective support for the proclamation of the "Futile Section" (moghavāra).
Indeed, an extremely limited objective support serves as the condition for the proclamation of the Futile Section.

Otherwise, since the movement of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) occurs only within its own respective domain, [if the object were not limited], in the case of an extremely limited objective support for the final section—
If there were no occurrence [of consciousness], the statement that "they are the objects of the four modes" would be difficult to justify.

16. In the five doors, the process-minds arise as appropriate according to each respective door, according to their respective conditions, and according to their respective objects and so forth—namely, by way of adverting, seeing (or hearing, etc.), receiving, investigating, determining, javana, and registration.

Without distinction, there are seven types. Alternatively, there are fourteen types of consciousnesses arising according to the separate emergence of each thought-moment, by way of the five beginning with adverting (āvajjana), the seven impulsions (javana), and the two registration (tadārammaṇa) moments.
In detail, however, there are fifty-four, because all these sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) consciousnesses arise therein as far as possible.
"Herein" means in the summary of the occurrence of objects.
The commentary on the cognitive process of the five doors is finished.
The cognitive process of the mind door.
Commentary on the Minor Impulsion Series (Parittajavana):
Since objects of the mind-door consciousnesses exist even in the past and future, it is impossible to define their range of objects by means of categories such as "very great" and so forth.
Therefore, this is restricted solely by way of being "clear" (vibhūta) or "unclear" (avibhūta), and thus the passage beginning with "If the object is clear" was stated.

19. "Therein" means in the mind-door (*manodvāra*). There are forty-one [types of consciousness] because thirteen types of consciousness—namely, the five door-advertences, the two sets of fivefold sense-cognitions, and the three mind-elements (*manodhātu*)—do not occur therein.
The commentary on the section on limited impulsions (*parittajavana*) is concluded.
Now follows the commentary on the section on absorption impulsions (*appanājavana*).
20. There is no distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest, because absorption occurs only at the time when the object is manifest.
21. In this context, the connection is that any given impulsion among the twenty-six sublime and supramundane impulsion-javanas enters the cognitive process of absorption (*appanā-vīthi*).
The construction is that they arise and cease in succession, being designated as preparation (*parikamma*), access (*upacāra*), conformity (*anuloma*), and change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*).
For the first consciousness is "preliminary work" (*parikamma*) because it serves as the preparation for absorption and acts as the agent of reflection.
The second is "access" (*upacāra*) because it moves in the vicinity [of absorption]. For even that which does not occur too close nor too far away is called "moving in the vicinity";

or alternatively, it is "access" because it proceeds having approached absorption. The third is so called because it is favorable both to the preliminary works in its prior stage and to the absorption that follows.

In forward order: it is called *gotrabhū* because it overcomes the limited lineage (*parittagotta*) and the worldling lineage (*puthujjanagotta*), and because it develops and expands the exalted lineage (*mahaggatagotta*) and the supramundane lineage (*lokuttaragotta*).

These four names are obtained in their entirety during its fourfold occurrence; however, during its threefold occurrence, it is known only by the names *access*, *conformity*, and *change-of-lineage*.

[They] are obtained. In the commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*), however, the names "preliminary work" (*parikamma*) and so forth are stated for the first three [stages], or for two [stages] without distinction;
the intention is that the fifth or the fourth [stage] should arise four times or three times respectively, according to the absorption (*appanā*) to be attained.
The word "four times" is used to show the number of occurrences obtainable for each name, such as "preliminary work," without exception.
It was stated at the beginning [as "the fourth"], but at the conclusion it is stated as "or the fifth" according to the sequence of counting.

"As appropriate" means in accordance with whether one possesses quick or sluggish direct knowledge (*abhiññā*). For one of quick direct knowledge, the fourth absorption consciousness (*appanā-citta*) arises immediately after three occurrences of sense-sphere javanas (*javana*).
For one of sluggish direct knowledge, it arises immediately after four occurrences of javanas.
The fifth [moment] arises as absorption (appanā). However, because conformity (anuloma) cannot produce change-of-lineage (gotrabhu) unless it has been practiced repeatedly,
and because even if it has been practiced, the sixth and seventh moments— due to their proximity to the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)—
cannot establish themselves through absorption, like a person standing near a precipice, therefore [absorption occurs] after the fourth and before the fifth.

It should be understood that absorption (appanā) does not occur. "In accordance with the initial resolution" means in conformity with the directing of the mind toward the development of serenity and insight corresponding to the form, formless, or supramundane paths and fruits;

thus, the path of absorption is called the "absorption-path" (appanāvīthi). When it is stated only that "after that, there is merely a lapse into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)," this refers to the fourth or fifth moment after the descent into absorption:
after that, there is merely a lapse into the life-continuum, and not a fruition-consciousness immediately following the path.
Furthermore, since the jhāna-resultant consciousnesses might repeatedly seize [the object] during the cognitive process of attainment (*samāpatti-vīthi*), it is stated again:

"At the conclusion of absorption" (*appanā-vasāne*). It is said that those belonging to other schools describe the occurrence of even sense-sphere javanas two or three times after the first absorption in order to complete the seventh javana; this is stated for the purpose of refuting their view.
“Or falling back into the life-continuum (bhavaṅga)” is stated with this restriction.
22. *Tattha* means: among those eight sense-sphere javanas associated with knowledge, and among those twenty-six sublime and supramundane javanas.
Or, *tattha* means: in that section on absorption (*appanā*). *Somanassasahagatajavanānantaraṃ* means: immediately after a javana accompanied by joy.
Immediately after the four wholesome functional javanas.

"Accompanied by joy" means that they are accompanied by joy by way of the fourfold jhāna and the path and fruit of those such as the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*), but not accompanied by equanimity;
for it is not stated that different feelings can serve as mutual repetition-conditions (*āsevanapaccaya*). They are "to be expected."
It is said that [these] are to be praised and are to be desired. "There too" means even in that single impulsion-moment of a single feeling.
Following a wholesome impulsion associated with the fourfold knowledge, a wholesome impulsion occurs; it is not a functional (kiriyā) impulsion, because that arises in a different continuum.
And it follows the three lower fruits; this is the intended meaning regarding the cognitive process of attainment (samāpatti-vīthi).

23. Following the two types of wholesome consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with three roots (*somanassasahagata-tihetuka-kusala*), there are thirty-two [impulsions] by way of the mundane and supramundane fourfold jhānas, excluding the fruition of the highest fruit (*aggaphala-vipāka*) and the functional (*kiriya*).
Following the two types of wholesome consciousness accompanied by equanimity and associated with three roots, there are likewise twelve [impulsions] by way of the five jhānas.

Following the two types of functional consciousness accompanied by joy and associated with three roots, there are [impulsions] by way of the fourfold functional jhānas and the fourfold fruition of the highest fruit.
By way of the eight [types of consciousness] associated with equanimity, and beyond the two types associated with the three roots,

there arise six absorption attainments (appanā) by way of the fivefold functional consciousnesses of the fine-material and immaterial spheres accompanied by equanimity, as well as by way of the fruit of Arahantship (aggaphala).
"In this context" refers to the section on the compendium of cognitive processes (vīthisaṅgaha).
The commentary on the section on absorption-javana is finished.
The commentary on the cognitive series of the mind-door is finished.
The commentary on the section on absorption-javana is finished.
Commentary on the Rule for the Registration [Resultant] (Tadārammaṇa-niyamavaṇṇanā): 25. “In all cases” means in both the five doors and the mind door.

26. “Desirable” refers to the desirable and the neutral. For an extremely desirable object will be mentioned separately. The wholesome resultants are the five sense-consciousnesses, the receiving consciousness, the investigating consciousness, and the registration consciousness.

Regarding the connection: since the investigating and registration consciousnesses associated with the desirable and the neutral are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) alone, he says, "But those associated with the extremely desirable are accompanied by joy (*somanassa*) alone.
For when a resultant [consciousness] proceeds by the power of karma, there is no grasping through conceptualization—as if seeing the reflection of a face in a mirror;
therefore, its association with feeling occurs exactly according to the object, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome.

However, because it occurs within mental continua where the perversions have not been abandoned, there is a grasping of even what is extremely desirable as having the aspects of the desirable, the neutral, and the undesirable;
and of even what is undesirable as having the aspects of the desirable, the desirable-neutral, and the neutral.

For instance, even regarding extremely desirable objects such as the Buddha and so forth, those lacking faith and others experience a javana of equanimity; likewise, heretics and others experience a javana of displeasure (domanassa); and those of deep disposition and so forth [experience other modes].
When the object is repulsive, there is a javana of equanimity; however, for dogs and the like, there is a javana of joy in that same situation.

As for the resultant consciousnesses occurring in the preceding and succeeding moments, they arise according to their respective physical bases. Furthermore, this applies to dogs and others who feel pleasure at the sight of impurity.
As for the reason why eye-consciousness and the rest are accompanied by equanimity even when they occur toward extremely desirable or undesirable objects, that has already been explained below.

27. *Tatthāpi* means "even in those [moments] having that as their object. *Somanassasahagatakiriyajavanāvasāne* means "at the conclusion of functional javanas accompanied by joy," which refers to the conclusion of the fivefold functional javanas accompanied by pleasure, whether they are with-root (*sahetuka*) or without-root (*ahetuka*).

It is said "at the conclusion of functional javanas accompanied by joy" and so forth because, for those whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*), even functional javanas proceed only according to the object due to the absence of perversion of mind (*cittavipallāsa*).
However, some teachers [cite] the *Paṭṭhāna*: "In wholesome and unwholesome..."

They say: "When [the javana] has ceased, the registration (tadārammaṇa) arises; thus, since registration is stated to occur only immediately after wholesome or unwholesome [javana], there is no arising of registration immediately after functional (kiriya) javana. To this it is replied:

If registration were said to occur even immediately after the indeterminate (abyākata), then it would also occur immediately after the determining consciousness (voṭṭhabbana) when the object is limited (paritta).

Regarding the phrase "they might imagine its occurrence," it is said that the "registration" (tadārammaṇa) does not follow immediately after the functional impulsion (kiriya-javana) because it is not mentioned there, not because it is impossible to obtain.
For even when something is obtainable, it is seen that it is not mentioned in certain contexts for some specific purpose;
just as, for example, the heart-base (hadayavatthu), though obtainable in the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, was not mentioned in order to avoid complicating the classification of the teaching.

28. [The jhāna factors] are accompanied by mental distress (*domanassa*)... pe ...and are accompanied only by equanimity (*upekkhā*), not by joy (*somanassa*), because they are mutually contradictory in nature.
For this very reason, in the *Paṭṭhāna*, joy is not mentioned immediately after mental distress, nor is mental distress mentioned immediately after that [joy].
Thus, it is said: "A state associated with pleasant feeling..."
"Conditioned by a state associated [with feeling] through the relation of proximity," and so forth;

thus, states associated with pleasant and painful feelings are stated in two pairs of sections as having the nature of the proximity-condition for those states associated with their own respective identical feelings and for those associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Those associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling...
However, because states associated with a single feeling and those associated with the other two feelings serve as immediate conditions (*anantarapaccaya*) for one another within the three sections,
exactly seven sections on the immediate condition are stated for the triad of feelings.
Furthermore, if joy were to arise immediately after grief, or grief immediately after joy, then [states] associated with pleasant and painful feelings would also [be included].
If one were to increase [the sequence] by two rounds each time through the condition of immediate succession (*anantarapaccaya*), there would be nine rounds to be stated;

however, they are not stated in that way. Therefore, there is no arising of those [mental states] immediately after one another. And here, by the phrase "at the conclusion of functional javanas accompanied by joy," etc., this rule is also authorized.
“Limited wholesome, faultless, meritorious, and functional;
one among these five has that as its object, toward those who are happy, as appropriate.
Also, the ‘unwholesome,’ ‘desireless,’ and ‘beautiful’ [realms], as well as the functional, are associated with equanimity.”
“In the case of the equanimous [javana], it has that as its object;

in the six [others], it is one or the other accordingly. This rule regarding the registration (tadārammaṇa) following the impulsion (javana) is indeed invariable. However, the application of the method beginning with “From an impulsion associated with knowledge, there is a registration associated with knowledge,” and so forth, is not absolute.
For generally, in the case of one who is habituated to unwholesome impulsions, [registration may occur] occasionally even from wholesome impulsions.

When unwholesome impulsions (javana) arise, or when one who has cultivated wholesome impulsions occasionally experiences unwholesome impulsions, due to the habituation of proceeding immediately after the unwholesome, there occurs a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) lacking roots even following a three-rooted impulsion.

Likewise, due to the habituation of proceeding immediately after the wholesome, there may also occur a three-rooted registration consciousness following an unwholesome impulsion. This is because of the karma that produces rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi).
However, there is no need to speak of the occurrence of registration (tadārammaṇa) by means of any other kamma. And so it is said in the Paṭṭhāna:
"When they practice insight into the rootless aggregates as impermanent, suffering, and non-self, when the wholesome or unwholesome [kamma] has ceased, a rootless resultant arises as registration;
when the wholesome or unwholesome [kamma] has ceased, a root-possessing resultant arises as registration."

Therefore, since they are accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*) alone at the conclusion of the impulsion (*javana*) of displeasure (*domanassa*), the connection is that the investigation (*santīraṇa*) accompanied by equanimity arises at the conclusion of the impulsion accompanied by displeasure.
By the phrase "of one whose rebirth-linking was accompanied by joy" (*somanassapaṭisandhikassa*), the absence of a lapse into the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is already indicated;
because there is no joy immediately following displeasure, that [lapse] is not mentioned, and instead only the absence of an object-representation (*tadārammaṇa*) is stated.
Reflecting on this, he said: "If there is no occurrence of that object.

This is because, even for a heretic or similar person who has a rebirth-linking consciousness accompanied by joy, when their mind is repelled by an extremely desirable object such as the Buddha, and a mental process (javana) accompanied by displeasure (domanassa) has occurred according to the method already stated, neither a registration consciousness (tadārammaṇa) accompanied by joy nor one accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā) arises with respect to that extremely desirable object; or else, due to some unsuitable condition.

With reference to a mundane jhāna that has been lost, for one who generates regret, thinking, "A sublime state has been lost by me," if there is a javana of mental grief (*domanassa*), then—since there is no registration (*tadārammaṇa*) when the object belongs to the sense-sphere (*akāmāvacara*)—the intention is that there is no possibility for the arising of registration at that time.

"Previously cultivated" means cultivated in the past; it refers to what was mostly grasped in that previous existence. This refers to the investigating consciousness (*santīraṇa*) accompanied by equanimity.
A faultless consciousness also arises, as intended by the fruition-consciousness of one emerging from cessation. As it has been said:
"How can it be that a faultless consciousness does not exist? This is not accepted [as a fact].
There is no restriction [that it must be faulty] without a fault, because the fruition is seen after cessation."
By what function does this consciousness proceed? First, it does not proceed by the function of registration (*tadārammaṇa*), because it does not grasp the object of the impulsion (*javana*).
Nor does it proceed by the function of investigation (*santīraṇa*), because it does not proceed by way of investigating that which has already been received.

It cannot be said to exist in the moments of rebirth-linking or death. Therefore, by process of elimination, since it serves as a factor of existence (*bhava*), it proceeds by the function of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*).
This would be appropriate. For this very point was indeed shown by the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla as well.

As for what he will say regarding the identity of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) in terms of both their intrinsic nature (dhamma) and their object (ārammaṇa), that should be understood as referring to the majority of cases;
for there is no dissimilarity between rebirth-linking and the life-continuum except in this one instance. "Immediately after that" means immediately after that [consciousness] of its own...
"Immediately after" means having made it uninterrupted; that is to say, immediately following that. 29.

Regarding the passage "They desire the sense-sphere... and so forth: here, they desire the object (*tadārammaṇa*) only at the conclusion of the sense-sphere impulsion (*javana*), because [that rebirth-linking consciousness] is produced by karma rooted in craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*).
For it is not produced by karma caused by craving for sense-pleasures, since it does not possess that same nature (*ataṃsabhāva*).
It arises immediately after a javana pertaining to the fine-material sphere, the immaterial sphere, or the supramundane. What is the reason?

Because it is not a producer [of rebirth], and because it lacks the quality of being similar to a producer. For just as a child who wishes to go out from a house goes out by taking hold of a producer—such as his father—or something similar to him like a finger, but not someone else such as a royal official, so too the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) proceeding elsewhere than toward the object of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) [does not produce rebirth].
The wholesome or unwholesome consciousness of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) that acts as the producer, or a similar functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*) of the sense-sphere, follows upon it;
however, dissimilar impulsions of the sublime (*mahaggata*) or supramundane (*lokuttara*) realms do not.

Likewise, they maintain that only sentient beings of the sense-sphere can have that [sublime state] as an object (*tadārammaṇa*), because for the Brahmās there is an absence of the seed of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhibīja*) in the sense-sphere, which would serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for such an object.
Likewise, they desire only those phenomena belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara) when these serve as objects;

not others, because of a lack of familiarity with them. For just as that child, even while following his father or someone like him, does not follow when he goes to an unfamiliar place such as a forest, but follows only in familiar places such as the courtyard in front of the house, so too this [consciousness] does not take as its object anything unfamiliar, such as the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).

It does not follow after that which has arisen by way of having something as its object. Furthermore, because it is produced by kamma dependent on craving for sense-pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*), this meaning already stated—that it occurs only toward limited phenomena (*parittadhamma*) which are objects of craving for sense-pleasures—is established. And there are these verses here:
“The impulsion (*javana*) follows after that which produces [the rebirth-linking] or that which is similar to it;”
But there is no other object for that [consciousness], like the play of a young child.
Indeed, even for Brahmā, this [rebirth-linking] lacks a seed;
for the seed of rebirth-consciousness is designated as belonging to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
“In a familiar place alone, like a child, it follows after that [object] and not elsewhere, or rather, it does so by way of craving.
But has it not been stated that “because of the absence of the seed of rebirth-linking in the sense-sphere”?

And if that were so, would it not follow that eye-consciousness and the rest would also be absent? It does not follow, because of the power of the functioning of the faculties and because of the restriction of consciousness according to the distinction between doors and cognitive processes.
The commentary on the rule for the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) is finished.
**Commentary on the Rule for the Impulsion Consciousness** 32.

"In its slow occurrence" means that at the time near death, because the physical basis is weak, the momentum has become slackened; thus, it occurs slowly. "At the time of death, etc."—by the word "etc.," the time of fainting is included.

33. Regarding the Blessed One’s... [they] say: at times such as the Twin Miracle, for the purpose of emitting masses of water and masses of fire and so forth, the Blessed One enters the respective preliminary absorptions (pādakajjhāna), emerges from them, and adverts to each of the factors of those absorptions individually.

Because he has reached the pinnacle of mastery over adverting (āvajjanavasitā), his mental application (cittābhinīhāra) is intent solely on adverting; thus, the objects are the factors of the absorption as they were adverted to.
The commentators state that four or five javana-cognitions of reflection arise.
And the phrase "of the Blessed One" is merely an illustration, for even others such as the Dhamma-Senāpati (Sāriputta) and so forth have javanas that do not reach completion during such urgent times.
Thus it is said in the commentary: "And this [state] has reached its ultimate limit..."
"The mastery [of the Blessed One] was at the time of the Twin Miracle, or at other such times.
Furthermore, the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla has stated that "four or five" should be understood according to whether one's faculties are sharp or dull;
therefore, it appears appropriate to take it as four for the Blessed One and five for others.
34. "For a beginner" means for one who has just begun the preliminary work (*yogakamma*). The first absorption (*appanā*) that arises is the "first attainment" (*paṭhamakappanā*).
Since there might be a doubt that the term "first attainment" could also apply to the impulsions of direct knowledge (*abhiññājavana*), he said "at all times";
this means that both at the time of initial arising and when mastery has been gained, the five impulsions of direct knowledge impel only once.
35. "Arising of the path" (*magguppāda*) refers to the arising of the path itself. "As appropriate" (*yathārahaṃ*) means according to the path that has arisen, whether it be the fifth or the fourth.

For in a single adverting cognitive process (*ekāvajjana-vīthi*), there are at most seven impulsion moments; thus, after a path that has arisen as the fourth, there are three fruition consciousnesses (*phala-citta*), and after a path that has arisen as the fifth, there are two.

36. "At the time of the attainment of cessation" means prior to the actual cessation. "The impulsion of the fourth formless realm" refers to any one of the wholesome functional (kiriya) impulsions pertaining to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Only non-returners (anāgāmi) whose taints are exhausted attain the attainment of cessation, not stream-enterers (sotāpanna) or once-returners (sakadāgāmi);
thus it is said, "either the fruit of non-returning or the fruit of arahantship. This is a change of grammatical case (vibhattivipallāsa).
And here it should be understood as "either in the fruit of non-returning or in the fruit of arahantship. Therefore he said, "when [the consciousness] has ceased.

"As appropriate" means according to the suitability of each respective individual. 38. "In every case in the cognitive process of attainment" refers to the entire cognitive process of meditative absorption (jhāna-samāpatti) and the cognitive process of the fruition-attainment (phala-samāpatti).

39. At the maximum limit, limited impulsion consciousnesses are considered to occur seven times. However, path-consciousness and direct-knowledge consciousnesses are considered to occur only once, a single time.

As for the remaining sublime and supramundane impulsion consciousnesses—excluding those associated with direct knowledge—they may occur many times within the cognitive process of meditative attainment (*samāpatti-vīthi*), as they can persist even throughout day and night. By the word "api" (also/even), mundane jhānas are included in the first eon.

The two final fruits [the non-returner and the arahant] arise once immediately after cessation, while the fruition-consciousnesses arise two or three times immediately after the path; thus they are combined.
The commentary on the determination of impulsions is finished. Now begins the commentary on the classification of individuals (*puggalabhedavaṇṇanā*).

40. Now, in order to demonstrate the delimitation of the cognitive processes (*vīthicitta*) that arise in twelve types of persons—namely, four types of worldlings (*puthujjana*), distinguished by being double-rooted, rootless, belonging to the woeful states, or triple-rooted;

and eight types of noble ones (*ariya*), distinguished by being on the path or established in the fruit—the author first states "of those who are double-rooted and rootless," etc., in order to show the types of consciousness that must be excluded for them.
"Two-rooted" (dvihetuka) means that these [consciousnesses] possess two roots by way of the greed and hatred accompanying rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*).

"Rootless" (*ahetuka*) is due to the absence of such roots. The letter *m* is used for euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). Absorption (*appanā*) and impulsion (*javana*) are not obtained because of the presence of the obstruction of fruition (*vipākāvaraṇa*).
Indeed, rebirth-linking with two roots or no roots is called the "obstruction of fruition. Precisely because of the absence of absorption and impulsion, [there is no attainment of] Arahantship.
It is said that functional javanas do not occur [in this state].

Regarding the statement in the text, “A root-cause-accompanied bhavaṅga is a condition for a root-cause-free bhavaṅga by way of proximity-condition,” it follows from this that even for those [beings] without root-causes, a two-root-cause tadārammaṇa can arise through various kamma;
however, for those with two root-causes, this need not even be mentioned.
There is none. However, because of the dullness of the root-linking (mūlasandhi), there is no three-rooted registration (tadārammaṇa) for either of the two;

thus he said, "likewise, the resultants associated with knowledge. But since the Elder Ācariya Jotipāla stated "the bhavaṅga with roots" without qualification, one might assume that even for those [resultants] without roots, there is a three-rooted registration; therefore, the statement here regarding the absence of resultants associated with knowledge [is made to clarify this].
It was said jokingly, "He alone should be asked who is its maker";
yet even though it was spoken as a joke, it stands like a statement made for the sake of gaining knowledge after having questioned the teacher.
For the reason for this has been stated by the teacher himself in the *Paramatthavinicchaya*:
“Knowledge does not arise because of the dullness of the root-junction.

However, others explain that just as for those with no roots (ahetuka), there is a resultant state with roots having that same object (sahetu-tadārammaṇa), so too for those with two roots (dvihetuka), there is a resultant state with three roots having that same object (tihetu-tadārammaṇa).
And in accordance with their view, here too the exclusion of the knowledge-associated resultant applies only to those with no roots.

They say this with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). However, because there is no authoritative textual passage (*pamāṇapāṭha*) on that point, the Teacher, after stating the reason why there is an absence of resultant consciousness associated with knowledge for both [types of beings], has shown the delimitation of the mind in exactly the same way for both;
therefore, their statement should be accepted after careful investigation. And here, in relation to those who are rootless (*ahetuka*), the term "in a happy destination" (*sugatiyam*) is used.
That statement, however, is intended to show that, in actual fact, the two-rooted resultant states permitted [by the Buddha] arise in those very same circumstances.
Therefore he said, "But in the miserable destinies," and so forth.

43. "Among those with three roots" refers to the nine types of persons, such as worldlings (puthujjana) and others, who possess three roots by way of greed, hatred, and delusion accompanying rebirth-linking consciousness.

45. Regarding "views" … pe … "of those in training" (*sekkhā*): because they have not yet fulfilled the training and possess the nature of one who is still training, they are given the name "those in training.
These refer to individuals who are stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmī*).

Since personality-belief (*sakkāyadiṭṭhi*) and doubt (*vicikicchā*) have been abandoned by the first path itself, neither the impulsion moments associated with them, nor—by virtue of the word "and"—the functional impulsion moments unique to those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), are found [among them].
46. "And the impulsion-moments of repulsion" refers both to the impulsion-moments of mental grief (*domanassa*) and to functional impulsion-moments associated with views and accompanied by doubt.
47. Regarding the phrase "supramundane... arise": because the four paths exist for only a single moment of consciousness, they cannot occur simultaneously in different individuals;
furthermore, because lower and lower attainments have not been mastered prior to the higher ones, and because [the qualities of] successive individuals [are distinct].

Because the defilements of kamma have not been eradicated and because [the defilements] have been subsided in stream-enterers—unlike ordinary worldlings—and because they have attained the state of distinct individuals such as stream-enterers, all eight supramundane javanas arise only for noble ones (ariyas) at their respective stages of the path and fruit. 48.
Now, excluding the javanas that have been specifically prohibited for each of these individuals, the javanas obtainable by way of elimination are as follows:
To show them collectively, the passage beginning with "of the Asekhas" was stated.

Because they fulfill the threefold training, for the Asekhas—the Khīṇāsavas—there are twenty-three [types of consciousness] remaining after excluding forty-five, by way of the thirty-three types of wholesome and unwholesome [consciousness], the three lower fruits, and the nine supramundane resultant states that are outside the cognitive process (vīthimutta). These consist of the twenty-three sense-sphere resultants, the twenty functional states, and the fruit of Arahatship.

Forty-four types of process-consciousness (vīthicitta) may arise according to their availability; they are enumerated here with reference to those established in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava).

Excluding thirty-three—namely, the eighteen functional javanas (kiriyajavana), the five associated with views and doubt, and the sublime resultants (mahaggatavipāka) of the four paths and fruits—one should understand them by way of the twenty-three sense-sphere resultants, the two types of adverting consciousness (āvajjana), the twenty-one wholesome states, the seven unwholesome states, and the three lower fruits.
One should enumerate fifty-six types of process-thoughts (*vīthicitta*) according to their occurrence without distinction. However, with respect to specific distinctions:

for *Sotāpannas* and *Sakadāgāmis*, there are fifty-one; for *Anāgāmis*, forty-nine; and for the remaining four types of worldlings (*puthujjana*), there are thirty-five—excluding the eighteen functional impulsions (*kiriyajavana*), all supramundane states, and sublime-resultant states—and these consist of the remaining sense-sphere resultants, the two types of adverting consciousness, and mundane wholesome and unwholesome states.

The fifty-four process-thoughts (vīthicitta) should be enumerated according to their occurrence without distinction. However, when distinguished: for those with three-rooted (tihetuka) consciousness, exactly fifty-four are obtained;

for those with two-rooted (dvihetuka) and rootless (ahetuka) consciousness, forty-one are obtained, excluding the knowledge-associated (ñāṇasampayutta), the resultant (vipāka), the absorption (appanā), and the impulsion (javana);

and for those destined for the states of deprivation (āpāyika), it should be understood that there are thirty-seven process-thoughts, which are the same as those [for the two-rooted] excluding the two-rooted resultant.
The classification of persons (*puggalabheda*) refers to the differentiation in the occurrence of consciousness according to types of individuals.
The commentary on the classification of persons is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the analysis of the planes (*bhūmivibhāga*).

49. All process-thoughts (vīthicitta) are found in all six doors because they can arise therein for all individuals. “Accordingly” means in accordance with each respective existence (bhava) and in accordance with each respective individual.

52. By the words beginning with “those,” the rejection of nose-consciousness and the others will follow; thus, in the fine-material-sphere plane (rūpāvacarabhūmi), only the impulsion (javana) and registration (tadārammaṇa) moments involving resistance (paṭigha) are rejected. “In all places” means in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava), the fine-material-sphere existence (rūpabhava), and the immaterial-sphere existence (arūpabhava).

54. In the sensual existence (*kāmabhava*), there are eighty types of process-consciousness (*vīthicitta*), excluding those that arise outside of a cognitive process (*vīthimutta*) as appropriate. In the fine-material existence (*rūpabhava*), there are sixty-four types, excluding twenty-five—namely, the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion (*paṭigha*), the eight types of consciousness with that same object (*tadārammaṇa*), and the sixfold group of nose-door and other sense-door consciousnesses (*ghānādiviññāṇachakka*)—and including the rest, which consist of two types of adverting (*āvajjana*), nine rootless resultants (*ahetuka-vipāka*), fifty-five impulsions (*javana*), and the mental element (*manodhātu*).

In the immaterial existence (*arūpabhava*), there are twenty-three types, consisting of the twenty-three sensual-sphere resultants, the first fifteen paths (*magga*), the two types of consciousness accompanied by aversion, the immaterial-sphere resultants, the functional mental element (*kiriyamanodhātu*), and the smile-producing consciousness (*hasana*).

Excluding forty-seven, the remaining twenty-six consciousnesses are obtained and found as forty-two types of consciousness by way of the limited (paritta) javanas, the eight formless-sphere (āruppa) javanas, the seven supramundane (lokuttara) javanas, and the mind-door adverting consciousness (manodvārāvajjana). However,

some maintain that because there is an absence of undesirable objects in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), unwholesome-resultant (akusalavipāka) consciousness can only arise for those Brahmās who have actually come here [from the lower realms].
They say that by excluding those [sixteen], there are only sixty process-thoughts in the fine-material realm (rūpabhava), together with the five types of limited-resultant consciousness.
However, in this context, it is impossible to maintain that undesirable objects are non-existent even for those who remain there while looking upon this world;
therefore, sixty-four are stated there along with those [sixteen]. And having done so, it was said:

In the *Dhammānusāraṇī*: "When the Brahmās take as their object an undesirable object belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), then even in a happy destination (*sugati*), the arising of unwholesome-resultant eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, mind-element, and investigating consciousness is possible.
This is the analysis by way of plane; it is the analysis of planes.
The commentary on the analysis of the stages (*bhūmivibhāga*) is finished. 55.
*Yathāsambhavam*: according to what is possible, that is, in accordance with the possibilities at each respective door or in each respective state of existence. *Yāvatāyukam*:

for the duration of the life-span, beginning from the mental process (*cittavīthi*) associated with the mind-door that occurs after rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) due to a desire for existence, and ending with the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*).

The intention is that non-perception (asati) occurs either at the end of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) that had been proceeding prior to that, or as an uninterrupted [state] during the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
Thus ends the commentary on the Chapter on the Cognitive Process (Vīthipariccheda) in the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, titled the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
5. Commentary on the Section on Process-Freed Consciousness 1.
Having thus far shown the compendium of cognitive processes (*vīthisaṅgaha*), he now begins to show the compendium of process-freed consciousness (*vīthimuttasaṅgaha*), saying:
"By way of process-consciousness alone," and so forth. Thus, by the method already stated, regarding the occurrence by way of process-consciousness starting from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*):

In the latter part, the compendium of occurrence (*pavattisaṅgaha*)—which concludes with death (*cuti*)—has been proclaimed. Now, immediately following that, the connection (*sandhi*) at the time of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is discussed;
the construction is that because of its proximity, the compendium of occurrence is stated by means of that very [term for rebirth-linking], which includes the time of death as well.
Commentary on the Fourfold Soil (*Bhūmicatukka-vaṇṇanā*).

3. It is called an *apāya* (state of loss) because it is for the most part devoid of what is considered merit. That very thing becomes the ground (*bhūmi*) where beings exist, hence it is an *apāyabhūmi*.
Because it is a beautiful place to go to and to be reborn in, owing to its being the basis for manifold success, it is a *sugati* (happy destiny).
A happy destiny accompanied by craving for sense-pleasures is a *kāmasugati*; that very thing is the ground, hence it is a *kāmasugatibhūmi*. The same applies to the remaining [categories].

4. It is called *niraya* because beings have gone forth (*niggata*) from it toward suffering (*ayata*). They are called *tiracchāna* because they are bent across (*tiro añcita*); the womb of those is the "animal womb" (*tiracchānayoni*).

It is called a "womb" (*yoni*) because by means of it, beings—though not actually mixed—are as if mixed due to their commonality of birth. In its actual sense, however, it is a specific mode of the manifestation of the aggregates (*khandha*).

They are called *peta* because they have gone (*itā*) or departed (*gatā*) toward what is preeminent in suffering (*sukha*); this refers to those divided into the types such as the *nijjhāmataṇhika*, etc.

The realm of the *petas* is the *pettivisaya*. Here, however, by the mention of the animal womb (*tiracchānayoni*) and the *pettivisaya*, only the aggregates (*khandha*) themselves are intended, because they lack such a delimited physical space.

Alternatively, "space" should also be understood in terms of the specific locations—such as forests, mountain foothills, and so forth—where they dwell in a fixed habitation. They do not rejoice through sovereignty, play, or similar pleasures.
They are called *asura* because they do not shine (*na dibbanti*), thus "petāsura" (hungry ghost-asuras).

Others, however, are *asura* because they are the opposite of *sura* (gods), yet here only the "petāsura" are intended to be included, since the inclusion of the others is desired among the Tāvatiṃsa gods. For it has been stated by the Teacher:
"Among the Tāvatiṃsa gods, the Vepacitti-asuras have gone."
5. "Humans" (*manussa*) are those in whom the mind is predominant due to qualities such as mindfulness, wisdom, the state of being celibate, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
For even the Buddhas and others, who have attained supreme mindfulness, equanimity, and so forth, are indeed human beings.
Furthermore, among these, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa are humans in the primary sense. Together with the inhabitants of the minor islands, they share a commonality of form and other characteristics.
Those dwelling on the other great continents are also called "human beings" (*manussa*). However, worldly people say, "Human beings are the offspring and sons of Manu, the first Kṣatriya.
Here, "human beings" refers to the land that serves as the dwelling place for human beings. The same applies to the remaining cases.
They have devotion toward the Four Great Kings, or [the term] *Cātumahārāja* refers to those who are the dwelling places of the Four Great Kings.

And there are the Cātumahārājika [devas]. Because thirty-three [beings] were reborn here together with the young brahmin Māgha as co-performers of merit, that place associated with them is called "Tettiṃsa";
that very place is "Tāvatiṃsa," and those whose dwelling is there are called "Tāvatiṃsa," so they say.
Furthermore, because of the statement: "A thousand Cātumahārājikas, a thousand Tāvatiṃsas..."

In other world-systems as well, there are the six sense-sphere heavens (kāmāvacara-devaloka); therefore, one should understand that this [particular] heaven is merely a name for that class of deities.

They are called Yāmas because they have gone forth from suffering (dukkha). They are called Tusitas because they have attained (itā) satisfaction (tusaṃ), that is, joy, through their own excellence of glory.
They are called Nimmānaratis because delight (rati) resides in their own creations (nimmāna). They are called Paranimmitavasavattīs because they exercise mastery over enjoyments created by others.
[They are] the Paranimmitavasavattīs.
7. Because they serve as attendants (*paricārikā*) to the Mahābrahmās, they exist in their assembly and are thus called *Brahmapārisajjā*.

Because they stand in the position of chaplains (*purohita*) to them, they are the *Brahmapurohitā*. They are called *Brahmā* because they have been increased and grown great by various specific qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
Because they possess beauty as well as long life and other qualities, and because they are great among the Brahmapārisajja and other classes, they are called "Great Brahmās" (Mahābrahmā).
These three [classes] dwell upon surfaces illuminated by the radiance of exquisite jewels. 8.
Those who have limited light are the Parittābhā (Limited Light). Those who have immeasurable light are the Appamāṇābhā (Immeasurable Light).

They are called *ābhassara* (radiant) because light radiates and issues forth from them in every direction, like lightning from a cloud, due to their continuity of aggregates produced by jhāna accompanied by rapture (*sappītika-jhāna*).
Or, they are called *ābhassara* because light radiates and issues forth from their bodies in fragments, as if falling away bit by bit, like the flame of a torch.
Alternatively, they are called *ābhassara* because they are characterized by shining with the aforementioned effulgence.
These three also dwell on a single level illuminated by the radiance of exquisite jewels.

(9) "Subha" refers to a bodily luster that is uniform, dense, and immovable; because they are limited (*paritta*) by the higher Brahmās in this regard, they are called the Limited-Lustrous (*Parittasubha*).

Because their luster is immeasurable (*appamāṇa*), they are called the Immeasurable-Lustrous (*Appamāṇasubha*). They are "crowded" (*ākiṇṇa*) with beauties (*subha*) consisting of the arising of radiance.

“Subhakiṇhā. Although it should be called “Subhākiṇṇā,” the vowel *ā* has been shortened and the final letter *ṇa* changed to *ha*, thus it is stated as “Subhakiṇhā. These beings also dwell upon a single floor illuminated by the radiance of exquisite jewels. 10.

Because they possess vast fruits produced by the development of jhāna, they are called Vehapphalas. This is because they consist merely of a continuity of form produced by the cultivation of dispassion toward perception (*saññā*).
There is no perception (*saññā*); because they lack it, the remaining immaterial aggregates (*arūpakkhandha*) are their [domain], thus they are "non-percipient" (*asañña*).
These very beings are the "non-percipient beings" (*asaññasatta*). They too dwell in a single place illuminated by the splendor of exquisite jewels.

They are the "Pure Abodes" (*suddhāvāsa*) because they are the dwellings of only those who are pure—namely, non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants—or because their dwelling is pure due to the absence of attraction (*anunaya*) and aversion (*paṭigha*). Of them...
The dwelling place is also the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa). 11.
Furthermore, those who dwell on the first floor do not leave their own place for a short time; thus they are called Avihā (the Unforsaking).
Those who dwell on the second floor are not tormented by anything; thus they are called Atappā (the Untormentable). Those who dwell on the third floor, because of their supremely beautiful form—
They are called *sudassā* because they are easily seen. The inhabitants of the fourth level are called *sudassino* because, owing to their perfectly pure vision, they see easily.
As for the inhabitants of the fifth level, because they possess the highest attainment (*ukkaṭṭhasampatti*), there is no one among them who is junior; thus they are the *akaniṭṭhā*. 12.

Only the four aggregates that constitute the resultant state of the first immaterial realm (*āruppa*) occurring in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāsānañcāyatana*) are [the beings]; or rather, the plane of the sphere of infinite space is the spatial extent delimited by those aggregates. The same applies to the remaining [immaterial realms].

13. The connection is as follows: "Ordinary persons (*puthujjana*), stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*), and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) are not found at all in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*). By the exclusion of ordinary persons and the others, it is stated that only non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and arahants are found there. 14.

"In the remaining places" means in those remaining places excluding the Pure Abodes, the woeful states (*apāya*), and the non-percipient beings (*asaññin*). In these remaining places, both noble ones (*ariya*) and non-noble ones (*anariya*) are found.
The commentary on the fourfold classification of planes (*bhūmicatukka*) is concluded.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Rebirth-linking (Paṭisandhicatukkavaṇṇanā): 16. "At the moment of descent" means at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). 17.

"Born blind" (*jaccandha*) means one who is blind by birth. Although all those born from eggs or from a womb are indeed without eyes at the very moment of birth, [the term "born blind" specifically refers to those who lack eyes throughout their entire life].

Nevertheless, even at a time when the arising of the eye and so forth is due, a being who—due to a rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) granted by karma whose potency has been obstructed by karma that hinders the production of the eye, or by another such karma—is one for whom the eye is not produced, is called "blind from birth" (jaccandha).
Others, however, say: "Blind from birth means blind at the very moment of delivery; he is one who has emerged after having been blind within the mother's womb."
They say: "Therefore, it is established that for those with two roots and three roots, the eye-faculty does not fail within the mother’s womb.

Regarding the phrase "those born blind and so forth," the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*) encompasses those who are congenitally deaf, congenitally mute, congenitally dull-witted, congenitally insane, eunuchs, hermaphrodites, neuters, and the mentally deranged.

However, others maintain: "Certain individuals with rootless rebirth-linking (*ahetuka-patisandhi*), though possessing unimpaired faculties, are by nature somewhat inclined toward discursive thought (*vicāra*)."
They say that by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those of such a kind are also included. "Dependent on the earth-deities" (*bhummassitā*) means being based upon or belonging to them.
"Falling from the mass of happiness" means those who have fallen into the states of misery (*vinipātikā*).
In all instances, "in the happy destinies of sense-sphere existence" (*kāmasugatiyaṃ*) refers to the sevenfold happy destinies of sense-sphere existence consisting of gods and humans.

21. "Among those" refers to the persons endowed with the aforementioned rebirth-linking, or to those in the states of misery and so forth. There is no fixed rule regarding the calculation of the measure of their lifespan, because some have long lives and others have even longer lives.
Thus it has been said: "There is no limit to the lifespan of those in the states of misery or of humans."
"For thus was Mandhātā long-lived, as were certain yakkhas.
Indeed, in the states of misery, karma alone is the measure; for those reborn there, as long as their karma has not been exhausted, there is no passing away.
The same applies to the earth-deities (*bhummadeva*). For among those born there, some remain for a period of seven days and so forth, while others remain even for an entire eon (*kappa*).
