Likewise, it is the same for humans: sometimes their lifespan is incalculable (*asaṅkhyeyya*), and sometimes it is only ten years.
As it is said: "He who lives long lives for a hundred years, or slightly more; he does not reach a second hundred years."
This, however, was said with reference to the present day.

22. "Five hundred divine years": fifty human years constitute one day [for them]; accordingly, by defining months and years, their life span is five hundred years by divine measure. And this has been said:
"Those fifty years which are a single day for humans there,"
"Thirty nights and days make a month, and twelve months make a year;
by that reckoning of years, their divine lifespan is considered to be five hundred.
"By human calculation" means by the calculation of human years. "Four times that" refers to the lifespan of the Cātumahārājika devas.

A day [of the Tāvatiṃsa devas] is measured by fifty human years; and having doubled five hundred divine years, there arise one thousand divine years for the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Thus, by way of doubling both the day and the year, it is fourfold;
yet that is one thousand years by divine reckoning, which by human reckoning amounts to twelve million six hundred thousand years.
It is so. Four times that amount is for the Yāma devas;

according to the method stated from the measure of the lifespan of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, it is four times as much, which by divine reckoning is two thousand years, and by human reckoning is fourteen billion years plus four million.
Four times that amount is for the Tusita devas, which is four thousand divine years, and by human reckoning—
Fifty-seven koṭis and six hundred thousand years. Four times that is for the Nimmānarati devas, which is eight thousand celestial years;
by human calculation, this is two hundred and forty-four koṭis and three hundred thousand years.
Four times that is for the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, which is sixteen thousand celestial years.
23. Showing the calculation of human beings himself, he said, "nine hundred," and so forth. The connection is as follows:

the lifespan for those who exercise mastery (*vasavattī*) is nine hundred and twenty-one crores of years, as well as sixty hundred thousand years. 25. Regarding the phrase "in the plane of the second jhāna":

this is stated according to the fourfold method (*catukkanaya*). Beyond that, in its occurrence during life and at the time of death, it proceeds and ceases precisely in that manner by way of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and the death-consciousness (*cuti*); such is the construction.

29. "Among them" (*tesu*) refers to those Brahmās who have taken rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) through those [deities]. "Of an aeon" (*kappassa*) refers to an incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*).

For it is not possible for the lifespan-limit of the three classes beginning with the Brahma-pārisajjas to be determined by means of a great aeon (*mahākappa*), because they do not perish even within a single aeon;
thus, a full aeon is impossible for them. For this world has been consumed by fire seven times.
It is destroyed by fire on the first occasion, by water on the eighth; again, for seven occasions it is destroyed by fire, and on the eighth occasion by water.
Thus, when eight sets of eight [occasions] are completed, it is destroyed by wind on the final occasion.

In this regard, starting from the level of the first jhāna, it is destroyed by fire; starting from the levels of the second and third jhānas, it is destroyed by water; and starting from the level of the fourth jhāna—
It is destroyed by the wind. And this has also been said:
"Seven times it is struck by the fire of beings, and at every eighth time by water;
when sixty-four [cycles] are thus completed, there shall be one supreme wind."
“By fire, [the worlds] below the Ābhassara [heaven] are destroyed; by water, [those] below the Subhakiṇha;
by wind, [those] below the Vehapphala—thus the world is destroyed.
Therefore, because there is no destruction even during a single eon for the first three levels of the jhānas, their existence persists throughout the entire eon.
Regarding the phrase "there is none," the limit of their lifespan should be understood by way of incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*).
However, starting from the second jhāna and above, it is by way of a full great aeon (*mahākappa*), not by way of an incalculable aeon.

And as for an "incalculable aeon," it is defined by the removal of one seed at a time—each the size of a white mustard seed—from a sphere measuring a league in length and breadth, once every hundred years, until all have been removed.
Even when mustard seeds have been exhausted, a fourth part of a great eon (*mahākappa*)—which is by nature inexhaustible—remains.

However, when many beings have met their destruction through one of the calamities of war, disease, or famine, by the power of the wholesome karma that causes the continuity of the remaining beings' existence, there arise beings whose lifespan gradually increases from ten years up to the measure of an incalculable eon (*asaṅkhyeyya-āyukappa*).
Then, once again, due to the undertaking of unwholesome practices (*asaddhamma-samādāna*),...
Having gradually declined until beings are born with a lifespan of ten years, through the destruction of beings by one of the calamities such as disease,
it is defined as "this is one intermediate aeon" (*antarakappa*); by way of such an intermediate aeon, its measure is sixty-four intermediate aeons,
though some also say its measure is twenty intermediate aeons.
45. They approach the base of infinite space; thus they are "those who approach the base of infinite space" (*ākāsānañcāyatanūpagā*).
49. "In one way alone" means identical in terms of plane, birth, associated phenomena, and formations. "Of one birth" means in a single existence.
The commentary on the fourfold set of rebirth-linking is finished.
Commentary on the Tetrad of Karma 50.
Now, in order to show the tetrad of karma by way of four aspects, the passage beginning with “janakaṃ” is commenced.

It is called *janaka* because it generates (*janayati*). It is called *upatthambhaka* because it supports (*upatthambheti*). It is called *upapīḷaka* because it oppresses after having approached (*upagantvā pīḷeti*). Having approached...
It is called "destructive" (*upaghātaka*) because it destroys.
In that context, wholesome and unwholesome volitions (*cetanā*) that produce rebirth-linking and the occurrences of existence, as well as resultant and kamma-produced matter, are called "productive.
Even though they themselves are unable to produce a result, [they assist] in the production of a result from another karma after a long interval.
Wholesome and unwholesome kamma that serves as a condition for the prolongation of a resultant state—whether that resultant itself be pleasure or pain—is called "supportive" (*upatthambhaka*).

This is because it provides a condition for the non-interruption of the resultant and a condition for its intensification, acting as a basis for its much longer duration in accordance with the generative capacity of the original kamma.

Conversely, [kamma] that obstructs the much longer duration of a resultant produced by another kamma—by means of disturbances such as disease or an imbalance of the bodily elements—is [called "destructive"].

Any action whatsoever is called "obstructive" (*upapīḷaka*). However, when an action that is weak in its power to produce a result is countered by the arising of a condition that cuts it off after it has already begun, thereby preventing its fruition, that [stronger] action is called "destructive" (*upaghātaka*).
This is the distinction between the producer (*janaka*) and the destructive: the producer does not cut off the fruition of another action, but rather...
"It produces a result that is obstructive and preceded by interruption"—this, first of all, is the conclusion reached in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*).
However, other teachers maintain: "Obstructive karma (*upapīḷaka-kamma*) afflicts the ripening of another karma from time to time by bringing about conditions such as frequent illness.
Obstructive karma (*upaghātaka*), on the other hand, completely cuts off that [other karma] and [produces its own result]."
They say: "It provides space, but it does not itself produce the result. For in this way, its distinction from the productive [kamma] is clearly evident.
"By way of function" means by way of the functions of producing, supporting, obstructing, and cutting off. 51.
"Heavy" means highly blameworthy and of great power—a kamma that cannot be resisted by another kamma.
"Proximate" (*āsanna*) refers to what is recollected at the time of death, or what was performed at that time. "Habitual" (*āciṇṇa*) refers to what has been done repeatedly;

or even if done only once, it is that which has been frequently cultivated. "Kamma by way of having been performed" (*kaṭattā-kamma*) refers to an action that is simply called "kamma" because it has been performed, without having reached the status of being weighty (*garuka*) and so forth.
In that regard, whether it be wholesome or unwholesome, among heavy and light karmas, that which is heavy—on the side of the unwholesome, such as the deed of matricide and so forth;

or on the side of the wholesome, sublime (mahaggata) karma—that alone ripens first, even in the presence of proximate and other types of karma, just as a great flood flows along after having submerged the shallow water. For that reason, it is called "heavy. In that case...
When there is nothing near or far, that which is remembered at the time of death ripens first; there is simply no need to speak of what was done at a distant time.

When even that is absent, among habitual and non-habitual deeds, that which is habitual—whether it be good conduct or bad conduct—ripens first. However, *kaṭattā-kamma* (kamma performed and stored) [ripens] when it has gained the opportunity for its habituation.
Because it draws in rebirth-linking through the absence of prior [kamma], the weighty (garuka) kamma ripens first of all. In the absence of the weighty, the proximate (āsanna) ripens;

in its absence, the habitual (āciṇṇa); and in its absence, the kamma of the present existence (kaṭattā-kamma). Therefore he said, "by way of the giving of its result," which means according to the sequence of the yielding of fruition.
However, in the *Abhidhammāvatāra* and other texts, the habitual is stated to ripen first after the proximate.

This has been stated. Just as when the gate of a cattle-pen full of a herd of cows is opened, even though there are later on young bulls, stallions, and heifers, it is only that which is nearest the gate—even if it be a weak, old, worn-out cow—that goes out first;
so too, although other wholesome and unwholesome states exist, because of its proximity to the time of death, that which is held most dear [goes out first].
"First, it gives its result in close proximity"—thus it is mentioned first here. 52.

*Diṭṭhadhamma* refers to the present personal existence (*attabhāva*) which has become manifest; that which is to be experienced there by way of the experiencing of its result is *diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*.
That which is to be experienced after being reborn immediately following the present life is *upapajjavedanīya*.
Kamma to be experienced in some other state of existence—whether in this very life or in some other future existence—is *aparāpariyavedanīya*.
Kamma that can be described as "there was indeed the kamma, but its result did not yet occur; it exists [now], and it will exist [in the future]" is *ahosikamma*.
In that regard, it has attained a state of strength through not being overcome by opposing factors and through having acquired specific excellence by means of particular conditions.
The first impulsion volition (*paṭhamajavana-cetanā*) that yields its fruit in that very same existence— having become preeminent by way of such prior karmic formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhāra*)—
is called "to be experienced in the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*). For, in a continuum possessing strong impulsion as described,
it proceeds by way of benefit or non-benefit toward those endowed with specific virtues, and due to the lack of repetition (*āsevana*), it possesses little ripening (*vipāka*).

Unlike the other two types [of wholesome karma], this karma does not depend upon the cessation of the ongoing stream of existence (*pavattasantāna*) nor upon the acquisition of a specific realm (*okāsa*).
Therefore, it yields only a result of fruition (*vipāka*) during the course of existence (*pavatti*), like a mere flower in this very life—an unrooted fruit (*ahetukaphala*).

However, the seventh impulsion consciousness (*javana-cetanā*), which is the decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) that accomplishes the purpose, having acquired its specific distinction according to the method already described, [yields its result] in the immediately following existence.

That which gives its result is called "to-be-experienced-in-the-next-birth" (*upapajjavedanīya*). And that [kamma] gives its process-result (*pavattivipāka*) only after it has given rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
There is no case where it gives a process-result when rebirth-linking has not been given; for the opportunity for what is to be experienced in the next birth arises immediately after death.

However, once rebirth-linking has been given, the teachers maintain that it gives its process-result even across hundreds of births, because it lacks the aforementioned causes [for immediate ripening].

The five volitions occurring between the initial and final volitions—which have not yet attained the status of being experienced in the present life (diṭṭhadhammavedanīya) and so forth—because their nature of yielding fruition remains uninterrupted, produce fruition during either rebirth-linking or the course of existence whenever an opportunity arises;
these are called "to-be-experienced-in-a-subsequent-life" (aparāpariyavedanīya). As for the two preceding types of kamma, they have passed away at their respective times.
And when the third [rebirth] has also been cut off from the process of *saṃsāra*, it is called "past-deed" (*ahosikamma*).

"By way of the time of ripening" means: by way of the times as previously delimited for the first three—namely, in the present, immediately after that, or at some time—and by way of the absence of such a time for the other.
For the designation "past-deed" applies precisely because its time has passed.
53. "By way of the place of ripening" means by way of the plane where rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) matures. 54.

Now, in order to show the occurrence of unwholesome and other types of kamma by way of the doors of bodily action and so forth, and to show their tenfold and other classifications by way of such acts as killing living beings, the passage beginning with "Therein, unwholesome... is commenced.
Action occurring through the door of the body is bodily action (*kāyakamma*). Likewise for verbal action and the rest. 55.

Taking life by causing it to fall excessively, without allowing the living being to escape, is the destruction of life (*pāṇātipāta*). The taking of what is not given through body or speech is the taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*). Engaging improperly in sensual pleasures characterized by sexual misconduct is misconduct in sensual pleasures (*kāmesu micchācāra*).

In this context, "living being" (*pāṇa*) is, from the conventional standpoint, a sentient being; from the ultimate standpoint, it is the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*). Regarding that living being, one who perceives it as a living being...
The volition of killing, which originates from the application of an act that severs the life-faculty, is the destruction of life.
The volition of theft, which originates from the application of taking another's property by one who perceives it as such, is the taking of what is not given.

Sexual misconduct is the volition of transgressing against a place where one should not go, proceeding through the door of the body by way of indulging in unrighteous sexual practices. The drinking of fermented liquor is also included herein.
They say [this is so] because of the state of misconduct (*micchācāra*) regarding sensual pleasures (*kāma*) reckoned as tastes.

Regarding the "body-door" (*kāyadvāra*), which is reckoned as bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*): it is so called because intention is made known by means of the body, and because it itself is cognizable by the body. It is a modification of the aggregate of wind-element-impulses (*vāyodhātu-javā*) produced by the mind that generates forward movement and so forth;

it is so called because it serves as a cooperative cause for rigidity and other such states, due to its nature as the "wind-body" (*copana-kāya*), and because it is the gateway for the occurrence of kamma.
And [it occurs] at the door of action known as the body-door.

For although that intimation is produced solely by the arising of consciousness accompanied by this or that specific action, nevertheless, while it is occurring in such a manner, the designation "bodily action" and so forth applies to the action that originates it;
thus, because it serves as the gateway for its manifestation, it belongs to that very [action].

It is appropriate to say this. If only the phrase "because it is stated in the context of the body-door" were used, one might object: "If that were so, there would be no definition of the doors of action (kammadvāra).
For what occurs in the body-door is called 'bodily action' (kāyakamma), and that which serves as the gateway for the occurrence of bodily action is called the 'body-door.
However, when one commands another by speech to commit killing and so forth, that bodily action also occurs in the door of speech."

"If there were no determination of the door by way of the action, then for one who performs lying and so forth through a bodily gesture, verbal action would also occur at the bodily door; thus, there would be no determination of the door by way of the action.

Anticipating this objection, it was said "by way of preponderance" (bāhullavuttito) in order to show that the determination is made on the basis of what occurs most frequently. For bodily action occurs only at the bodily door.
It occurs predominantly through the body; it occurs little through the door of speech.

Therefore, because it occurs predominantly through the door of the body alone, its status as bodily action (*kāyakamma*) is established, just as the status of being a forest-dweller and so forth is established for those who live in the forest. Likewise, bodily action itself occurs mostly through the door of the body, not the others;
therefore, because bodily action occurs mostly in this very place, it has the status of being the door of bodily action.
The meaning here is this: the status of being a "brahmin village" and so forth for actual brahmin villages and the like is established;
there is no obstacle whatsoever in defining the doors of kamma.
56. *Musā* means an unreal matter; it is called *musāvāda* because one speaks that [matter] falsely (*tacchato*) by means of it. It grinds away (*pisati*) concord.
It is *pisuṇā* because it crushes and scatters, or because it makes the state of endearment empty.

It is *pharusā* because it makes both oneself and others harsh, or because its contact is rough like a saw. *Samphaṃ* is that which bears fruit as pleasure and welfare, yet disperses and destroys them;
it is any kind of useless talk that does not benefit oneself or others, and one prattles such things with this [speech], hence it is *samphappalāpa*.
In this context, lying (musāvāda) is the volition that originates from the application of making known an unreal matter as being real to one who desires to have it understood as such.
This becomes a path of kamma only when it causes a breach between others; otherwise, it is merely kamma.

It is the defiled volition that originates from a verbal application intended to cause a breach between others—whether out of a desire to cause such a breach or out of a desire for one's own pleasure.

Slanderous speech (*pisuṇavācā*) is also a course of kamma only when there are two parties already divided. Harsh speech (*pharusavācā*) is an absolutely cruel volition that originates an application of speech intended to cut another’s vital points;
for if there is gentleness of mind, it does not constitute harsh speech.
Idle chatter (*samphappalāpa*) is a defiled volition that originates an application for conveying useless matters, such as the *Sītāharaṇa* and so forth.
However, that [course of action] is established only when others have grasped that harmful intent. Regarding the "door of speech," which is designated as vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*):

it makes known the speaker's intention through speech, and it is itself made known by speech. This is because, due to the absence of mere conventional speech—which is a modification of the aggregate consisting of the earth element augmented by mind-originated matter that gives rise to the effort producing vocal differentiation designated as vocal intimation—and because it serves as the gateway for the occurrence of kamma, it is designated as the "door of speech."
Regarding the doors of action (*kammadvāra*): "By way of habitual practice" is exactly as previously explained. 57.

*Abhijjhā* (covetousness) is so called because one meditates upon or thinks with greed toward the prosperity of others. *Vyāpāda* (ill will) is so called because by means of it one becomes afflicted regarding welfare and happiness. *Micchā-diṭṭhi* (wrong view) is so called because one sees wrongly and perversely.
Therein, coveting another's property in the manner of "O, may this be mine! is *abhijjhā*; that [covetousness] [relates] to another's property...
The path of action (kamma-patha) occurs through one’s own naming [of the victim]. Mental corruption in the form, “Oh, may this being perish,” is ill-will (byāpāda).
Wrong view (micchā-diṭṭhi) is a distorted perception according to the method beginning with, “There is no giving,” and so forth.

Here, however, the division of the paths of action occurs only through the views of nihilism (natthika), causelessness (ahetuka), and non-doing (akiriya). Now, by way of defining their factors (aṅga) and so on:
"Proliferation" (papañca) should be understood according to the method presented in various other places.

"Even apart from intimation" means even without bodily or verbal intimation, that is, even without having originated it. And here, covetousness and the rest associated with the consciousness that originates intimation belong to the side of volition (cetanā).
58. "They arise with hatred as their root" means they arise through conditions such as co-nascence (sahajāta) etc., having that which is termed hatred as their root;
or they arise with a mind rooted in hatred, not from roots such as greed. For even when laughing, kings command the taking of life only with a mind of hatred;
likewise, this should be understood accordingly for harsh speech and ill-will. Regarding the objects upon which wrong view is fixed:
Because one clings [to an object] preceded by greed, it is said: "And wrong view has greed as its root. As for the remaining four [unwholesome courses of action], they all arise from two roots.

First, when someone takes away a desired object, or takes away an undesired object with the purpose of protecting themselves, their relatives, or their possessions, their taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) has greed as its root. For one who takes [an object] for the sake of retaliating against an enemy...

By the root of hatred. From the authority of those who recite the *nīti* (political ethics), kings and brahmins—who seize the property of others for the sake of punishing the wicked—say such things as, "All this was given to the brahmins by the kings;
however, because they are all very weak, others enjoy it, whereas the brahmins enjoy only what is their own," and so forth, acting with the perception that it is their own.

Thus, for those who take anything at all and for those who deny the connection between action and its fruit, [this state] arises through the root of delusion (*moha*). In the same way, this should be applied accordingly to false speech and the other [unwholesome courses of action]. 63.
Although this [resultant consciousness] arises with respect to the six objects by means of the threefold action, it arises according to a threefold restriction.

He said: "In the same way, by way of generosity, virtue, and meditation. For when the [ten] are demonstrated as two, then again as two, and then as three, they are included respectively within those very three—generosity and so forth. We shall explain the reason for this later.
However, the application of their occurrence among the six objects and the three doors of action should be understood according to the method handed down in the commentaries and other sources.
65. It is called *dāna* because one gives (*dīyati*) by means of it; it is the volition of relinquishment. The same applies to the remaining terms. It is called *sīla* because one cools (*sīlati*);

the meaning is that one composes (*samādahati*) bodily and verbal actions, or places them correctly (*sammā ṭhapeti*). Alternatively, it is called *sīla* because one maintains (*sīlayati*) or sustains (*upadhāreti*);
here, "sustaining" refers to the state of being firmly established in wholesome states. For it has been said: "Being established in virtue," and so forth. One develops (*bhāveti*) the wholesome.
"Bhāvanā" is so called because one cultivates and increases the Dhamma by means of it. "Apacāyana" is that by which one honors and performs proper service (sāmīci) through the mode of worship.
"Veyyāvacca" is the state of being occupied with the performance of various duties. "Pattidāna" is that by which the merit (patti) produced within one's own continuum is given away.
"Pattānumodanā" is that by which one rejoices in the merit. [The word] "Dhamma" [is used].

"Listening to the Dhamma" (*dhammassavana*) means that by means of this, one listens. "Teaching the Dhamma" (*dhammadesanā*) means that by means of this, they teach the Dhamma. "Rectification of view" (*diṭṭhijukamma*) is the straightening of one's views.

In that regard, for one whose mental continuum possesses underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), the volition (*cetanā*) that proceeds from the relinquishing of existing objects out of a desire to honor and assist others is called "giving" (*dāna*).
This [volition] occurs by way of seeking the objects of giving, and by way of recollecting with a joyful mind what has been given.
And the volitions belonging to the preceding and succeeding phases of that process converge precisely here. In this same way, it should be understood accordingly for the remaining cases as well:

for one undertaking, fulfilling, or even refraining from bodily and verbal misconduct as it occurs—even without formally undertaking them—the five, eight, or ten precepts (sīla) by way of the perpetual precepts (niccasīla), or for one going forth (pabbajjā) or receiving full ordination (upasampadā) at the ordination hall.
The volition that arises when one undertakes the vows (*saṃvara*) and fulfills the fourfold pure virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) is called "virtue" (*sīla*).

The volition that proceeds by means of preliminary work and reflection upon the forty meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and the stages (*bhūmi*) such as the aggregates (*khandha*), reaching up to the stage of the lineage-change (*gotrabhu*) but not yet attaining absorption (*appanā*), is called "development" (*bhāvanā*); this also includes the volition involved in mastering blameless sciences and so forth.
In this very context, the summary is as follows:

For those who are senior by age and superior in virtue, the volition of showing great respect—consisting in rising from one's seat, offering a seat, and so forth, performed with a mind free from defilement and without expectation of robes or other requisites—is called "reverence" (apacāyanā).
And for those same persons, as well as for those who are ill, [it is performed] with the aforementioned disposition.

The volition of performing various duties is called *veyyāvacca* (service). The volition of aspiring for the sharing with others of the merit produced within one’s own continuum is called *pattidāna* (the giving of merit).

The volition of sympathetic rejoicing (*abbhānumodanā*)—with a mind free from the stain of stinginess—toward merit given by others or even that which has not been given, is called *pattānumodanā* (rejoicing in merit).
Having heard this Dhamma and practicing therein according to the method described, one thinks:
"I shall partake in the distinction of mundane and supramundane qualities," or, "Having become learned, I shall assist others through the teaching of the Dhamma and so forth.
Thus, with an undefiled underlying intention (ajjhāsaya) proceeding from the diffusion of welfare toward oneself or others, there arises the volition of hearing the instruction on welfare.
"Listening to the Dhamma" includes here even the volition of listening to blameless sciences and the like.
"Teaching the Dhamma" refers to the volition of instructing for the benefit of one who attends to the mind with wise attention (*yoniso manasikāra*) out of indifference to gain, honor, and so forth;
it also includes the volition of pointing out blameless sciences and the like. Through right view proceeding by way of the formula beginning with "there is giving," etc., [it is included].
Rectification is called the rectification of view (*diṭṭhijukamma*).
If this is so, would it not follow that a mental state dissociated from knowledge cannot possess the nature of a meritorious action consisting in the rectification of view?
No, it does not fail to obtain; for even the preceding and succeeding volitions are included within those very same meritorious actions. Moreover—

For at the moment of straightening [the view], the consciousness is associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa-sampayutta*) alone; however, in its preceding and succeeding phases, it may also be dissociated from knowledge (*ñāṇa-vippayutta*).
Thus, even that [dissociated state] can be considered a "straightening of views. Enough of this excessive elaboration.
Among these ten [meritorious deeds], the giving of a gift and the rejoicing in merit are included within the category of giving (*dāna*), because they share the same essential nature. Giving, too...

For these two are the opposites of envy (*issā*) and avarice (*macchariya*). Therefore, because they share the same opposite and possess the same characteristic, they are included within the basis of meritorious action consisting in giving (*dānamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*).

Reverence (*apacāyana*) and service (*veyyāvacca*) are included within the basis of meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya*), because they have the nature of conduct-virtue (*cāritta-sīla*).

However, teaching, listening, and the straightening of views are included within that consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), because they have the nature of practicing wholesome states (*kusaladhamma-sevana*).
“They are included [in the category of development]” is what the Elder Ācariya Dhammapāla stated. Others, however, say:
“When teaching and when listening, one teaches and listens by penetrating each characteristic through directing knowledge according to the teaching;
and since those acts of teaching and listening bring about penetration itself, they are included in the development consisting of teaching and listening.”
They say this. Furthermore, it can be said that teaching belongs within the category of giving because of its essential nature as a gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*).

For it has been stated: "The gift of the Dhamma surpasses all other gifts. Likewise, the rectification of views (*diṭṭhijukamma*) applies in every respect, because it possesses the characteristic of determining everything for all beings.
Indeed, among the perfections such as giving, whatever occurs in the manner of "there is what is given" and so forth—
When purified by right view, it becomes of great fruit and great benefit; and having established this, it is stated in the *Dīghanikāya-aṭṭhakathā*:

"The straightening of views is the defining characteristic of all [wholesome deeds]. Thus, because the other two are included within the three categories of giving, virtue, and meditation, it should be understood that, in brief, there are only three bases for the performance of merit.
And it has been shown thus by the Teacher below.
67. Mental action alone [is intended here], because it does not occur in the doors of body and so forth due to its lack of being an originator of intimation (*viññatti*).

And that is wholesome of the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), consisting in meditation (*bhāvanāmaya*), because it does not occur by way of giving and so forth. It is that which has reached absorption (*appanā*), excluding those occurring in the preliminary stage (*pubbabhāga*).

By way of the state belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-bhāva*). "By way of the distinction of jhāna factors" means that although there are many types due to distinctions such as the path of practice (*paṭipadā*), it is fivefold according to the distinction of the jhāna factors produced by the process of transcending those factors. 68.

"By way of the distinction of objects" means by way of the distinction among these four objects: the space remaining after the removal of the kasiṇa, the mind having space as its domain, the absence of that [space], and the consciousness taking that [absence] as its object.

69. "In this context" means among these four kinds of kamma categorized according to their manifesting conditions. "Free from restlessness" refers to the eleven types of unwholesome kamma that are devoid of volition accompanied by restlessness.

What, then, is the reason here that doubt-accompanied kamma—which is the weakest of all due to its lack of conviction—draws forth rebirth-linking, while that which is associated with conviction, though stronger than it, does not?
Does it not draw [the rebirth-linking] when accompanied by restlessness? Because it lacks the essential nature of giving rebirth-linking.
For this investigation—whether it draws strongly or does not draw weakly—applies only to those states that possess the essential nature of giving rebirth-linking.
But for that which lacks even the essential nature of giving rebirth-linking, its state of strength is not a cause for drawing rebirth-linking.
But how is this to be understood: that there is no nature of giving rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) for [consciousness] accompanied by restlessness (*uddhacca*)?

Because it does not exist among those [states] to be abandoned by vision (*dassana*). For unwholesome states are threefold: those to be abandoned by vision, those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and those which may be abandoned by vision or may be abandoned by cultivation.
Among these, the arising of consciousness accompanied by wrong view (*diṭṭhi*) and accompanied by doubt (*vicikicchā*)...

Those called "to be abandoned by seeing" (dassanena pahātabba) are so named because they are to be abandoned by the path of stream-entry (sotāpatti-magga), which receives the name "seeing" (dassana) by virtue of its initial vision of Nibbāna.

The arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness (uddhacca-sahagata-cittuppāda) is called "to be abandoned by cultivation" (bhāvanāya pahātabba) because it is to be abandoned by the final path (agga-magga).
For, in the three higher paths, one cultivates—by way of cultivation—the Nibbāna already seen by the first path.

Because it causes [the path] to proceed, it is called "development" (bhāvanā). However, states of consciousness dissociated from views and accompanied by mental grief may be abandonable by seeing, or they may be abandonable by development;

for they are abandoned by the first path in their stage of producing rebirth in the lower realms, and by the higher paths in their remaining stages of being dense or less dense. In this regard, it might be asked:
Even that which is to be abandoned by seeing is designated here as "to be abandoned by seeing" by virtue of its commonality with what is to be abandoned by seeing.

Furthermore, if restlessness-accompanied [kamma] were to grant rebirth-linking, then, since an unwholesome rebirth-linking is impossible in a happy destination, it would have to grant it only in the woeful states.
And that which leads to the woeful states must necessarily be abandonable by seeing.
Otherwise, because that which leads to the states of misery has not been abandoned, it would follow that those in training (sekkhas) could still be reborn in the states of misery;
yet this is not tenable, as it contradicts such statements as, "He is liberated from the four states of misery and is no longer subject to falling into the lower realms.
Furthermore, if these [defilements] were to be abandoned by vision, they would have appeared in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase, "There may be those to be abandoned by vision."

It might be said that this has not been stated. Now, one might argue: "Since greed, hatred, delusion, and the defilements associated with them are stated among those to be abandoned by seeing as 'leading to the states of deprivation,' it is possible to include volition accompanied by restlessness there.
That is not so, because it is stated that such [volition] is to be abandoned exclusively by means of cultivation (bhāvanā).
For this has been said: “Which states are to be abandoned by development? A consciousness-arising accompanied by restlessness.
Therefore, its non-mention among those [states] to be abandoned by vision establishes that it does not give rebirth-linking.
But is it not said in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*—?
“At whatever time an unwholesome state of consciousness has arisen, accompanied by equanimity, associated with restlessness, having a visible form as its object...
pe... or having mental phenomena as its object, or whatever it may be directed toward—at that time there is contact...
pe... there is non-distraction. These states are unwholesome. Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).”
“Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

Having thus extracted the arising of consciousness accompanied by restlessness, its result has also been extracted. How, then, can it be accepted that this [restless consciousness] lacks the capacity to provide rebirth-linking?
This was not extracted with reference to providing rebirth-linking; rather, it was extracted as a result occurring during the course of existence (pavatti-vipāka).
Having intended this. In the *Paṭṭhāna*, however, it is said:
"Concomitant volition to be abandoned by vision is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for mind-produced matter;
asynchronous volition to be abandoned by vision is a condition for resultant aggregates and for matter produced by kamma."
"An object-condition by way of kamma-condition"—
having thus extracted the state of being a conascent and asynchronous kamma-condition for volition alone that is to be abandoned by seeing, [the text] then states:
"Conascent volition to be abandoned by cultivation is a condition, by way of kamma-condition, for mind-originated matter."
Only the state of being a co-nascent kamma-condition for volition to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*) has been extracted here;
however, the state of being a asynchronous kamma-condition has not. Furthermore, there is no drawing forth of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) without an asynchronous kamma-condition;
therefore, that [volition] does not give rebirth-linking in any way whatsoever. As for what some say: "The volition of restlessness (*uddhacca-cetanā*) gives both types of fruition..."
As for the claim that “it is not given [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] because the state of asynchronous kamma-condition (*nānākkhaṇika-kamma-paccaya*) has not been mentioned,” that is merely their own opinion;
for in the *Paṭisambhidā-vibhaṅga*, the occurrence-result (*pavatti-vipāka*) of even agitation-accompanied states is mentioned, and in the *Paṭṭhāna*,
the state of asynchronous kamma-condition was not mentioned specifically with reference only to rebirth-result (*paṭisandhi-vipāka*).

For if the state of being a kamma-condition at different moments were stated with reference to the resultant [consciousness] of the course of existence (*pavattivipāka*), then one might suppose it applied to the rebirth-linking result (*paṭisandhivipāka*) as well;
therefore, the state of being a kamma-condition at different moments is not stated by way of the resultant of the course of existence even though it exists.
Consequently, it is not possible to deny its resultant of the course of existence. Hence he said: "But in the course of existence... and so forth.

Ācariya Buddhamitta and others, however, maintain that there is restlessness-accompanied [unwholesome consciousness] which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and there is also that which is not to be abandoned by cultivation.
Among these, that which is to be abandoned by cultivation occurs in the mental continuum (*santāna*) of those in training (*sekkha*);

the other occurs in the mental continuum of worldlings (*puthujjana*). Furthermore, the yielding of its fruit belongs only to that occurring in the mental continuum of worldlings, and not to the other.
Having thus divided the restlessness-accompanied [kamma] into two types—describing one as giving both kinds of result and the other as being entirely devoid of result—they explain it in this way.

As for their analysis herein, the refutation thereof, and the rejection of the opinion of those who maintain that there is no result whatsoever, all of that has not been stated here; it is found in works such as the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.
And particularly, it should be understood according to the method explained in the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*, the commentary on the *Abhidhammāvatāra*.

"In all places in the sense-sphere world" (*sabbatthāpi kāmaloke*) means in every part of the sense-sphere world, both in the happy destinies and the miserable destinies. "As appropriate" (*yathārahaṃ*) means in accordance with the doors and the objects.
Even in the states of misery, there is the resultant consciousness whose object is the great prosperity of *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and so forth, as well as that of the inhabitants of hell.
Resultant consciousness arises during such events as the sight of the Elder Mahāmoggallāna; this is the fruit of wholesome kamma alone.
For an undesirable result cannot possibly arise from unwholesome kamma. Indeed, it has been said:

"Bhikkhus, it is impossible, it is out of the question, that a desirable and pleasing result should accrue from unwholesome kamma. Therefore, even in the woeful states, wholesome kamma [produces its fruit].
It produces rootless resultant [consciousness]. Because there is no resultant consciousness of one plane arising from karma of another plane;

because it is impossible for the cultivation of dispassion toward sense-desires to produce a consciousness whose object is sense-desire craving; and because the sublime and supramundane wholesome states have exclusively similar results, there is no arising of rootless resultants through form-sphere karma;
thus, even in the fine-material world, [it produces] objects such as visible forms according to the circumstances.
"It produces them" refers to what was stated as "in all places within the sense-sphere world," and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to show that karma ripening in this way ripens in three ways—by way of sixteen, twelve, and eight [factors]—it was stated, "Even there," and so forth.
"Even there" means even when wholesome karma is ripening in this manner. "Exalted" (ukkaṭṭha) means...
It is distinguished either by being accompanied by wholesome states or by its subsequent occurrence through repetition.

For that karma which, at the time of its own occurrence, is surrounded by wholesome karmas occurring in the preceding and succeeding phases, or which is subsequently practiced through the attainment of repetition—that is superior.
However, that which at the time of performance is surrounded by unwholesome karmas, and subsequently...
Or, that which is permeated by the arising of remorse, thinking, "This was an evil deed committed by me," should be understood as "inferior.
"Rebirth-linking" (paṭisandhi) refers to only a single rebirth-linking; for there is no rebirth-linking in multiple births by means of a single kamma.
However, the result of the process (pavatti-vipāka) occurs even in a hundred births or a thousand births. As it is said: "A gift given to an animal..."

"Having given, a hundredfold reward should be expected. However, because in this case knowledge is the antidote to delusion—the cause of misfortune such as being born blind—or indeed to all unwholesome states, the kamma associated with it does not become a condition for such misfortunes.
Therefore, even though it may be extremely weak, if it is three-rooted (tihetuka), it draws forth only a two-rooted rebirth-linking (duhetuka-paṭisandhi), and never a rootless one (ahetuka).

And because it lacks association with knowledge (*ñāṇa*), double-rooted (*duhetuka*) kamma is incapable of producing the fruit of knowledge, just as unwholesome kamma—due to its lack of association with non-greed (*alobha*)—is incapable of producing the fruit of non-greed.
Thus, even when it is extremely intense, such double-rooted kamma draws only a double-rooted rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), not a triple-rooted one;
hence it is said: "The weak is triple-rooted, while the strong is double-rooted," and so forth.
Here it might be asked: Just as in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* it is said, "Through the excellence of destiny, rebirth occurs by way of the condition of eight roots associated with knowledge," so too,

there is rebirth associated with knowledge through the condition of eight roots— by way of three roots at the moment of impulsion of wholesome kamma, two roots at the moment of attachment, and three roots at the moment of rebirth-linking.

Likewise, regarding the statement: "In the case of a rebirth associated with a fortunate destination but dissociated from knowledge, rebirth occurs by way of six roots as conditions," this refers to a rebirth dissociated from knowledge through the condition of six roots:
two roots at the moment of impulsion (*javana*), two roots at the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), and two roots at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
Thus, "in the case of a fortunate destination, dissociated from knowledge... [the text continues].
Is it not the case that there is no drawing forth of a two-rooted rebirth-linking by a three-rooted [kamma], because it is not stated that rebirth occurs through the conditions of seven roots?

This is not so; for just as a weak two-rooted kamma [draws forth] an arooted rebirth-linking, so too a weak three-rooted kamma, by its own capacity, [draws forth] precisely a two-rooted rebirth-linking according to its suitability.
Because it ought to be given, however, the Great Elder left the reading incomplete in order to demonstrate that the result resembles the action.

Otherwise, since there would be no statement saying "the conditions for the four roots," it would follow that even rebirth without roots (ahetuka) could not occur through an action with two roots (duhetuka).
Therefore, just as in the case of a miserable rebirth, one avoids rebirth without roots—such as being born blind or deaf in a happy realm—by means of [actions with] roots...

It should be understood that rebirth with two roots (duhetuka) alone is mentioned for the purpose of showing rebirth with roots in a fortunate realm (gatisampatti), and not rebirth without roots (ahetuka);
likewise, rebirth with three roots (tihetuka) alone is mentioned by means of karma with three roots for the purpose of showing a result corresponding to the cause (kammasarikkhaka),
and not rebirth with two roots, but this is not because [rebirth with two roots] cannot be obtained.

74. Thus, having demonstrated the occurrence of resultant consciousness according to the doctrine of the Venerable Tipiṭaka-Cūḷanāga Thera— stating that by means of a single volition there are sixteen results,
wherein the twelvefold path and the eightfold path without roots (ahetuka) occur— it must now also be shown according to the doctrine of the Venerable Mahādhammarakkhita Thera,
resident of Moravāpi, who maintains that by means of a single volition there are twelve results, wherein the tenfold path and the eightfold path without roots occur.
To show this by way of example, it was said: "without effort" (*asaṅkhāra*) and "with effort-result" (*sasaṅkhāra-vipāka*), and so forth.
Just as when the face moves, the reflection of the face moves on the surface of a mirror, even so, for wholesome [kamma] without effort, there is only a result without effort, not one with effort;
thus, the distinction of effort is due to the very nature of its arrival. This is the intended meaning here. However, as for the distinction of effort regarding the result...
This is intended by way of condition, not by way of kamma; therefore, this particular doctrine has been formulated.
"Of these" means of those who hold such a view. "In due order" means according to the sequence of three-rooted, weak (kukkuṭṭha), and so forth.
"Twelve resultants" means, by way of three-rooted, weak, unprompted, and prompted kamma, respectively, [the twelve] excluding the prompted fourfold [set].
There are twelve resultant [consciousnesses] excluding the four unprompted (asaṅkhārika) sets;
likewise, ten resultants excluding both the prompted (sasaṅkhāra) and unprompted types associated with double-rooted (duhetuka) inferior (omaka) karma;
and eight resultants excluding the two double-rooted types associated with double-rooted superior (ukkaṭṭha) karma.
Following the method described above by the passage beginning with “tihetuka-mukkaṭṭha,” etc., recite [the suttas] according to their possibility, in accordance with what is appropriate for each.

75. That which is limited (*paritta*) is so called because it is, as it were, cut down on all sides and possesses little power. That which has been brought to an exalted state is *paṇīta* (exquisite).
That which exists between the two is the intermediate (*majjhima*).

Regarding this, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* without distinction that "merely acquired and not yet cultivated is limited (*paritta*)," and likewise: "not well-cultivated and lacking full mastery is intermediate;
but exceedingly well-cultivated and possessing complete mastery is sublime (*paṇīta*). However, the Teacher [Buddhaghosa] here...
It appears that even a slight degree of cultivation, provided it has been attained, is what is intended.
For instance, in the *Nāmarūpapariccheda* by Ācariya Anuruddha, it is said:
“When a similar cultivation has been attained and is present with great strength, But one does not attain such a cause, higher knowledge does not ripen.”

Having stated that sublime states (*mahaggata-dhammā*) give rise to results because they possess strength through the acquisition of repeated practice (*āsevana-lābha*) within their own plane, it was said that direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) does not ripen because that [condition] is absent.
Alternatively, what is produced by inferior desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation is "limited" (*paritta*);
by middling desire and so forth, it is "middling"; and by superior [desire and so forth], it is "exalted. Enough of this excessive elaboration.
"Having developed the fifth jhāna" means having developed all three types of the fifth jhāna that have not yet reached the state of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

However, the fact that for one who has attained the state of direct knowledge there is no result (*avipāka*) has been established by the Teacher (*ācariya*) through such passages as "not having obtained such [a state]," and so forth.
But the authors of the *Mūlaṭīkā* and others establish it otherwise. That, however, in brief, therein—
In this regard, the details should be understood according to the method explained in the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī*.

"Having developed dispassion toward perception" means: by seeing the disadvantage in the occurrence of the formless through such methods as "perception is a disease, perception is a tumor," or "the mind is wavering, the mind is distracted," and by determining that its absence constitutes a state of excellence.

According to the opinion of some, having developed the meditation on the fading away of the formless (*arūpavirāgabhāvanā*)—by means of the power of meditation upon either the air-kasina (*vāyokasiṇa*) or the limited space-kasina (*paricchinnākāsakasiṇa*), in order to bring about the non-arising nature of the formless which is to be attained by that [meditation]—those heretics who maintain the doctrine of the efficacy of karma (*kammakiriyavādin*) arise among other beings;
this is the intended meaning. Furthermore, they die here in whatever posture (*iriyāpatha*) they may have been in.
It should be understood that they are reborn there for that very reason.

86. As for the non-returners (anāgāmin), they arise in the Pure Abodes (suddhāvāsa). Thus, it is only the noble ones (ariya) who are non-returners—whether at the time they were ordinary worldlings (puthujjana) or later—having cultivated all three types of the fifth jhāna, according to the gradual sequence of the differences in their faculties such as faith.
They arise in the five Pure Abodes.
87. The construction is: "having developed [the jhānas] in successive order, they arise in the formless realms (ārūpya) in successive order.
"In successive order" means by way of the sequence beginning with the first formless attainment. And all of this is according to the specific, unique stage of each respective jhāna.

It has been said. However, when there is attachment (*nikanti*), ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*) and others are reborn anywhere—at any level included within the fine-material realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*)—according to the jhāna they have attained;
likewise, they may also be reborn in the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) by the power of sense-sphere karma.
For it is said: “The mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds, bhikkhus, because of its purity. But for a non-returner (*anāgāmin*), due to the complete [abandonment] of sensual lust...
Because they have abandoned attachment to sense-sphere existence (*kāma-bhava*), they do not generate it;

thus, they are reborn anywhere within the planes of jhāna as they have been attained, excluding the sense-world. For there is a fixed rule that only non-returners (*anāgāmin*) are reborn in the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*).
However, there is no fixed rule that they are not reborn elsewhere. And having established this, the Teacher said:
“Non-returner persons are reborn in the Suddhāvāsa [Pure Abode] realms;
those who have not attained the state of non-returning are born in the sense-sphere realm (kāmadhātu).
Furthermore, even these dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka) invariably produce meditative attainment (samāpatti) at the time of death, due to their concentration.

It should be understood as "the state of being one who fulfills [the conditions]. However, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "Whether they be noble (ariya) or non-noble, women who have attained the eight meditative attainments (aṭṭhasamāpatti) are reborn only among the Retinue of Brahmā (brahmapārisajja).

Furthermore, because the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and the fourth formless realm existences constitute the most excellent states of existence, noble ones born there do not arise elsewhere; likewise, among the remaining [realms], those higher and higher...
They are reborn in the Brahma-worlds, each in the lowest of the lower ones. For this was said by the Teacher:
“Established in the Vehapphala, Akaniṭṭha, and Bhavagga realms, All noble persons (ariyapuggala) are not born anywhere else again.”
"Those noble ones who have gone to the Brahma-world do not reappear below.
The commentary on the fourfold classification of kamma is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the sequence of death and rebirth-linking.

89. Regarding the phrases beginning with "by the exhaustion of the life-span" (*āyukkhayena*): although the power of karma remains, death due to the complete exhaustion of the life-span as it was determined for each respective realm of existence is "death by the exhaustion of the life-span" (*āyukkhayamaraṇa*).

Although there is still a remainder of the determined life-span in those various states, and the collection of conditions such as the time of the destiny (*gati*) is present, death occurs because the karma that accomplishes that particular existence has reached the completion of its fruition;
this is "death by the exhaustion of karma" (*kammakkhayamaraṇa*). [This refers to] the exhaustion of both the life-span and the karma.
Because both [the life-force and the kamma] perish simultaneously, death is "death by the destruction of both. Even though that [simultaneous destruction] exists,
for some whose continuity is severed by means such as being struck with a weapon through the power of a certain "severing kamma" established in a previous existence,
or for those whose capacity has been warded off by a severing kamma accumulated through some action performed against those great in virtue—

Death that occurs by being displaced from one’s position at that very moment—due to the fact that karma lacks the capacity to project a particular individual existence (attabhāva), as in the cases of Dusī Māra, Kalāburāja, and others—is called "death by interruption" (upacchedaka-maraṇa).
This, however, does not occur for denizens of hell, inhabitants of Uttarakuru, or certain deities. Thus it has been said:
“Either by violence or by some action that cuts short [life].
The arising and occurrence of death is “the arising of death.
90. At the time of death means at the moment proximate to death. “Accordingly” means in accordance with the beings who are to arise in their respective destinies (*gati*).

In some cases, however, for one whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava) and who does not give rise [to new kamma], only the phenomena of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and so forth as they have appeared go to the state of being the object of the final moments of death, and not kamma or the signs of kamma (kamma-nimitta) and so forth.
"Previously acquired" means acquired previously by way of seeing a shrine (cetiya) and so forth. "Serving as an instrument" means serving as an instrument by way of flowers and so forth.

"Upalabhitabbaṃ" means that which is to be experienced. "Upabhogabhūtaṃ" means that which is to be enjoyed, such as celestial nymphs (*accharā*), celestial palaces (*vimāna*), wish-fulfilling trees (*kapparukkha*), the fires of hell (*nirayaggi*), and so forth.
For the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) residing in celestial nymphs, celestial palaces, wish-fulfilling trees, the mother’s womb, and so on, is a sign of a happy destination (*sugati*).

That which resides in the fires of hell, the guardians of hell (*nirayapāla*), and so on, is a sign of an unhappy destination (*duggati*). A "sign of a destination" (*gatinimitta*) is a sign pertaining to a particular state of existence (*gati*).
"By the power of kamma" means by the influence of wholesome or unwholesome kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
"Of the six doors" refers, according to the method to be explained, to the six doors of rebirth as they occur;
if wholesome kamma ripens, then a pure wholesome consciousness (*kusala-citta*) occurs, but if unwholesome kamma does, then a defiled unwholesome consciousness occurs.
He said: "While it is ripening... [and so on] ...or defiled. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Bhikkhus, consciousness, while persisting, persists either clinging to the gratification in signs or clinging to the gratification in secondary characteristics.
If at that time one should die, it is possible that one would be reborn in one of two destinations."
“Or hell, or the animal realm. Regarding the phrase *tatthoṇataṃ vā*: it means as if bent toward that state of existence in which one is to be reborn;

or alternatively, the word-division is *tatthoṇataṃ eva*. As for the intention behind the term *bāhullena* (by way of majority), it should be understood according to the method stated in the passage beginning with *yebhuyyena bhavantare* (for the most part in another existence).
Alternatively, that [intention] can be understood by the very expression *yathārahaṃ* (as appropriate).

Regarding the phrase "as a means of inclusion": by the word "for the most part" (*bāhullena*), it is understood that this indicates [the practice] is not constant, unlike those whose lives are suddenly cut short who die as if slowly.
"By way of making it new" (*abhinavakaraṇavasena*) means by way of making oneself new, as if it were being done at that very moment.

91. "Of one whose death is imminent" means of one whose death is near due to a lifespan of the measure of a single cognitive process (*vīthicitta*), or of one whose death is near due to a lifespan slightly longer than that.

"At the conclusion of the cognitive process" means at the end of those cognitive processes that conclude with the registration consciousness (*tadārammaṇa*) or those that conclude with the impulsion (*javana*).
In this regard, for those who, having passed away from the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*), are reborn in that very same place, [the processes] conclude with the registration consciousness.
"For the others, [they cease] at the conclusion of the impulsion," as stated in the *Dhammānusāraṇī*. "At the exhaustion of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*)" means:
if there were more than one cognitive series (*javana-vīthi*) remaining of the life-span, then it arises and ceases at the end of the life-continuum;

but if there were only one moment of consciousness remaining of the life-span, then it ceases at the end of the cognitive-series consciousness, and that [consciousness] has only past kamma and so forth as its object. By the phrase "immediately after that,"...
He rejects the doctrine of those who maintain the existence of an intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

"According to what is appropriate" means in accordance with the time for performing an action and the time for the yielding of its result. Alternatively, it means according to the maturing karma, by way of underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), or by way of being co-nascent with the impulsive moment (*javana*);
that is to say, in accordance with the mode of occurrence. But is it not said: "enveloped by the underlying tendency of ignorance," and so forth?
It has been said. But how can there be the state of underlying tendency (*anusaya*) for those things co-nascent with the impulsive moment (*javana*)?

This is not a fault, because they too are designated as "underlying tendencies" due to their similarity to the underlying tendencies. Otherwise, there would be no inclusion of those things co-nascent with unwholesome karma, or those co-nascent with craving for existence, or those co-nascent with the impulsive moments immediately preceding death.
Because ignorance itself persists and continues to exist in the sense of being unabandoned, it is an underlying tendency; and by that which is thus encompassed...
"Encompassed. It has "craving as its root" (*taṇhānusayamūlaka*) because craving itself is the root, the primary factor, and the concomitant cause of this [existence].

"By volitional formations" (*saṅkhārena*) means by wholesome or unwholesome kamma, or by the collection of phenomena such as contact that arise together with that kamma, or by those arising together with the javana-mind-moments proximate to death; it is that which is being generated by these.
For craving directs [the mind] toward objects whose dangers are concealed by ignorance, and it is designated as the "volitional formation" that hurls [one into existence].
The aforementioned formations hurl [beings] forth, as it has been said:
"By those born together with ignorance, craving, and formations— which obscure the danger of sense objects and do not allow one to see— beings go to states of woe."
“By those [factors] not yet abandoned, there is the concealing and the inclining of the remaining ones;
moreover, the formations are swift, and they become exclusively wholesome.
Regarding “being grasped by associated factors”: this means being grasped by the factors associated with itself, such as contact and so forth, through the condition of association and the like.
When it is grasped while being surrounded, it becomes the precursor by way of its status as the foundation for those factors that arise simultaneously;
thus, it is the primary factor through its state of being the support for those co-arising phenomena. For it is said: "Phenomena are preceded by the mind.
By way of the linking of different existences means by way of the linking together of the preceding existence and the subsequent existence as if they were a single continuous chain.
It is established at the very moment of its arising; the intention is not that it goes from here to another place.

For no phenomenon included within a previous existence transmigrates to another existence, nor does it arise without causes included within a previous existence, like an echo, a lamp, or a seal-impression. Enough of this excessive elaboration.

92. "Slowly occurring" means those that proceed slowly. The intended meaning is that when present objects have come into the range of the sense-doors, [these consciousnesses arise] by way of the sign of movement in the mind-door, and by way of the sign of action in the five doors.
Since even rebirth-linking and the life-continuum possess present objects, first, in the case of the mind-door, there are four types of life-continuum following rebirth-linking.
However, in the case of the five doors, the state of having a present object is obtained only at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For instance,

when someone’s death-consciousness (*cuticitta*) arises immediately after a cognitive process (*cittavīthi*)— which culminates in registration (*tadārammaṇa*)— has arisen in the mind-door with respect to a present sign of destiny (*gatinimitta*) that has entered its range, then, in the very next moment, within an object lasting for five mind-moments...

The occurrence with respect to a present object occurs in the rebirth-linking that follows immediately after the death-consciousness— which lasts for a single mind-moment and occurs upon an object [determined] by the four life-continuum moments following the active rebirth-linking,

as well as by the mental process occurring appropriately regarding the color and other qualities of the gifts presented by kinsmen and others at the five sense-doors. This is the occurrence with respect to a present object.

"It is apprehended"—this is the summary here; the detailed explanation, however, should be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, in the commentary on the *Vibhaṅga*, or in the commentary on the section concerning "consciousness conditioned by formations. Regarding "apprehended by the six doors":
the sign of the deed (*kamma-nimitta*) is apprehended by the six doors, and the sign of the destination (*gati-nimitta*) is apprehended by the sixth door, as applicable.
It should be applied [in this way]. However, others explain it without making such distinctions. With that same intention, it is stated in the *Saccasaṅkhepa*:
"There may be a junction at the five doors, even without karma, when there is a double range.
But in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, because it is said, "The sign of the destiny comes into the range of the mind-door," [this refers] to the registration consciousness.
Furthermore, because the rebirth-linking consciousness of the five doors has not been shown [in that context], and because the *Mūlaṭīkā* and other works have specifically stated—defining it thus:

"The visible-object base (vaṇṇāyatana) presented by the power of kamma becomes an object of the mind-door alone, as in the case of one seeing a dream or through the divine eye"—the teachers do not accept their [opposing] statement. [This refers to the phrase: "And the present..."

In this context, while it is appropriate for the sign of destiny (*gatinimitta*) to have a present object, the sign of kamma (*kammanimitta*) is intended here as the sign of the very kamma that produces rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
How, then, could its status as a present object be possible when it has been grasped by the impulsions (*javana*) immediately preceding death?
For it cannot be the case that the very same thing which presents the object is also the producer of rebirth-linking, because of the absence of the state of having been accumulated (*upacita*).

And because of its being relished. For, according to the statement, "Because it has been done and accumulated," it is precisely karma that has been repeatedly practiced which draws forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

Furthermore, since in the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* it is stated that even for a rebirth-linking with roots, two roots serve as conditions at the moment of attachment (*nikanti*), karma that has been done and accumulated is indeed relished by craving (*taṇhā*).
When it produces its result, how could the javanas occurring at the moment of death—occurring in the same cognitive series as the rebirth-linking consciousness—be considered repeatedly practiced?
And how could they be touched by the dark [kamma] at that time?
Furthermore, the present kamma-sign is the object of the five-door javanas occurring near the moment of death.
It is true that it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: “Kamma pertaining to the five doors does not become the object of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi-nimitta*) because of its extreme weakness.

However, since death can occur while flowers and other offerings presented by kinsmen and others are still present, there is the possibility of rebirth-linking occurring with respect to their color and so forth.
This refers to those [mental states] capable of producing rebirth-linking that arise in the portion preceding the death-proximate cognitive process (*cuti-āsanna-vīthi*).

Because it is equal in status to the object of the javanas occurring at the mind-door, even that which is grasped by the death-proximate javana—though it has fallen within the same single continuum—is described as "present" in the sense of being a kamma-nimitta, such as a visible form and so forth. And having established this, the teacher Ānanda stated:
"And in the case of the five doors, the present kamma-nimitta that comes into range [is grasped] within the continuum of the object of the action performed in proximity."
"Arising" and "similar to that" should be understood [in this way]. 94.
*Yathārahaṃ* (accordingly): in accordance with the second, fourth, first, and third types of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). 98.
After death from the formless realm (*ārūppa*), there are rebirth-linkings in the formless realms—excluding the lower formless realms—for those who attain higher and higher formless states.

Because there is no accumulation of lower and lower kamma, and because access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) is powerful, the resultant rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*) are those with the three roots of the sense-sphere (*kāma-tihetuka*).

Following death (*cuti*) in the fine-material sphere (*rūpāvacara*), there may be rebirth-linkings with two roots or three roots—excluding those without roots—solely through the power of access concentration.
Following death from a sense-sphere state with three roots, all [subsequent rebirths] included within the sense, fine-material, and immaterial realms [are likewise determined].

Accordingly, there may be rootless (*ahetuka*) and other types of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). For the other [type of being], after death from a double-rooted or rootless state, there may be triple-rooted and other types of rebirth-linking only within the sense-sphere existences (*kāma-bhava*).
The commentary on the sequence of death and rebirth-linking is concluded.
99. "Immediately after the cessation of rebirth-linking" means immediately after the cessation of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-nirodhānantara*).
"That very same consciousness" refers to it being designated as such because of its similarity [to the preceding], just as one says, "those very same medicines.
"When there is no arising of process-consciousnesses" means when there is no arising of process-consciousnesses at intervals; having become the death-consciousness (*cuti-citta*), it ceases.
"That very mind" is the connection [of the sentence].
101. "They turn and proceed" means they continue until the complete cutting off of the root of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). 102.

Just as in this present existence there is rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), the cognitive processes (*vīthi*), and the death-moment (*cuti*), so too in another future existence.
The construction is as follows: "This continuity of consciousness (cittasantati) revolves in such a manner, beginning with rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) and the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).

However, some maintain that because only the treatment of the "extra-stream" (vīthimutta) is shown in this section, it is more appropriate here to include only rebirth-linking, the life-continuum, and death;

thus, they interpret the phrase "rebirth-linking, life-continuum, and cognitive processes" (paṭisandhibhavaṅgavīthiyo) as "the flow of rebirth-linking and the life-continuum" (paṭisandhibhavaṅgappavāhā).

They say it is for the sake of the goal; however, that is merely their opinion, because at the conclusion of the demonstration of the inclusion of the process, the intention is to provide a concluding summary for everything included therein.

For if this were the case, the reference by means of the word "this" (*etaṃ*) to everything [previously mentioned] in the passage, "But having reflected, this is not lasting," would be perfectly appropriate. This refers to what has been stated above.
Having reflected upon and contemplated the round of existence as unstable, impermanent, and subject to dissolution,
the wise and enlightened ones, having long been well-disciplined, attain the deathless, stable, and unchanging state of Nibbāna;
and having realized it through the knowledge of the path and its fruit, they thereby completely sever the bonds of attachment and enter the equal element of Nibbāna without residue.
They will exist; they will attain [it].
Thus ends the commentary on the Chapter on the Modes Apart from the Cognitive Series (*vīthimutta*) within the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, titled *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
6. Explanation of the Analysis of Matter (Rūpapariccheda) 1.

Having thus first shown the two-fold Abhidhamma subject matter by way of consciousness and mental factors, he now begins to show matter and, immediately following that, Nibbāna, saying "At this point," and so forth.
[This is] by way of enumeration, exposition, and detailed exposition, including their classifications and modes of occurrence.

Since mental states (citta) and mental factors (cetasika) have been analyzed by way of five divisions— those possessing the distinctions stated by way of three divisions, and those possessing the occurrence described by way of two divisions, namely, occurrence (pavatti) and rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi)—
the connection [of the following] is: "Now, matter (rūpa) will be explained according to its sequence."
2. Now, in order to establish the matrix (*mātikā*) for the purpose of analyzing matter as it was promised, the words beginning with "enumeration" (*samuddesa*) are stated.
Briefly, *samuddesa* means enumeration. *Vibhāga* means analysis by way of singlefold categories and so forth. *Samuṭṭhāna* means that from which [matter] arises or originates;
these are the conditions that generate matter, such as kamma and the rest. *Kalāpas* refers to groups such as the eye-decad and so forth. This is according to the sequence of their occurrence.

And thus, according to the classification of beings by way of the periods of existence and the sequence of the arising of material phenomena. This concludes the commentary on the summary of matter. 3.

Having become great through the elements together with their constituent parts within the continua of both the clung-to (upādinnā) and the unclung-to (anupādinnā), they have manifested; thus they are called "beings" (bhūtā).

The great elements (*mahābhūtā*). Alternatively, they are called "great elements" because they possess great wonders through the display of various kinds of extraordinary qualities, or because they display many non-existent things;

or because these [elements] contain great wonders or non-existent things, as in the case of illusionists and the like. Because they themselves lack an intrinsic nature such as blue and yet appear as the perception of derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) such as blue, they are called "great elements.
Or else, they are deceivers of sentient beings by means of pleasing colors, shapes, and so forth.

They are called "great elements" (*mahābhūtā*) because great non-existent things (*abhūtāni*) exist within them, since they deceive beings by appearing as agreeable objects such as the forms of desirable men, like the *yakkhinī* and others.
For it has been said: "They are 'great' because they have manifested, or they are called 'great elements' because they are equal to the great."
“Because of their deceptive nature through falsehood, they are called ‘great elements’ (mahābhūtā).
Alternatively, they are called *mahābhūtā* because the derivative forms (*upādārūpa*) exist within them as something great, and they themselves are elemental (*bhūta*).
Form that proceeds by depending upon the great elements is derivative form (*upādāyarūpa*). If this is so, [then] in dependence on one great element...
[Objection: From such statements as "Then the great elements... and so forth, each individual great element serves as a support for the remaining great elements;
therefore, does this not entail that they too possess the nature of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)? [Reply:

This is not so, because the designation is established only for those material phenomena that proceed by depending [on the great elements]. For that which depends upon the great elements and is itself depended upon by others is not derived matter. However, that which...

It is indeed derived, yet it is not derived by anything; thus, that very thing is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), and there is no possibility of applying that designation to the primary elements (*bhūta*).
Furthermore, since it is "derived matter from the four great elements," it possesses the characteristic of derived matter;
therefore, there is no lack of derived-matter-ness in those things that proceed as derived.
