4. In the sense of extending (*pathana*), it is "earth" (*pathavī*). Like natural earth such as trees and mountains, it manifests—meaning it stands forth—as the basis for the co-nascent material phenomena.

It is called "earth-element" (*pathavī-dhātu*) because it is earth itself as an element, due to its maintenance of its own characteristic and so forth, and because, in the sense of being devoid of a sentient being or a soul, it resembles the elements that constitute the parts of a body or a rock. It brings forth and extends the co-nascent material phenomena.

It comes together (*āpāyati*), or it coheres (*brūheti*), or it increases (*vaḍḍheti*); thus, it is *āpo*. It heats (*tejeti*) and ripens (*paripāceti*), or it settles (*niseti*) by means of its sharpness, warming the other three elements;
thus, it is *tejo*. It blows (*vāyati*) and carries the aggregate of elements to different locations; thus, it is *vāyo*.
Furthermore, these four should be understood as having, respectively, the characteristics of hardness, cohesion, heat, and distension.

5. The etymological meaning of "eye" (*cakkhu*) and the other [faculties] has already been explained above. What is called "sensory matter" (*pasāda-rūpa*) is so named because it is caused by the clarity of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

Furthermore, that [sensory matter], in its respective order, is characterized by the clarity of the elements originated by kamma, having as its proximate cause the desire to see, the desire to hear, the desire to smell, the desire to taste, and the desire to touch.
Among these, the eye first resides in the location where the bodily shape arises for those standing directly in front, at a point in the center of the black pupil the size of a louse's head.
Like a prince who has spread out seven layers of fine cloth over layers of cotton wool and is supported by four nurses— whose duties are holding, bathing, adorning, and fanning—
this body is assisted by the four elements whose functions are supporting, binding, maturing, and moving, is sustained by temperature, mind, and nutriment, and is maintained by life-force.
Surrounded by color and other qualities, it functions according to its respective role as the basis and door for eye-consciousness and the rest;
the other is called the "eye with its constituent parts. Likewise, the ear and the others function in their respective order:

the ear is within the ear-cavity, having the shape of a finger-ring and being covered with fine, thin, brown hair; the nose is within the nostril, shaped like a goat’s hoof; and in the middle of the tongue...

They occur pervading a portion of the body shaped like the tip of a lotus petal; however, setting that aside, they occur covering the rest of the entire body—excluding the locations where the fire born of karma (*kammaja-tejo*) is established, as well as the hair-tips, body-hair-tips, nail-tips, and dry skin.
Even so, there is no confusion between this [fire] and the others, because their bases and characteristics are distinct. This is true even for those [fires] that share a common basis.
For visible forms, tastes, and so forth are unmixed by way of their distinct characteristics; how much more so, then, are the sensitive organs (pasāda) which have different bases?
Because it is impossible to touch the water element due to its subtle nature, it is said: "The water element is excluded from what is comprised by the [other] three elements.
For although coldness is perceived through touch, that is actually only heat (tejo). When it is weak...
For indeed, there is the perception of cold in what is hot because of the absence of any quality designated as "coldness.

This is understood from the instability of the perception of cold, just as in the case of the near and far shores. For instance, those who stand in the heat during the summer season and then enter the shade have the perception of cold;
yet for those who remain in that very same place for a long time, there arises the perception of heat. And if it were the water element...
Coldness might be perceived within a single aggregate together with the state of heat;

however, it is not so perceived. Therefore, it is understood that "the water element is not coldness. As for those who say, "The water element is fluidity, and that is apprehended by touch," they should be told:
"That which is called fluidity is apprehended by touch—this [is what] the Venerable Ones [hold]."
“[The world] is intoxicated by conceit regarding its own configuration. For this was said by the ancients:
“Touching the three elements that dwell together with the divine, this world conceives the conceit: ‘I am touching the divine.’”
"Just as one who grasps with the mind the shape of a being after having touched it, so too should a deity be understood [to be known] through the thought, 'I touch it directly.

That which is called "objective form" (gocararūpa) is so named because it is the objective domain of the five types of consciousness. It is called "range" (gocara) because the sense faculties (indriya) move within it.

For this is the name for an object (*ārammaṇa*). Moreover, these five types [of objects] have, respectively, the characteristic of being the domain (*gocara*) of eye-consciousness and so forth, or the characteristic of impinging upon the eye and so forth. 7.

The state of a woman is femininity (*itthatta*); the state of a man is masculinity (*purisatta*). Therein, [femininity] has the characteristic of being the cause of female gender marks, signs, postures, and deportment.
"Female state" (*itthatta*) refers to masculinity (*purisatta*), characterized by being the cause for the male gender-mark and so forth.

In this context, the female sex organ is the "female gender-mark" (*itthiliṅga*). It is the female sign (*itthinimitta*) because it serves as the condition for the perception "woman" in one who intends [to perceive] a woman. The movement, sitting, and so forth of one who is not clear-minded constitute "female gestures" (*itthikutta*). The female physical form is the "female appearance" (*itthākappa*).
The male gender-mark and the rest should also be understood according to the method already stated.
In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, the feminine gender and so forth are described differently. Summarizing that, they say:
“The gender (*liṅga*) is the shape of the hands and so on; the sign (*nimitta*) is the smile and so on;
the sport (*kutta*) is playing with a shuttlecock and so on; and the deportment (*ākappa*) is the manner of walking and so on.”

It is called "of the nature of existence" (*bhāvarūpa*) because by means of it there occurs such designations as "woman" and so forth, and because it constitutes the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, this [heart-base] remains pervading the entire body, just like the body-faculty (*kāyindriya*).

8. It is the "heart-base" (*hadayavatthu*) because the heart itself is the physical basis (*vatthu*) for the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*). For it is characterized by being the support for those two elements; and that [base] is the size of half a *pasata* within the cavity of the heart.
It occurs depending upon the blood. Although this has not been mentioned in the *Rūpakaṇḍa*, its existence should be understood from both scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yutti*).
In that regard, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) proceed depending upon that material form:
"That material form which, by way of being a support-condition (*nissayapaccaya*), [serves] for the mind-element, the mind-consciousness-element, and the states associated with them..."
The word *āgama* refers to the statement from the *Paṭṭhāna* that has come down thus: "condition. As for the *yutti*, it should be understood as follows:
"The two elements of the realm of desire and form, which are produced, substantial, and serve as a basis, persist in association with material form, just like eye-consciousness and the rest."
“These [mental states] are not dependent on the eye and so forth, because they have that [consciousness] as their support;
nor are they dependent on visible forms and so forth, because they also occur externally.
Nor is life itself [the support], because it is occupied with other functions.”
And there are not two entities therein, even though it proceeds when [the object] is non-existent.
Therefore, knowing that "it is the basis" (vatthu) and "it is the becoming" (bhūti),
this is a distinction in teaching due to the pair of basis and object.
"In the recitation of the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, it was not explained by the Great Seer.

It is called "life" (*jīvita*) because beings live by means of it. Precisely that [life] is the "life-faculty" (*jīvitindriya*) because of its sovereignty (*ādhipacca*) in the maintenance of material form born of kamma.
For it has the characteristic of maintaining material form born of kamma. Even for those things that persist only for their own respective moments, [it performs this function].
For it is indeed as the cause for the maintenance of co-nascent [phenomena] that it acts as their protector.

For karma alone is not the cause of their persistence, just as food and so forth are for those born from nutriment and so on, because of the absence of that [sustaining] function at the very moment of the karma's occurrence.
This [heat], however, proceeds by pervading the entire acquired body along with the digestive fire.
10. Because it is swallowed after being made into a mouthful, it is called "edible food" (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*); this is stated in order to show that food has a physical basis.

However, the nutritive essence (*ojā*)—which is the cause for the support of the body together with its sense faculties, which follows through every limb and member, and which consists of the moisture of swallowed food—is what is meant here by "nutritive material form" (*āhāra-rūpa*). For it is characterized precisely by its state as the cause for the support of the body together with its sense faculties.
Or, it is characterized by the extraction of the eightfold material qualities such as *ojā*.
11. It is called "materiality by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvarūpa*) because it is apprehended through its own respective individual essence, such as hardness and so forth.

It is "possessing characteristics" (*salakkhaṇa*) because it is accompanied by characteristics such as arising and so forth, or impermanence and so forth. Without the state of delimitation and so forth, [it exists] through itself...

It is called "derived matter" (nipphā-rūpa) because it is produced by conditions such as kamma through its very intrinsic nature. Matter has the intrinsic nature of being subject to transformation (ruppana);
therefore, that which is associated with this [nature] is also matter, just as one says "the noble person" (ariyasava) or "blue lotus" (nīluppala).

Since this word *rūpa* occurs even for things that do not possess that intrinsic nature by way of conventional usage (ruḷhi), it is specified by another word *rūpa* and thus called "matter-matter" (*rūpa-rūpa*), just as one says "suffering-suffering" (*dukkha-dukkha*).

It is "comprehension-form" (*sammasana-rūpa*) because it is worthy of being comprehended by means of applying the three characteristics, since it is apprehended as its own intrinsic nature even after transcending states such as delimitation. 12.

It is not cut (*na kassati*) thus it is space (*ākāsa*). Space itself is "space" (*ākāsa*); it is an "element" (*dhātu*) in the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva-ṭṭhena*), thus it is the "space-element" (*ākāsadhātu*). [This refers to] the material phenomena included within each individual group (*kalāpa*), such as the eye-decad and so forth.

Limiting materiality (*pariccheda-rūpa*) is that which delimits by way of producing a state of non-intermixture with other material groups, or that which is delimited by them, or the mere delimitation of those [groups]. For it acts as if it were delimiting each respective material group.
And even though there exists a state of contact between material groups belonging to one group and those belonging to another group, [it still functions as a delimiter].
Space is the state of being secluded from this or that form; it is the limit of form. And it is not touched by those very forms which constitute its boundary.
Otherwise, there would be no such delimitation, because those forms would attain a state of pervasiveness. Non-pervasiveness indeed constitutes non-contact.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "It is untouched by the four great elements."
13. That which makes known one’s intention by means of a moving body, and which itself is made known by that [body], is bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

That which makes known one’s intention by means of speech—consisting of vocal sounds accompanied by consciousness—and which itself is made known by that [speech], is verbal intimation (*vacīviññatti*).

In this context, [bodily intimation] is that which, acting as a cooperative cause for the stiffening, supporting, and movement produced by the air-element (*vāyodhātu*) originated by the consciousness that generates walking and so forth, is distinct from the air-element that is the cause of the quivering of the quivering body.

Bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) is the modification perceived as the condition for the quivering of the material body, like the exertion of one lifting a large stone with all one's might at the moment of grasping it.

For that [intimation] makes known the intention by means of the quivering body. Indeed, in the case of tree-shaking and so forth—which are devoid of such intimating modifications—one does not say, "He is causing this."

“The seeing” refers to the grasping of the intention (*adhippāya*). And in the case of hand-movements and so forth, because they are grasped by the mental-door impulsions (*manodvāra-javana*) occurring immediately after the imperceptible [impulsions] following the perception of the flickering body, they are themselves cognized by the body.
But how do hand-movements and so forth occur by way of intimation (*viññatti*)? It is said: in the cognitive process (*vīthi*) consisting of a single adverting [consciousness].

Among the seven impulsion moments, the air element produced by the seventh impulsion, accompanied by the transformation of intimation, causes that which is born of consciousness to move by acting as the cause for its arising in another location, having received support from the air elements produced by the first and subsequent impulsions.
However, those produced by the preceding impulsions serve merely to provide stability and maintenance as an aid to it. For just as with seven yokes...
When a cart is to be pulled, only the oxen yoked to the seventh yoke move the cart, having received support from the oxen yoked to the six yokes below;
however, those yoked to the first yoke and so forth merely provide the necessary support and stability, thus acting as an assistance to them.
This should be understood in the same way.
And here, "motion" is simply arising in another location, because there is no transference of phenomena even by the measure of a hair-tip from the place where they have arisen.
Otherwise, their lack of activity and their momentariness would not be possible.

And "being the cause for arising in another location" means that, just as co-nascent material phenomena [arise] elsewhere than the place established by the material phenomena originated by the preceding impulsion (*javana*).

They arise; thus it should be understood that they arise there together with them. In this context, however, when there is movement born of consciousness (*cittaja*), the other [element] also moves through connection with it, like a dry lump of cow dung thrown into the current of a river.

Even those wind-elements produced by the first impulsion (*paṭhamajavana*) and so forth, which are unable to move [the body] in that way, are indeed accompanied by the transformation of informative intimation (*viññatti*). By means of which...
Because this [directional part] is capable of undergoing a modification toward the state of being directed toward that [object], it desires to perform the acts of approaching and so forth.
And by establishing it thus, he will later state that even the adverting of the mind-door possesses the quality of originating intimation (*viññatti*).

Vocal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*) is a single modification which, acting as a condition through impact, occurs together with the derived matter (*upādinnarūpa*) located at the site of syllable-production within the earth-element originated by the consciousness that produces vocal differentiation.
Whatever needs to be said here should be understood according to the method already stated for bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).

However, this is the distinction: just as there it was said, "immediately after the grasping of the quivering body," so here it should be construed as "immediately after hearing the sound being heard.
And here, because of the absence of stiffening and so forth, the method beginning with "arisen from the seventh impulsion" (*sattamajavanasamuṭṭhita*) applies.
It is not obtained. For sound arises simultaneously with the impact itself; and such impact is indeed obtainable even in the case of the first impulsion (*javana*) and those that follow.

And here, just as when one sees forms such as cow-heads or palm-leaf fans made by gluing them together, there arises at the mind-door a cognitive process (*manodvāra-vīthi*) occurring immediately thereafter whose sequence is imperceptible, and which serves as a mnemonic sign (*saññāṇa*) for the cow-heads and so forth in the form of their association with water.
Just as there is the grasping of water by taking hold of the vessel, so too, by grasping the sound of the body as it is uttered while quivering,

there is the grasping of the intentional modification through the mental-door process— which arises immediately thereafter, is imperceptible in its interval, and possesses a relationship established by what preceded it;
this is the simile common to both.
14. Lightness is *lahubhāva*; malleability is *mudutā*; wieldiness is *kammaññatā*.
These should be understood, respectively, as the lack of heaviness in material phenomena like that of one who is healthy; their lack of rigidity like well-polished leather;
and their state of being suitable for bodily activities like well-refined gold. For even though this triad of lightness and so forth does not mutually abandon one another—
The diversity [of material phenomena] is spoken of in terms of their various specific modifications.
Lightness (*lahutā*) is a modification of matter produced by conditions that are the opposites of the disturbance of the elements that cause rigidity.

Pliancy (*mudutā*) is produced by conditions that are the opposites of the disturbance of the elements that cause stiffness. Agility (*kammaññatā*) is produced by conditions that are the opposites of the disturbance of the elements that cause a state unfavorable to bodily activities.
15. Accumulation (*upacaya*) means piling up; it has the sense of "the first piling," as the prefix *upa-* indicates the sense of "first" in words such as *upaññatta* ("first laid down").

Continuity (*santati*) means a continuous flow; it has the sense of a succession. Therein, the arising of material phenomena from the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) until the emergence of the decads of the eye and so forth is called accumulation. Beyond that is continuity.
[The term] *nāma*. Aging (*jarā*) is the process of decaying by way of the state of being oriented toward cessation in those material phenomena (*rūpa*) that each abide for only a moment;

that very [aging] is "age-ness" (*jaratā*). It is "impermanent" (*anicca*) because it should not be approached as permanent or stable; its state is "impermanence" (*aniccatā*), which is the disintegration of matter.
It is called "characteristic-form" (*lakkhaṇarūpa*) because it serves as the cause of the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) of phenomena according to their respective states.
16. "Only the form of birth" (*jātirūpa*): Because of the state of arising moment by moment of material phenomena starting from rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it is designated as "birth.
Furthermore, because its existence is bound to the fourfold continuity of matter through the state of the arising of matter, it is reckoned as "matter.

It is spoken of as the "continuity of accumulation" (*upacaya-santati*) according to the distinction in the modes of occurrence known as the first and subsequent cessations, in accordance with those to be trained (*veneyya*).

Because it is stated after analyzing [the terms] as "accumulation" (*upacaya*) and "continuity" (*santati*). And having done so, in order to show that there is no difference in meaning between them in their respective expositions, it is said:
"That which is the accumulation of the sense bases (*āyatana*) is the accumulation of matter; that which is the accumulation of matter is the continuity of matter.
"Even elevenfold" means even in eleven modes by way of homogeneous inclusion (*sabhāga-saṅgaha*).

17. The four primary elements, the five sensitive organs, the four objects, the two kinds of being, and heart-matter—these, together with the two [factors] of life-force and nutriment, constitute eighteen kinds.
Likewise, there is delimitation, the two kinds of intimation, the three kinds of transformation, and the four kinds of characteristics;
these exist separately from the states of delimitation, transformation, and so forth among material phenomena.
Because they are not produced by conditions, these ten are "unproduced" (anipphanna); thus, there would be twenty-eight kinds [of matter].
The commentary on the enumeration of matter is finished.
The commentary on the classification of matter.
18. Now, in order to show the method of the singlefold and so forth for those [factors] as they have been enumerated, it is said:
"And all this... and so on. It is "rootless" (*ahetuka*) due to the absence of associated roots such as non-greed (*alobha*).

It is "with conditions" (*sappaccaya*) because it possesses its own respective conditions. It is "with taints" (*sāsava*) because it is accompanied by the taints of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*) and so forth that arise with reference to a self. By means of conditions...

It is "conditioned" (*saṅkhata*) because it is constructed (*abhisaṅkhatattā*). It is "mundane" (*lokiya*) because it is connected with the world known as the aggregates of clinging (*upādānakkhandha*).

It is "belonging to the sense sphere" (*kāmāvacara*) because it ranges within the craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmataṇhā*). It is "without an object" (*anārammaṇa*) because, unlike immaterial phenomena, it does not grasp any object.

It is "not to be abandoned" (*appahātabba*) because it cannot be abandoned by means of the "factor-abandonment" (*tadaṅga*) and other such methods. The word "iti" [indicates the end of the definition].
This is the sense of "mode" (*pakāra*); by means of it, the entire singlefold method beginning with "the indeterminate" (*abyākata*) is subsumed.
19. Internal material form (*ajjhattika-rūpa*) so called because it occurs in reference to or directed toward the self (*attānaṃ*) designated as the personal existence (*attabhāva*).
Granted that there are other things produced internally, yet by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhī*), only the eye and so forth are "internal. Now...

Or, because they are of such exceptional service to the personal existence (*attabhāva*), as if saying, "If we do not exist, you will be like a mere wooden post," the eye and so forth are specifically called "internal" (*ajjhattika*).
Alternatively, it is "internal" because it functions as the door for the mind, which is designated as the "self";
that very [mind] is the internal. Because they are external to that, [the objects] are external.
The other is twenty-three-fold external matter.
(20) The other is twenty-two-fold non-basis matter.
(22) All eight kinds of faculty-matter possess predominance because they exercise sovereignty over the five consciousnesses, over the gender signs, and over the maintenance of co-nascent matter.
For the fivefold translucent matter exercises sovereignty over eye-consciousness and the rest by means of its own sharpness, dullness, and so forth, because it induces sharpness, dullness,
and so forth in them as well. Furthermore, both types of sex characteristics exercise sovereignty over the feminine gender and so forth,
because even when those [characteristics] arise from their respective conditions, they for the most part arise in that particular form only within a continuum whose nature is already established.

But it is not so by way of being a faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*). Furthermore, life-force (*jīvita*) has predominance in the protection of what is produced by karma, because their respective momentary states are dependent upon the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*).
And it proceeds by its own connection with the phenomena established by itself, like a boatman.
23. It is gross material form (*oḷārika-rūpa*) because of its coarseness due to having attained the state of being an object and a subject.
Precisely for that reason, it is called proximate form (*āsanna-rūpa*) or near form, because it is easy to apprehend.

That which is the state of being face-to-face with those that have arrived—both by way of their own nature and by way of dependence—and the mutual falling upon one another, is "resistance" (*paṭigha*), as if there were a striking against one another. For just as when there is a striking...
There is a movement of that which is weak; thus, when they are in a state of mutual opposition, there is a movement of the weak life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) because it lacks a material nature.
That which possesses resistance is "with resistance" (*sappaṭigha*). In this context, the excellence belongs to the tangible object itself;
by way of its support, the excellence belongs to the nose, tongue, and body, along with odors, tastes, and tangibles; yet in both cases, there is no excellence [in the consciousness].

It should be understood that [this refers to] the eye, ear, visible forms, and sounds. The other sixteenfold [category], such as subtle matter and so forth, is so called because it lacks the nature of grossness and the rest.

24. The eighteenfold clung-to matter (*upādinnarūpa*) is born from kamma; it is so called because it has been taken up and grasped by kamma endowed with craving and views as its own fruit. The other tenfold unclung-to matter (*anupādinnarūpa*) is so called by way of a negative compound (*na-upādinnarūpa*). 25.

That which exists together with a demonstration (*nidassana*), defined as the state of being visible, is "with-demonstration" (*sanidassana*). This refers to the state of being the objective domain of eye-consciousness.

"Visible" (*sanidassana*) is said [in the compound] together with "demonstrable" (*nidassana*). Although that [visible object] is not different from the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), it is appropriate to speak of it as if it were something else in order to distinguish it from other phenomena; thus, it is "with demonstration.

For when phenomena have become unified through their commonality of being "phenomena" (*dhamma*), it is fitting to apply a metaphorical designation (*upacara*) to that specific distinction which creates differentiation, treating it as if it were something else.
For in this way there is an understanding of the specific meaning.
26. "By way of not reaching" means by way of the object-sphere not reached by oneself, or by way of not reaching the region of the sense-object oneself.
For the eye and ear do not reach visible forms and sounds; or rather, they themselves do not reach [those objects].
They seize their respective objects. Therefore, this is said:
“But among these, the eye and the ear Are graspers of what is encountered;
Because they are causes for the arising of consciousness, Their range extends to what is near and far.”
“For indeed, the eye perceives the color of things situated at a distance, obscured by crystal and the like, and even those as large as mountains and so forth.
It perceives what is situated in space and what lies between the belly and the skin.”
And the sound of bells and the like is a large object within the range of the ear.
If it is argued that [the sense] goes to the region of the object and grasps it after pervading it,
then that [sound] would also be the range of the [sense] in its mode of determination.
“If that [body], through its connection with the primary elements, proceeds toward the collection of sense faculties,
then color and sound produced by the power of kamma and mind are born of mind.
They do not become objects for those [faculties], for they do not exist outside.”
And although these are taught without distinction, in the text they refer specifically to that [object].
"If this pair [of eyes] perceives only what is near to itself,
it would likewise see the color of the eye, as well as the root of the eyebrow."
“There would be no determination of direction or location for sound;
yet for one who shoots an arrow, there would be the falling of the arrow upon his own ear.

This is because the material phenomenon that grasps its respective object, being presided over by consciousness, has the intrinsic nature of grasping those various objects. The other twenty-three types of material phenomena are non-object-grasping, owing to the absence of such grasping.

27. *Vaṇṇa* (color/appearance) is so called because it is to be seen (*daṭṭhabba*) and described (*vaṇṇitabba*). *Ojā* (nutritive essence) is that which generates material form immediately after its own arising.
As for "indivisible matter" (*avinibbhoga-rūpa*), this is because there is nowhere any separate occurrence through the disintegration of one from another.
For even the opinion of those who maintain that odors and so forth do not exist in the fine-material world (*rūpaloka*) has been rejected by teachers in various places.

28. *Iccevaṃ*: here too, the word *iti* has the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). By this, it includes all the various types of matter not mentioned here, such as the threefold division of suffering (*dukkatikādi*) and so forth.
The commentary on the analysis of matter (*rūpavibhāgavaṇṇanā*) is finished.
[Now begins] the commentary on the method of the origination of matter (*rūpasamuṭṭhānanayavaṇṇanā*).
29. But what are those [factors] such as kamma, etc.; how, where, and when do they originate matter? To this he says, “Therein,” and so forth.
“Starting from rebirth-linking” means starting from the moment of arising of the rebirth-linking consciousness.

“In each and every moment” means in the three moments of each individual consciousness; it is said that [matter arises] without interruption. Others, however, [refer to] the moment of the consciousness’s duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*).
And they deny the arising of material phenomena at the moment of dissolution.
Although the proof for this and what must be said regarding it in the absence of a moment of duration have already been stated below, here too, for the sake of easy comprehension,
it is stated by summarizing the proof along with what must be said regarding that [moment of dissolution] in the absence of the arising of material phenomena at the moment of dissolution:
“In the *Vibhaṅga*, regarding such terms as ‘arisen’ (*uppanna*) and ‘arising’ (*uppajjamāna*):

at the moment of dissolution (*bhaṅgakkhaṇa*), it is ‘arisen’ but not ‘arising. [In the *Paṭṭhāna*], by such statements as ‘arising while arising’ (*uppajjamānam-uppāde*) and ‘arisen’ (*uppanna*),” and so forth.
Only the arising and passing away are declared, not the moment of the mind’s persistence.
If it is held that "persistence exists" because it was said: "Arising, passing away, and the alteration of what persists are discerned."
“Because change-of-state is not found in a single phenomenon,
and because of the expression ‘knowledge’ (paññāṇa), there is also a continuous persistence therein.
Therefore, it is said that no stability of the mind is seen in the Canon.”
In the Abhidhamma, even non-existence is in every way a negation. When it is asked,
"When the origin of that [suffering] ceases, what then arises for it?",
the answer "Suffering arises" is negated by the word "no."
“‘The arising of form does not occur at the moment of its destruction; therefore, all conditions are causes of form only for the arising of consciousness’—so say some.
To this it is replied: Just as it is accepted that [conditions] apply to a single phenomenon (dhamma) therein,”
The state of dissolution is likewise distinct from the state of arising.
This state of being oriented toward dissolution should be understood as "stability" (ṭhiti) through the method of seeing the underlying principle (*naya*),
though it was not explicitly taught in the *Vibhaṅga*.
“Because the characteristics of arising and so forth are taught as belonging only to the conditioned,
continuity is not stated there as ‘stability. Since prefixes function only to modify the meaning of roots,
[the prefix *sam-* does not alter the sense of the root *sthā*].”
"It is manifested" means that its meaning is understood.

For it was indeed stated in the *Yamaka* with reference either to the non-arising of matter at the moment of its dissolution due to the influence of mind-born [matter], or else with reference to the formless realm (*ārūpya*).
“This is simply the nature of things: that application occurs according to what is available.
Therefore, there is no stability of consciousness at the moment of dissolution, nor is there an absence of material form.

(31) Because the cause for producing the development of dispassion toward material form is absent, and because of the incompatibility [of such a state] with it, and due to the lack of opportunity, there are no immaterial resultant states.

Because they lack association with the jhāna factors that serve as specific conditions for the production of material form, fourteen types of consciousness—namely, the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness and the two [types of] resultant consciousness of the immaterial sphere—do not originate material form; thus it is said: "excluding the immaterial-sphere resultants and the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness.

Furthermore, the rebirth-linking consciousness and the death-consciousness are included within the nineteen moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga), and therefore do not constitute a separate interval of consciousness.
"It does not exist" means that no announcement (vajjana) has been made for it. Although no such announcement was made,
and although it is devoid of the postnascent condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), nevertheless, because it proceeds by depending on a weak physical basis that is not sustained by nutriment and so forth,

and because it occupies the place of mind-originated material phenomena among the kamma-born material phenomena due to its adventitious nature, the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhi-citta*) [is established].
It does not produce matter. Regarding the death-consciousness (*cuticitta*), however, it is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary) that:

"In a continuity (*santāna*) whose root-process has subsided, the death-consciousness of one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*)—due to its exceptionally peaceful mode of existence—does not produce matter.
But masters such as Ānanda and others maintain that "the death-consciousness of all beings does not produce matter."
Their detailed analysis, however, should be understood according to the method explained in the *Mūlaṭīkā* and other works in brief, and in the *Abhidhammatthavikāsinī* in detail.
"Starting from the first bhavaṅga" means starting from the first bhavaṅga that arises immediately after rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).

It causes [the consciousness] to arise only while it is being born, and not while it is stationary or in the process of dissolving, due to the acquisition of conditions such as the immediate condition (*anantara-paccaya*).
Because it possesses the capacity to produce [matter] precisely at the moment of its own arising. 32.

*Iriyāpatha* (posture) is so called because it is the path of occurrence for bodily activity (*kāyikakiriyā*), such as walking and so forth; in actual meaning, it is the occurrence of matter in that particular state.
It sustains that [matter], supporting it as it occurs. For just as by means of the "street-minds" (*vīthicitta*)...
When the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) flows in an uninterrupted stream, the factors [of posture] sink;

this is not the case with these thirty-two types [of postures], nor when the twenty-six types of wakeful consciousness (*jāgaraṇacitta*) that will be mentioned hereafter are occurring. At those times, however, the factors remain firm and proceed precisely according to the state of the posture as it occurs.
(33) They also originate intimation (*viññatti*), not merely physical postures alone. Although there is no specific distinction made here...
It should be understood that only the javanas occurring in the mind-door (manodvāra) that produce intimation (viññatti) likewise generate laughter;
this is because those [javana-cittas] occurring in the five doors (pañcadvāra) are weak.

Granted, in this context there is no posture (iriyāpatha) or intimation apart from material form (rūpa); nevertheless, not every consciousness that originates material form is capable of sustaining a posture.

And it is that which produces a modification of intimation. However, that consciousness which produces intimation invariably supports the postures, because the posture is inseparable from its intimation.
The separate mention of the postures and intimations from matter is for the purpose of showing this distinction: that [the former] support the postures while [the latter] produce matter.
34. There are thirteen [types of consciousness]: four from the wholesome, four from the unwholesome, and five from the functional.
Among these, ordinary worldlings laugh with eight—both wholesome and unwholesome; those in training (sekkhā) with the five excluding those accompanied by wrong view;
and those beyond training (asekkhā) with the five functional consciousnesses. Furthermore, among them, Buddhas laugh only with the four functional consciousnesses accompanied by roots.

It is not without cause; for it is said: "Having attained unimpeded knowledge regarding the past and so forth, every bodily action of the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these three qualities, is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge.

They say that it is not fitting for the Buddhas to engage in even a smile-producing state of mind devoid of investigative wisdom (*vicāraṇapaññā*). [This refers to] the smile-producing consciousness (*hasituppādacitta*).

However, even while occurring in the course of daily activity, their smile-making is indeed a concomitant of knowledge (*ñāṇānuparivatti*), because it follows upon the knowledge of past lives, the knowledge of future births, and the knowledge of omniscience. And this being so, it is stated in the Commentary:
"At the conclusion of the exercise of those knowledges, this consciousness arises gladdening [the mind]. Therefore, it is not possible to prevent its occurrence in Buddhas.

35. Because it receives support from conditions such as those arising subsequently (*pacchājāta-paccaya*), the fire element (*tejo-dhātu*) attains strength precisely at the moment of its presence; thus it is said: "The fire element has reached stability," and so forth. 37.

Among these, the nine material phenomena consisting of the heart-base and the sense-faculties are exclusively "born of kamma" (*kammaja*), because they arise solely from kamma. For whatever has arisen, is arising, or will arise [from kamma] is called "born of kamma," just as [the term] "milk" is used for that which has been, is being, or will be milked.

40. Because they depend on present conditions, the triad of lightness (*lahutā*) and the others is not born of kamma; otherwise, they would have to exist at all times. Therefore it is said: "The triad of lightness and the others arise from temperature, consciousness, and nutriment.
43. Nine [material phenomena] are exclusively born of kamma. Among the fourfold groups, nine are born of kamma, making eighteen born of kamma in total.

Fifteen are born of consciousness, by way of the fivefold transformation-forms, sound, inseparable material phenomena, and space. Thirteen are born of temperature: sound, the triad of lightness and the others, inseparable material phenomena, and space.
There are twelve types of nutriment-born [matter], by way of the inseparability of the triad of lightness and so forth, and by way of space.

44. It is explained that the characteristics do not arise through certain conditions; for while they are merely the intrinsic nature (sabhāvamatta) because they possess the nature of matter that is being born, ripening, and dissolving, they lack their own specific characteristics such as birth and so forth in the absence of that intrinsic nature.
For the characteristics such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth exist for the eye and other [bases] that are associated with arising; it is not so for birth and the others themselves.

If birth and the others were to have their own births and so forth, there would result an infinite regress (*anavasthāna*). As for the fact that being "born from something" is admitted for birth in passages such as, "The visible-object base...
[and] physical nutriment (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*): these states are mind-originated," [it refers to a different sense of origination].

This too should be understood as referring to the fact that even birth (*jāti*) is perceived as a modification of a phenomenon arising at the very moment when the conditions that produce form have attained the state of being conditions for the production of form, their functional activity having not yet ceased. As it is said:
"Monks, birth is impermanent, conditioned, and dependently arisen. Aging-and-death, monks, is impermanent, conditioned..."

Regarding the expression “dependently arisen,” the intended meaning here is that it refers to the state of being the characteristic of those things that are dependently arisen. Thus the ancients said:

“Because it is born from something in the text, because it is a synonym for birth, and because it is the intrinsic nature of conditioned things—the state of being conditioned is taught in all three [instances].”
The commentary on the method of the origination of material phenomena is finished.
Commentary on the Application of Groups (Kalāpayojanā): 45.
Furthermore, since these material phenomena, even when arising from karma and so forth, do not originate individually, then...
It is indeed a cluster (*piṇḍa*). Therefore, in order to show the numerical limit and the specific nature of these clusters, it is said:

"arising together" (*ekuppādā*), and so forth. "Arising together" means arising simultaneously in the sense of being contained within individual groups (*kalāpa*), not by way of all groups arising simultaneously with one another.

46. "Ten" means having ten as its measure; this is a collective name for the group. That which is characterized by the eye, or that group in which the eye is predominant, is the "eye-decad" (*cakkhudasaka*).

The same applies to the remaining [decads]. 47. By the inclusion of "vocal intimation" (*vacīviññatti*), sound is also included because it is inseparable from it; thus it is called the "vocal-intimation decad. 50.
But do all these twenty-one groups exist everywhere, or are some present only in certain places? To this he says: "Therein," etc.
The commentary on the *Kalāpayojanā* is finished.
**Commentary on the Sequence of the Arising of Matter (Rūpapavattikkamavaṇṇanā)** 52.

Now, in order to show their arising by way of their occurrence, by way of rebirth-linking, and by way of the modes of birth (*yoni*), it is said: “But all these... and so forth. “Accordingly” (*yathārahaṃ*) means in accordance with those whose sense bases are complete in their intrinsic nature.
53. Those born in moist places such as the interior cavities of lotuses and the like are *saṃsedaja* (moisture-born).

They are called *opapātika* (spontaneously born) because they possess *upapāta* (rebirth); here, however, a distinguished form of rebirth is intended by way of its excellence and limit, just as one says, "A maiden should be given to a handsome man.
Seven sets of ten [factors] manifest, because they are perceived through the state of having fully developed sense bases (*āyatana*).
Sometimes these are not obtained due to those who are blind from birth, deaf from birth, noseless from birth, eunuchs, or those belonging to the first aeon (paṭhamakappika).
In that regard, for those of spontaneous birth (opapātika) reborn in a happy destination through karma of great power, there is no deficiency of faculties;
thus they do not obtain the eye, ear, or nose. Furthermore, there is a lack of sex organs in moisture-born beings, and also in the case of those of spontaneous birth belonging to the first aeon.

However, in the miserable destinies (*duggati*), it should be understood that the non-acquisition of both the eye and the ear occurs by way of both [types of birth], while the non-acquisition of the nose occurs only by way of moisture-born beings (*saṃsedaja*) and not by way of apparitional beings (*opapātika*). For thus it is said in the *Dhammahadayavibhaṅga*:
"At the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*), for some eleven bases (*āyatana*) appear; for some ten; and for others yet more..."

Based on the statement, "For some ten, for some nine, for some seven," it is said that for a spontaneously born being (*opapātika*) with complete faculties, there are eleven bases (*āyatana*), excluding the base of sound.
For the blind, there are ten, excluding the eye-base; likewise for the deaf, excluding the ear-base;

for those who are both blind and deaf, there are nine, excluding both of those; and for one in the womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*), there are seven bases, excluding the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and sound bases.

[These] have been stated. However, if there could be a spontaneously born being (opapātika) who lacks a nose, then ten bases would have to be mentioned three times by way of those who are blind, deaf, and noseless;
nine bases three times by way of those who are blind, deaf, and both blind and deaf, as well as noseless;
and eight bases by way of one who is blind, deaf, and noseless. But they have not been stated thus. Therefore, there is no spontaneously born being [who lacks a nose].
"Absence of the nose. And so it is stated in the *Yamaka-aṭṭhakathā*: "There is no spontaneously born (opapātika) being without a nose.
If there were, one would have to say that some possess eight bases (āyatana).
However, the absence of a nose in moisture-born beings cannot be denied by such scriptural passages as "at the moment of rebirth in the sense-sphere realm," and so forth.
This is said with reference specifically to the spontaneously born (*opapātika*) mode of birth, because the inclusion of the seven bases (*sattāyatana*) is impossible for others [than those beings],
and it was stated with reference specifically to those born from a womb (*gabbhaseyyaka*). As for the commentarial statement that "moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) beings,
by virtue of possessing complete bases, are included among the spontaneously born," that too refers only to those moisture-born beings who possess complete bases among the spontaneously born.

This was stated by way of inclusion. However, others explain that since the coexistence of the nose and tongue is mentioned in the *Yamaka*, and because it is impossible for there to be a tongueless being, there can likewise be no being without a nose;

even in that case, they argue that while the eye and ear function in the form realm (*rūpabhava*) without the nose and tongue, the nose and tongue do not function without each other, as both [are required].
"Because they do not arise in the fine-material existence (rūpabhava)"—thus, their concomitance has been stated by way of their non-occurrence separately in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava);
therefore, it is not impossible to say so.
54. They lie in the womb, in the mother’s belly, thus they are "womb-dwellers" (gabbhaseyyaka); those very beings are called "beings" (satta) because of their attachment to form and the rest.
Beings born from a womb. These are the egg-born and the womb-born. Three sets of ten [material qualities] become manifest, which are called "embryo-form" (*kalalarūpa*);

when these are massed together, they are like clear, translucent drops remaining at the tip of a strand of hair from a birth-wool that has been dipped in clarified sesame oil and then lifted out. Sometimes this is not obtained.

By way of the existence of non-existent beings. "After that" means after the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*). "In the period of the course of existence" (*pavattikāle*) means on the seventh day;

according to the opinion of the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), it is on the eleventh day. "Successively" means: after the lapse of seven days from the manifestation of the eye-decad (*cakkhudasaka*), the ear-decad (*sotadasaka*);
after the lapse of another seven days from that, the nose-decad (*ghānadasaka*); and after the lapse of another seven days from that, the tongue-decad (*jivhādasaka*).
Thus, in due order. For this very meaning is also shown in the *Aṭṭhakathā*.

55. "The time of subsistence" means the time of subsistence of the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*). For the temperature co-nascent with the rebirth-linking consciousness, having reached its stage of subsistence, produces the pure octad at the moment of that [consciousness's] subsistence.
Then, by the sequence beginning with "arisen at the moment of dissolution," and so forth...

The temperature produces material form. "Depending on the diffusion of nutritive essence" means: for an embryo in the womb, from the time the nutritive essence derived from the food swallowed by the mother begins to pervade the body via the nutrient-carrying channels;

and for moisture-born and spontaneously born beings, from the time the nutritive essence derived from the mucus in the mouth and so forth begins to pervade the body via the nutrient-carrying channels.

56. "Above the death-consciousness" means that which has the death-consciousness as its upper limit. Kamma-born material phenomena do not arise [after that point], because there is no death at the moment of their arising. For it is only when the continuity of kamma-born material phenomena is severed that one is said to be "dead. As it is said:
“When vitality, heat, and consciousness abandon this body, then it lies cast away like a useless log.
“Earlier” refers to the moment of arising of the seventeenth [consciousness]. After that, the mind-born and nutriment-born materiality also ceases.
In the continuity of non-living beings, because there is no arising of those [material phenomena], the mind-born and nutriment-born materiality,
having arisen accordingly, continue for some time and then cease. However, other teachers explain that "mind-born materiality is cut off even prior to the death-consciousness."
58. The reason for the absence of the nose, tongue, and body [faculties] in the fine-material world (rūpaloka) has already been stated.
Furthermore, the two types of nutriment do not function there because they are dependent conditions for intense sensual lust, which is absent among the Brahmās;

and material groups produced by nutriment are not found there because, in the absence of swallowed food, even the nutriment present within the body lacks the capacity to generate materiality. For external temperature and nutriment serve as the necessary support.
Having obtained temperature and nutriment, they give rise to material form. The "life-nonad" refers to the life-nonad that takes the place of the body-decad due to the absence of a physical body.
59. It exceeds [the number] because it remains as something to be found in the rebirth-linking and the course of existence of other Brahmās;
however, at the time of death, since there is no casting off of a body for Brahmās, all [material phenomena] have three origins.
And those [material qualities] arising from two [causes] cease simultaneously.
(61) Among material phenomena, twenty-three [types] exist because of the absence of five—namely, the nose, tongue, body, and the two sexes. However, some say:
"Even the triad of lightness and so forth is not present among them, because there is no disturbance of the elements that causes heaviness and the like"; this [they maintain].
This is not the reason. For there is no dependence on something to be pacified for the arising of a state opposed to it;

if that were so, it would follow that buoyancy and the other [characteristics] would be absent from functional consciousnesses (kiriyacitta) which possess roots. The statement beginning with "sound is a transformation" is spoken as a commonality applicable to all.
The commentary on the sequence of the occurrence of matter is concluded.
Commentary on the Divisions of Nibbāna: 62.
Having thus far demonstrated mind, mental factors, and matter by way of their divisions, he now speaks the words beginning with “Nibbāna, moreover,” while demonstrating Nibbāna.
By the phrase “to be realized by the knowledge of the four paths,” [he shows] Nibbāna’s relation to the various noble persons.

This demonstrates that [the object] is established through direct perception (*paccakkha*). By the phrase "being the object of the paths and fruits," it shows that for noble worldlings (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*), it is established through inference (*anumāna*).

For indeed, knowledge whose object is a conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhata-dhamma*) or a conceptual designation (*paññatti*) is incapable of completely cutting off or pacifying the defilements (*kilesa*);
yet, there exists in the world the complete cutting off of defilements and so forth. Therefore, there exists [an object] that is contrary to conditioned phenomena and conventional designations.

It is established that Nibbāna is a single phenomenon (dhamma) which serves as the object (ārammaṇa) for the paths and fruits that bring about the eradication and subsiding of the defilements (kilesa).
By demonstrating that it is established through direct perception and inference, he refutes the doctrine of those who have fallen into the error of claiming that Nibbāna is a mere non-existence.
Enough of this excessive elaboration. [Now, regarding] the phenomena of the three planes, classified into aggregates (khandha) and so forth...

Because it has emerged from craving—which is designated as "weaving" (*vāna*) due to its nature of weaving together or binding by way of lower and higher [realms]—and because it has transcended its objects, it is "past.
(63) "By way of intrinsic nature" means by its own characteristic of subsiding. That which is grasped by the clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*) and so forth is "clinging" (*upādi*);

this is a designation for the five aggregates. Because the remainder of the defilements still clings to it, it is "with-clinging-remainder" (*upādisesa*). That which exists together with that is "possessing a residue of clinging" (*saupādisesa*).
"That very [state] is the Nibbāna-element" refers to the Nibbāna-element with residue remaining (*saupādisesa-nibbānadhātu*).

"By way of cause" means by way of the trace (*lesa*) of the presence or absence of the residue remaining, which serves as the cause for designating [Nibbāna] as "with residue remaining" and so forth. 64.
It is "empty" (*suñña*) because it is empty of lust, hatred, and delusion by way of its object (*ārammaṇa*) and by way of association (*sampayoga*); emptiness itself is "emptiness" (*suññatā*).
Likewise, it is signless (*animitta*) because it is devoid of the signs of lust and so forth; it is wishless (*appaṇihita*) because it is devoid of the longing for lust and so forth;
or it is emptiness (*suññatā*) because it is empty of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*). It is signless because of the absence of the signs of all conditioned phenomena;

it is wishless because of the absence of the longing of craving (*taṇhā*). 65. It is deathless (*accuta*) because of the absence of passing away; it is absolute (*accanta*) because it transcends the end or limit; [it is unconditioned] by way of conditions...

It is "unconditioned" (*asaṅkhata*) because of its unconditioned nature. It is "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there is no one superior to itself, or because there is no further state to be described in accordance with the Dhamma.
It is "free from craving" (*vānamuttā*) because it is liberated from craving (*vāna*), or because it is entirely devoid of it.
They are "great seers" (*mahesiyo*) because they seek and search for the great aggregates of virtue and so forth. The passage beginning with "Thus, O Citta" consists of six sections.
This is the conclusion regarding the analysis of consciousness and the other categories.
The commentary on the classification of Nibbāna is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, titled the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
The commentary on the section on the delimitation of material form is finished.
7. Commentary on the Section on Compendium:
1. Regarding the characteristics: there are seventy-two types [of phenomena] based on their own specific characteristics, namely: consciousness, mental factors, derived matter, and Nibbāna.
The *vatthu-dhammas* (basis-phenomena) have been described as *sabhāva-dhammas* (intrinsic-nature phenomena). Now, the connection is as follows:

"I shall explain the compendium—the collection—classified according to its application, such as the 'Compendium of the Unwholesome' (*akusalasaṅgaha*), by way of the individual and collective grouping of those *sabhāva-dhammas* as appropriate. 2.

The "Compendium of the Unwholesome" (*akusalasaṅgaha*) is the grouping of only unwholesome states by way of their common characteristics (*sabhāga-dhamma*). [The following] refers to mixed states by way of the wholesome and so forth.

“Compendium” means a mixed compendium. “The compendium of the factors conducive to enlightenment” (bodhipakkhiya-saṅgaha) refers to the grouping together, by way of their common basis, of the factors conducive to enlightenment—namely, the noble path characterized as the full awakening to truth—which consist of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
“The compendium of all” (sabba-saṅgaha) refers to the grouping together of all things by way of the aggregates and so forth.

Commentary on the Compendium of the Unwholesome (Akusalasaṅgaha): 3. They are called *āsava* (taints) because they have existed for a long time in the sense of having been stored away since the beginningless past; or because they flow out toward objects through the eyes and other [senses], like pus flowing from a wound.
Alternatively, they are so called because they flow from existence up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), or from phenomena up to the state of lineage (*gotrabhū*).
They are called *āsava* because they flow (*savanti*) or proceed. Here, the prefix *ā-* has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*), and that limit is twofold:

by way of exclusion (*maryādā*) and by way of inclusion (*abhividhi*). Among these, the exclusionary limit is one that proceeds by setting the action outside [the limit], as in "The rain fell as far as Pāṭaliputta.
The inclusive limit is one that proceeds by pervading the action, as in "The sound rose up as far as the realm of existence (*ābhavagga*)."

But here, it should be understood in the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*). For they occur both in the peak of existence (*bhavagga*), which is their place of arising, and in the state of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*), which is their object.

Furthermore, while other defilements such as conceit exist and flow up to the peak of existence and the state of change-of-lineage, these [taints] are so called because they pervade by way of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self;
thus, in the sense of producing intoxication, they resemble a taint (*āsava*) due to their similarity to a fermenting agent.

And it should be understood that these very [defilements] are established by way of being "outflows" (*āsava*). Sensual desire itself is the outflow of sensual desire (*kāmāsava*), which is sensual lust.

Lust for existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms is the outflow of existence (*bhavāsava*). Lust accompanied by craving for meditative absorption and the view of eternalism is included right here [in this category].
Among these, the first is lust for rebirth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*), the second is for kamma-existence (*kamma-bhava*), and the third is accompanied by the view of existence.

The sixty-two types of views constitute the taint of views (*diṭṭhāsava*). Ignorance regarding the four truths—suffering and so forth—the prior limit, the subsequent limit, both the prior and subsequent limits, and dependent origination;
that is, ignorance regarding these eight points, constitutes the taint of ignorance (*avijjāsava*).
It is called a "flood" (*ogha*) because it carries one away by overwhelming, or because it strikes down by casting one below, or because it causes one to sink.

The flood-currents (*ogha*) are so called because they resemble a torrent of water; for these [taints] overwhelm and strike down beings, as if causing them to sink into the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).
Furthermore, it is the taints (*āsava*) themselves that are here called "flood-currents" in the sense already stated. 5.

They are called "yokes" (*yoga*) because they yoke beings—either within the cycle of existence or at the end of an existence—to another state of existence through kamma and its result, or to suffering. These are the same phenomena mentioned below.
6. They bind the form-body (rūpakāya) with the name-body (nāmakāya), or they bind the future body with the present body;
they wrap it so that it is difficult to release—thus they are called "body-fetters" (kāyagantha).

The grasping of purity through virtue such as the cow-vow (gosīla), through observances (vata), or through both, is "clinging" (parāmāsa), because it touches upon what is external and lacks true reality. "This alone is the truth, all else is vain"—this is adherence, a firm grasping.
This is adherence to the belief in truth (*saccābhiniveso*). 7.
They are called "clinging" (*upādānāni*) because they grasp an object very firmly and intensely, like a snake seizing a frog.

Sensual desire itself is clinging; or, it is "clinging to sensual pleasures" (*kāmupādāna*) because one clings to sensual pleasures. [It is] thus regarding precepts, vows, and so forth: "By means of these precepts, vows, and so forth, there shall be purification from cyclic existence for me. Thus [regarding] precepts, vows, and so forth...
Grasping is the clinging to rules and observances (*sīlabbatupādāna*). That which they speak by means of it is "doctrine" (*vāda*);

the doctrine of a self—imagined in twenty ways as being either distinct from or non-distinct from the aggregates—is "self-doctrine" (*attavāda*). That very thing is the clinging; thus, it is "clinging to self-doctrine" (*attavādupādāna*). 8.
They obstruct wholesome consciousness arising through jhāna and so forth, and thus do not allow it to arise in that way.
The hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*): they are called hindrances in the sense that they obstruct the eye of wisdom (*paññā-cakku*).

Sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) is simply desire (*kāma*)—defined as excessive lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure—in the sense of longing; thus it is "sensual desire. That very thing is a hindrance, hence "the hindrance of sensual desire" (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*).

Ill will (*byāpāda*) is so called because by it the mind becomes corrupted and ruined; its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) consists of the nine grounds for resentment, such as the thought, "He has done me harm," and so forth.
Hate (*dosa*) is ninefold, or tenfold when including resentment (*aṭṭhānakopa*); that itself is the hindrance, thus it is the "hindrance of ill-will" (*byāpādanīvaraṇa*).
Stiffness-and-torpor (*thinamiddha*) itself is the hindrance, thus it is the "hindrance of stiffness-and-torpor. Likewise for the "hindrance of restlessness-and-worry" (*uddhaccakukkuccanīvaraṇa*).
But why are these distinct phenomena stated as two pairs under the status of a single hindrance each? [It is] because of their function, nutriment, and opposites.

Because their functions are identical. For the function of inducing sluggishness in an arising state of consciousness is common to both sloth and torpor; likewise, the cause for the lack of tranquility is common to both restlessness and worry.

Similarly, for the former two, drowsiness and yawning are the nutriment—in the sense of being the cause—while for the latter two, it is the brooding over misfortunes such as the loss of relatives. Furthermore, energy is the specific antidote to the former two.
"Peace is for those who follow after": thus the ancients have said— "Because of the unity of what is to be done, nutriment, and opposites, there is indeed oneness here;
For how could restlessness-and-worry and sloth-and-torpor exist in one such as this?"
“Languor, lethargy, duty, sloth, and thoughts of kin—these are the causes [of hindrances]; energy and serenity are their opposites.

(9) In the sense of not being abandoned, they lie latent (*anu-senti*) in the continuum (*santāne*) one after another (*anu-anu*); thus they are called *anusayas*. The meaning is that they arise upon obtaining a corresponding cause.
For the defilements that have not been abandoned are liable to arise when their conditions are met;
they lie latent within the continuum as it were, and thus in that state they are called "latent dispositions" (*anusaya*). In the ultimate sense, however, these are future defilements;

though those of the past and present are also so called, it is because they possess that same nature. For there is no difference in the intrinsic nature of phenomena due to a difference in time. If...
"In the sense of being unabandoned" refers to the underlying tendencies (*anusaya*). But would not all defilements (*kilesa*), being unabandoned, thereby become underlying tendencies?

We do not say they are "underlying tendencies" merely by virtue of being unabandoned; rather, underlying tendencies are those defilements that have become firmly rooted in the sense of being unabandoned.

Furthermore, this state of becoming firmly rooted is the unique, individual nature (*sabhāva*) of sensual lust and the other [defilements] alone, which is not shared with anything else. Enough of this dispute.
The underlying tendency that is itself sensual lust is the underlying tendency of sensual lust (*kāmarāgānusaya*).
10. They are called fetters (*saṃyojana*) because they fetter and bind.
12. They are called defilements (*kilesa*) because by means of them the mind is defiled, tormented, or afflicted.

13. "By the name of the sense-sphere existence" (kāmabhava) means by the name of the objects designated as sense-sphere existence. "Proceeding in that manner" means proceeding by way of touching and so forth external to moral conduct, vows, and the like. 14.
The taints (āsava), floods (ogha), yokes (yoga), and ties (gantha) are threefold according to their basis (vatthu) and their nature (dhamma), as explained by the method already stated.

Likewise, two kinds of clinging (upādāna) are mentioned, namely craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi). There may be eight hindrances (nīvaraṇa), [consisting of] sloth-and-torpor, restlessness, and worry.

By way of separate inclusion: there are six underlying tendencies (*anusaya*), because the underlying tendencies of sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) and the underlying tendency of existence (*bhavarāga*) are taken together as being of the nature of craving (*taṇhā*).
Nine fetters (*saṃyojana*) are recognized, because those mentioned in both contexts that are of the nature of craving and those of the nature of views are each included as one.
Furthermore, defilements (*kilesa*) are ten according to the Suttanta method and also ten according to the Abhidhamma method. Thus it is.
The inclusion of evil unwholesome states is said to be ninefold. And herein: Greed and views are included in nine ways;
ignorance and aversion are included in seven ways; [the remaining] five are included in five ways, and four are included in four ways.
Doubt is included in three [fetters], pride and restlessness in one, and sloth is included in two.
Remorse, torpor, shamelessness, and fearlessness are grouped together as concealment;
these evil states are thus comprised in nine groups.
The commentary on the inclusion of the unwholesome is finished.
Commentary on the inclusion of the mixed: 15.
That which is to be said regarding the roots has already been stated above.
16. Having approached the object, they are called *jhānas* in the sense of close contemplation (*upanijjhāyana*)—that is, reflection—and in the sense of burning away opposing states as appropriate.
They are called *jhāna-aṅgas* (factors of absorption) because they are known (*ñāyanti*) as being "limbs" (*aṅgiyanti*) by virtue of their constituent parts within the aggregate.
And although there is no whole apart from its parts, just as in the case of army-parts, chariot-parts, and so forth, each one [is considered separately].
They are called factors because, having come together as a single unit, they constitute the state of jhāna. Herein, mental distress (*domanassa*) is an unwholesome jhāna-factor;
the remaining ones are wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate jhāna-factors. 17.
They are called "paths" because they lead toward happy destinies, unhappy destinies, and Nibbāna; they are the tracks that serve as the way for these.
The factors are the factors of the eightfold path, or *maggaṅgāni*. One sees rightly, without error, thus it is right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*).
That, moreover, is tenfold by way of [the conviction] "there is a gift," and so forth; or it is fourfold by way of the functions such as full understanding (*pariññā*).

They conceive rightly by means of this, thus it is right intention (*sammā-saṅkappo*). It is threefold by way of the intention of renunciation (*nekkhamma*), the intention of non-ill will (*abyāpāda*), and the intention of non-cruelty (*avihiṃsā*).
It is threefold. Right speech and the others have already been explained below. One exerts oneself rightly by means of this, thus it is right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
One remembers rightly by means of this, thus it is right mindfulness (*sammāsati*). The classification of these, however, will be stated further on.

The mind is rightly and personally concentrated by means of this, thus it is right concentration (*sammāsamādhi*); it is fivefold one-pointedness according to the first jhāna and so forth. Wrong view and the others...
They are path-factors because they belong to the path leading away from an unhappy rebirth.

(18) Regarding seeing and so forth: [the path is known] by means of eye-consciousness and the rest; generally, by means of signs and the like during the occurrence of a mental continuum associated with them;
during life, by means of those phenomena associated with kamma-born materiality that are present while living; and during the act of thinking and knowing, by means of the associated phenomena.

In the state of being happy and so forth, [the factors] that cause the self to conform are the mental states (dhammas) that, by way of sovereignty, act as faculties (indriyas): those that arise simultaneously with happiness and so forth;

those that proceed by way of faith and so forth among the [five spiritual faculties] such as faith; those that proceed in the same manner during the process of "I shall know the unknown" (*anaññātaṃ ñassāmī*);
and those that arise simultaneously with the proceeding by way of full understanding (*ājānana*) and the state of having known (*aññātāvibhāva*). These are the faculties in the sense of being lords.

He says "name" by referring to "the eye-faculty," and so forth. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, other meanings of "faculty" (*indriya*) such as the sense of "lord" (*indaliṅga*) and others are also stated.
The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) is twofold, according to whether it is material or immaterial.
For one who has practiced with the underlying intention: "In this beginningless cycle of existence, may I know the Deathless State not yet known, or indeed the Dhamma of the Four Truths."

The faculty is the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*). It is the "faculty of final knowledge" (*aññindriya*) because it knows—meaning it understands by means of the first path, knowing without transgressing the boundary of what has been seen.
The "faculty of one who has already known" (*aññātāvindriya*) is the faculty of an Arhat who stands having penetrated the four truths.
And here, the inclusion of the "faculty of wisdom" (*paññindriya*) is for the purpose of clarifying the specific nature of the phenomenon.

The inclusion of the "I-shall-come-to-know-the-unknown" faculty (*anaññātaññassāmītindriya*) and the others is for the purpose of clarifying the distinctions among individuals, their inclinations, and their specific functions.
Herein, the internal sense bases (*ajjhattikāyatana*) are mentioned first because they serve as the qualifiers and supports for the designation of sentient beings (*sattapaññatti*).

However, although the mind faculty (*manindriya*) could have been mentioned right here due to its commonality with the status of being an internal sense base, it is instead treated together with the formless faculties (*arūpindriya*).

The life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) was mentioned immediately after [the faculties] for the purpose of showing [their function]; this designation [of "female" and "male"] undergoes differentiation as "woman" and "man" by means of these two.
Immediately after that, the pair of [sexual] characteristics (*bhāva*) is mentioned for the purpose of showing how they are distinguished;

following that, the life-faculty is mentioned again for the purpose of showing that these appropriated phenomena (*upādinnadhamma*) persist by means of it. [Thus,] it is a mass of phenomena designated as a "sentient being."
The pentad of feeling is taught next in order to show that when [the mind] proceeds by way of bondage, it becomes defiled by these feelings;
then, the pentad beginning with faith is taught to show the equipment for purification for those desiring purity through those [faculties];

and finally, the pentad of the powers is taught at the end to show that those who have accumulated the equipment for purification are purified by these [powers], and that they have attained purity and completed their task.
Three have been stated. Since the intended meaning is established by this much, there is no mention of others;
this is the reason for their teaching in this particular order.
Enough of this excessive elaboration. 19. By means of the opposing states known as lack of faith, laziness, negligence, restlessness, ignorance, lack of moral shame, and lack of moral dread...
The seven powers, beginning with faith (*saddhā*), are so called in the sense of being unshakable and because of their stability among associated states (*sampayutta-dhamma*);

the pair of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*), however, are so called solely because of their stability among associated states. Factors that serve as the counteragents to those states that function under the influence of self are the predominants (*adhipati*). As it is said: "For one who possesses desire (*chanda*), what indeed is not accomplished? and so forth.

For when a consciousness arises having obtained the support of previous volitional formations (*pubbābhisaṅkhārūpanissaya*), desire and the other [mental factors] function as the primary factors (*dhura*), accomplishing their associated states;
and they function by virtue of those [states], thus they function as the very counterparts of those states that are dependent on themselves.
This is by way of precluding the dominant influence (*adhipatibhāva*) of other dominant factors.

Sovereignty (*issariya*) is predominance (*adhipatitā*). Even though other faculties exist, the mere fact of being made to conform to seeing and so forth by means of eye-consciousness and the rest is what constitutes "faculty-ness" (*indriyatā*);
this is the distinction between the predominant faculty (*adhipatindriya*) and the others. 21.

They are called "nutriments" (*āhāra*) because they bring in (*āharanti*) the nutritive essence and the eightfold materiality, etc. For edible food brings in the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence.

The nutriment of contact nourishes the three kinds of feeling; the nutriment of mental volition, which is wholesome and unwholesome kamma, nourishes rebirth-linking within the three realms of existence.
The nutriment of consciousness, which is the rebirth-linking consciousness, nourishes the co-nascent mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*).

Although there are other factors that nourish what arises from their respective conditions, [consciousness] is specifically designated as a nutriment because it is the particular condition for the internal continuity.
These very four are called "nutriments.
For beings who subsist on physical food, edible nutriment is the specific condition for the material body;
even though that body is produced by kamma and other factors, its continued existence for ten years or more occurs only through the supporting power of edible nutriment. Thus it is said:
It was said: "Like a nurse for a child, like a supporting pillar for a house.

Contact (*phassa*) also becomes a condition for the persistence of beings by means of the occurrence of pleasant and other feelings, precisely as it touches the object which serves as the basis for those pleasant feelings and so forth.

Mental volition (*manosañcetanā*) is a condition for the persistence of beings because, by way of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, it exerts itself (*āyūhamānā*) precisely in order to bring about the root of existence (*bhava*).
Consciousness, by means of discerning through the process of the manifestation of name-and-form, serves as the condition for the persistence of beings;

thus, these very factors are called "nutriments" because they are the specific conditions for the internal continuum. The status of contact and the others as the second and subsequent [nutriments] is according to the order of the teaching, not the order of their arising.

26. Because the five types of sensory consciousness (pañcaviññāṇa) merely strike at their objects due to the absence of applied thought (vitakka), the equanimity, pleasure, and pain existing within them are not enumerated as factors of absorption (jhānaṅga), owing to the absence of the mode of sustained contemplation (upanijjhānākāra).
