For it is said: "The factors of absorption end with applied thought.
This applies to the sixteen types of consciousness by way of the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness, the triple mind-element (manodhātu), and the triple investigating consciousness (santīraṇa).
Due to the absence of energy (*vīriya*), even though concentration (*samādhi*) exists there, it does not attain the state of a power (*bala*).

For it is said: "Energy is the final [factor] of the powers. Likewise, among the eighteen rootless (*aheütuka*) states, the path-factors (*maggaṅga*) are not found because of the lack of roots (*hetu*). For it is said: "The root is the final [factor] of the path-factors.
Bearing this point in mind, he said: "In the two sets of fivefold sense-consciousness," and so forth.
The connection is: "the jhāna factors are not obtained. 27.

Because it is devoid of resolution (*adhimokkha*), the one-pointedness in a mind accompanied by doubt is merely a state of mental stability; it does not, however, receive the designation of "wrong concentration," "concentration faculty," or "concentration power. Thus he says, "Likewise, in a mind accompanied by doubt," and so forth. 28.

By mentioning the two-rooted and three-rooted [consciousnesses], he shows the absence of predominance (*adhipati*) in those with a single root. [This applies] only to the impulsion (*javana*) consciousnesses.
The restriction is for the purpose of showing that dominant factors (adhipatis) are impossible in the case of mundane resultant (vipāka) states.

For those [resultants] do not proceed preceded by desire (chanda) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "as far as possible," he says this with reference to the fact that while investigation-dominant (vīmaṃsādhipati) states are impossible in two-rooted impulsion (javana) moments, they are obtainable in accordance with the presence of the mental formation and the appropriate physical support (upanissaya). Only one [such factor] is obtained.
Otherwise, because the status of predominance would be untenable, the Blessed One— just as in the exposition of the root-condition (*hetupaccaya*) where he states,

"A root is a condition, by way of root-condition, for those phenomena associated with the root," and so forth— did not state regarding the predominance-condition, "Predominance is a condition for those associated with predominance," etc.,

but rather formulated the predominance-condition according to each individual predominance, stating, "The predominance of desire (*chandādhipati*) is a condition for those associated with desire," and so forth.

29. By way of basis (vatthu) and by way of phenomena (dhamma), there are six root-phenomena (hetu-dhamma); five jhāna-factors, because they are taken together as feeling (vedanā) through the inclusion of mental joy, grief, and equanimity;

nine path-factors, because right intention, right effort, and right concentration are taken together with right thought, right energy, and one-pointedness of mind respectively due to their common nature as thought, energy, and mental unification.
There are sixteen faculty-phenomena (indriya-dhamma), [including] the five faculties of feeling...
Because the three supramundane faculties and the faculty of wisdom are taken together due to their commonality of feeling (*vedanā-sāmañña*) and their commonality of knowledge (*ñāṇa-sāmañña*),
and because the material and immaterial life-faculties are taken separately; furthermore, nine factors of power (*bala-dhamma*) are stated according to the method already mentioned,
four dominant factors (*adhipati-dhamma*) are stated, and likewise four nutriments (*āhāra*) are stated— thus [they are classified] by way of the wholesome (*kusala*) and so forth.
The "Mixed Compendium" (Missakasaṅgaha) is so named because it is composed of these three [compendia]; thus, this compendium is said to be sevenfold. And herein:
Wisdom is comprised of five factors; Exertion and one-pointedness, however, Are comprised of four factors;
Mindfulness is comprised of three.
Volition, feeling, and faith are considered to be comprised within two [factors];
the remaining twenty-eight are said to be comprised within one each.
The commentary on the mixed compendium is finished.
Commentary on the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment (Bodhipakkhiyasaṅgahavaṇṇanā) 30.
It is called *paṭṭhāna* because it "stands forth" (*paṭṭhāti*). The meaning is that, having entered by way of apprehending the foul and so forth, it proceeds with respect to objects such as the body.

Mindfulness itself is the *paṭṭhāna*; thus it is "foundation of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*). That, moreover, occurs by way of apprehending the aspects of foulness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self with respect to the body, feelings, mind, and mental phenomena.

It is said that there are "four foundations of mindfulness" by way of abandoning the four perversions of perception—namely, regarding the foul as beautiful, the painful as pleasant, the impermanent as permanent, and the non-self as self.

The body (*kāya*) is so called because it is the source (*āya*) of loathsome things such as head-hair and so forth; it is the physical frame. Alternatively, the body is the collection of inhalations and exhalations.

Contemplation (*anupassanā*) of that body—by way of preliminary practice and by way of insight—is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyānupassanā*). [This refers to] those things which consist of the suffering of suffering, the suffering of change, and the suffering of formations.
Contemplation by way of feelings is the contemplation of feelings (*vedanānupassanā*).

Likewise, contemplation of the mind (*cittānupassanā*) is the contemplation of the mind itself as it is differentiated by lust, loftiness, and so forth, according to its associated states and its various planes. Contemplation of mental phenomena (*dhammānupassanā*) is the contemplation of mental phenomena such as perception and formations, which possess distinct characteristics.
31. It is called *sammappadhāna* because one exerts oneself rightly by means of it; thus, it is effort (*vāyāma*).

And since that effort is fourfold according to its function, he says, "the four right endeavors," and so forth. Effort (*vāyāma*) is the exertion consisting in the practice of meditation subjects such as the contemplation of the foul (*asubha*). "For the sake of further increase" means for the sake of growth.

32. One succeeds by means of this; thus it is *iddhi*. Knowledge of the various kinds of success (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*) is a "foot" (*pāda*) of success; hence, *iddhipāda*. Will itself as a foot of success is *chandiddhipāda*.
35. One awakens (*bujjhati*); thus it is *bodhi*. This refers to the practitioner (*yogāvacara*) starting from the time he has initiated insight (*vipassanā*).

Or, it is that harmony of states (*dhammasāmaggi*), such as mindfulness and the rest, by which he awakens—that is, penetrates the Truths—or by which he rises up from the sleep of the defilements (*kilesa-niddā*), due to the absence of the contraction caused by the defilements.
Or, it blooms for the attainment of the path and its fruits; that harmony of factors is *bodhi*.
Those factors which have become limbs or causes of that *bodhi*—or of that awakening—are the *bojjhaṅgas*. Furthermore, since they are sevenfold by way of their constituent phenomena, he said:

"The mindfulness factor of complete awakening" (*satisambojjhaṅga*), and so forth. Mindfulness itself is the beautiful factor of awakening, or [it belongs] to the beautiful awakening, or to the beautiful [awakening].

Or, it is a factor of enlightenment; thus, it is the mindfulness enlightenment factor (*satisambojjhaṅga*). It investigates and examines phenomena, thus it is the investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor (*dhammavicaya*), which is the wisdom of insight (*vipassanāpaññā*).
Equanimity (*upekkhā*) here refers to the equanimity of neutrality (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
Having stated, "Therein, the grouping is sevenfold," he says again "tranquility of intention" (*saṅkappapassaddhi*) and so forth, in order to demonstrate that [grouping].

It has been stated. In that context, energy (*vīriya*) has nine bases because it performs nine functions by way of the four right efforts, the basis of psychic power of energy, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, the enlightenment factor of energy, and right effort.

Mindfulness (*sati*) has eight bases because it performs eight functions by way of the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, the enlightenment factor of mindfulness, and right mindfulness.
Concentration (*samādhi*) has four bases by way of the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and right concentration.

Wisdom has four functions because it possesses five bases by way of the basis of psychic power consisting of investigation, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, as well as right view.
Faith has two bases because it possesses two functions by way of the faculty of faith and the power of faith.
This is the most excellent and supreme classification of the thirty-seven states that are distinguished by their status as factors conducive to enlightenment.
41. In all eight types of supramundane consciousness, there are all thirty-seven factors; however, they may or may not include *vitakka* (initial application) and *pīti* (joy).
They are absent in the second jhāna because of the impossibility of *vitakka*, and in the fourth and fifth jhānas because of the impossibility of *pīti*.

In mundane consciousness as well, during the occurrence of the six purifications beginning with purification of virtue (*sīlavisuddhi*), these factors are present according to their respective functions.
According to their respective suitability, some [factors] exist separately in certain instances, while in others they do not.
The commentary on the inclusion of the factors conducive to enlightenment is concluded. The commentary on the total inclusion is finished.
42. Those various phenomena (dhammas), distinguished by such divisions as past, future, and present, are called "aggregates" (khandhas) in the sense of being a heap when gathered together into one.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Having gathered that together and condensed it, this is called the aggregate of form," and so forth.
Furthermore, these aggregates are fivefold according to the classification of the vessel, the food, the condiment, the cook, and the eater.
He said, "The aggregate of form," and so forth. For form is like a vessel because it is the support for feeling;
feeling is like food because it is what is to be consumed; perception is like seasoning because it is the cause for obtaining the relish of feeling;
mental formations are like a cook because they perform the preparation; and consciousness is like the eater because it is the consumer.
And to this extent, the intended meaning is accomplished; thus, only five [factors] are mentioned. This is also the reason for the sequence of the teaching:
because he wishes to show, in their proper order, where one eats, what one eats, by what means one eats, who is the provider, and who is the eater.
43. The aggregates that are the objective domain of clinging are the "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānakkhandha*).
Since these consist specifically of the five [aggregates] beginning with form, which are grasped as the objects of clinging, it is said: "the aggregate of form-clinging," and so forth.

Indeed, for the purpose of including all phenomena belonging to the same class, both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) phenomena are taught without distinction as the "five aggregates. This is for the purpose of indicating the plane of insight (*vipassanā-bhūmi*).
However, only those [aggregates] that are subject to taints (sāsrava) are called "aggregates of clinging" (upādānaskandha).

Now, while feeling and the other aggregates here may be either with taints or without taints, form is not so, because it belongs exclusively to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara). It should be understood, however, that form is taught among the aggregates by way of its similarity as a heap, and it is taught among the aggregates of clinging by way of its being subject to clinging and its nature as a heap.
44. They are called *āyatanas* because the mind and mental factors, through their respective functions, strive and exert themselves toward the various doors and objects therein;
or because they extend and expand those states that constitute their own source (*āya*); or because they lead and cause the long-lasting suffering of *saṃsāra* to proceed;
or because they serve as the causes for eye-consciousness and the rest. Furthermore, in common worldly usage, it refers to a place of residence, a mine, a meeting point, or a place of birth.
It is called an "āyatana" (base); therefore, these too are so called because they are the dwelling places for eye-consciousness and the rest, which have their respective doors and respective objects;
because they are the source-places for those very [consciousnesses] as they occur in a crowded state;
because they are the meeting-places for those [consciousnesses] converging from the doors and the objects; and because they are the birth-places for those arising right there.
The sense bases (*āyatana*). These, moreover, are twelvefold: the six internal sense bases which function as doors, and the six external sense bases which function as objects.
Thus he says, "the eye base," and so forth. It is the eye and it is a base, hence "eye base" (*cakkhāyatana*). The same applies to the rest.
Herein, among the internal sense bases, the eye base is "manifest" (*vibhūta*) because its object is visible and impinging.
That was stated first; immediately after that, the others whose objects are non-demonstrable and impinging were stated.
Even among those, the ear-base was stated immediately after the eye-base because of their commonality in not grasping an object through direct contact.
Among the remaining ones, the nose-base was stated first because it is capable of grasping an object more rapidly than the others. For when an object is merely placed in front of it...

The odor of food and so forth strikes the nose by means of the wind; immediately after that, however, the tongue-base (jivhāyatana) is mentioned because it shares the common characteristic of functioning in a specific location.
Following that is the body-base (kāyāyatana), which is omnipresent. Then comes the mind-base (manāyatana), which is capable of apprehending the objects of all five [senses].
Finally, the objects of those aforementioned bases—namely, the visible-form base (rūpāyatana) and so forth—are mentioned in their respective order.
45. They are called *dhātus* because they bear their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*). Alternatively, they burn the manifold suffering of *saṃsāra* according to its occurrence;
and like a burden carried by porters, they are borne or maintained by sentient beings.
Because they lack self-mastery, they are merely the manifestation of suffering, and through them, the suffering of *saṃsāra* is experienced by sentient beings; and thus it is manifested.

These very [aggregates] are measured and established, like the elements that are constituent parts of the body such as lymph and blood, and like the elements that are constituent parts of rocks such as yellow orpiment and realgar;
they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) because they are constituent parts of the knowable. As it has been said:
"It discerns and it is a discerning, it is held and it is established; ... (the remainder of the verse follows) ..."
"It is that by which one is sustained here, or it is that which is considered a constituent (dhātu) because it is a source;
thus they are called 'constituents' (dhātus), like the constituents of the body or the elements of a mountain.

Having divided the mind-base (manāyatana) into sevenfold according to the seven types of consciousness-constituents, and together with the remaining eleven bases, eighteen constituents have been stated; thus he says "eye-constituent" and so forth. The reason for their sequential order should be understood according to the method already explained.
46. They are "noble" (ariya) because they belong to the noble ones (ariya), and they are "truths" (sacca) because of their state of being suchness; thus they are the "Noble Truths" (ariyasacca).

For these establish the eight noble persons—namely, the four who have entered the path and the four who abide in the fruit—because, in the absence of the penetration of truth, they do not attain the state of a noble one, whereas when that penetration exists, they invariably attain that state. [This applies] specifically to suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

However, they are true by way of their characteristics—defined as being restricted to those specific objects and pervading them—which consist respectively in their being oppressive, their being a source, their being an escape, and their being a means of deliverance;
and this quality of being oppressive and so forth belongs only to suffering and the rest, not to anything else, nor does it consist in their being non-oppressive and so forth.
Therefore, these are true. Thus said the Ancients:
“Four [factors] are conducive to enlightenment, severing the four stains;
and four [factors] bring about the Arahant individuals whose defilements are exhausted.
For elsewhere, qualities such as being obstructive and so forth are not found in these.”
"Because these do not cause affliction, they are called 'truths' (sacca), just as a carpenter's tools are called 'truths' [for their reliability].

Alternatively, they are "Noble Truths" (ariyasacca) because they are to be penetrated by the Noble Ones (ariya), or because they were taught by the Noble One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha (sammāsambuddha).
Furthermore, they are fourfold by way of being defiled or undefiled, and by way of fruit and cause.
He said: “The four noble truths,” and so forth. Therein, it is *dukkha* because of its loathsomeness and emptiness.
It is the *samudaya* (origin) because, when conditions such as karma are determined, it is the cause for the arising of suffering; that is, taking it as "suffering arises from this.
It is the *nirodha* (cessation) of suffering because suffering does not arise therein, or by means of this. [It is] the cessation of suffering.
It goes toward [cessation] and they practice by means of it; thus, it is the "practice leading to the cessation of suffering" (*dukkhanirodhagāminīpaṭipadā*). 47.

By way of the mental factors (*cetasika*), the sixteen subtle material phenomena (*sukhumarūpa*), and Nibbāna, sixty-nine states are designated as the "base of mental objects" (*dhammāyatana*) among the bases, and as the "element of mental objects" (*dhammadhātu*) among the elements.
49. "The remaining mental factors" refers to the fifty mental factors remaining after excluding feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saññā*). But why are feeling and perception treated separately?
Why are they called "the three"? Because of their state of being the gratification and the equipment for the phenomena of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadhamma*).

For among the phenomena of the three planes, feeling proceeds as the gratification; and perception, by way of the perversion of perceiving the beautiful in the unattractive and so forth, proceeds with that same aspect as its equipment.
Therefore, because these are the primary causes of saṃsāra, they have been taught separately. For this was said by the Teacher:
“The two aggregates were mentioned in order to demonstrate, by way of analysis, the gratification in the phenomena of the round and the pursuit of that gratification. [Question:
But surely Nibbāna is included within the bases (āyatana) and the elements (dhātu); why is it not included among the aggregates (khandha)? [In response, he said:]

“By the absence of differentiation,” and so forth. For the designation "aggregate" (khandha) is used in the sense of a collection for those things differentiated by distinctions such as past and so on; since Nibbāna lacks differentiation, it is excluded from the inclusion within the aggregates—meaning it is free from them. 51.
By the distinction between the six doors and the six objects, there are twelve bases (āyatana). Of the six...
By way of the doors, the objects, and both combined, there arise just as many consciousnesses;
thus, in a figurative sense and by way of sequence, there are eighteen elements (dhātu). 52.

That which has three planes (bhūmi) belongs to this [consciousness] is "three-planed" (tibhūma); that which is three-planed is precisely "belonging to the three planes" (tebhūmaka). Herein, karma operates.
And the ripening of that [craving] is the round of existence (vaṭṭa). Craving is threefold by way of craving for sense-pleasures and so forth;
it is eighteenfold by way of the six objects; it is fifty-fourfold by way of the past, future, and present;
and it is divided into one hundred and eight types by way of the internal and external. But why, when there are other causes of suffering, is craving alone the origin?

Why is it so stated? Because it is the primary cause. For craving is the specific cause of suffering because it is the cause of the variety of suffering—both by being the reason for the diversity of kamma and by becoming an auxiliary to kamma.

Regarding the phrase "the path is called the way leading to the cessation of suffering," the term "path" should be connected again with the statement "the supramundane path is considered [to be that path]."

53. Those associated with the path—excluding the eight factors themselves—and the remaining factors such as contact (phassa) associated with the path, as well as the fruit together with its associated states:
these are, in the primary sense (nippariyāyato), excluded from and outside the four truths.

However, in the secondary sense (pariyāyato), because it is stated in the exposition of the faculty of one who has already known (*aññātāvindriya*) that "it is a path factor and included in the path," the factors of right view and so forth among the phenomena of the fruit are [included] within the truth of the path.

Furthermore, it is possible to include the other factors associated with the paths and fruits within the truth of suffering by virtue of their commonality with the suffering of formations (*saṅkhāra-dukkha*).
For if this is the case, the all-inclusive nature of the teaching on the truths is also established.

But why have these many phenomena, such as the aggregates and so forth, been mentioned? Because they were taught in that very way by the Blessed One. And why did the Blessed One teach them in that way?

Because it is intended as a support for three kinds of beings. For there are three kinds of beings: those confused about mind-and-matter (nāma-rūpa) and both together, according to whether their faculties are sharp, moderately sharp, or dull; and according to whether they prefer a concise, medium, or detailed exposition.

Among these, the mention of the aggregates (khandha) is for those confused about mind, because mind is analyzed in four ways therein; the mention of the sense-bases (āyatana) is for those confused about matter, because matter is [analyzed] therein...

Because it is analyzed in eleven ways for those who are confused about both [the aggregates and the elements], the mention of the "elements" (dhātu) is for the sake of those confused about both, since they are analyzed there in detail;
likewise, the mention of the "aggregates" (khandha) is for those with sharp faculties and those who prefer brevity—this should be applied accordingly.
Furthermore, these three types [of analysis] are indeed beneficial when seen by way of the occurrence, the cessation, and the cause of both.
"No otherwise" should be understood as the grasping of truth.
The commentary on the *Sabbasaṅgaha* is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*, titled the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
The commentary on the Section on Compendium is finished.
8. Commentary on the Section on Conditions (Paccayapariccheda). 1.

Now, in order to demonstrate the conditions of the aforementioned phenomena of mind and matter by way of the methods of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) and the Foundations of Mindfulness (paṭṭhāna):

The passage beginning with "Yesaṃ" has commenced. For those conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata*)—that is, those things arisen through conditions—the various conditions which are helpful for their persistence and their arising, and in whatever manner or form those conditions are so helpful:
the classification of those arisen phenomena, of those conditions, and of that mode of conditionality (*paccayākāra*), [is explained] here, in this [work].

The construction is as follows: immediately after the section on the Compendium of Categories (*samuccayasaṅgaha*), I shall now explain—in each appropriate place—how, when the various phenomena arisen from their respective conditions exist, those conditions possess the specific modes of being conditions corresponding to their respective natures. 2.

In this context, *paṭiccasamuppāda* (dependent origination) is so called because it is that wherein the arising of fruits occurs equally, having depended upon the completeness of conditions (*paccayasāmaggi*).

The mode of conditions (*paccayākāra*). *Paṭṭhāna* is so called because various types of states (*ṭhāna*) are the conditions (*paccaya*) therein, and so forth; it is the great treatise (*mahāpakaraṇa*) known as the *Anantanayasamantapaṭṭhāna*.
The method taught therein is the *paṭṭhānanaya*.
3. *Tattha* means "in those two methods. Its nature (*bhāva*) is that which has the habit of existing (*bhavanasīla*) by virtue of the state of being a conditioning phenomenon (*paccayadhamma*).

The state of being present when that [condition] is present is itself merely a mode; it is "characterized by that" in the sense of being characterized by that mere mode of being present when that is present.

By this very [explanation], its being characterized by the mere mode of not being present when that is absent is also shown by implication. For the characteristic of a condition must be demonstrated by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "When this exists, that comes to be; with the arising of this..."
“This arises; when this is absent, that does not come to be; with the cessation of this, that ceases.
That from which the fruit proceeds is a condition (*paccaya*). It is a station (*ṭhiti*) because the fruit stands there, depending on it for its existence.

A station that functions by being specifically determined [by a cause] is called a “determining-condition-station” (*āhacca-paccaya-ṭhiti*). This is the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda-naya*).

For while that [general conditionality] proceeds by taking merely the aspect of "existence when that exists" (*tadbhāvabhāvibhāvākāramatta*) and thus proceeds without distinction, disregarding the specific determination of causes and other conditions;

this [specific conditionality], however, proceeds with distinction by taking the specific aspect of the capacity of each respective cause or condition to function as a condition for each respective distinct phenomenon. Thus, it begins from the standpoint of the status of a "direct condition" (*āhañcapaccaya*).
It is said [thus]. However, some explain that "the duration spoken by striking against the throat, palate, and so forth is 'duration through impact' (*āhacca-paccaya-ṭhiti*).
But this merely reveals that their words are to be ridiculed on account of their mere hearing;

for it is not possible to teach the method of dependent origination, or any other method, without striking against the throat, palate, and so forth. "Having mixed together" refers even to the *Paṭṭhāna* method.

The teachers, such as the compilers [of the Abhidhamma], include [these factors] within dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) itself, and having mixed them together by way of their being the presence of that [result] when that [cause] is present, and by way of the conditions such as the root-cause (hetu), they elaborate upon and expand them; however, our intention is to show them separately.
Commentary on the Method of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppādanayavaṇṇanā)

4. It is ignorance (*avijjā*) because it does not cognize; or, it finds or acquires that which should not be found, such as bodily misconduct and the like, or it does not find that which should be found, such as bodily good conduct and the like;
or, it does not make known that which is to be known, such as the Four Noble Truths and so forth;
or, it causes one to run toward what does not exist, or fails to cause one to run toward what does exist—thus it is ignorance with respect to the Four Noble Truths, the past limit, and so on.

This is the name for ignorance regarding the four [truths]. Ignorance itself as a condition is "ignorance-condition" (*avijjāpaccaya*). From that ignorance-condition, because they construct the conditioned (*saṅkhata*), they are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*);

these are wholesome and unwholesome kamma. They are threefold: the formation of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*), the formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), and the formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*).

Among these, the thirteen wholesome volitions (*cetanā*) pertaining to the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere constitute the formation of merit; the twelve unwholesome volitions [constitute the formation of demerit].

The formation of demerit (*apuññābhisaṅkhāra*), the four types of immaterial volition, and the formation of the imperturbable (*āneñjābhisaṅkhāra*)—thus these twenty-nine types of volition are called formations (*saṅkhāra*).

Resultant consciousness (*vipākacitta*) is called consciousness (*viññāṇa*); it is of nineteen kinds by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) and thirty-two kinds by way of the course of existence (*pavatti*).
Name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) consists of name (*nāma*) and form (*rūpa*). Therein, "name" refers here to the triad of aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*).

Matter (rūpa), moreover, is twofold according to the distinction between the primary elements (bhūta) and derived matter (upādāya): namely, kamma-originated matter. Both of these should be understood here as being accompanied by rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa).

Regarding the phrase "conditioned by name-and-form" (nāmarūpa-paccayā): here, "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) is to be understood as a collective singular compound (sarūpeka-sesa), meaning both "name" (nāma) and "form" (rūpa).
The six internal bases (ajjhattika-āyatana) are the eye and so forth; according to the opinion of some, the six external bases (bāhira-āyatana), such as visible forms and so forth, are also included.
Or it is called the "base" (*āyatana*). The six bases and the sixth base together constitute the "sixfold base" (*saḷāyatana*).
Contact, which has six doors by way of visual contact and so forth, is called "contact. Feeling is threefold by way of pleasure, pain, and equanimity. Craving is threefold:
craving for sense-pleasures, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. Furthermore, by way of the six objects and so forth, it is divided into eight hundred types.

There are four types of clinging (*upādāna*), beginning with clinging to sense-pleasures (*kāmupādāna*). In this context, weak craving is called "craving" (*taṇhā*), while strong [craving] is "clinging.
Alternatively, craving is the longing for an object not yet attained, like a thief reaching out his hand in the dark;
clinging is the grasping of an object already attained, like a thief seizing what has come into his hand. It is the opposite of fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*).
Craving (*taṇhā*) is the opposite of contentment, while clinging (*upādāna*) is grasping. Craving is the root of the suffering of seeking, whereas clinging is the root of the suffering of guarding;
this is the distinction between them. Existence (*bhava*) is twofold: existence as kamma (*kammabhava*) and existence as rebirth (*upapattibhava*).

Therein, the first is called "existence" because the fruit arises from it; it is of twenty-nine kinds, according to the wholesome and unwholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), and so forth.
But "becoming" (bhava) is that which comes to be; it is ninefold by way of the sense-sphere becoming (*kāmabhava*) and so forth.

Herein, in the formula "with clinging as condition, becoming," both the process-of-rebirth becoming (*upapattibhava*) is intended. In the formula "with becoming as condition, birth" (*jāti*), only the kamma-becoming is meant, for that alone is the condition for birth, not the other.
For that [process-of-rebirth becoming] is indeed birth itself, having the nature of the aggregates first produced [at conception]; yet it is not that very same thing [which is the condition].
The reason for this is appropriate. Birth (*jāti*) is the acquisition of a personal existence (*attabhāva*) for various beings in their respective destinies and so forth.

Aging (*jarā*) is the state of decay of that very personal existence once it has been produced in such a way. Death (*maraṇa*) is the termination of this same existence as delimited by a single lifetime.
Sorrow (*soka*) is the mental anguish of one who is struck by calamities such as the loss of kinsmen. Lamentation (*parideva*) is the verbal outpouring of that same person.
Lamentation (*parideva*). Bodily painful feeling is suffering (*dukkha*). Mental painful feeling is grief (*domanassa*).
For one who is struck by the loss of relatives and so forth, the intense mental distress manifested as excessive anguish is despair (*upāyāsa*).
And here, although other conditions such as the basis and the object exist, the mention of specific conditions like ignorance (*avijjā*) and so on is because they are the predominant factors.

And it should be understood as being "due to its manifest state. Herein, because formations proceed as phenomena subject to ripening only within a continuum that is underlain by ignorance, there is the occurrence of formations conditioned by ignorance;
and consciousness, having been generated by formations, becomes established in another existence.
For its arising would not be possible in the absence of a producer; therefore, "consciousness is conditioned by formations. And as for name-and-form:

Supported by consciousness, which acts as the precursor and the foundation, it establishes itself during both rebirth-linking and the course of existence; thus, "with consciousness as condition, mind-and-form.
And the sixfold sense base arises, depending precisely upon that mind-and-form, as the gateway for the six kinds of contact according to their respective functions and not otherwise;
thus, "with mind-and-form as condition, the sixfold sense base. Furthermore, contact occurs only when the sixfold sense base has come into being, having an object [of perception].
It touches. For there can be no arising of that [contact] in the absence of the sense doors; thus, "with the sixfold base as condition, contact arises.
One experiences feeling only while touching an object—whether desirable, undesirable, or neutral—and not otherwise; thus, "with contact as condition, feeling arises.
And when one contemplates gratification in phenomena that are objects of feeling, craving originates with feeling as its cause; thus, "with feeling as condition, craving arises."
Furthermore, being parched by the moisture of craving, they lead to the strengthening of grasping toward phenomena that are subject to grasping.

For, by repeatedly relishing forms and so forth through craving, one falls into a state of thirsting for sense pleasures; thus, craving is the condition for the clinging to sense pleasures (*kāmupādāna*).
Likewise, one who is infatuated with the various categories such as form develops wrong view—such as "there is no giving"—and [clings] to the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

One who desires liberation, yet clings to the path of purity within the impure path, grasps both the two views of self-theory (*attavāda-dassana*)—which consist in the apprehension of the aggregates as self or belonging to self—and thus craving becomes a condition even for the clinging to views and so forth;

this is "clinging conditioned by craving. Furthermore, it is precisely because beings are established in clinging through their respective associations and underlying tendencies (*anusaya*) that they lead to the accumulation of kamma; thus, clinging is a condition for becoming (*bhava*).
And birth, which is designated as rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*), has only kamma-existence (*kammabhava*) as its cause.
Because it is found here and there like a sprout from a seed, existence is called the condition for birth. And when there is birth, there is the occurrence of aging and death;
for there is no occurrence of aging and death for those who are unborn. Thus, birth is the condition for aging and death—in this way, these [links] [are related].
The existence of this [result] should be seen as occurring through the existence of that [cause].

Thus, "there is the origin of this entire mass of suffering" means by way of the aforementioned sequence of conditional relations, and not through the creation of a Lord (Issaranimmāna) or other such causes;
nor does it refer to an "entire" mass of suffering that is unmixed with pleasure and so forth, but rather to that which is designated as the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa).
Or rather, for the entire mass of suffering, the heap of suffering, there is no arising or production of pleasure, beauty, and so forth.
Herein, in this context of the compendium of conditions, *addhā* means time;
it is so called because it constantly moves (*atati*), goes, and proceeds.
6. Ignorance and volitional formations constitute the past time, because it is only the causes included within past existence that are intended here.
Furthermore, by the mention of "time" (*addhā*), only the phenomena (*dhamma*) such as ignorance and so forth are meant, since no time whatsoever is found apart from them.
For it is only phenomena—characterized by having ceased or not yet arisen—that are included within the three moments of arising and so forth, according to the divisions of past and future time.
And they are designated by way of the present time. Birth, aging, and death are the future period because they arise in the future from causes that are present.
The middle period is the present, because it has the nature of a fruit produced here from past causes, and because it has the nature of causes for a future fruit;
thus, the eight factors beginning with consciousness in the middle are the present period.

8. One might object: "Should not sorrow, lamentation, and so forth also be mentioned as constituent factors? To this he says: "The mention of sorrow and so forth," etc. The meaning is that the mention of sorrow and so forth is merely an illustration of the secondary fruit of birth, and not a presentation of them as separate constituent factors.
9. Craving, clinging, and becoming are also included. Because they share the common nature of being defilements (*kilesa*), craving and clinging are included by the inclusion of ignorance (*avijjā*);

because they share the common nature of being kamma-becoming, kamma-becoming is included by the inclusion of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*). Likewise, by the inclusion of craving, clinging, and becoming...

And the connection is that ignorance (*avijjā*) and volitional formations (*saṅkhārā*) are included. Here too, by the method already stated, their inclusion should be understood through their mention;

and since consciousness (*viññāṇa*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*saḷāyatana*), contact (*phassa*), and feeling (*vedanā*), as well as birth, aging, and dissolution, are stated to be "birth, aging, and death" (*jātijarāmaraṇa*), he says:
"by the mention of birth, aging, and death," and so forth.

10. "Five causes in the past": this refers to five causes produced in a past existence as conditions for a present fruit. These are stated according to their specific nature (*sarūpato*) as the two—ignorance (*avijjā*) and formations (*saṅkhāra*)—and according to their inclusion (*saṅgahavasena*) as the three—craving (*taṇhā*), clinging (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).
Now, regarding the "fivefold fruit": that which has arisen here in the present through the conditions of those past causes.
The pentad of results beginning with consciousness. Now, regarding "the five causes":

by way of the three factors beginning with craving that are stated according to their specific nature (*sarūpato*), and by way of the two factors, ignorance and volitional formations, which are included [therein], there are now five causes as conditions for the result in the future.
The "pentad of results in the future" is stated by means of the inclusion of birth, aging, and death; these arise from present causal conditions.

The fivefold fruit, beginning with the consciousness that arises in the future, constitutes the twenty modes; thus they are called "modes" (ākāra) because they are scattered here and there throughout the past and so forth.

There is one junction between the past causes and the present fivefold fruit, one between the present fivefold fruit and the present causes, and one between the present causes and the future fruit; thus, there are three junctions.
For this has been said: "There is one junction between formations and consciousness, one between feeling and craving, and one between existence and birth.
Herein, the first junction is the connection between cause and fruit because of the state of uninterrupted occurrence of the fruit from the cause;
likewise the third; but the second is so called because of the state of uninterrupted occurrence of the cause from the fruit.
It is that which constitutes the relationship between cause and fruit. For even a phenomenon that has become a fruit is a condition for another phenomenon whose intrinsic nature is that of a cause.
Herein, ignorance and the rest, as well as consciousness and the rest, are condensed; thus it is a "condensation" (*saṅkhepa*). There are four condensations:
past cause, present result, present cause, and future result. These are the "four condensations."

11. Regarding the phrase "a portion of existence known as kamma-existence" (*kammabhava*): here, volition that serves as the condition for rebirth-linking in the future is called "existence" (*bhava*);
whereas volition that serves as the condition for rebirth-linking here in this present life, within the previous kamma-existence, should be understood as "formations" (*saṅkhāra*).
"The rest" refers to the sevenfold [factors] beginning with consciousness, categorized by way of birth, aging, and death, in terms of their present fruit.

These are the phenomena already mentioned. Furthermore, that which is designated as "a portion of existence" (bhavekadesa) consisting of rebirth-existence (upapattibhava) should be understood as being included within the future.
Since the term "existence" (bhava) also refers to kamma-existence (kammabhava), the expression "a portion of existence" was used [to distinguish it].
12. Ignorance is the root of the past; craving is the root of the future. Thus he said, "there are two roots by way of ignorance and craving."

13. Through the cessation of those very roots of the cycle of existence—namely, ignorance and craving—and through the attainment of the state of non-arising by means of the penetration of the Truths, the cycle ceases due to this non-occurrence.

Furthermore, for beings who are repeatedly and constantly oppressed by the intoxication known as aging and death, and who are beset by sorrow and the like, there arises again the influx of the taints, such as the taint of sensual desire.
And ignorance also proceeds. For it is said: "With the arising of the taints (āsava), there is the arising of ignorance.
By this, the condition for ignorance is also shown; otherwise, the wheel of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda-cakka) would remain unconnected.

Thus, in the manner described, it is bound together, uninterrupted, beginningless, and devoid of a start. Because it is included within the three planes, it is "belonging to the three planes" (tebhūmaka), consisting of defilements (kilesa), karma, and their result (vipāka).
The Great Sage, the Perfectly Enlightened One, established and set forth dependent origination as consisting of three cycles.
The commentary on the method of dependent origination is finished.
The commentary on the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* [follows].

14. Having thus shown the method of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) by way of its analysis, [the text] now states "root-condition" (*hetupaccayo*), etc., in order to show the method of the *Paṭṭhāna*.

Therein, it is called a "root" (*hetu*) because one is supported (*hinoti*) or established by means of it. Since verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *hi* should be understood here in the sense of "supporting.
Alternatively, one is led upward (*hinoti*) by means of this, which serves as the cause for action and brings forth nourishment (*oja*).
Just as a tree, by means of its root, attains, proceeds toward, reaches growth, and maturity through its fruit, it is therefore a "cause" (*hetu*).
Being both a cause and a condition, it is called a "causal condition" (*hetupaccaya*). It is said to be a condition by way of being a cause, or a condition through its state as a cause.
Briefly stated, it is a cause in the sense of being a root, and a condition in the sense of being an assistance; thus, it is an assister by way of being a root.

The state-condition (*dhamma-hetupaccaya*) should be understood as follows: during the course of existence, it consists of six states that assist the mind-originated material phenomena, and at rebirth-linking, those same six that assist the kamma-originated material phenomena, as well as the associated mental states in both instances; they function in the sense of being a "root" (*mula*), meaning they establish a firm foundation, just like the roots of a tree.
It is called an *ārammaṇa* because it is "grasped" (*ālambīyati*) by the mind and mental factors, just as a staff or similar object is grasped by a weak person.

Indeed, whatever phenomenon (*dhamma*) the mind and mental factors proceed by taking as their basis, those respective phenomena are termed the "object-condition" (*ārammaṇapaccaya*) for those respective states.
There is no such phenomenon that would not become an object-condition for the mind and mental factors.
The condition that serves as the counterpart for those things that proceed under their own control is the *adhipati-paccaya* (dominant condition).

Because there is no interval between this condition and that which has arisen through it, it is the *anantara-paccaya* (proximate condition). Due to the absence of any spatial configuration, it is a perfectly proximate condition;
thus, it is the *samanantara-paccaya* (immediately preceding condition). It is capable of producing a corresponding arising of consciousness immediately after itself.
A phenomenon that has ceased immediately prior is called both the "proximate condition" (*anantara-paccaya*) and the "immediately preceding condition" (*samanantara-paccaya*).
For their distinction lies merely in the phrasing; in meaning, however, both are synonyms for that which has ceased immediately before.
Indeed, no difference between them is found in their actual sense. As for what some say—that the "proximate condition" refers to the state of being proximate in meaning—[that is not so].

The statement, "It is a proximity condition by way of immediate succession in time," contradicts such passages as: "For one emerging from cessation, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is a condition for the attainment of fruition by way of a proximity condition.

For indeed, the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, having ceased seven days or more prior, serves as the proximity condition for the attainment of fruition; therefore, [one should abandon] this dogmatic adherence.
One should understand that the distinction here is merely in the phrasing and not in the meaning.

For cessation is the "proximate condition" (anantara-paccaya) because it possesses the capacity to produce a subsequent state by acting as an interval between the cessation of a preceding state and the arising of a succeeding state.
It is like [the mind] thoroughly bringing about a sense of unity with itself, thinking, "This is above this, this is below this, and this is all around."

Cessation is the "immediately antecedent condition" (samanantara-paccaya) because it is capable of producing [the subsequent state] by way of immediate succession; thus, the distinction lies merely in the phrasing.

For even in the case of the cessation-condition, there is an interval between the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (nevasaññānāsaññāyatana), the preceding death-consciousness (cuti-citta), and the resultant rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) that arises at a later time; yet, by way of a homogeneous [state], [it serves as the condition].

Because there is no intervention by a non-material phenomenon (arūpadhamma), and because material phenomena of different classes are incapable of acting as an intervention, they possess the capacity to produce [subsequent states] by bringing about a state of unity through uninterrupted arising;
thus, the status of being an immediate and proximate condition (anantara-samanantara-paccaya) is obtained for them as well.
Therefore, although there is no distinction in terms of their nature as phenomena (dhamma), in such and such a manner...
The distinction [between types of conditions] should be understood as being merely due to differences in the meaning of the prefixes, according to the disciples who are to be enlightened.

Because it does not arise even when those things that arise together with it do not arise, and because it acts as a condition for those things that arise together with it by virtue of arising simultaneously—like a lamp for its light—it is the "conascence-condition" (*sahajāta-paccaya*). This refers to the four immaterial aggregates and the four great elements.
At the moment of rebirth-linking, there are also the resultant states of the physical bases.
Mutuality-condition (aññamañña-paccaya) is a condition by way of its supporting nature for those states that assist it, just as three staffs support one another.
And the state of being a mutuality-condition is simply the state of assisting by way of mutual dependence.
"It is not by mere co-nascence"—this is the distinction between these two.

For indeed, some things that function as co-nascent conditions do not function as mutuality conditions; this is because the mutuality conditionality of mind with respect to mind-born material phenomena, of mentality with respect to derived material phenomena, and of the primary elements with respect to derived material phenomena has not been mentioned [in the context of mutuality]. If...
For if the state of being a mutual condition (*aññamañña-paccayatā*) were to consist merely in the fact that [factors] assist one another by way of simultaneous arising (*sahajāta-bhāva*),
then it would follow that they must be identical to the conditions of simultaneous and mutual arising (*sahajāta-aññamañña-paccaya*).

Just as a cloth is the support for a painting, so too the four aggregates (*catukka-khandha*), which serve as the support for simultaneously arisen mind and matter (*nāma-rūpa*), are like trees, mountains, and so forth.

Just as the earth is the support for things placed upon it, so too the primary material phenomena (*bhūtarūpa*) are, respectively, the supports and the bases for the seven co-nascent material phenomena and the consciousness-element; thus these are called the "support-condition" (*nissaya-paccaya*), because they are supported by those that depend on them.

Because they act as a support through their powerful nature, they are the "decisive support-condition" (*upanissaya-paccaya*), since the prefix *upa-* indicates intensity; its classification, however, will be explained later.
The six bases and the six objects— these, having arisen first from among the conditionally arisen states,
are the pre-nascence condition (*purejāta-paccaya*) by virtue of their being supportive through their state of existing while [the effect] is occurring.

The post-nascence condition (*pacchājāta-paccaya*) consists of the mental states and mental factors that arise subsequently and are supportive by way of providing support for the body, which would otherwise lack the cause for the persistence of its continuity in the absence of the post-nascence condition.
Thus, it should be regarded as like the volition (cetanā) that craves food for the bodies of young vultures.

Habitual practice (āsevana) is the grasping of a subsequent text as being similar to itself—by way of its state of skillfulness and so forth—in terms of its familiarity, strength, and specific nature, just as with a previously familiar text;
by means of that condition, there arise phenomena of the same class (sajātiyadhammā).
Only states of the same genus (sajātiya-dhamma) are the condition by repetition (āsevana-paccaya).

For states of a different genus cannot cause those of a different genus to take their own course—defined as the state of being wholesome (kusala) and so forth—by means of the excellence and strength of the repetition; nor do they themselves take that course from them.
However, it should be understood that these are the immediately preceding mundane wholesome and unwholesome states, as well as the functional (kiriya) javanas that are not advertings (anāvajjana).
Volition that assists co-nascent and asynchronous resultant states, as well as kamma-produced matter (kaṭattārūpa), by means of its nature as a functional activity conditioned by mental application,
is the kamma-condition (kammapaccaya).
Those [states] which assist co-nascent mind-and-matter to attain a state of effortless tranquility by means of their own effortless and tranquil nature [are the nutriment-conditions].

Resultant consciousness and mental factors are the resultant condition (*vipāka-paccaya*). For these, because they are not to be accomplished by effort (*payoga*), they arise merely from the performance of karma;
thus, they possess a tranquil state devoid of exertion, rather than a tranquility consisting in the subsiding of defilements (*kilesa-vūpasama*).
Precisely because they possess such a tranquil state, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and other such states are difficult to discern. They consist merely in impingement, reception, and investigating.
However, the results (vipāka) are indeed difficult to discern; their status as grasping at form and so forth is understood only through the occurrence of the impulsion (javana).
The four nutriments (āhāra), which assist by way of supporting both the material and the immaterial, constitute the nutriment-condition (āhāra-paccaya).

For even though they possess the quality of producing, the primary function of nutriment is precisely that of supporting. Even while producing, the nutriment supports by way of preventing interruption.
Or, the state of nourishing is the state of being nutriment (*āhāra*).

The faculty-condition (*indriya-paccaya*) is a condition in the sense of predominance (*adhipati*), which consists in causing the phenomena arisen from conditions to conform to itself with respect to their respective functions.

Thought-conception (*vitakka*) and the others, having approached by way of reflecting upon the object (*ārammaṇūpanijjhāna*) and reflecting upon the characteristic (*lakkhaṇūpanijjhāna*), reflect upon the object.

The jhāna-condition: right view and the other factors that are helpful in the sense of leading out from an unhappy destination due to merit, or from a happy destination due to evil, are the path-condition.

Even though they are distinct in the ultimate sense, mental phenomena (nāmadhamma) that have attained a state as if unified—being helpful by way of the characteristic of association, which consists in simultaneous arising and so forth—are the associated-condition. They are likewise [path-conditions] because they are joined through mutual connection.

The dissociated condition (*vippayuttapaccaya*) consists of the bases, consciousness, and mental factors which are beneficial by virtue of their state of dissociation, their lack of conjunction, and their departure from diversity.

The presence condition (*atthipaccaya*) consists of those factors to be explained later—beginning with "conascent" (*sahajāta*) and "pre-arisen" (*purejāta*)—which are beneficial by way of supporting a similar state through their existence, which is defined as having a present intrinsic nature (*paccuppannasabhāva*). For even though they possess the quality of being producers (*janakatta*), [they function as support].
The function of the presence conditions (*atthipaccaya*) is preeminent precisely in regard to stability; thus, their role as "supporters" (*upatthambhaka*) is what is grasped here.

When a single aggregate of contact and so forth is occurring, because there is no room for a second [aggregate] due to its absence, those [preceding aggregates] that have just ceased are helpful by way of providing space for the immediately succeeding consciousness and mental factors, which would otherwise not obtain the opportunity for their own stability.
Mind and mental factors are the non-presence condition (*natthipaccaya*).
Phenomena that assist by way of their absence—namely, those not currently occurring because they have not departed from their own intrinsic nature—are the disappearance condition (*vigatapaccaya*).

Those that assist by way of not having entered cessation are simply presence conditions (*atthipaccaya*), which are the non-disappearance condition (*avigatapaccaya*) merely by virtue of possessing their own intrinsic nature.
The state of being a conditionality (paccayatā) should be understood as a distinction between these factors, even though the factors themselves are not distinct:

the state of being a presence-condition (atthipaccayatā) consists in the assistance rendered by way of not departing from cessation, while the state of being a non-disappearance-condition (avigatapaccayatā) consists in the assistance rendered by way of not having entered into cessation.

Indeed, it was after knowing the specific capacity of phenomena in every aspect that the Blessed One taught the twenty-four conditions; thus, through faith in the Blessed One, one should understand: "These factors are distinguished in this way."

Having generated knowledge consisting of what has been heard (*sutamaya-ñāṇa*), one should apply oneself to the realization of that [truth] through the types of knowledge consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

For although the collection of factors (*dhammasāmaggi*) is the same without distinction, it should be understood that the condition stated previously is mentioned again in a different manner according to the persons to be trained in various ways—
just as, for example, after stating the dyad of "rootless" (*ahetuka-duka*), the dyad of "dissociated from roots" (*hetu-vippayutta-duka*) is stated.
15. Name, which is comprised of the four aggregates, is a condition for a similar name in six ways; that same [name] is a condition for the combined [aggregates of] name-and-form in five ways;
furthermore, it is a condition for form—distinguished as primary elements and derived matter—in one way;
and form is a condition for name in one way; and concepts, name, and form are conditions for name in two ways.
The conditions are of two kinds: the pair consisting of name-and-form together acts as a ninefold condition for another such pair of name-and-form;
thus, the conditions are established as sixfold.
16. Resultant indeterminate states have attained the state of result by way of kamma, as if they had fallen, impelled by the momentum of kamma.
Having grasped its own inherent nature as it occurs and having cultivated it, it does not cause anything else to occur, nor does it arise by taking up the influence of a previous result (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, because of the statement, "There is no single [condition] in repetition due to the path-condition," and because repetition is specifically excluded for the smile-producing consciousness among the rootless functional states (*ahetuka-kiriya*), the two types of adverting consciousness do not constitute a repetition-condition (*āsevana-paccaya*); therefore, only the impulsion consciousnesses possess the state of being a repetition-condition.

He says, "The preceding impulsions," and so forth. Although this is stated without qualification, here only mundane wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate impulsions are to be understood, because supramundane impulsions have not been mentioned as having the status of repetition-condition (*āsevanabhāva*).
And having done so, it is stated in the *Paṭṭhāna-aṭṭhakathā*: "But there is no such thing as a supramundane repetition-condition."
For in that case, because wholesome [consciousness] precedes one of a different class, it does not cause the preceding state to acquire the quality of repetition (*āsevanaguṇa*).

Furthermore, although resultant and functional consciousnesses arise by way of impulsion (*javana*), they do not take repetition as their object according to the method explained for the indeterminate resultants, nor do they cause another to take it.
As for what was said by the teacher, the Elder Dhammapāla: "There is no impulsion devoid of repetition."

That which was stated [in the *Paṭṭhāna*] should be understood as being stated by way of the majority. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the Teacher having spoken without due consideration.

As for the path, however, it does not receive the condition of repetition (*āsevana*) from the change-of-lineage (*gotrabhu*), because the state of being of different kinds by way of plane and so forth is not intended here.
For it is said in the *Paṭṭhāna*: “The change-of-lineage is a condition for the path by way of the condition of repetition.”
“Purification is a condition for the path by way of the condition of repetition.

Because the characteristics of association—such as arising together and so forth—in fourfold ways are absent, there is no state of being associated even for material phenomena that arise simultaneously; thus it is said, “mental states and mental concomitants [are conditions] for one another.”
17. The causal factors of jhāna and the path factors are related to co-nascent mind and matter as root conditions and so forth.

These three [factors] act as conditions by way of root condition, etc., for both the matter produced by kamma at rebirth-linking and the matter produced by consciousness during the course of existence, as well as for the co-nascent mind in both instances.
For it is said that "co-nascent matter" refers everywhere to matter produced by kamma at rebirth-linking and during the course of existence.
He will say, “of mind-originated [matter]. “Conascent volition” includes even volition conascent with eye-consciousness and so forth.
“Of conascent name-and-form”: all volition is [the cause] of name; volition accompanying rebirth-linking is the cause of kamma-originated matter;
and volition conascent with the consciousness that originates matter during the course of existence is the cause of mind-originated matter. [As for] asynchronous [volition]:
Volition (*cetanā*) refers to wholesome and unwholesome volitions produced in past existences and other times, distinct from the moment of fruition (*vipākakkhaṇa*).

"Of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpānaṃ*) applies to both instances [in the text]. "Fruition aggregates" (*vipākakkhandhā*) refers to the immaterial (mental) aggregates of fruition, beginning with rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*).
For even matter originated by kamma does not receive the designation "fruition" because it is material in nature and because it lacks the quality of having an object (*sārammaṇabhāva*).
And because the term "result" (*vipāka*) is conventionally established only for immaterial phenomena that are similar to kamma. 18.
"Of this pre-arisen body": of this material body that has arisen prior to the conditioning phenomenon.
But how can there be a conditionality of a posteriorly arisen [phenomenon] toward that which has already arisen through conditions? Has it not been said?
"Because, in the absence of the postnascent condition (*pacchājātapaccaya*), it would not attain the state of being the cause for the persistence of the continuum (*santāna*).
Therefore, there is no contradiction in saying that its function is to provide support for the causal state of the evolving continuum.
19. Because the bases such as the eye are impossible at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), and because when they do exist, [they serve as the basis] for their respective consciousnesses...

Because they do not enter into the state of being conditions [for rebirth-linking], and because the heart-base—which arises simultaneously with the rebirth-linking consciousness—lacks the status of being pre-arisen (*purejāta*), it is said:

"Six bases [are conditions] during the course of existence. And the statement, "The five objects [are conditions] for the cognitive series of the fivefold sense-consciousness," was spoken with reference to what appears in the exposition of the object-as-pre-arisen (*ārammaṇa-purejāta-niddesa*).
However, in the section on questions (*pañhāvāra*), it says: "Whether they be trainees (*sekkhā*) or worldlings (*puthujjanā*)..."

Because [the Suttas] state, "or one who contemplates the eye as impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and so forth, including the present eye and other faculties without distinction, the mental-object (dhamma) as an object-prenascence is also obtained for the cognitive series of mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa). This is established by implication:
that when a cognitive series proceeding through the mind-door (manodvārika-vīthi) occurs having grasped a present mental-object as its object, [that object is an object-prenascence].
That [object] is its object-prenascence (*ārammaṇapurejāta*). 22.
Natural (*pakati*) means by its own nature alone, devoid of other conditions; thus, natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) is so called.
What is meant is that there is some kind of decisive support that is distinct and unmixed with objects or immediate antecedents (*ārammaṇānantara*). Alternatively, it is "natural" (*pakata*)...
The decisive support (*upanissaya*) is the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*). Here, the prefix *pa-* in the word *pakata* is an intensifier;
it indicates that [the quality] has been produced within the continuum by virtue of its capacity to bring about its own fruit, as well as the state of having been cultivated.

Therefore, lust and so forth, or faith and so forth, which have been produced within one's own continuum, or the weather and food which have been cultivated, constitute the natural decisive support. It is described exactly in this way.

23. *Garukataṃ* means that which has been reflected upon with reverence. For it is said: "Having given a gift, having undertaken virtue, and having performed the Uposatha duty, one reflects upon that with reverence," and so forth.

Thus, the description of this [reflection] proceeds by way of reflecting with reverence upon such things as giving, virtue, the Uposatha duty, previous well-performed deeds, jhāna, the lineage-knowledge (*gotrabhu*), purification (*vodāna*), and the Path.

24. Because the *anantarūpanissaya* (proximate decisive support) is presented without making a distinction from the *anantarapaccaya* (proximate condition) by way of the method beginning with, “Preceding wholesome aggregates are a condition for subsequent wholesome aggregates by way of decisive support,” it is stated as “those that have ceased immediately before,” and so forth.
Even so, [it functions] by way of the arising of a corresponding consciousness immediately following itself.
The immediate condition (*anantarapaccaya*) and the proximity-strong-support condition (*anantarūpanissayapaccaya*)—the latter by way of being a powerful cause—this is the distinction between them.

25. The construction is as follows: "lust and so forth, both internally and externally, as appropriate... [and] lodgings. For lust and so forth are produced internally, while persons and so forth are cultivated externally. Thus it has been said by the Teacher:
"States such as lust and faith are perfumed internally..."
"And the seven conditioned phenomena, cultivated externally.
Alternatively, the construction is simply according to how they exist: "internal and external wholesome and other phenomena.
For one's own lust and so forth [are internal], while one's own wholesome and other phenomena [are external]; and by relying on the faith and so forth of a good friend, the wholesome [arises].
And they become the supports for others who perform them.

In this context, based upon sensual lust and the other [defilements], there arise the cultivation of generosity, virtue, the Uposatha, jhāna, direct knowledge (abhiññā), insight (vipassanā), and the path, for the purpose of rebirth in the realms of sense-desire existence (kāmabhava) and so forth, and for the purpose of the subsiding of lust and the rest;
as do the successive stages of lust and the rest which have lust and the rest as their cause.
"They exist" should be understood according to what is appropriate. For whatever arises in dependence upon whatever, that very thing is the natural decisive support (*pakatūpanissaya*) for it.
This is indeed the "Great Authority on Conditions," namely that which is called the "decisive support condition" (*upanissayapaccaya*).
Thus it has been said: "The natural decisive support is manifold. "Faith and so forth" refers to virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom.
For it is well known that one’s own acts of giving, virtue, and so forth arise depending upon one’s own faith and other qualities;

likewise, the giving, virtue, and so forth of others arise depending upon the faith and other qualities of one’s spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitta). "Pleasure" and "pain" refer to bodily pleasure and pain.
"Person" refers to a person such as a spiritual friend. "Food" refers to suitable food and the like; "season" is of the same nature.
27. To expand upon the meaning stated in brief as “they are conditions through predominance…,” it is said: “In this context, the object that has been treated with esteem,” and so forth.

An “object treated with esteem” is an object that has been rendered weighty by means of reviewing, relishing, and so on. For such an object—whether it be distinguished as jhāna, the path, the fruit, insight, nibbāna, or the like—makes the phenomena of the path, fruit, and so on dependent upon itself by means of reviewing, relishing, and so forth; thus, it is called “predominance of the object.”

The object-dominance condition (*ārammaṇādhipati*) consists merely in the state of being treated with esteem. The object-strong-dependence condition (*ārammaṇūpanissaya*), however, is distinguished from this by the sense of being a powerful cause;
this is the difference between them. Regarding "conascent... name-and-form":

the fourfold conascent dominance—consisting of desire, consciousness, energy, and investigation—is a condition for conascent name-and-form through the mode of conascent dominance, according to its respective suitability, specifically during the occurrence of that name-and-form.

28. It is said that the state of being a conascent condition (*sahajāta-paccayatā*) of a form-dhamma (*rūpa-dhamma*) with respect to a non-form-dhamma (*arūpa-dhamma*) is stated by way of the physical basis (*vatthu*) during rebirth-linking;

thus it says, “the physical basis and the resultant [mental states] are mutually [related]. 30. However, since the state of being a mutuality condition (*aññamañña-paccayatā*) occurs only through mutual support and not merely by way of co-arising, form is not a mutuality condition for name in the course of existence (*pavatti*); therefore it is said, “mind and mental factors [are mutually related].”
"Mutually. Likewise, since derived material phenomena (*upādārūpa*) are not mutual conditions for primary material phenomena (*bhūtarūpa*), it is said:
"The great elements are mutually [related]. 31.

But has it not been stated that "the immaterial nutriments (*arūpino āhārā*) [are conditions] for co-nascent mind-and-matter (*nāmarūpa*)"? And if this is so, then for those without perception (*asaññīnam*)...
If it is asked: "Since it is impossible for food to be co-nascent [with the beings themselves], how is this statement 'all beings subsist by means of nutriment' to be understood? It is said in reply:

By taking the figurative sense of being a condition—namely, that karma which proceeds by way of the nutriment of mental volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*), or the other remaining nutriments associated with it, act as conditions through the relations of kamma and decisive support (*upanissaya*)—the fact that all beings subsist by means of nutriment is stated;
it is not, however, in the sense of being a direct nutriment-condition (*āhārapaccaya*).

32. Regarding the passage beginning with “five translucent [faculties]” (*pañca pasādā*), one might ask: are not the female faculty (*itthindriya*) and the male faculty (*purisindriya*) included? True, they are not included.
Even though these two are to be followed by the physical marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, that is not by way of being a condition (*paccaya*).
For just as there are those who protect and support life and nutriment because they are their conditions, so too [the other faculties] exist as non-disappearance conditions (*avigata-paccaya*).
Furthermore, the female and male states do not assist the gender-markers (*liṅga*) and so forth through any kind of assistance.
Rather, when the gender-markers and so forth arise solely through their own respective conditions such as karma, they serve as the condition for the apprehension of "female" and so on;
because they do not occur in any other manner within the continuum associated with them, there is a state of being followed by the gender-markers.
And because their state as faculties is mentioned, the status of those [faculties] as a faculty-condition is not stated [here].

33. Only for those names—such as the eye and so forth—which proceed as if emerging from within, and for those material phenomena which arise in dependence upon name, there is the possibility of association; for these alone does the status of dissociation-condition apply.
However, there is no suspicion of association between material phenomena (rūpa) and other material phenomena.

Since those [mental states] that arise solely by depending on a physical basis (vatthu) have "object" (ārammaṇa) as their mere status as an objective field, there is likewise no suspicion of association with them either.

Thus, it is said that the condition of dissociation (vippayutta-paccaya) is stated only for those cases where there is a suspicion of association; hence he says, "at the moment of descent into the womb, the bases," and so forth.

34. In every way and in all aspects, according to what is appropriate by name, there are three kinds of conascent conditions, two kinds of prenascence conditions, and one kind of postnascence condition.

Among the nutriments, edible food and the material life-faculty—these five kinds—are both presence conditions and non-disappearance conditions, by virtue of their existence as presently arisen entities.

Because it does not assist by its presence in the manner of supporting such a state (dhamma), but rather assists only through its own mere existence, it lacks the status of an *atthipaccaya* (presence condition) for Nibbāna, which exists at all times; nor does it have the status of an *avigatapaccaya* (non-disappearance condition).

Alternatively, [the definition of these conditions] is incompatible with the assistance rendered by the state of non-existence (*natthibhāva*) in things associated with arising and so forth, and incompatible with the assistance rendered by the state of disappearance (*vigatabhāva*).
And because the state of being a benefactor consists of such things as the condition of presence (*atthipaccaya*), there is no undesirable consequence of its being that specific condition.
Furthermore, the material life-faculty (*rūpajīvitindriya*) is mentioned separately here because, like nutritive essence (*ojā*), it is a benefactor only at the moment of subsistence (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*);

thus, it is not included among the co-nascent conditions (*sahajātapaccaya*). 35. Now, in order to show that all conditions, even in brief, fall into exactly four categories, [the text says]: "The object... they go."

It has been said: "For there is no condition whatsoever that does not become an object for consciousness and mental factors, nor one that does not become a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for that which arises through its own respective conditions.
Furthermore, because the occurrence of the world has karma as its cause, all things do not transcend the nature of karma by way of the metaphorical designation of 'cause' applied to the fruit;
and these [things], from the ultimate standpoint, exist by way of worldly convention."
And since they exist [only] as such, all of them together constitute the synthesis within the four [aggregates]. 36.

Now, in order to show that all those instances mentioned here and there as "conascent matter" (sahajātarūpa) are not to be understood without qualification, it is said: "Conascent matter," and so forth.
For in the case of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), there is an absence of matter originated by consciousness (cittasamuṭṭhānarūpa).

In the course of existence (*pavatti*), because there is no fixed rule for the simultaneous arising of matter originated by kamma together with consciousness and mental factors, "co-nascent matter" (*sahajāta-rūpa*) is twofold:

in all cases during the course of existence, it refers to matter originated by consciousness; and at rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it refers to kamma-born matter, which is termed "matter produced by what has been done" (*kaṭattā-rūpa*).
Matter that arises because kamma has been performed is "matter produced by what has been done."
37. Thus, according to the method stated, conditions are possessed of the three times by way of their occurrence as follows:

those occurring in all three times include the five past-time conditions by way of proximity, contiguity, repetition, absence, and disappearance; the two-time condition, namely the kamma-condition, by way of its past and present occurrence;
the three-time conditions, namely the object, predominance, and decisive-support conditions; and the remaining fifteen conditions, which are present-time conditions.
