Briefly, phenomena (dhammas) are threefold by way of designation and name-and-form: those liberated from time by way of the designation of Nibbāna; those internal by way of eye, lust, faith, and so forth;
and those external to that by way of person, weather, food, and so forth;
those conditioned by way of being arisen through conditions; and those unconditioned by way of being the opposite of that.
The construction is as follows: "In the *Paṭṭhāna*, the treatise consisting of infinite methods and the *Samanta-paṭṭhāna*, the conditions are reckoned as twenty-four in every respect.
38. "Therein" means among those [categories of] name and form as they have been defined.
The commentary on the method of the *Paṭṭhāna* is concluded.
Commentary on the Classification of Designations (Paññattibhedavaṇṇanā): 39.

It was stated that designations are twofold, distinguished by the "expressed" (*vacanīya*) and the "expresser" (*vācaka*). This is shown in the passage beginning with “because they are to be made known” (*paññāpiyattā*).

“Because they are to be made known” means because they must be communicated in various ways; by this, the distinctions among phenomena such as form—such as their aggregates, continuities, bases, and specific states—are indicated.
The designation of meaning (*atthapaññatti*), which consists of conventional truth and is termed "derived designation" (*upādāpaññatti*), has been stated.

For that [meaning-designation] is made known by means of the designation of names (*nāmapaññatti*). By way of "making known," it is because the designation of meaning is made known through various modes.

By this [statement], the designation of names—which is the verbal expression (*abhidhāna*) for those things that have acquired the name "designation" because they designate [their objects]—has been stated.

40. "By way of the mode of transformation of the primary elements" means by taking as a basis and support the mode of transformation—designated as the state of having been transformed—which occurs in the manner of extension, cohesion, and so forth, through the continuous succession of the great elements such as earth and the rest.

"In such and such a way" refers to [the distinctions] of earth and so forth. "Earth, mountains, and so forth" refers to the conceptual designation (*paññatti*) of a continuum consisting of earth, mountains, trees, and the like.

The "form of the arrangement of constituent parts" refers to the specific mode of arrangement, the particularity of construction, and the shape of the constituent materials and requisites such as wood, clay, and thread.
"Chariots, carts, and so forth" refers to collective designations for things such as chariots, carts, villages, pots, and cloth.
"The revolution of the moon and so forth" refers to the moon, sun, and constellations revolving clockwise around Mount Sineru.
The mode of revolving such as arising and so forth. "Directions, time, and so forth" refers to the designation of directions such as the eastern direction;
the designation of time such as forenoon and so forth; and the designation of months and so forth, distinguished by their respective names, such as the month of Vesākha.

"The mode of non-contact" refers to the mode of hollow spaces and so forth, which are not in contact with the various groups of material form. "Wells, caves, and so forth" refers to wells, caves, apertures, and the like.
The designation of space (*ākāsapaññatti*). "The sign of each respective primary element" refers to the sign of each respective primary element, such as the earth-kasiṇa and so forth.
"Distinction in development" refers to the specific continuity of development consisting of the preliminary stage (*parikamma*) and its divisions.

"The kasiṇa-signs and so forth" refers to the designations of signs that appear to yogis, divided into the kasiṇas, the sign of the foul (*asubha*), and so on, further categorized as the learning sign (*uggahanimitta*), the counterpart sign (*paṭibhāganimitta*), and so forth. "Distinguished in this way and so forth" refers to the divisions such as the space remaining after removing the kasiṇa (*kasiṇugghāṭima-ākāsa*) and the cessation-kasiṇa (*nirodhakasiṇa*).
*Ca*. "In the manner of a shadow of meaning" means in the manner of a reflection, that is, in the manner of a counterpart-image (*paṭibhāga*) of the ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*).
41. "By way of the six names such as *nāma*, *nāmakamma*, etc. refers to these six names: *nāma*, *nāmakamma*, *nāmadheyya*, *nirutti*, *byañjana*, and *abhilāpa*.
Among these, it is called *nāma* because it bends (*namati*) toward meanings. It is twofold according to the distinction between etymological derivation (*anvattha*) and conventional usage (*ruḷhi*).
The fourfold [classification] is according to the desire for the performance of qualities common [to all]. *Nāma* itself is *nāmakamma*; likewise, it is *nāmadheyya*.

*Nirutti* is the speaking (*kathana*) of a meaning by extracting it through the medium of syllables. It is called *byañjana* because it manifests (*byañjayati*) the meaning. It is called *abhilāpa* because it expresses (*abhilapati*);

it is the sequence of the arrangement of syllables as they occur in sound. Furthermore, this designation by name (*nāmapaññatti*) is [further divided] by way of the combination of the existent, the non-existent, and both.

To show that it is sixfold, the words “designation of what exists” (*vijjamānapaññatti*) and so forth were stated; they designate by means of this [designation] through such expressions as “form,” “feeling,” and so on.

42. “Of both” means of the two: the existent and the non-existent. One who possesses the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*)—that is, six higher knowledges—is one “possessed of the six higher knowledges” (*chaḷabhiñño*). And here, because the higher knowledges exist, [the designation applies] to the person who has attained them.
And because this [term] does not exist [as a substance], it is called a "designation of the non-existent by means of the existent.
Likewise, because a woman does not exist [as a substance] and the sound exists, the term "woman's sound" (*itthisadda*) is a designation of the existent by means of the non-existent.
Because the sensitive eye-faculty and the consciousness dependent upon it both exist, the term "eye-consciousness" (*cakkhuviññāṇa*) is a designation of the existent by means of the existent.
Because both the king and the son are conventional truths (*sammutisacca*), the term "prince" is a designation of the non-existent by means of the non-existent.

43. "In accordance with the sound of speech": following, pursuing, recollecting, and taking as an object the vocal sound consisting of words such as "earth," "mountain," "form," or "feeling"—immediately after the occurrence of the stream of ear-consciousness (*sotaviññāṇa-vīthi*) that has arisen [thereby]...
For the mind-door— meaning for the continuum of mind-door consciousness that proceeds in the mode of contemplating names—

the objects (gocara) which have become the support (ārammaṇa) for the names, based on the prior acquisition of conventions such as "this is the name for such-and-such a thing," are the meanings (attha) which follow along by way of the guidance of the designation of names (nāmapaññatti) pertaining to the conventional and ultimate levels, subsequent to the grasping of those names.
Designations (paññatti) are understood to be divided into conventional (sammuti) and ultimate (paramattha).

This [conventional designation], consisting of earth, mountains, form, feeling, and so forth—which makes known the things to be made known—is constructed by worldly convention and established through worldly usage;
it is grasped at the door of the mind, consists of strings of syllables, and is to be understood as "conceptual designation" (nāma-paññatti), being designated as such because it designates [objects].

And here, the mind-door cognitive process that occurs immediately after the ear-consciousness process is included within the mention of the "ear-consciousness process" itself; thus it is called "the ear-consciousness process.

For one hearing a sound such as a pot, there are two rounds of impulsion (javana) for each individual sound, occurring with respect to both present and past objects. These [impulsions] take as their object the name-concept (nāma-paññatti) grasped by the intellect...

The teachers maintain that, beginning with the sequence of syllables, there is first the apprehension of the designation (paññatti) by means of the mental process (javanavīthi) which follows immediately upon the ear-consciousness process and has the past sound as its object; after that, there is the comprehension of the meaning.
The explanation of the divisions of designation is concluded.
Thus ends the commentary on the Chapter on Conditions in the *Abhidhammattha-saṅgaha-vaṇṇanā*, titled the *Abhidhammattha-vibhāvinī*. 9.
Commentary on the Chapter on Meditation Subjects (*Kammaṭṭhāna*).

1. Following this exposition of conditions, there is the object that constitutes the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) for both types of development— the two kinds of cultivation known as serenity (*samatha*), in the sense of calming the hindrances, and insight (*vipassanā*), in the sense of seeing things in their various aspects such as impermanence—
because it is the basis for the occurrence of the twofold work of development, and because it serves as the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for successive stages of yogic practice.

The construction is as follows: "I shall explain, in due order, the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) and the path of development (*bhāvanāvīthi*) according to the sequence of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
[Now begins] the Description of the Classification of Temperaments (*caritabhedavaṇṇanā*), concerning the meditation subject for serenity (*samathakammaṭṭhāna*).

3. Those whose temperament (*carita*) is passion (*rāga*) by nature are "passion-temperamented" (*rāgacarita*). The same applies to those with hatred-temperament (*dosacarita*) and so forth. "The compendium of temperaments" refers to the classification of persons (*puggala*) according to their fundamental temperaments; however, by way of association (*saṃsagga*), there are sixty-three temperaments.

For it is said: "In the triads beginning with passion, there are seven; in the triads beginning with faith, there are seven; in the cases where the roots are one, two, or three, there are seven times seven through their combination."

For here, there is one set of seven consisting of the triads beginning with lust: those of lustful temperament, those of hating temperament, those of deluded temperament, those of lust-and-hate temperament, those of lust-and-delusion temperament, those of hate-and-delusion temperament, and those of lust-and-hate-and-delusion temperament.

Likewise, there are those of faithful temperament, those of intellectual temperament, those of discursive temperament, those of faith-and-intellect temperament, those of faith-and-intellect-and-discursiveness temperament, those of intellect-and-discursiveness temperament, and those of faith-and-intellect-and-discursiveness temperament.
In the triads beginning with faith (*saddhā*), by mixing them in this way two by two, there are fourteen temperaments (*carita*).
Furthermore, when the triads beginning with lust (*rāga*) are joined with the triad beginning with faith according to their single, double, and triple roots, there arise:

the temperament of lust and faith (*rāgasaddhācarita*), the temperament of lust and intellect (*rāgabuddhicarita*), the temperament of lust and applied thought (*rāgavitakkacarita*), the temperament of lust, faith, and intellect (*rāgasaddhābuddhicarita*), the temperament of lust, faith, and applied thought (*rāgasaddhāvitakkacarita*), and the temperament of lust, intellect, and applied thought (*rāgabuddhivitakkacarita*).
"Those of greedy faith, greedy intellect, greedy temperament, and greedy thought" constitute one set of seven according to the method based on greed as the root.

Likewise, "those of hateful faith, hateful temperament, hateful intellect, and hateful thought," and so forth, constitutes one set according to the method based on hatred as the root. And "those of deluded faith," and so forth, constitutes one set according to the method based on delusion as the root.
Thus, there are three sets of seven according to the method of single roots. And just as it is here, so it is also according to the method of double roots.

“Those whose temperament is dominated by lust and hatred, those whose intellect is dominated by lust and hatred, those whose thoughts are dominated by lust and hatred,” and so forth—this constitutes the first triad of sevens.
In the method based on the three roots, however, there is one further set of seven beginning with “those whose temperament is dominated by lust, hatred, and delusion, and faith,” and so forth.
Thus, by way of these mixed groups of seven, there are forty-nine temperaments. Therefore, these forty-nine together with the previous fourteen—
Sixty-three types of temperament (carita) are to be seen. Some, however, describe them as "sixty-four" by including views (diṭṭhi).
The explanation of the classification of temperaments is finished.
Now follows the explanation of the classification of development (bhāvanā).
4. That development which consists of preliminary reflection or initial action is called "preliminary development" (*parikamma-bhāvanā*).

The development pertaining to the sense sphere (*kāmāvacara*), beginning from the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and ending with the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*), is called "access development" (*upacāra-bhāvanā*), because it proceeds in proximity to absorption (*appanā*), just as one speaks of the "vicinity of a village" (*gāmūpacāra*) and so forth.
Development that has reached the state of the sublime (*mahaggata*) is "absorption development" (*appanā-bhāvanā*).

It is called "access" (appanā) because it has applied thought (vitakka), which is designated as access, as its forerunner. It is called "access" because it functions as if placing the associated states upon the object;
thus it is defined as "access (appanā) and directed-access (byappanā).
Furthermore, by virtue of having that [access] as their forerunner, all sublime and supramundane jhāna factors are also termed "access."
The Explanation of the Different Types of Meditation is finished.
5. The Explanation of the Different Types of Signs:
The sign of the preliminary work is the object; thus it is the "preliminary-sign" (*parikammanimitta*), such as the kasiṇa disk and so forth. That very same [sign]...

The sign to be grasped by the mind as if seen with the eye is the "learning sign" (*uggaha-nimitta*); alternatively, it is called the learning sign because it is the sign grasped by one who is learning.

The "counterpart sign" (*paṭibhāga-nimitta*) is the sign that resembles that [learning sign], being free from the defects of color and so forth, and serving as the object for access and absorption. 6.

Earth itself is the "kasiṇa" (totality) in the sense of its being "entire" (*sakala*), because it is to be pervaded as infinite without remaining in a single place; thus it is the "earth-kasiṇa" (*pathavī-kasiṇa*).
The kasiṇa-disk, its counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta), and the jhāna having that as its object, is called the “earth kasiṇa.
The same applies to the water kasiṇa and the others. In this context, it should be understood that earth and the other three are the four primary-element kasiṇas;
blue and the other three are the four color kasiṇas; delimited space is the space kasiṇa; and the light of the moon and so forth is the light kasiṇa.
7. A bloated corpse is one that is swollen up; it is called "bloated" (uddhumātaka) in the sense of being loathsome. The same applies to the remaining [meditations on the foul].
A corpse that is mostly blue-black in color, mixed with white, red, and so forth, is called "livid" (vinīlaka), specifically because it is blue.
One from which pus has flowed out is "festering" (vipubbaka). One cut in two in the middle is "cut open" (vicchiddaka).

The *vikkhāyitaka* is that which has been gnawed and mangled by dogs, jackals, and other such creatures in various ways. The *vikkhittaka* is that which has been cut into pieces by dogs, jackals, and others in various ways and scattered here and there.
The *hatavikkhittaka* is that which has been struck with a weapon in the manner of a crow’s footprint and so forth, and then scattered in various ways.
The *lohitaka* is that from which blood is trickling. The [corpse] from which swarms of worms are trickling is the *puļuvaka*.
The worm-infested [corpse]. Even down to a single bone is "the skeleton. 8.
Recollection (anussati) is mindfulness directed toward each respective object. Recollection having the qualities of the Buddha, such as his being an Arahant, as its object is *buddhānussati*.

Recollection having the qualities of the Dhamma, such as its being well-expounded, as its object is *dhammānussati*. Recollection having the qualities of the Saṅgha, such as its being well-practiced, as its object is *saṅghānussati*.
Recollection of one’s own virtue (*sīla*) that is perfectly purified by way of its being unbroken and so forth is *sīlānussati*.

Recollection of one’s own generosity (*cāga*) by way of its being free from the stain of stinginess and so forth is *cāgānussati*. Recollection of one’s own qualities such as faith by placing deities in the position of witnesses, thinking, "I possess such qualities as those with which the deities were endowed when they attained the state of devas," is [devatānussati].
Recollection of the deities (*devatānussati*). Recollection of the qualities of Nibbāna, which is the allaying of all suffering, is the recollection of peace (*upasamānussati*).
Recollection of death, which is the cutting off of the life-faculty, is the recollection of death (*maraṇānussati*).

Mindfulness that has gone to, and is directed toward, the bodily parts such as head-hair and so forth, is mindfulness occupied with the body (*kāyagatāsati*). Inhalation and exhalation are *ānāpāna*; mindfulness having those as its object is mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassati*).

9. It is called *mettā* because it gladdens (*mijjati*) and cleanses (*siniyhati*), or because it exists among friends (*mitteṣu bhavā*). Its characteristic is the bringing about of welfare and happiness for sentient beings. Its characteristic is the desire to remove the suffering of others;

this is *karuṇā*. Its characteristic is the joy in the success of others; this is *muditā*. Its characteristic is the occurrence of an attitude of equanimity toward both the desirable and the undesirable;

this is *upekkhā*. They are called "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*) because they have immeasurable sentient beings as their object. [They are so called] because they constitute the state of the supreme abodes (*vihāra*).
Or, it is the "divine abode" (*brahmavihāra*) because it is the state of dwelling in the supreme [states]. 10.

The perception that occurs as "repulsive" regarding edible food by way of reflecting on its going, seeking, consumption, and so forth, is the "perception of repulsiveness in nutriment" (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*). 11.

The defining of the four elements, such as the earth element and the rest, by way of their specific characteristics and by way of their constituent parts, such as head-hairs and so forth, is the "defining of the four elements" (*catudhātuvavatthāna*).
12. The immaterial states are those that occur with an immaterial object.
The commentary on the classification by way of signs is finished.
The commentary on the classification by way of suitability.
13. Now, in order to show the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) suitable for the temperament of each respective individual, he says:
"But among the temperaments," and so forth. One whose temperament or nature is lust is called "one of lustful temperament" (rāgacarita); such a person is one in whom lust abounds.

Because the meditation subject of the foul (asubha) is the direct opposite of lust, it is suitable for him. Mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) is suitable for one of deluded temperament (mohacarita) and for one of discursive temperament (vitakkacarita).

The recollections of the Buddha and so forth are suitable for one of a faith temperament (*saddhā-carita*) because they are the antidotes to delusion by virtue of being objects of the intellect, and because they prevent the wandering of discursive thought (*vitakka*). The perception of death, the perception of peace,
and the foundations of mindfulness are suitable for one of an intellectual temperament (*buddhi-carita*), because of their profound nature and because they are objects of the intellect alone.
18. "The remaining ones" refers to ten kinds [of kasinas], consisting of the fourfold primary-element kasinas, the space kasina, the light kasina, and the four formless [kasinas].

"Among those" means among these ten meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*). A broad [kasina] is suitable for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*), because the mind becomes excessively confused in a cramped space.
A small [kasina] is suitable for one of discursive-thought temperament (*vitakkacarita*), because of the large object of focus.
This is stated because [the object] serves as a condition for the non-wandering of applied thought (*vitakka*), both by being its direct opposite and by being extremely suitable.
Indeed, there is no development of the kasiṇas or other objects that does not suppress lust and the other defilements, or that does not assist faith and the other faculties.
The commentary on the classification of what is suitable is finished.
Commentary on the Different Types of Meditation (Bhāvanābhedavaṇṇanā) 19. In all these cases—that is, even among the forty meditation subjects—there is no attainment of absorption (appanā).

This is because the qualities of the Buddha and so forth exist as ultimate realities (paramattha), because they are manifold, and because even a single one of them is profound. This applies to the ten meditation subjects beginning with the recollection of the Buddha (buddhānussati).

Because it is impossible for concentration to become established by way of absorption (appanā), concentration fails to reach the state of absorption and instead becomes established in the state of access (upacāra).

However, supramundane concentration and the concentrations of the second and fourth immaterial attainments reach absorption even with respect to phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (sabhāvadhamma) due to the excellence of their cultivation.
For indeed, through the sequence of the stages of purification in cultivation, the supramundane reaches absorption.

[It] attains [it]. Formless-sphere concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*) occurs by way of the development that transcends the object. For the mere transcending of the object belongs only to the fourth-jhāna concentration when it has reached absorption (*appanā*).
21. They possess five jhānas, or they are "five-jhāna" because they are connected with them.

22. Because its object is repulsive due to the cultivation of foulness (asubha), the mind proceeds there by the power of applied thought (vitakka) alone, like a boat on a river with a violent current by means of the power of its rudder.
Thus, since jhāna without applied thought is impossible in this meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) of foulness, it is stated that it "belongs to the first jhāna."

23. Because they abandon ill will, cruelty, and lack of delight—which are accompanied by mental distress—these three, beginning with loving-kindness (*mettā*), are appropriately associated with mental joy (*somanassa*) as the direct opposite of mental distress; thus it is said: "The three beginning with loving-kindness consist of four jhānas. 24.

Having abandoned the three modes of activity occurring during the day, such as: "May all beings be happy," "May they be freed from suffering," and "May they not be deprived of the attainment of happiness already gained," [the practitioner] develops a state of equanimity toward beings through the vision of the ownership of kamma (*kammassakatā*). From this development arises [the fourth jhāna].
Because equanimity as neutrality is more powerful there, and because the divine abiding of equanimity cannot coexist with pleasure,
it is said that "equanimity belongs to the fifth jhāna.
The commentary on the distinctions in development is finished.
Commentary on the Different Spheres of Activity (Gocarabheda-vaṇṇanā) 26.

"According to what is appropriate" means according to the suitability of each respective object. It is said "by way of a figurative expression" because for some objects, the sign is not clearly manifest.
27. For it is only in the case of the kasiṇas, the foulness subjects, and mindfulness of breathing that a clearly manifest sign can arise.

28. Regarding "one who is grasping the sign in the earth-circle, etc.": First of all, having purified the fourfold purification of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*), having severed the ten kinds of impediments (*palibodha*), and having approached a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) endowed with qualities such as being dear, venerable, and worthy of respect, one should take up a meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*) suitable to one's own temperament, and [avoid] the eighteen kinds of unsuitable dwellings.
Having abandoned [distractions] and dwelling in a suitable residence endowed with the five factors, having severed minor impediments such as the removal of hair and nails,

and having placed the mind upon the earth-kasiṇa and other objects according to their respective stages of meditation— beginning with the preliminary kasiṇa-maṇḍalas and so forth, and sitting down by fixing the mind on the sections of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna) and so on—
one [meditates] upon the earth-kasiṇa and other such objects through the sequence of those respective meditations, [reciting] "earth, earth," and so forth.
This is the summary here regarding one who is grasping the sign. For the detailed method of development, however, it should be taken from the *Visuddhimagga*.
Indeed, both methods of development have been stated here by the Teacher in extreme brief;
and since there would be excessive prolixity if the detailed system were brought in for the sake of explaining that meaning, we too shall not elaborate upon it. But when...
"That sign has been well grasped by the mind" means that when that preliminary sign has been correctly apprehended by the mind through the process of successive development.
"It has come into the range of the mind-door" means that even for one who has closed their eyes or gone elsewhere while attending to it,
it appears exactly like the kasiṇa disk and comes within the range of the mind-door impulsion consciousnesses.
29. "He becomes concentrated" (samādhiyati) means that, specifically through the attainment of one-pointedness of mind, he becomes concentrated.
30. Because the person too is concentrated by virtue of the concentration of the mind, it is said, "of one thus concentrated. "Resembling that" means similar to the learning sign (uggahanimitta);
for that very reason, it is called the "counterpart sign" (paṭibhāganimitta). Furthermore, compared to the learning sign—

It is exceedingly pure. "Released from the basis-object" (*vatthudhamma-vimutta*) means released from the ultimate reality (*paramattha-dhamma*), or alternatively, released from the basis-object—that is, from the defects inherent in the kasiṇa-circle.
It is "consisting of development" (*bhāvanāmaya*) because it is produced by meditation.
"Well-fixed" (*samappita*) means thoroughly fixed.
31. "From that time onwards" means from the moment the counterpart sign (paṭibhāga-nimitta) arises.

33. Mastery over adverting (āvajjana-vasitā) is the capacity to repeatedly advert to the jhāna factors immediately after the adverting consciousness has arisen upon each respective object among the five jhāna factors, without proceeding beyond four or five impulsion moments (javana) or a few moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga).
This occurs immediately following the desire to attain absorption (samāpatti).
The capacity to attain [jhāna] immediately after the arising of the adverting consciousness, without proceeding further than a few moments of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga),

is called "mastery in attainment" (samāpajjana-vasitā). The capacity to arrest the current of the life-continuum— which flows like the rapid torrent of a river— by means of a dam, and to maintain the jhāna for a predetermined duration,
thereby being fit to protect it from lapsing back into the life-continuum, is called "mastery in resolution" (adhiṭṭhāna-vasitā).
The mastery of emergence (*vuṭṭhāna-vasitā*) is the capacity to emerge from jhāna without exceeding the time previously delimited.
Alternatively, the mastery of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-vasitā*) is the capacity to maintain [the jhāna] by not allowing it to proceed beyond the time previously delimited.
The capacity to emerge precisely according to the time [delimited], without emerging before the time previously delimited has passed, is [mastery of emergence].
"Mastering emergence" means enough with this excessive elaboration. "Mastery of reviewing," however, is established by mastery of adverting itself;
for the reviewing impulsions are indeed nothing other than the impulsions immediately following the adverting consciousness.

"For the abandoning of the gross factors such as applied thought" means for the non-arising of the gross factors such as applied thought at the moment of the second jhāna and so forth. "Exerting" means...

For one performing the preliminary work (*parikamma*), it should be understood that access concentration (*upacāra-bhāvanā*) is said to be accomplished from the moment the craving for applied thought (*vitakka*) and so forth is suppressed.
"As appropriate" means in accordance with the respective object, such as the kasiṇa, for the attainment of each specific jhāna.
It is stated, "excluding space," because it is impossible to remove the space-kasiṇa. "Kasiṇa" refers to...
The counterpart sign of the kasiṇa. "Having removed" means having lifted it up by way of non-attention.

"For one performing the preliminary work (parikamma) by way of infinity" means for one performing the preliminary work directed toward space, thinking, "Infinite space, infinite space," and not merely "infinite, infinite. The same applies to the base of infinite consciousness (viññāṇañcāyatana). "Infinite."
The teachers say that even without entering [the attainment], it is permissible to attend to it as "space is space" or "consciousness is consciousness.

39. "For one who performs the preliminary work with the thought, 'This is peaceful, this is sublime'" means for one who develops it with the thought, "This is peaceful, this is sublime," because the object is a mere absence.
40. "And among the rest" refers to those among the recollections of the Buddha and so forth that remain after excluding the meditation subjects that lead to absorption, such as the kasiṇas.
In the eight [foundations of mindfulness] and the four bases for the establishment of perception—thus, in these ten meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*).

"Having performed the preliminary work" means having performed the preliminary work according to the method stated thus: "That Blessed One is indeed an Arahant, he is indeed a Perfectly Enlightened One," and so forth.
"Well-mastered" means well-learned by way of making the mind inclined, leaning, and bent toward the qualities of the Buddha and so forth. And the preliminary work becomes concentrated.

The development of the preliminary work (parikamma-bhāvanā) succeeds when concentrated; and access is accomplished, meaning that while suppressing the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), access-concentration (upacāra-samādhi) arises.

41. "Occurring by way of direct knowledge" (abhiññā-vasena) means by way of the five mundane direct knowledges, such as the various supernormal powers (iddhividha), in the sense of knowing with special distinction.
"Having emerged from the fifth jhāna that serves as the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā)" means:
having tamed the mind through the fourteen modes beginning with conformity to the kasiṇa, and having made it capable of being directed toward the goal;

then, because of its suitability due to its association with equanimity and one-pointedness, one enters that very fifth fine-material-sphere jhāna which is the basis and foundation for the direct knowledges, having the earth-kasiṇa or other such objects as its support. Having attained that—

Having emerged from that, one should bring to mind the resolution and so forth: at the time of the preliminary work for the knowledge of the modes of supernormal power (*iddhividha-ñāṇa*), one should resolve upon the various forms to be manifested, such as those of a hundredfold nature or the form of a youth;
at the time of the preliminary work for the divine ear (*dibbasota*), upon sounds categorized as gross or subtle;
and at the time of the preliminary work for the knowledge of others' minds (*cetopariya-ñāṇa*), upon the distinctions of lust and so forth by means of perceiving the color of another's heart-mind.

Regarding the mind: at the time of the preliminary exercise for the knowledge of recollecting past lives, one adverts to the aggregates previously inhabited in former existences, such as the death-consciousness and so forth;
or, at the time of the preliminary exercise for the divine eye, one adverts to the visible form located in the place pervaded by the light.
"For one performing the preliminary exercise" means for one performing the preliminary exercise by thinking, "May I be a hundred," "May I be a thousand," and so forth.

"Regarding form and so forth" means regarding the objects that have become the basis for the preliminary work (*parikamma*), which are divided into: the formative jhāna (*pādakajjhāna*), the body, visible forms and so forth as the bases of resolve, sounds, the minds of others, and the aggregates of past lives.
Herein, for the knowledge of the various supernormal powers (*iddhividhañāṇa*) first of all, there are six objects:

the formative jhāna, the body, and the visible forms and so forth as the bases of resolve for visible forms and so forth. Among these, the formative jhāna is exclusively past; the body is present; the rest—
[The objects of the other supernormal powers] are either present or future. However, for the divine ear, it is sound alone, and that too is present.

As for the knowledge of others' minds, the teachers of the Great Commentary (Mahā-ṭīkā) maintain that the object is any consciousness—whether limited and so forth—that has occurred within seven days in the past or will occur within seven days in the future, belonging to all three periods of time.
The authors of the *Saṅgaha*, however, state that "there are four aggregates. But how can it have a present consciousness as its object?
Is it not the case that the object grasped by the adverting consciousness (*āvajjanā*) becomes the object for the supernormal power consciousness (*iddhicitta*)?

And since the adverting consciousness ceases having made a present consciousness its object, at that very same moment the other person’s consciousness also ceases; thus, [the object] of both the adverting and the impulsion (*javana*)...

On account of time, would there not be a single object [for both]? And how is it that having a different object for the adverting consciousness and the impulsion consciousness—other than in the course of the path and its fruition—is not intended?
First, in the Commentary, the state of having a present object belonging to the continuity-period (*santati-addhā*) is applied.
However, Master Ānanda says: "Having emerged from the foundational jhāna, [the distinction of] the present and so forth..."
Without performing any preliminary work other than simply thinking, "I know this person's mind," he again enters the foundational jhāna,
emerges, adverts to the mind without distinction, and immediately after three or four preliminary applications,
penetrates the other's mind with the knowledge of penetration of minds (cetopariya-ñāṇa), just as one sees a visible form with the divine eye.
Subsequently, by means of a sense-sphere consciousness, one also performs the determination of [the object] as "with lust" and so forth, just like the determination of blue and so on.

And all these [determinations] have only the present mind and its object as their basis; furthermore, in the case of an undesirable state, there is no fault of having multiple objects, because they proceed with an undifferentiated mode of appearance.
For the knowledge of recollection of past lives, the aggregates previously inhabited and those things connected to the aggregates...
Furthermore, names and clans, as well as Nibbāna, become objects [of knowledge], whereas for the divine eye, only present visible form is the object;
this is the distinction between their objects. "Enters according to what is appropriate" means it enters in accordance with its respective preliminary work (*parikamma*). 42.
Now, in order to show the classification of the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) by way of their objects, he says: "The modes of psychic power," and so forth. *Adhiṭṭhānādi* (resolution, etc.).
The various modes of supernormal power (*iddhi*) are its methods; thus it is called "the modes of supernormal power" (*iddhividhā*).

Because it resembles the divine ear and because it is dependent upon the divine abodes (*dibbavihāra*), it is both divine and an ear—thus, "the divine ear" (*dibbasota*). By means of this, the minds of others are known; thus it is "knowledge of the minds of others" (*paracittavijānanā*).
[It is so called] by way of having resided within one's own continuum and by way of dwelling upon them as its object, regarding the aggregates (*khandha*) and so forth in previous past existences.
Recollection is the recollection of past lives (*pubbenivāsānussati*). According to the method already stated, it is "divine" and it is "vision," thus it is the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu*).

Furthermore, the "knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings" (*cutūpapātañāṇa*) is also called the divine eye itself. The knowledge of the destiny according to deeds (*yathākammūpagañāṇa*) and the knowledge of the future (*anāgataṃsañāṇa*) are also accomplished by means of the divine eye alone;
for there is no separate preliminary practice (*parikamma*) for them. Among these, as for the knowledge of the future:
Whatever object there may be— whether it is the consciousness and mental factors that will occur from the seventh day onwards in the future,
or those that will occur starting from the second day— that indeed has the range of the omniscient knowledge within its own domain.
However, it should be understood that for the knowledge of the destiny of kamma, the object consists of volition termed wholesome or unwholesome, or else all four aggregates.
The classification by way of objective field is the "classification of objective fields.
The commentary on the classification of objective fields is finished.
The commentary on the meditation subjects for serenity is finished.
**The Description of the Different Kinds of Purification in the Meditation Subject of Insight (Vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna)** 43.

It is called *vipassanā* because it sees in various ways by way of impermanence and so forth; it is the wisdom of development consisting of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and the rest.
Its meditation subject, or that very [insight] itself as the meditation subject, is the insight meditation subject (*vipassanā-kammaṭṭhāna*).
The connection is that within this insight meditation subject there is a compendium of purification in seven ways. 44.

Impermanence itself is the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*); or, it is the "characteristic of impermanence" because by means of it something is characterized. The state of suffering, which consists in being oppressed by arising and passing away, [is likewise a characteristic].

Or, "characteristic" means the characteristic of suffering (*dukkhalakkhaṇa*). The absence of a self as imagined by others is "selflessness" (*anattatā*); that itself is the characteristic, thus it is the "characteristic of non-self" (*anattalakkhaṇa*).
45. The contemplation of each of these three characteristics is the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā*) and so forth.
46. Knowledge that proceeds by way of contemplating the aggregates and so forth as groups is knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*).

Knowledge that proceeds by way of contemplating arising and dissolution is knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*). Knowledge that occurs after releasing [the focus on] arising and proceeding toward dissolution is knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*).

Knowledge that proceeds by way of contemplating formations as fearful is knowledge of fear (*bhaya-ñāṇa*), [and it proceeds] by way of observing those things seen as fearsome from the perspective of their disadvantage (*ādīnava*).

Knowledge that occurs as the perception of the process [of conditioned phenomena] is knowledge of danger (*ādīnava-ñāṇa*). Knowledge that occurs by way of dispassion toward those things in which danger has been seen is knowledge of dispassion (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*).
Knowledge that occurs by way of the desire for liberation from formations after having become dispassionate is knowledge of the desire for liberation (*muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa*).
Knowledge that occurs again by way of the examination of formations for the purpose of applying the means to liberation is knowledge of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhā-ñāṇa*).

Knowledge that occurs by maintaining equanimity toward phenomena already analyzed, through the avoidance of both fear and delight, is knowledge of equanimity regarding formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*).

Knowledge that is conducive to the accomplishment of the functions of the preceding nine knowledges and to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*) that follow is conformity knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*).

47. It is “empty” (suññata) because of its emptiness of self (attasuññatā). It is “liberation” (vimokkha) in the sense of being liberated from the fetters and so forth. It is “signless” (animitta) due to the absence of the sign of permanence and so on. It is “wishless” (appaṇihita) due to the absence of directed longing (taṇhāpaṇidhi). 49.

That which protects one from the sufferings of the states of misery and so forth is called the *pātimokkha*. Because it restrains one from bodily misconduct and the like, it is “restraint” (*saṃvara*);

and because it has the sense of composing and upholding, it is “virtue” (*sīla*). Thus, it is the virtue of restraint by the *pātimokkha* (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasīla*). [This pertains to] the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth...
Virtue consisting in the restraint of the sense faculties with regard to forms and so forth is virtue of restraint of the sense faculties (*indriyasaṃvara-sīla*).
Virtue consisting in the practice of complete purity of livelihood by avoiding wrong livelihood is virtue of purification of livelihood (*ājīvapārisuddhi-sīla*).

Virtue consisting in the reflection upon requisites based on their necessity—that is, reflecting on them with the thought "this is for this purpose"—is virtue dependent on requisites (*paccayasannissita-sīla*). These are fourfold by way of teaching, restraint, seeking, and reflection.
And because it is completely pure, it is called the "fourfold purity of virtue" (*catupārisuddhisīla*). 50.

"Purification of mind" (*cittavisuddhi*) is so called because it purifies by way of bringing about the state of the mind being free from hindrances; or because it is designated by way of the term "mind"; or because it is purified. 51.

"The general common nature of phenomena is their characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*); their function and fulfillment are their flavor (*rasa*); their mode of manifestation is their proximate cause (*upatthānākāra*); and their fruit is their result (*phala*)."

The definition of the truth of suffering (*dukkhasacca-vavatthāna*) is the grasping of the characteristics and so forth— spoken thus as "contact has the characteristic of touching" and "earth has the characteristic of hardness," and so on in detail,
and "name has the characteristic of bending" and "form has the characteristic of being affected," and so on in brief—
by way of their individual characteristics and the like, distinguishing and apprehending them.

“Purification of View” (diṭṭhivisuddhi) is so called because it is both a "view" (diṭṭhi) in the sense of seeing that "there is no self apart from name-and-form," and a "purification" (visuddhi) in the sense of cleansing the stain of the view of self.
52. "Comprehension of Conditions" (paccayapariggaha) refers to how, at the moment of rebirth-linking, both name and form arise by way of the causes of ignorance, craving, clinging, and kamma.

It arises. In the course of existence (*pavatti*), material phenomena arise by way of the conditions of kamma, consciousness, temperature, and nutriment; mental phenomena arise by way of the conditions of support, object, and so forth, based on the eye and other material bases;

and specifically, wholesome states arise through the attainment of the fourfold sets beginning with wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*), unwholesome states arise as their opposite, resultant states arise by way of the wholesome and unwholesome, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) and so forth arise as resultants, and functional impulsion (*kiriyajavana*) arises in the continuum of one whose taints are exhausted.

"And adverting arises"—thus, by way of both common and uncommon factors, the discernment of the conditions such as kamma, which are established through direct perception regarding the occurrence of mentality-materiality throughout the three periods of time, is the definition of the truth of origination and is called purification by overcoming doubt.
This consists of the sixteenfold investigation beginning with, "Did I exist in the past? and so forth.
It is called "crossing over doubt" (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇā*) because of crossing over—that is, transcending—the eightfold doubts beginning with "doubt regarding the Teacher.
It is called "purity" (*visuddhi*) because it purifies the stains of views concerning causelessness and irregular causes.
53. Following that, after the discernment of conditions, there is the definition by way of the individual characteristics and so forth of those conditions thus discerned.
Having discerned, by way of the determination of conditions, the mentality-materiality included within the three planes— excluding the supramundane— which is divided into past and other periods,
one should take as a basis the method of the aggregates and so forth; and having condensed that method of the aggregates and so forth as it appears by way of the five aggregates,
the six doors, the six objects, and the phenomena occurring at the six doors, into groups and clusters, [one contemplates] whatever has arisen in the past.
Form that has passed away has already ceased. Form that will arise in the future will cease right there as well.
That which is present ceases right here without reaching the future. The same applies to internal and external, subtle and gross, inferior and superior forms, and so forth.

Therefore, it is "impermanent" (anicca) in the sense that it should not be approached as a self or anything similar; it is "suffering" (dukkha) in the sense of destruction, because it goes to its destruction.

"In the sense of being fearful because they cause fear; and 'non-self' (anattā) in the sense of being coreless, due to the absence of a self-core and so forth"—and by means of the knowledge of comprehension (*sammasana-ñāṇa*) according to the periods of time such as the past, according to the continuity such as the past, and according to the moments such as the past, [one contemplates]: "The eye is impermanent... the mind is impermanent. Visible forms... mental objects are impermanent. Eye-consciousness... mind-consciousness is impermanent, suffering, and non-self," and so forth.

For one who is comprehending and repeatedly reflecting upon the three characteristics—defined by the modes of non-existence, arising and passing away, oppression, and lack of mastery—by means of the knowledge of comprehension of aggregates (*kalāpasammasanañāṇa*) which proceeds through the process of comprehending those three characteristics;
and when that knowledge of comprehension has arisen, [he sees] again regarding those very same formations: "With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form..."

“With the arising of craving, karma, and nutriment, there is the arising of form; likewise, with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form; and with the cessation of craving, karma, and nutriment, there is the cessation of form.
Having thus applied this to the aggregate of form, and having removed nutriment from the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, one adds contact, saying:
“With the arising of contact... with the cessation of contact... And for the aggregate of consciousness: “With the arising of name-and-form...”
"By the cessation of name-and-form": having included name-and-form, there is [contemplation] by way of the arising of conditions and by way of the cessation of conditions;

and by way of the moment, through seeing merely the characteristic of origination and merely the characteristic of change in the present aggregates without referring to the conditions—thus, for each aggregate, there are four ways by way of conditions and four ways by way of moments.
"Arising in one way and five ways" refers to the light known as the radiance that issues from the body,

produced by the insight-consciousness of a practitioner who has begun insight meditation and who contemplates arising and falling through the knowledge of arising and falling (udayabbaya-ñāṇa) in fifty modes— by seeing ten instances of arising and ten instances of falling—
and which is conascent with the insight-consciousness; it consists of the fivefold types beginning with the "minor" (khuddika).
Rapture (*pīti*); likewise, tranquility (*passaddhi*), characterized by the subsiding of bodily and mental distress, which is twofold according to body and mind;
resolution (*adhimokkha*), consisting of the powerful faculty of faith; exertion (*paggaha*), consisting of the enlightenment factor of energy that accomplishes the function of the right efforts;
exceedingly sublime bliss; knowledge (*ñāṇa*) consisting of insight into the three characteristics, which is like a diamond released from Indra; and the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*).
Mindfulness, known as "establishment," is capable of recollecting past events such as long-term actions;

equanimity consists of two types: the equanimity of specific neutrality, which arises simultaneously with insight (vipassanā) that has attained balance and constitutes the equanimity enlightenment factor (upekkhā-sambojjhaṅga), and the equanimity of adverting at the mind-door.
Regarding the appearance of light and other phenomena, [it functions] by thinking, "Indeed, never before has such an appearance arisen for me," and so forth.

By this method, while establishing a basis (*ālaya*) therein, one should not—when the ten imperfections of insight (*vipassanupakkilesa*), such as the "radiance" (*obhāsa*), have arisen—take them to be "surely I have attained the Path, surely I have attained the Fruit," thinking that such radiances and so forth had never arisen before.
Rather, one should understand: "These radiances and so forth are not the Path, because they serve as the basis for craving, views, and conceit. Then...
"These are indeed the imperfections of insight; however, the knowledge of insight that has entered the path, being free from those imperfections, is the Path.

Thus, because it defines and determines the characteristics of the path and the non-path, and because it knows and sees the path and the non-path, and because it purifies the perception of the path where there is no path, it is called "Purification by Knowledge and Vision of What Is and Is Not the Path" (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).
54. "As far as conformity" means up to the knowledge of conformity to the truths (*saccānuloma-ñāṇa*). Regarding the "nine insight knowledges":

there is the knowledge of rise and fall (*udayabbaya-ñāṇa*), which knows the arising and passing away of the aggregates; the knowledge of dissolution (*bhaṅga-ñāṇa*), which, having let go of the arising, is equanimous toward mere dissolution;

the knowledge of fear (*bhaya-ñāṇa*), which, by way of dissolution, is equanimous toward the aspect of what is to be feared in those things that appear [as such], like lions and other [dangers]; and for those things thus viewed with equanimity...

Knowledge of danger is like one who observes the aspect of peril in a burning house; knowledge of disenchantment proceeds by way of becoming disenchanted with those things whose dangers have been seen;
knowledge of the desire for deliverance proceeds by way of the wish to be freed from those phenomena of the three planes, just as fish and other creatures [desire to escape] from a net and so forth;
and [knowledge of the way] is like a sea-bird that, for the sake of finding a means of escape, [observes] even those things whose dangers have been seen.
The knowledge of contemplation by reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānupassanā-ñāṇa*) reaches its culmination through repeated synthesis;
the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa*) proceeds in the mode of equanimity toward those formations whose dangers have been seen, like a man who has lost his wealth;
and [it stands] above the eight preceding insight-knowledges that proceeded by way of the insight into characteristics such as impermanence, and below those to be attained at the moment of the path.

And the ninth, conformity knowledge— known as the knowledge conforming to the truths— which occurs prior to the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū) within the path-moment by way of conformity to the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment:
these nine knowledges constitute the purification by knowledge and vision because they function as the path,
in the sense of knowing the three characteristics, in the sense of seeing through direct experience, and in the sense of being purified from opposing factors.
And this is called purification by knowledge and vision of the way (paṭipadā-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi).
55. The ripening of insight is "insight-ripening" (vipassanā-paripāka); it is the knowledge of equanimity towards formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). Depending upon and relying on that, [one thinks]:
"Now absorption will arise," meaning, "Now the supramundane path, which is termed absorption, will arise."
At the moment it ought to be spoken. "Whatever" refers to any one of the three [objects] grasped by equanimity towards formations (*saṅkhārupekkhā*).

56. It has reached the summit through the attainment of the pinnacle of insight (*vipassanā*); because it is accompanied by conformity-knowledge (*anuloma-ñāṇa*), it is "with conformity" (*sānuloma*);

and because it is indifferent toward formations, it is precisely that "equanimity towards formations. From the states of woe and so forth, and from the sign of formations, according to what is appropriate...
And because it goes toward the path known as emergence from the point of emerging, it is called "leading to emergence" (*vuṭṭhānagāminī*).
57. *Abhisambhontaṃ* means reaching. 58.
*Parijānanto* means knowing by way of delimitation: "Suffering is only this much; there is nothing less or more than this. *Sacchikaronto* means realizing.

Making it manifest by way of taking it as an object. "By way of developing the truth of the path" means by way of increasing [it] by acting as a co-nascent condition, etc., for the fourth truth, which is designated as the truth of the path and consists of the associated path-factors.
The accomplishment of the four functions by a single knowledge is seen from the example of a lamp, etc., performing its four functions such as burning the wick; thus: "He who..."
"And, monks, one sees suffering," and so forth; thus it should be accepted from the scripture (*āgama*). 59.
Regarding the phrase "two or three fruition-consciousnesses having occurred":

in accordance with the arising of the path, two or three fruition-consciousnesses occur even when the defilements have been severed, like water poured from jars upon a place where a fire has been extinguished, for the purpose of cooling the heat.
Having arisen as factors that pacify distress within the mental continuum—meaning, having proceeded through their occurrence—it is said:

"The knowledges of review. These are sense-sphere knowledges having the path, fruit, and so forth as their object, with reference to which it was said: "When there is liberation, the knowledge arises: 'It is liberated.'"
60. Now, in order to show the stage of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇā*), it is said: “The path and the fruit,” and so forth.

Therein, the wise person reviews the path, thinking: “Indeed, by this very path have I come. Then, he reviews its fruit, thinking: “This is the benefit I have obtained. Then, he reviews Nibbāna, thinking: “This is the Dhamma that has been realized by me as an object.”

He reviews them. Then he either reviews the defilements already abandoned, thinking, "These specific defilements have been abandoned by me," or he reviews the remaining defilements, thinking, "These specific ones still remain. In this regard, some trainees (sekha) review them while others do not;
herein, there is freedom of choice—that is the intention. For instance, the Sakyan Mahānāma [asked], "What indeed is that Dhamma within myself..."

"Not abandoned" refers to his questioning regarding defilements that have not been abandoned. However, for an Arahant, there is no reviewing of remaining defilements because all defilements have been abandoned;
therefore, it should be understood that there are nineteen kinds of reviewing knowledge: fifteen for the three trainees (sekha) and four for the Arahant.

"By way of the sequence of the six purifications" means by way of the sequence of these six purifications: the two that constitute the foundation, namely purification of virtue and purification of mind;
and the four that constitute the body, namely purification of view and so forth.

It is called "purification by knowledge and vision" because it consists in the knowing of the four truths, because it brings them into direct experience, and because it is purified from the stains of the defilements.
"Herein" means in the meditation subject of insight (vipassanā).
The commentary on the classification of purifications is finished.
Now follows the commentary on the classification of liberations (vimokkha).

61. Therein, in that aforementioned context, regarding volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*), the adherence (*abhinivesa*)—the firm grasping—in the form, "That which is the doer of karma and the experiencer of its fruit, this is my self," is what is released by the contemplation (*anupassanā*) that proceeds as "not-self" (*anattā*).

Because it contemplates the aspect of the emptiness of a self (*attasuññatākāra*), it is called the "contemplation of emptiness" (*suññatānupassanā*), a gateway to liberation (*vimokkhamukha*) from the opposing side.
By way of liberation, it serves as the gateway to the supramundane path and fruit known as "liberation.

62. Contemplation occurring as "impermanent" with respect to formations is "signless contemplation," because it releases and abandons the sign of perversion—consisting of the perversions of perception, consciousness, and view that occur as "permanent" in what is impermanent—and because it contemplates in a mode free from such signs of perversion.
The connection is: "it is called a door to liberation.

63. Regarding the term "suffering": it is the contemplation of the process [of existence] that releases the longing, the aspiration, and the yearning for craving—consisting of craving for sensual pleasures and existence—which proceeds with respect to formations according to the method "this is mine, this is my pleasure," and so forth; it does so by means of seeing the aspect of suffering.
Because it relinquishes aspects that are devoid of longing (*paṇidhi*), it is called "contemplation of the wishless" (*appaṇihitānupassanā*). 64.

Therefore, since these three names belong to these three [insights], if the insight leading to emergence contemplates as non-self (*anattato*), then the path is called the "emptiness liberation" (*suññato vimokkho*) because it receives its name by way of its arrival.

66. "By way of the arrival of insight" means by way of the arrival designated as insight. That by which the path and the fruit arrive is here called "arrival," namely, the path of insight (*vipassanāmagga*).
67. "By the method already stated" means by way of the contemplation of non-self (*anattā*) and so forth, which were mentioned previously.

"Even while its own fruit is arising" means that even though its own fruit—which is the fruit of the path already attained—is arising, it receives the three names not by way of the path's progression, but solely by way of insight (*vipassanā*), at the time of the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*); for at that time, there is no occurrence of the path.

Because it is not suitable to be its door. "By way of the object" means by way of Nibbāna, which possesses the names *suññata* (emptiness), *animitta* (signless), and *appaṇihita* (wishless) because it is empty of all formations, devoid of the sign of formations, and free from the longing of craving; [the path] proceeds by taking that as its object.
"By way of its own nature" means because it is empty of lust and so forth, devoid of objects such as the signs of form, and free from the longing of the defilements.
By virtue of its own qualities. "In all instances" means in the cognitive process of the path and in the cognitive process of the attainment of fruition.
"Of all" means of both the path and the fruition.
The commentary on the classification of deliverance is finished.
Commentary on the Classification of Individuals (Puggalabhedavaṇṇanā) 68.

"One for whom seven births at most" (*sattakkhattuparamo*) means one whose maximum number of rebirth-linkings (*paṭisandhi*) within the fortunate realms of sense-sphere existence (*kāmasugati*) across seven cycles is seven;
the intention is that such a person does not go to an eighth or subsequent existence in the sense-sphere realm. It is with reference to this that it was said: [as follows].
“They do not take up an eighth existence,” it is said. However, the teachers maintain that existence in the happy realms of the fine-material and immaterial worlds continues even beyond seven rounds.
69. Regarding the phrase “of lust, hatred, and delusion,” the inclusion of delusion (*moha*) should be understood as referring to the delusion that accompanies lust and hatred.

70. One whose taints (*āsava*) are exhausted is called an *khīṇāsava*. Because he is the foremost among those worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇāraha*), he is the supreme recipient of offerings (*aggadakkhiṇeyya*).
The commentary on the classification of individuals is finished.
Commentary on the classification of attainments:
72. “Of all” means of all four types of noble persons.
73. *Nirodhasamāpatti* is the attainment (*samāpatti*) of cessation (*nirodha*), which is defined as the non-occurrence of mind and mental factors;
it is dwelling having reached the cessation of mind in this very life (*diṭṭheva dhamme*).

"Of non-returners" (*anāgāmīnaṃ*) refers specifically to those non-returners who have attained the eight meditative attainments (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*)—that is, those established in the realms of sense-desire and form—as well as those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsavā*). "Therein" (*tattha*) means in the attainment of cessation.

"Having gone as far as the base of nothingness" means having proceeded thus by way of establishing the union of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*) up to the base of nothingness. "The resolve, etc.

refers to the resolve that robes and other requisites, or houses and so forth—which have been set aside separately after setting aside those attached to the body—will not be destroyed by fire and the like; it also includes the honoring of the Saṅgha and the Teacher’s exhortation.
Having performed the fourfold preliminary duty beginning with the determination— namely, emerging earlier than usual and observing the manifestation of the life-formations within seven days—
the explanation of the different types of attainments is finished.
The explanation of the meditation subject of insight is finished.
75. Commentary on the Encouragement:

"The enjoyment of the flavor of practice" refers to the enjoyment of the flavor of the practice of serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*), which is divided into the bliss of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), the bliss of the fruit, and so forth.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha* titled the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*.
The commentary on the section on meditation subjects (*kammaṭṭhāna*) is finished. Regarding the concluding commentary (Ka):
by him whose birth occurred in a noble family resplendent with conduct and family tradition, [this work was composed] concerning the sphere of action and so forth.
The construction is as follows: by him who has grown through faith and whose arising of qualities such as generosity and virtue is utterly pure;

by one called by that name, by one with that appellation; having directed his aspiration—having made a wish—for compassion for others, which is characterized by helping others to cross over easily and to reach maturity in the Teaching, that treatise which was thus wished for and requested is now, at this point, completed.
(Kha) By means of that vast merit arising from his devotion to this work— purified by the wisdom of the Noble Path and adorned with virtues such as moral discipline—
the modest monks [dedicated it] for the sake of auspiciousness, which is the source of the manifestation of their meritorious power,
to the monastery named Mūlasoma, which is the dwelling place of the fortunate, ever-prospering, and pre-eminently renowned.
"May those dwelling there think me worthy of honor; may the resident monks be such as this"—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the conclusion is finished.
And thus, this work called the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī* is completed.
Abhidhammatthasaṅgahaṭīkā.
Concluding Remarks 1.
In the delightful city of Pulatthi, the sovereign of cities,
Built by King Parakkamabhuja of the mighty arm,
he dwells in the Jetavana monastery,
which is delightful with its excellent, beautiful, and noble groves and arched gateways.
Honored by a multitude of disciples who were mines of virtue, perfected in morality, self-control, restraint, and contentment,
he attained [mastery] over numerous texts beginning with the words of the Lord of Sages.
And among those born [into this lineage], his status as a teacher was honored by the wise.
Furthermore, the commentaries on the Vinaya-ṭṭhakathā and other works here indicate the power of his knowledge.
Delighting the virtuous by elucidating the essence of the sweet meaning through the *Sāratthadīpanī*, [this work]—
out of compassion for that [text], Sāriputta...
Of that Elder, who was a mine of the qualities of firm and essential virtue,
and who attained proficiency in the domain of many texts—
this manifestation of his knowledge is the sole cause for [his] worldly success.
5. Therefore, by the power of this perfectly pure exertion, I shall become an heir to the true dispensation of the Teacher Metteyya. 6.
At that time, I shall illuminate his pure-minded dispensation as it shines forth.
May I honor and revere the venerable Sāriputta.
Just as this commentary has been completed in twenty-four days,
may those of virtuous intention quickly attain success, O living beings!
Thus ends the commentary on the *Abhidhammatthasaṅgaha*,
titled the *Abhidhammatthavibhāvinī*,
composed by the disciple of the Venerable Elder Sāriputta.
